author: Marcelo Rovai
subtitle: Professor at Universidade Federal de Itajubá
content:
🦾 Running Gemma4 on a Raspberry Pi 5 — with only 2 GB of RAM.

Most people reach for Ollama when they want a local LLM on a Raspberry Pi. Ollama is great — I use it constantly. But last week I ran the same Gemma 4 E2B model with Google's LiteRT-LM, and the difference in memory footprint stopped me in my tracks:

• Ollama + Gemma4:E2B → 7.7 GB RAM + 4 GB swap
• LiteRT-LM + Gemma4:E2B → 2.1 GB RAM + ~1 GB swap

Same model. Same Pi. Roughly 3× less memory.

LiteRT-LM is Google AI Edge's production-ready inference framework — the same runtime that runs inside Pixel Watch, Chromebook Plus, and Chrome. It uses the .litertlm model format (INT4 quantized, tokenizer + metadata in a single file) and runs entirely in-process: no daemon, no port 11434, no server to manage.

For my "Edge AI Engineering" e-book (https://lnkd.in/eRrvn9FF), I wrote a full chapter covering:

✅ The architecture: Engine → Conversation → XNNPACK executor
✅ pip install in a venv — that's it for setup
✅ Single-turn queries vs. persistent multi-turn chat
✅ Tool calling (JSON-based function dispatch)
✅ Streaming with TTFT, total latency, and tokens/sec metrics

The key mental model: the Engine loads weights once (expensive), and each Conversation object keeps its own KV cache automatically. No manual history management — unlike raw REST APIs.

One number from my testing: ~4–7 tokens/sec on Gemma 4:E2B with a warm engine. Not blazing fast, but for an always-on IoT assistant running locally, it's perfectly usable.

The real payoff of LiteRT-LM isn't the Pi, though — it's that the same .litertlm file you test on your Pi runs without modification on Android, Jetson Orin, and any Qualcomm device. One binary. Every platform.

📓 Study notebook: https://lnkd.in/etDZ5WCu

author: Leo L.
subtitle: AI Infrastructure | HPC, GPU & AI Networking | Guided AI Engineering
content:
This week’s vLLM-MoE Round 3 result is encouraging.

A 26B MoE model that would normally expect around 80GB GPU memory now reaches 128.59 tok/s on a single A100 40GB.

That is up from 60.31 tok/s in Round 2 — a 2.13× improvement.

For comparison, an 8×A100 40GB NVLink setup can reach around 2000 tok/s total, or about 250 tok/s per GPU. Our current single-GPU result is already about 51% of that per-GPU throughput, without NVLink and without tensor parallelism.

This comparison becomes even more interesting when we consider that NVLink-based systems are much more expensive than non-NVLink setups.

A few takeaways for me:

1. Fine-tuning vLLM inference for MoE still has plenty of room.
2. It may be time to reevaluate NVLink in large-model inference from both cost and performance perspectives.
3. With the right software–hardware co-design, some pure hardware performance advantages may be partially hidden, amortized, or reshaped by smarter inference architecture.

The final question is token per dollar.

Raw tok/s tells us how fast the system runs.
token/$ tells us whether the system makes economic sense.

In inference, the winner may not be the system with the highest peak throughput.

It may be the system with the best tokeneconomics.

author: Darshan Baslani
subtitle: AI Systems Engineer | Building LLMs & Autograd Engines from Scratch | CUDA & Inference Optimization
content:
Most of the time in LLM inference isn’t spent doing math; it’s spent waiting on memory.

I’ve been spending time deep in the PyTorch Profiler traces of Qwen 3.5, trying to squeeze every drop of performance out of a B200. The traces revealed a massive bottleneck: standard PyTorch operations were heavily memory-bound, specifically around RMSNorm and the residual stream additions.

The CPU was wasting time launching tiny, fragmented kernels, and the GPU was constantly reading and writing the residual to HBM.

To fix this, I decided to drop down to Triton to write a custom, highly optimized fusion kernel. But instead of just writing a basic single-pass norm, I re-architected the model's forward pass to mimic production inference engines like vLLM.

Here is what the optimization pipeline looked like: 
1️⃣ The Baseline: Standard PyTorch nn.Module boundaries forced sequential HBM trips (Add -> Write -> Read -> Norm -> Write). 
2️⃣ The Triton Kernel: Built a custom Fused Zero-Centered RMSNorm specifically for Qwen’s FP32-upcast precision requirements. 
3️⃣ Breaking the Boundaries: Modified the Hugging Face Qwen3_5DecoderLayer to pass a tuple of (hidden_states, residual) between layers. By breaking strict OOP rules, I fused the residual addition from the end of one layer directly into the input norm of the next layer entirely in SRAM.

📊 The Results (Benchmarked on Nvidia B200):
Kernel Latency: ~5.7x reduction across all hidden dimensions.
Overall Throughput: Jumped from a baseline of ~16 tok/s to nearly 50 tok/s.

It's one thing to read about kernel launch overhead and memory bandwidth limits, but writing the pointers, handling the shape routing, and watching the throughput 5x on bare metal is an incredible feeling.

Next up: Tackling the chunked sequential memory recurrence of Qwen's Gated Delta Networks.

author: Deep Sheth
subtitle: AI Engineer | Multi-Agent Systems · RAG Pipelines · CUDA · LLM Infrastructure | USC MS CS | Open to AI/ML Roles
content:
I built a KV cache compression engine that serves 104,000 users per second from a single GPU.
Benchmarked on real Criteo ad data. On real NVIDIA hardware. With real profiling.

The problem: LLM-based recommendation systems run out of GPU memory fast. Each user's context lives in a KV cache, and at BF16 precision, you can only fit a few thousand concurrent users per GPU. More users = more GPUs = millions in infrastructure costs.

I built OmniStack-RS to fix this. It compresses KV caches 3.37x using a fused INT4+QJL codec: getting BF16 down to 4.75 bits per element with practically zero quality loss (max error vs FP32: 0.0024).
What that means in practice: 3.37x more users per GPU. 3.37x lower serving costs.

Results on Criteo Day 23 data (NVIDIA A10): 
• P99 latency: 0.69 ms (144x under MLPerf's 100ms deadline) 
• Throughput: 1,634 queries/sec, 104,571 users/sec 
• Compression: 3.37x (beat the 3.2x design target) 
• Numerical parity vs FP32: PASS

Under the hood: 
• INT4 Lloyd-Max quantization + 1-bit Rademacher QJL residual 
• Fused Triton attention kernel (dequant, softmax, and output in one pass) 
• O(1) Multi-LoRA dispatch for per-user personalization 
• Profiled with NVIDIA Nsight Compute (not just Python timers)

Built from scratch. No CUDA C, just pure Python and Triton. Looking to take these hardware-native optimizations to the next level: let's talk infra.

author: Anubhab Bandyopadhyay
subtitle: Founder & CEO, Neurafewz
content:
I stumbled across GPU kernel fusion 3–4 years ago. I understood the words, not what they meant. Yet, today at Neurafewz, fusion is one of the fundamental tools we use to squeeze #performance out of #inference pipelines.

Let's use the tail end of an #attention block as an example,
---
# seq_len=1024, hidden_dim=4096, bf16

attn_proj = matmul(attn_out, W)
attn_proj += residual
normed = norm_fn(attn_proj)
---
The activation #tensor is 1024 × 4096 × 2 bytes = 8MB.

Eager #execution does something like this:
- Projection #kernel reads 8MB from #DRAM, does the matrix multiplication, writes 8MB back.
- Add kernel reads it again, adds the residual, writes 8MB.
- The norm involves 2-3 more kernels, each with its own reads and writes plus FP32 per token intermediates

That's roughly ~50MB of #memory traffic to move the same bytes back and forth between compute and DRAM. Now compound that across batches and 80 #transformer layers — each of which has to finish before your first token appears.

You bought all this beautiful compute. Tensor cores, massive #parallelism, absurd #FLOPS. And your pipeline stalls because the #GPU is waiting for the same 8MB tensor to ping-pong between DRAM and the SMs.

Kernel fusion is the escape hatch.
Instead of `Proj → DRAM → Add → DRAM → Intermediate steps  → DRAM  → Norm → DRAM`
you do `Proj + Add + Norm → DRAM`.

Keep intermediates in registers and #SRAM, run all the math on the tile that's already hot, write once at the end. For this slice of the #model, memory traffic drops from ~50MB to ~16MB. Same math but fewer round trips and kernel launches.

So why not #fuse everything?
Because GPUs aren't fast because one thing runs quickly — they're fast because thousands of independent pieces of work run in #parallel. Some operations need global coordination: #reductions, #scatters, sync-heavy patterns. And in #CUDA, the most natural global sync point is often "finish the kernel, write to DRAM, launch the next one." Force fusion across that boundary with suboptimal #algorithm for a compute and you save memory #traffic but kill parallelism, #occupancy collapses, a few SMs become the bottleneck, while the rest of the GPU watches.
Congratulations: your "#optimized" version is slower. That's the part I didn't appreciate 3–4 years ago.

The fastest memory is the memory you never touch — until touching memory is the price you pay to keep the GPU parallel.

Abhishek Sarkar Donald D'Silva
#GPUComputing #HPC #AI #ML #KernelFusion #Inference #MatrixMultiplication

author: Vito Lin
subtitle: Software Engineer - Cuda & Rust
content:
🚀 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐂𝐔𝐃𝐀 𝐢𝐬 𝐞𝐱𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐆𝐏𝐔?

Between your .cu file and Tensor Cores, there is a high-stakes "translation task" happening inside the compiler process. 

🧠 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐈 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐝:
1. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐔𝐃𝐀 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧
→ Code goes through a multi-stage transformation:
   CUDA C++ → PTX (Virtual ISA) → ptxas (The Optimizer) → SASS (Real ISA)

Each step can either preserve your performance or destroy it through "Register Spilling". Register Spilling = too many variables → Registers overflow → Data spills into local memory → Performance drops.

2. 𝐏𝐓𝐗: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐕𝐢𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥 𝐈𝐒𝐀 𝐋𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐫
→ PTX (Parallel Thread Execution) is a Virtual ISA.
→ It uses infinite virtual registers (%r1, %r2, ...).
→ It acts as a stable contract: Write once in PTX, and it could be ran on future GPU generations with high compatibility.
→ It’s the "LLVM IR" of the NVIDIA world.

3. 𝐩𝐭𝐱𝐚𝐬: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐄𝐧𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐫
→ This is where the real drama happens. `ptxas` takes the infinite world of PTX and squeezes it into the finite physical world of the SM.
→ Register Allocation: It maps those infinite `%r` registers to the 255 physical registers available per thread.
→ The Danger Zone: If your kernel is too complex, `ptxas` triggers *Register Spilling*, moving data to slow Local Memory (VRAM), which leads to bad performance.

4. 𝐒𝐀𝐒𝐒: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐈𝐒𝐀 𝐋𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐫 
→ SASS (Streaming Assembler) is the Real ISA that the hardware actually executes.Unlike PTX, SASS is specific to your GPU architecture (e.g., `sm_90` for Hopper).
→ SASS contains low-level scheduling hints and hard-coded register assignments.
→ Programmer can see it using `cuobjdump -sass`.

5. 𝐖𝐡𝐲 "𝐅𝐚𝐭 𝐁𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬" 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫
→ To make software work on both an RTX 3090 and an H100, NVIDIA uses Fatbins.
→ A Fatbin stores:
    1. Multiple CUBINs (pre-compiled SASS for specific GPU versions).
    2. The PTX source (for JIT compilation on future GPUs).
→ Make sure AI model will not die when a new GPU architecture is released.

6. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐇𝐢𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐧 𝐎𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐈𝐧𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐏𝐓𝐗
→ Sometimes the `nvcc` compiler is too conservative, so power users inject Inline PTX directly into C++ to trigger specific hardware features like `cp.async` (Async Copy) or Tensor Core MMA instructions.
→ This bypasses high-level abstractions to talk directly to the hardware's capabilities.

💡 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭:
GPU performance isn't just about the algorithms you write in C++, but about how gracefully those algorithms survive the translation from Virtual PTX to Physical SASS. 

#CUDA #GPUComputing #ParallelProgramming #HPC #AIInfra #AI #NVidia #AMD

wanted to clear something up about wafer pass that keeps coming up in our discord. $10/wk for 5,000 requests/day on frontier coding models is not our vc-subsidized loss leader, our margins are great! let me explain:

once kernel optimization is mostly automated, the hardware story flips.

on stock SGLang or vLLM, an MI355X still leaves a huge chunk of the chip on the floor. that kills unit economics for cost-sensitive serving. but, with the wafer agent grinding on it for a few days, MI355X goes from viable to genuinely competitive on tokens per dollar. the numbers we've been getting on AMD have been better than conventional wisdom says is possible.

you can also squeeze a ton of perf from frontier hardware. blackwell has TMEM, 2-CTA MMA, async matmul, block-scaled FP4, and dozens of other features not a lot of people know how to use correctly. the agent finds them and uses them. so on a B300 the same model ends up faster than what humans can hand-tune, because the search space is too big to explore manually.

if you stack all of this together, you get the substrate that makes the price work. $10/week, 5,000 requests a day, 10x what claude code gives you on the equivalent pricing plan. we cost 2-3x less per request to operate than the unoptimized stack.

author: Elizabeth Thomas
subtitle: Independent LLM Inference Engineer · vLLM Contributor (4 merged PRs) · Quantization · Speculative Decoding · KV-Cache Optimization · ex-Target Principal Engineer
content:
Day 26/100: Zero-Downtime Deployment & Cost Estimation

Models change. New checkpoints, quantization swaps, runtime upgrades, configuration tweaks and none of it can ship with downtime on a live inference Application Programming Interface (API). Once the deployment problem is solved, the next question is what the hardware actually costs per million tokens.

Three deployment strategies bracket the safety-versus-capacity tradeoff. Blue-green runs two identical fleets: blue is currently serving, green is the new version. Once green passes health checks against a hold-out traffic slice, the load balancer flips weights atomically. Rollback is one weight flip. The cost: 2× Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) capacity during the overlap, typically 15–30 minutes for a careful cutover. Rolling updates replace replicas one at a time - cheapest, but some traffic always lands on the in-flight version during the swap. Canary shifts traffic in steps (1% → 5% → 25% → 100%) with automatic rollback if error rate or p99 latency breaches a threshold. Slowest path, but it catches subtle regressions that only show up at small traffic slices - prompt-format edge cases, numerical drift from a new quantization.

Cost estimation reduces to one formula: 
$/1M tokens = (GPU $/hr) ÷ (tokens/sec × utilization × 3600) × 10⁶

Three independent levers move that number, and each one can shift it by multiples.
1) GPU choice (H100 vs B200 vs A100) sets the rate. 
2) Throughput is set by High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) bandwidth and quantization: INT4 versus FP16 is roughly a 4× cost reduction per token because each token reads ¼ the weight bytes from HBM. 
3) Utilization is the silent killer: idle GPUs cost the same as busy ones. 

A 70B model on 4× H100 at 30% utilization costs ~2.3× more per token than the same fleet at 70% which is a queueing-and-batching problem, not a hardware problem. Quantization and utilization compound: INT4 at 70% utilization is ~12× cheaper per token than FP16 at 30%.

Graceful shutdown closes the loop. When a Kubernetes pod is replaced, the preStop hook deregisters it from the load balancer, in-flight requests drain, and only then does SIGTERM land. Drain timeout should be set to p99 request duration plus buffer. Too short kills long-tail requests mid-stream and produces user-visible errors during every rollout; too long and rollouts crawl, blocking subsequent rollouts.

Walkthrough with blue-green and canary simulators, a quantization-aware cost model, and a graceful-shutdown drain loop: (https://lnkd.in/ggu9Ry7J). Next up: performance benchmarking and profiling tooling.

author: Taofeek Olalekan
subtitle: Senior AI & HPC Infrastructure Engineer | Disaggregated LLM Inference | 10,000+ GPU Scale | Building Europe’s First Sovereign Industrial AI Cloud
content:
Spent the week optimising prefill/decode-disaggregated inference for GLM-5 NVFP4 on B200 — and came away with deeper respect for every Claude Code and Codex token I use daily.

Headline result: TTFT p50 collapsed 8× — from 61.5 s to 7.7 s — on a 40,000-request mixed bailian trace (coder + reasoning + normal). Throughput parity preserved at ~6,900 tok/s. 87-minute production gate, zero errors.

The path:

— GPU↔NIC same-NUMA placement via dranet + `UCX_MAX_RMA_RAILS=1`. Per-rank KV transfer hit 30+ GB/s peaks (~62% of NDR400 line rate) in the multi-frag zero-copy regime.

— SGLang server-side audit against published Blackwell recipes (SGLang GB200 PD reproduction, GLM-5 cookbook, DeepSeek-V3 bench scripts). Six flag/env additions our baseline was missing — including matching `--max-prefill-tokens` to `--chunked-prefill-size`, NVFP4-specific quant paths, and Blackwell collective fusion.

— Code-grounded retraction of two earlier hypotheses: page-size tuning was already auto-handled for GLM-5's NSA backend; the DeepSeek-V3 architectural flag set (DP-attention, dense-tp-size 1, EP=tp) didn't compound on top at our 16-GPU 2-node scale — that recipe is built for GB200 NVL72, not for our footprint.

The real lesson: at this scale, you're not throughput-bound on PD — you're tail-latency-bound. The decode KV pool is the binding ceiling, and TTFT collapses or explodes on whether prefill admission keeps up with it. p99 is still 34× off aggregate-router quality, but median is now a different conversation.

Asymmetric TP across prefill and decode looks promising in theory, but I haven't been able to validate it on this footprint yet — TP=2 model fit is the open question.

author: Mark Molchanov
subtitle: Senior AI/ML Engineer | 5+ Years in Machine Learning, NLP & Generative AI | Python | LLM Fine-Tuning | RAG | LangChain | LangGraph | AI Agents | AWS | AI-Powered Solutions
content:
I spent the last two years optimizing inference in production. And I can tell you one thing: most of what I knew about deploying models became useless the moment I started working with LLMs.

Classic ML inference is straightforward at its core. One forward pass, result is ready, GPU is free. XGBoost, CNN, BERT classifier - they all follow the same pattern.
LLMs completely broke my mental model.
One request is not one forward pass. It's hundreds of sequential passes, one token at a time. The prefill phase is compute-bound, decoding is memory bandwidth-bound, and running both on the same GPU is like having one pedal for both the gas and the brake.
Then you add KV cache into the mix. It grows with context length and can be shared across requests. Which means routing is no longer about "which server has the least load" - it's about "which replica already has the right prefix cached."
MoE models throw expert parallelism on top of all that.
This is exactly why a completely separate optimization stack exists just for LLM inference: speculative decoding, continuous batching, PagedAttention, quantization, prefix caching, tensor parallelism and dozens more techniques, each solving a specific production bottleneck.
I recently came across a map of 72 LLM inference optimization techniques grouped into 9 blocks. Every single one of them exists because someone hit a wall in production.
What LLM inference optimizations are you using? What do you think is the most underrated technique out there?
Drop it in the comments 👇

author: Nikolas Markou
subtitle: Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence Consultant | Head of AI @ Electi
content:
The cache is the bill.

A modern 70B LLM spends as much GPU memory remembering your prompt as running the model.

That memory is the KV cache. Every serious inference optimization that shipped in the last two years was a different attack on it.

Attention lets each generated token look at every prior token. Per layer, the model produces three vectors per token: a query (Q), a key (K), a value (V). The new token's Q is scored against every prior K to pick where to attend, and those scores weight the prior Vs into the output.

Done naively, token n recomputes K and V for tokens 1 through n minus 1. Quadratic in sequence length. No production system could pay that.

> Once a token's K and V are computed, they never change.

So you cache them. The new token computes only its own Q, K, V, multiplies Q against the cached K matrix, weights the cached V matrix, appends its own K and V to the store. Generation drops from O(n squared) to O(n). The cost shape did not disappear. It moved into memory.

The math is concrete. On a 70B model at 80 layers, 64 heads, head_dim 128, every token contributes around 320 KB per layer in FP16. At 128K context, 40 GB per sequence. The weights at 4-bit are 35 GB. The cache is now larger than the model.

This is what the demo does not show. Benchmarks run at 1K context. Production runs at the second integration, where someone wired in retrieval and the prompt ships a 30K-token preamble every turn.

Five optimizations the serving stack converged on.

1. GQA (grouped-query attention) shares each K and V across multiple Q heads. Llama 3 cut its cache by 8x with no measurable quality loss. The first thing any 2025 architecture does.

2. MLA (multi-head latent attention, DeepSeek V2 and V3) compresses K and V into a small latent vector and projects out per step. Roughly another 4x on top of GQA. The reason DeepSeek serves 128K context economically.

3. Sliding-window attention (Mistral, Gemma) caps the cache at a fixed window of W tokens. Cheap, lossy, useful for chat where the recent context is what matters.

4. PagedAttention (vLLM) allocates the cache in fixed-size blocks instead of contiguous tensors. Fragmentation drops from roughly 50% wasted to under 5%. The reason your batch size doubled when you migrated.

5. Prompt caching (Anthropic, OpenAI, every modern serving stack) stores the K and V of a shared prompt prefix and reuses it across requests. One system prompt fanned out to a thousand users computes the prefix once. This is the layer the recent "Claude limits" threads were arguing about without naming it.

Quantize K and V to INT8 on top of any of the above and a single H100 serves roughly five times the concurrent users at the same latency.

The cache is the bill.

author: Rishabh Misra
subtitle: Principal ML Lead - Generative Personalization | ML Book and Course Author | Researcher - LLMs & RecSys - 1k+ citations | Advisory @ Startups | Featured in TechCrunch, NBC, TheSun | AI Consultant
content:
Your $30,000 NVIDIA H100 is essentially a very expensive space heater for 80% of an LLM generation request.

Not because your engineers are incompetent. Because of *physics*.

After scaling high-throughput systems at Twitter and Amazon, I thought I understood performance bottlenecks. CPU cycles. Network I/O. Database locks.

LLM inference broke everything I knew. For the first time in computing history, the most powerful chips ever built spend most of their time doing absolutely nothing, just waiting for data.

Here's the counterintuitive truth most people miss:
→ Your inference bill isn't 10x higher than training because of "model size." It's because of something called the *Memory Wall*.

Think of it this way:
→ Your H100 can perform 989 TeraFLOPS of math per second 
→ But it can only move 3.35 TB per second from memory 
→ The ratio is roughly 300:1

What this means: Unless your code performs at least 300 operations for every byte it reads from memory, your compute cores sit idle, waiting.

During the "decode" phase (generating text token-by-token), we read the entire model weight matrix for every single token. A 70B parameter model requires 140GB of memory movement per token.

Physics dictates: You cannot generate tokens faster than you can pull weights from RAM to the chip. We're Not Computing; We're Just Moving Data. This is why throwing more compute at the problem yields zero latency improvement.

So if you're a CTO staring at a "low GPU utilization" graph: Don't fire your AI team. They're not lazy. They've hit the ceiling of physics.

This is Part 1 of a multipart deep dive into LLM inference optimization. In Part 2, we'll dissect the KV Cache bottleneck.

What's been your biggest "aha moment" when optimizing LLM inference?

author: Oleksiy Vlasenko
subtitle: Staff Technical Lead Manager at Google
content:
A big part of my work involves optimizing ML models to run efficiently on TPUs. It's not a trivial effort — every meaningful speedup requires a lot of domain knowledge spanning the compiler, the hardware, the framework internals, Pallas kernels, ML-specific knowledge and so on.

So I had an idea: what if Andrej Karpathy's autoresearch loop could automate this?

Turns out it works, but only when the autoresearch idea is extended into a more complete architecture:

Autoresearch — an optimization loop modified to tune model performance (tokens/sec, MFU), instead of optimizing how fast a model can train. It proposes ranked, falsifiable experiments, runs them on TPU, and either accepts or rejects them based on results. See https://lnkd.in/ecZE8hiG

LLM wiki — a knowledge base of TPU-specific domain information that informs every hypothesis (papers, codebases, kernels, plus the running record of every experiment). It also documents how to profile TPU models and interpret traces. See https://lnkd.in/efKPN3BA

XProf MCP server — an observer that grounds each iteration in real signal. For TPU perf, that's XProf wrapped as MCP, so the agent can read profiles, attribute ops back to HLO and source lines, and verify every claimed win against a real trace. See https://lnkd.in/eftmRcCt

When those ideas were combined together, everything worked like magic. 
Repo is available at: https://lnkd.in/ebywzwua

In less than a day, the agent ran 60+ experiments with minimal supervision and achieved performance comparable to the highly-optimized Llama3 8B model implementations in the MaxText repo (see wiki/experiments/llama3_8B_autoresearch_optimization folder).

Excited to see how far we'll be able to push this.

author: Sebastian Raschka, PhD
subtitle: ML/AI research engineer. Author of Build a Large Language Model From Scratch (amzn.to/4fqvn0D) and Ahead of AI (magazine.sebastianraschka.com), on how LLMs work and the latest developments in the field.
content:
April was a pretty strong month for open-weight LLM architecture releases:

1. Gemma 4
Continues the local/global attention recipe with sliding window attention, which is a classic yet "easy" way to extend context while making it cheaper than full attention.

2. GLM-5.1
A large MoE model that based on DeepSeek V3.2 with multi-head latent attention (MLA) and DeepSeek Sparse Attention

3. Qwen3.6
Keeps the Qwen3.5-style hybrid stack. I.e., mostly Gated DeltaNet / linear-attention-style layers, with periodic full attention layers. Next to the 35B-A3B MoE variant there now also is a 27B dense variant.

4. Kimi K2.6
A 1T-scale sparse MoE model with DeepSeek-style MLA and only a small fraction of parameters active per token. It is another good example of how frontier-scale models keep improving without major architecture changes (coming from DeepSeek V3) except increasing the size. (Lots of performance improvements are due to the training recipe.)

5. DeepSeek V4
Probably the most architecture-heavy release of the month. The Pro and Flash variants add manifold-constrained hyper-connections, compressed attention variants, hash-based routing in the early layers, and a 1M-token context window.

All of these are now added to the LLM Architecture Gallery.

I am keeping the notes short for now, especially for DeepSeek V4, because the details around mHC and compressed attention deserve a more careful writeup. More once I am fully back in May.

author: Mehul Batra
subtitle: Tinkering with AI x Multimodal DataCloud @DigitalOcean | Apache Fluss PPMC
content:
𝐆𝐏𝐔 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐟𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫. 𝐂𝐏𝐔 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐭.
A 25MB multilingual PDF that indexed in 98s on H100 took 213s on c16.  The reason was honest: Docling's layout detection (YOLO, table-transformer, OCR) is neural net inference, and neural nets are faster on GPU. Other formats (DOCX, markdown, CSV, JSON) don't touch the GPU during parsing. Only the ML-parsing path regressed.
The metric that mattered wasn't the one we were measuring.

𝐌𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐏𝐔 𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐡 𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞
Default PyTorch on CPU leaves performance on the floor. Docling shipped with num_threads=4 on a 16-vCPU node, 75% of the compute idle while the layout model ran. Bumping OMP_NUM_THREADS to 16 and enabling oneDNN with AVX-512 (the same vectorization trick SIMD uses, one instruction operating on 16 floats at once) closed most of the gap.

Same file, same model: 402s with defaults, 198s with tuning.

Tuning recovered what defaults left on the table. It didn't close the hardware gap, the H100 still ran this path in 81s. We moved OCR to CPU anyway, because the bottleneck on this workload wasn't compute, it was access to compute.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝
Per-job latency: how long one job takes once it starts. Queue latency: how long a job waits to start.
With dedicated H100s and per-job reservation, job N+1 waits in Pending. Bursty ingestion meant 15-30 minute queue times during peaks. Auto-scaling CPU nodes provisioned new capacity in seconds when a burst arrived. Average pod pending time dropped from  minutes to  second.
A 2.2× slower parse that waits 0 minutes beats a faster parse that waits 20. The math only matters if you measure the right thing.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐢𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 "𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐊𝐮𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐬𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠"
You can't autoscale an H100 fleet the way you autoscale CPU nodes. GPU node bring-up means nvidia-container-runtime, driver init, CUDA setup, and large ML image pulls. Cold starts were 5-10× longer than CPU nodes, and every per-job reservation paid that tax again. Spot availability is thinner. Most importantly, the GPU pool itself was capped: a fixed allocation we couldn't grow on demand. Bursty ingestion hit that ceiling and queued. CPU nodes have no such ceiling for this workload, the autoscaler adds capacity until the burst clears.
The freed GPUs didn't sit idle. They moved into a shared /v1/embeddings inference pool that warms once and stays warm. Scaling out the replica pool collapsed embed time from minutes to seconds via concurrent requests and Ray Serve dynamic batching. The startup cost is paid once at pool initialization, not per job.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐨𝐧
Per-job reservation made the GPU a job-local resource. Shared inference made it a platform resource.
Per-job latency is what you measure in a benchmark. Queue latency is what users feel.
#AIinfra #knowledgebases #embeddings #utilizationisKing

author: Alex Razvant
subtitle: Senior AI Engineer | Writing The AI Merge Newsletter
content:
AI inference and the merge between GPUs and DSAs

GPUs currently handle the largest chunk of AI Compute for both model training and inference at scale.

They won't go anywhere.

However, demand for AI inference is growing and many companies are designing Domain Specific Architectures (DSAs), their own hardware.

Some examples are:
1/ Google TPU (Tensor Processing Unit)
2/ Apple NPU (Neural Processing Unit)
3/ Groq LPU (Language Processing Unit)
4/ Cerebras
5/ Tenstorrent Blackhole
6/ AMD Instinct M
7/ SambaNova SN40L
8/ AWS Trainium/Inferentia
9/ NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX 

What's the problem DSAs are solving? > To minimize data movement.

They optimize the memory hierarchy and the compute-bound vs memory-bound trade-off. In GPUs, a data point has to pass through VRAM, then SRAM, and Registers etc.

Each component in this hierarchy increases in bandwidth but decreases in memory size.

VRAM (Slowest)> Gigabytes.
Caches (Faster) > Megabytes.
Registers (Fastest) > Kilobytes.

DSAs reorganize this hierarchy and reduce the time a data point spends in memory, to leave more for the compute part.

That's why LLM inference is so fast on Groq LPUs for example.

author: Lorenzo Bradanini
subtitle: Software Engineering & Systems Design Read by 15k+ engineers. I write about the deep structure of software: data engineering, computation, and the physical limits that shape technology. Author of The Software Frontier.
content:
Most people think GPUs are compute machines.

They’re not. They’re latency-hiding systems.

That single misunderstanding is why so much effort in AI infrastructure gets misallocated.

In training, we hide communication under compute.
In inference, we try to hide serial generation under parallelism.
In serving, we hide memory fragmentation behind smarter allocation.

Different layers. Same game.
Because the real constraint is never “how much compute you have.”

It’s what’s starving that compute:
– memory bandwidth
– communication
– or sequential dependencies

If one of these dominates, your trillion FLOPs don’t matter. The system stalls.
That’s why an H100 can generate tokens at human reading speed.

Not because it’s weak, but because it’s waiting.
Waiting on memory. Waiting on data. Waiting on the next step in a sequence it cannot parallelize.

The entire modern inference stack (batching, KV cache design, speculative decoding, scheduling) is just one thing:

A set of tricks to make sure something useful is happening while something else is blocked.

That’s the deeper pattern.

Not optimization as a checklist, but optimization as restructuring time.

And once you see systems this way, everything changes:
You stop asking “how do I make this faster?”

And start asking “what is idle right now, and why?”

author: Sreedath Panat
subtitle: MIT PhD | IITM | 100K+ LinkedIn | Co-founder Vizuara & Videsh | Making AI accessible for all
content:
KV cache is a simple idea in LLM inference.

When a transformer generates text one token at a time, it has to decide the next token by attending to all the previous tokens. Now here is the inefficient part: if we do this naively, then at every new decoding step, the model keeps re-processing the entire prefix again and again. That means for token 100, it is not just processing token 100. It is effectively revisiting tokens 1 to 99 as well, recomputing their attention-related representations repeatedly. This creates unnecessary compute, higher latency, and much slower generation.

This is exactly where KV cache comes in.

Inside self-attention, each token produces three vectors: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V). During autoregressive decoding, when a new token arrives, the model only needs the new token’s Query to compare against the Keys of all previous tokens, and then use the corresponding Values to compute attention. The important insight is that the Keys and Values for previous tokens do not change during inference. So instead of recomputing them every time, we store them in memory. That stored memory is called the KV cache.

At step t, the model computes Q, K, and V only for the new token, fetches the old K and V from the cache, performs attention over the full history, generates the next output, and then appends the new K and V into the cache. This means the model still “looks at” the full context, but it does not waste time rebuilding the same internal representations again and again.

Why does this matter so much?

Because without KV cache, decoding becomes increasingly expensive as the sequence grows. With KV cache, generation becomes dramatically faster, especially for long prompts and long responses. This is one of the core reasons why modern chat systems can stream tokens in a reasonably responsive way. If you have ever wondered how LLMs can answer in real time even after you give them a long prompt, KV cache is a major part of the answer.

But there is a tradeoff.

KV cache reduces compute, but increases memory usage. For every token in the context, and for every transformer layer, the model stores Keys and Values. So as context length grows, memory consumption grows too. This is why serving long-context LLMs is not just a compute problem, it is also a memory systems problem. In production, a lot of inference engineering is really about managing this tradeoff well: batching, paged attention, cache eviction, quantized KV cache, prefix sharing, and memory-efficient serving.

author: Raphael Pisoni
subtitle: Machine Learning Researcher | Representation Learning | LLMs | CV | Adaptable AI
content:
I never really considered how dangerous QK-norm actually is before working on RBF Attention. While solving some obvious issues, it can be the cause of some much less obvious ones.

QK-norm is definitely the industry standard right now. It stops "magnitude bullying" by projecting queries and keys onto a hypersphere before taking the dot product and makes training more stable. Sounds great right?

The problem hides in the backward pass. While the forward pass becomes scale-invariant, the gradients flowing backward through the norm layer actually scale inversely with the unnormalized inputs.
Big pre-norm vectors --> tiny gradients.

But why would those unnormalized vectors get so big in the first place? Think about the geometry. When your optimizer takes a linear step on a circular surface (the normalized hypersphere), the update vector inherently points outwards along the tangent.

Because of this, with every single optimization step, the pre-norm vector length increases. As these vectors inflate, the gradients shrink toward zero. This geometric drift is one reason for why we actually need weight decay. To constantly drag parameter norms back down.

Scaled RBF Attention offers a pretty clean workaround. If you measure similarity using negative squared Euclidean distance (-||Q - K||²) instead of a dot product, due to the softmax we end up with 2(Q⋅K)−||K||².

That term acts as a built-in, dynamic L2 regularizer. The architecture itself actively penalizes large keys. It naturally keeps vector magnitudes in check without ever forcing a projection onto a hypersphere.

Because RBF Attention actively avoids the explosion of pre-norm magnitudes, you don't need QK-norm. The network maintains healthy gradient flow natively, and you drop the weird tangent-drift artifacts entirely.

I wrote up the full explanation and math and even  implemented super-fast Triton kernels.

Small-scale runs look surprisingly stable, but obviously, we need to scale up experiments to see how these dynamics hold up.
Let me know if you can help with that!

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🔬 LLM-as-a-verifier

Stanford and Berkeley just released LLM-as-a-Verifier, a prompting recipe that pushes Gemini 2.5 Flash to SOTA on Terminal-Bench 2 (86.4%) and SWE-Bench Verified (77.8%) as a trajectory selector. It's a pretty cool general-purpose framework based on a simple trick.

→ Instead of picking one score token, they take the expectation **over the full logprob distribution of score tokens**. This gives a continuous reward signal for free!

→ Scaling granularity from 1 to 20 score levels keeps improving accuracy. The quantization error in scalar judges turns out to be much larger than people assumed, and finer scales let the verifier approximate a continuous reward more faithfully.

→ Repeated verification (k=1 to 16) and decomposing into 3 sub-criteria (specification compliance, output format, error signals) both add gains that compound. The decomposition matters because verifying simpler factors is easier than rating overall trajectory quality in one shot.

→ Verification accuracy hits 77.4% with zero ties at k=16, vs 70.2% with 5.4% ties for the judge baseline. Most of the gains come from being more discriminative with ties rather than flipping wrong decisions.

Reading token probabilities for verification has precedent (Generative Verifiers averages the "Yes" token probability across sampled CoTs), but turning score-token granularity into its own scaling axis is a nice contribution. The asymmetric setup is also surprising, with Flash ranking Opus 4.6 trajectories. My main concern is that the round-robin tournament is O(N²) verifier calls per task. Additional comparisons against trained generative RMs would have also been nice.

author: Pere Martra
subtitle: AI Research Engineer | Structured Pruning & LLM Efficiency | Fairness-Aware Optimization | Author “Rearchitecting LLMs” @Manning | 2K GitHub ⭐
content:
When you quantize model weights in vLLM, you're not just making the model smaller. You're buying yourself more context.

vLLM pre-allocates a fixed slice of GPU memory at startup: weights get one part, the KV block pool gets the rest. 

So every byte you save on weights automatically becomes available KV capacity. More blocks = longer sequences, bigger batches.

Hugging Face works differently. Weights and KV cache live in completely separate memory regions. Quantizing one has zero effect on the other. They're independent levers.

This diagram shows both worlds side by side:
→ In HF, the KV cache just grows token by token into whatever memory is free.
→ In vLLM with NF4 weights, the smaller model footprint expands the pre-allocated block pool.
→ In vLLM with quantized KV blocks (FP8), each block shrinks, fitting more tokens into the same pool.

Same GPU. Three very different memory behaviors depending on where you apply the compression.

This is from Chapter 8 of Rearchitecting LLMs (Manning), where we benchmark all three configurations on T4 and L4 GPUs.  And the results on older hardware are not what you'd expect.

Notebooks are on the github repository. Link in the comments.

author: Sriram Govindan
subtitle: ML Systems | GPU Kernel Engineer @Modular | Cofounder @Bench AI
content:
If you're in the AI performance space, you'll see countless blogs about custom GPU kernels that are 10, 30, or even 100% faster than NVIDIA's cuBLAS. Interestingly, the perf gains aren't the crazy part; it's how simple they are to achieve.

Performance comes from optimizations, and optimizations fall into two buckets: features and tuning. Feature implementation is what the engineers at Modular (yours truly), NVIDIA, and Hazy Research do. It's coming up with a fusion, memory loading pattern, scheduling technique, etc., and making it accessible. Tuning is what comes after. It's picking the right combination of optimizations and dispatching them based on your workload.

This is where we have an edge over cuBLAS. You see, cuBLAS is a generic library; algorithms like matmul need to be performant across a huge range of shapes. As Performance Engineers, we're not trying to support the generic case. We have a specific model in mind (Kimi, Deepseek, …), which uses fixed shapes (head_dim, weight matrix dimensions, …), and we know its dominant workloads (prefill, decode). So we can use this info to make a kernel tailored to our needs.

And here's the cool part: in tons of cases, the tailored kernel can be made with tuning alone. No custom GPU code required. All you need is a strong kernel library (Mojo Kernels, Cutlass, ThunderKittens) and the knowledge of when to apply an optimization.

To give you a head start, here are a couple of common scenarios and the appropriate optimization:

Matmul, Decode: Try SwapAB. The batch size sits in the M dimension, but tensor cores have a fixed M size; this wastes compute. With SwapAB, the A and B matrices switch positions, moving the batch size to the N dimension, where you have finer granularity. The tradeoff is that C needs to be transposed.

Prefill: Try a persistent kernel with a CLC scheduler. A large matmul launches lots of blocks across multiple waves; this puts heavy pressure on the block scheduler. Persistent kernels remove that pressure entirely. Each SM persists for the full kernel duration, and the CLC scheduler handles the assignment.

My next article will be an extensive list of optimizations and when to use them, so keep your eyes peeled for that. In the meantime, check out these great resources 👇

Vishal Padia's excellent blog on Flash Attention: https://lnkd.in/g9rzN939

author: Aanchal Karamchandani
subtitle: Senior ML Engineer | LLM Inference & Serving | Production AI Infrastructure
content:
A single H100 has 80 GB of memory.

One request with 10,000 tokens uses ~5 GB of KV cache.

100 concurrent users? 
That’s 500 GB.

This isn’t a model problem.

It’s a memory management problem.

Most discussions around LLM performance focus on model size, quantization, or architecture.

But in real systems, the bottleneck shows up somewhere else entirely:
memory.

My latest article breaks down how modern inference systems actually deal with this, not by making models smaller, but by making smarter decisions about memory.

Four questions drive everything:
→ What do you keep? 
→ What do you share? 
→ What do you move? 
→ What do you let go? 

Inside the article:

• PagedAttention → eliminates fragmentation and over-reservation (60–80% waste → <4%) 
• Prefix sharing → stores identical KV blocks once across many users 
• Prefill caching → avoids recomputation across time, not just concurrency 
• Attention-aware eviction → keeps what matters, not just what’s recent 
• KV cache quantization → reduces memory per token by 2–4x with minimal accuracy loss 

These are not isolated tricks.

They form a system.

Each layer reduces a different kind of waste, and makes the others more effective.

At every stage, the cost is not removed. 
It is moved, reduced, shared, or delayed.

When Google released Gemma 4 this month, the community quickly adopted Google Research's TurboQuant algorithm to compress the KV cache during inference. TurboQuant is a data-oblivious vector quantizer that matches the Shannon lower bound on distortion — with zero training and zero data passes.

I open-sourced pyturboquant  — a PyTorch implementation of TurboQuant aimed at embeddings and RAG. What that unlocks for on-premise deployments:
No codebook training. Add a document, it's indexed.
True streaming ingestion. No rebuild when the corpus grows.
Pure local. Pair it with an open-source embedding model and nothing leaves your machine.

content:
My first blog associated with the startup I joined, uncovers which torch.compile mode you should use as a kernel baseline and our team is hiring!

📖 The Blog: The right torch.compile mode to use

One of the first things that a Kernel Engineer does when they're tasked with creating an optimized kernel is, establishing a fair baseline.

Comparing against eager execution is unfair because all the code executes in python one line at a time introducing tons of overhead and inefficient global memory reads and writes.

Torch’s compile functionality is a simple decorator you need to wrap your PyTorch code in to obtain a fused and optimized Triton version of the eager kernel. However, torch’s compiler supports 4 modes and there’s no clear winner between which mode to choose.

In this blog we cover our experiments profiling 23 different kernels commonly used in LLMs/VLMs across all compilation modes and show how 𝗺𝗮𝘅-𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗲 is quite terrible, it sometimes even underperforms eager execution. 

We show that 𝗺𝗮𝘅-𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗲-𝗻𝗼-𝗰𝘂𝗱𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵𝘀 and even 𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁 win the most often.

As a kernel engineer your takeaway should be that if you’re benchmarking against a torch module use 𝗺𝗮𝘅-𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗲-𝗻𝗼-𝗰𝘂𝗱𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵𝘀 or 𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁 as the compilation mode.

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
One of the optimizations in Flash Attention-4 is approximating the exponential function. The need for this is tied to a hardware unit called Special Function Units (SFU) on GPUs.

🤝🏽 SFUs & Transcendental Math Functions

Transcendental math functions are functions that "transcend" algebra, they cannot be expressed as a finite sequence of algebraic operations. These functions are prevalent across deep learning, with prime examples being exp, log, sin, and cos.

The complicated nature of these operations, means that the circuitry needed to compute them is different than the Arithmetic Logic Units (ALUs) that make up CUDA cores and this is what SFUs do.

😟 The SFU Bottleneck

On both Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, there are 128 FP32 CUDA cores The asymmetry is worse with tensor cores: on the B200, tensor cores deliver 8,192 ops/clock/SM while SFUs deliver just 16 ops/clock/SM. That's a 512:1 ratio.

Flash Attention-3 addressed this by hiding softmax computation under asynchronous WGMMA. Overlapping the SFU-bound exponentials with tensor core work so neither stalls the other. But from Hopper to Blackwell, tensor core throughput grew from 1 to 2.25 PFLOPs while the SFU count stayed the same. The overlap strategy alone was no longer enough to mask the lower throughput of the SFUs.

⚡ Optimizing Transcendental Math Ops

𝗙𝗔-𝟰: 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. The FA-4 authors approximate exp2 using a cubic polynomial (Cody-Waite range reduction + Horner evaluation) that runs entirely on the FMA/CUDA cores, bypassing the SFU. 

This consumes extra registers, so it's applied to only 10–25% of entries in each softmax row, with the rest still computed via the SFUs.

𝗖𝘂𝘁𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀: 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗿𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 Setting `fastmath=True` in cutlass is a third, lighter-weight option. It skips the correction steps involved in computing these ops, trading precision for fewer total instructions.

The Colfax Research FA-4 blog post covers the polynomial coefficients and Cody-Waite decomposition in detail: https://lnkd.in/dm2KChhw

subtitle: No BS AI/ML Content | ML Engineer with a Plot Twist 🥷100M+ Views 📝
content:
I've been training models on GPU clusters for years.

I couldn't explain why Tensor Parallelism stops scaling at 8 GPUs.

HuggingFace ran 4,000+ scaling experiments on up to 512 GPUs and wrote everything down. Open source.

The Ultra-Scale Playbook. Here's what humbled me:

1️⃣ Activation memory is the silent killer
I knew it grew with batch size. I didn't know it grows quadratically with sequence length.
At 8K context, activations dwarf parameters, gradients, and optimizer states combined.
One interactive widget made this click in seconds.

2️⃣ ZeRO-3 and Pipeline Parallelism solve the same problem
One communicates weights. The other communicates activations.
I was combining them when I shouldn't have been. The benchmarks show exactly when each one wins.

3️⃣ That 43% throughput drop from TP=8 to TP=16
Tensor Parallelism uses NVLink inside a node. Cross-node requires slower interconnects.
I knew TP didn't scale well cross-node. I didn't know it was THIS bad.

4️⃣ Pipeline bubbles have been nearly eliminated
1F1B, interleaved stages, DualPipe, zero-bubble scheduling.
DeepSeek-V3 splits backward passes into input gradients and weight gradients to fill the bubble.
I was still using naive PP. Embarrassing.

5️⃣ FP8 training already works at scale
DeepSeek-V3 did it. Per-tile quantization: 1x128 for activations, 128x128 for weights.
50% memory reduction. Not theoretical. Production.

Reading time: 2-4 days. Worth every hour.

𝟖𝟔% of your VLM's prefill time is the vision encoder. Not the LLM. 🤔

And up to 𝟕𝟏% of those image patches are exact pixel duplicates of another patch in the same image. White margins. Solid backgrounds. Toolbars. Status bars. Your VLM encodes every single one.

𝐏𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐥𝐏𝐫𝐮𝐧𝐞 from 𝐎𝐏𝐏𝐎 𝐀𝐈 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 fixes this at the source — pruning redundant patches 𝐛𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 the ViT encoder even runs. Not after. Before. In raw pixel space.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡:

➡️ 𝟐𝐃 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 — the same principle behind PNG and JPEG-LS. Predict each patch from its three causal neighbors. If the prediction matches — drop it.

author: Alex Razvant
subtitle: Senior AI Engineer | Writing The AI Merge Newsletter
content:
The demand for AI inference, pushes for a merge between GPUs and DSAs.

GPUs currently handle the largest chunk of AI Compute for both model training and inference at scale.

They won't go anywhere.

However, demand for AI inference is growing and many companies are designing Domain Specific Architectures (DSAs), their own hardware.

Some examples are:
1/ Google TPU (Tensor Processing Unit)
2/ Apple NPU (Neural Processing Unit)
3/ Groq LPU (Language Processing Unit)
4/ Cerebras
5/ Tenstorrent Blackhole
6/ AMD Instinct M
7/ SambaNova SN40L
8/ AWS Trainium/Inferentia
9/ NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX 

What's the problem DSAs are solving? > To minimize data movement.

They optimize the memory hierarchy and the compute-bound vs memory-bound trade-off. In GPUs, a data point has to pass through VRAM, then SRAM, and Registers etc.

Each component in this hierarchy increases in bandwidth but decreases in memory size.

VRAM > Gigabytes.
Caches > Megabytes.
Registers > Kilobytes.

DSAs, amongst other things, propose to reorganize this hierarchy and reduce the time a data point spends in memory, to leave more for the compute part.

That's why LLM inference is so fast on Groq LPUs for example.

On the same note, the new NVIDIA's Vera Rubin line of GPUs + Groq LPUs, making the NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX Accelerator is super interesting in this regard.

Seems like itt brings the best of both worlds.

author: Ashwin Gopinath
subtitle: Fixing the Company Brain Problem | Organizational Memory for Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) | Ex-MIT Professor
content:
Google proved their KV cache compression was near-optimal, but we beat it by removing a feature. Turns out, 97% of the dimensions they were compressing are noise.

TurboQuant's error correction (QJL) faithfully fixes rounding errors on all 128 dimensions. The problem: only 4 of those dimensions carry actual signal. On the other 124, "correcting" noise just injects more noise. It's like running spell-check on random characters, it "fixes" gibberish into confident wrong words.

TurboQuant was a single compression paper that moved ~$100B in semiconductor market cap. Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron stock dropped within 48 hours of the announcement. It proved you could compress the inference memory bottleneck away, suddenly every company that had been buying premium high-memory GPUs was overprovisioned.

Our technique, SpectralQuant, gives 5.95x compression (vs TurboQuant's 5.02x), 4.5x faster attention decoding, identical perplexity (9.51 — same as uncompressed FP16), all with just 15 seconds of one-time calibration

There is a lot more counter-intuitive findings in there that might be fun for anyone working with transformers to read.

author: Elizabeth Thomas
subtitle: Independent LLM Inference Engineer · vLLM Contributor (4 merged PRs) · Quantization · Speculative Decoding · KV-Cache Optimization · ex-Target Principal Engineer
content:
100 days of LLM Inference: Inspired by Inference Engineering (https://lnkd.in/gfZMcK8k) by Philip Kiely (Baseten Books, 2026), I'm working on building a structured deep-dive into Inference Engineering from CUDA kernels to multi-cloud autoscaling.

Inference engineering is not the same problem as training. Serving generative models well requires three distinct layers - Runtime, Infrastructure and Tooling. Each builds on the one below it, and gaps in understanding at any layer surface as production problems at the layer above.

*Runtime* is everything that happens on a single GPU and it's where most of the leverage lives. Training is compute-bound; the bottleneck is FLOPS. Inference decode is memory-bandwidth-bound; the bottleneck is loading model weights from HBM for each forward pass. Serving frameworks like vLLM and SGLang are built around this constraint: vLLM's PagedAttention manages the KV cache in fixed-size pages to reduce fragmentation and raise batch utilization; SGLang's RadixAttention extends this with prefix sharing across requests to cut redundant prefill cost. Speculative decoding and disaggregated prefill/decode exist for the same reason - they're all attempts to keep the memory bus saturated.

*Infrastructure* is how that single-GPU runtime scales across a cluster. Tensor parallelism splits weight matrices across GPUs and requires an all-reduce
 == after every matrix multiply. Pipeline parallelism avoids the all-reduce but introduces idle bubbles between stages. Neither works well without a runtime layer that's already tuned.

*Tooling* is observability and benchmarking: TTFT, inter-token latency, queue  depth, GPU utilization, the instrumentation that makes the other two layers debuggable. Without it, optimization is guesswork.

I'm working through all three end-to-end, with every concept implemented as a runnable notebook/script and every claim verified with a benchmark on a two-node DGX Spark cluster. The goal is a mental model precise enough to look at a latency profile and know which layer the problem is in before opening a profiler.

Code and notebooks will be shared at https://lnkd.in/gVqhCAPc.              

 #LLMInference #InferenceEngineering #DGXSpark #vLLM #KVCache

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
⚖️ Training Better LLM Judges with 40x Less Data

Most generative judge models need 600-900k training samples. RISE-Judge matches SOTA on RewardBench with just 40k, using a two-stage SFT + DPO pipeline on Qwen2.5-32B.

→ The core idea is decomposing judge training into style adaptation (SFT) and preference accuracy (DPO). SFT teaches step-by-step CoT reasoning patterns, while DPO sharpens judgment on the hard cases where GPT-4o fails.

→ Position and length bias are handled at the data level: answers are swapped and re-evaluated, and only consistent judgments survive into the SFT set. Inconsistent ones become DPO hard negatives.

→ RISE-Judge-32B hits 92.7 on RewardBench, tying SFR-Judge-70B while using 17x less data (40k vs 680k) and being half the size. The 7B variant scores 88.2, beating CompassJudger-32B.

→ Training on judge data doesn't hurt general abilities. The model matches Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on MMLU, BBH, and MT-Bench, suggesting that critical evaluation tasks implicitly teach response quality.

→ When used to annotate DPO pairs for a policy model, RISE-Judge outperforms GPT-4o annotations on AlignBench.

It's a nice, straightforward paper that also releases training data (SFT and DPO). Note that this approach only handles pairwise comparisons (no absolute/pointwise scoring). It would also have been interesting to have benchmarks beyond RewardBench.

LLMs could write like Shakespeare but had never seen a sunset. ViTs could recognize an image of a cat, but couldn't tell you why it's cute.

👉 Qwen-VL: "Here's the image. Now talk to me about it." (generative, conversational)

The architecture is deceptively simple: Eyes (frozen ViT) + Brain (frozen LLM) + Translator (a tiny MLP). The LLM doesn't even know it's seeing an image; it just thinks it's reading a very strange language.

And now? You can show a model the inside of your fridge and get recipes. Show error screenshots and get a fix. Show it a dashboard and get a trend summary. 

High-res tiling means it reads text in screenshots too, so OCR comes for free. Video processing is also straightforward, since it's just more frames and so extra tokens to process. Vision models don't just see anymore. They speak.

content:
🌱 Rethinking GPU Computing as a Software Engineer

Most of us still associate GPUs with deep learning.

That’s true—but increasingly incomplete.

I recently reviewed “GPU-accelerated computing with Python 3 and CUDA”, and what stood out wasn’t just the tooling—it was how it reshapes the way we think about systems. Thanks to the PACKT team Loganathan K,Sujata Tripathi,Srishti Seth, Vinishka Kalra for inviting me to participate, and contribute.

The book spans quite a spectrum:
⇒ CUDA fundamentals and debugging
⇒ Multi-GPU execution
⇒ NumPy → CuPy
⇒ RAPIDS (cuDF, cuML)
⇒ JAX for optimisation
Even LLM workloads

What emerges is a continuum—from low-level kernels to full data and AI pipelines.

== A subtle but important shift =

At first glance, tools like cuDF and cuML feel familiar:
⇒ pandas → cuDF
⇒ scikit-learn → cuML

But underneath, everything changes.

⇒ Data lives on the device.
⇒ Execution is massively parallel.
⇒ And performance becomes sensitive to data movement.

== Some practical nuance ==

GPUs don’t automatically make everything faster, this book took an empirical approach around this.
⇒ Small datasets → CPU is often sufficient
⇒ Simple inference → GPU may not be necessary
⇒ Data transfer → can dominate runtime

There’s usually a scale threshold before GPU benefits become meaningful.

== What stayed with me ==

This isn’t just about acceleration—it’s about system design.

You start asking:
⇒ Where does data live?
⇒ How often does it move?
⇒ Can this pipeline stay on the GPU end-to-end?

== Closing Thoughts == 
We’ve seen shifts before—cloud, distributed systems, microservices.

This feels similar.

A move towards heterogeneous computing, where understanding hardware is once again part of good software engineering.

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
Have you ever wondered why deep learning kernels like contiguous tensors?

📖 What does it mean for a tensor to be contiguous?

A tensor is contiguous when its elements are stored in memory in the same order you'd visit them iterating through the logical dimensions. In PyTorch, this means the elements are laid out in row-major order with no gaps or jumps. The rightmost dimension varies fastest, and each row immediately follows the previous one.

The plots below show how a transposed tensor isn't contiguous.

💲 Cost of .contiguous()

The .contiguous() operation is ubiquitous across deep learning models, with its most common use case being in the attention layer. When applied to a non-contiguous tensor, it triggers a full copy. If you do something like 
A = A.contiguous() where A is non-contiguous, the operation:

1. Allocates new memory equal to the size of A.
2. Reads the contents of A from HBM (the highest-latency memory tier on a GPU).
3. Writes the contiguous version of A back to HBM.

For a 4096×4096 FP16 matrix, that's a 32MB round-trip through HBM, which is notoriously slow.

🤝🏽 Memory Coalescing
Despite the extra I/O, calling .contiguous() is often worth the cost because of how DRAM is physically accessed.

When we read a specific location in DRAM, the hardware doesn't just fetch that one value it returns the values of locations in a neighborhood referred to as the “cache line” (128 bytes on modern NVIDIA GPUs). CUDA devices can detect when all 32 threads in a warp are requesting data from the same cache line and "coalesce" those requests into a single memory transaction.

When a tensor isn't contiguous, each thread may be hitting a different cache line, turning what could be 1 memory transaction into as many as 32!

🎁 Wrap Up
Contiguous tensors ensure that sequential access patterns across threads can leverage memory coalescing, making the upfront copy cost well worth it.

author: James Noh
subtitle: Partner @a16z | AI Infra & Cloud GTM | Stanford 🌲
content:
10 based lessons learned from Baseten's inference book by Philip Kiely: 

1️⃣ Start with shared inference, and move to dedicated later. Pay-per-token APIs while finding PMF. Switch to dedicated GPUs only when 3 factors align: scale (volume makes per-GPU cheaper), specialization (custom models or tight latency needs), and orchestration (multi-model pipelines). 

2️⃣ Inference optimization is about constraints, not maximization. The best inference systems are specific, not general. They're tuned for a particular model, product, and traffic pattern. More constraints = higher performance.

3️⃣ KV cache is arguably the most important resource in LLM inference. Without it, attention is quadratic and inference would be unbearably slow. Managing where it lives, how much to allocate, and when to reuse it across requests is critical.

4️⃣ Tensor Parallelism (TP) is default multi-GPU strategy; Expert Parallelism (EP) improves throughput for MoE. TP splits tensor ops across GPUs for lower per-user latency but needs high-bandwidth NVLink. EP assigns experts to specific GPUs, reducing networking overhead and scaling better across nodes. Many deployments combine both.

5️⃣ Memory bandwidth, not compute, bottlenecks most LLM serving. Decode is memory-bound because model weights load for every generated token. Any optimization that reduces memory movement––quantization, kernel fusion, and PagedAttention––directly improves TPS.

6️⃣ Inference engines as tools for abstraction. vLLM (broadest support), SGLang (strong MoE & customization), and TensorRT-LLM (highest performance but steepest learning curve) all feature continuous batching, quantization, speculative decoding, prefix caching, parallelism, and disaggregation. Choose one based on your model, hardware & engineering bandwidth.

7️⃣ Measure latency in percentiles, not averages. This is because LLM latency is right-skewed. P99 (5x longer than the median) will ruin the user experience even when the avg looks fine. Track P50, P90, and P99 for both TTFT & TPS.

8️⃣ Long cold start times → inaccurate scale-down → compute over-provisioning. Cold starts pile up across GPU procurement, container loading, weight loading, and engine compilation. Quantizing weights, caching compiled engines, and loading from low-latency local storage all chip away at this.

9️⃣ Image gen models are composable. Every image system is a pipeline of a text encoder, denoising model, and VAE––each individually optimizable. Unlike LLMs, image inference is compute-bound and the quality-speed tradeoff is direct: fewer denoising steps = faster but worse output.

🔟 Client code is the often-overlooked last mile. TLS handshakes, session management, and protocol choice eat into latency budget. Reuse HTTP sessions, use WebSockets for real-time audio, and gRPC for structured service-to-service calls. For bulk workloads, async jobs with webhook callbacks unlock throughput sync requests can't match.

🔗 Link to Phil's full free book in comments ⬇️

author: Emilio Andere
subtitle: Co-Founder and CEO at Wafer - Hardware Acceleration for AI
content:
you might assume sampling is free in LLM inference, but at small batch sizes sampling eats 10-38% of decode time. 3 kernel launches to pick 1 token from 150k options. FlashSampling is a novel approach inspired by FlashAttention which fuses all of it into the matmul. here's how it works: 


the last layer of an LLM is a matrix multiply. the hidden state (4096 elements) times a vocabulary weight matrix (4096 x 150,000). the output is 150,000 logits, one score per possible next token. 

the standard pipeline writes all 150,000 to HBM, launches a softmax kernel that reads them back and writes 150,000 probabilities, then launches a sampling kernel that reads those probabilities and picks one token. three kernels and two full HBM round-trips to select a SINGLE integer.

at small batch sizes, this can cost 10-38% of decode time. you might think it's about bandwidth, but 600 KB of logits is nothing for a B300. the real cost is the kernel launches and synchronization barriers. three separate kernels means the GPU stalls twice waiting for one operation to finish before starting the next.

so why does sampling need softmax? softmax converts logits into probabilities that sum to 1. you sample by walking a cumulative distribution. the problem is that softmax requires ALL logits to find the max (numerical stability) and compute the global sum. you can't start sampling until every logit is known. that's why the full tensor gets written to HBM. the matmul produces logits tile by tile on SRAM, but softmax needs the global picture.

the Gumbel-Max trick removes this dependency entirely. add independent Gumbel(0,1) noise to each raw logit. take the argmax. the winning index is sampled with probability exp(logit_i) / sum exp(logit_j). exactly softmax w/ no normalization needed.

why does this help at all? because argmax decomposes. the global maximum equals the maximum of tile-local maxima. so the matmul can stay tile by tile on SRAM. for each tile, add noise, keep only the single best candidate (one index, one score), discard the rest. the 150,000-element tensor never leaves fast memory. only a handful of tile-local winners get written to HBM, and a tiny kernel picks the global winner.

FlashSampling implements this as a two-stage fused kernel. stage 1 runs the matmul and Gumbel perturbation together in the GEMM epilogue. stage 2 reduces tile candidates to one token. 

on B300: 1.84x over multinomial sampling, 2.52x over FlashInfer's top-k/top-p. end-to-end in vLLM on B200: 19% reduction in time per output token on Qwen3-1.7B.

this is the FlashAttention playbook applied to sampling. find a mathematical identity that makes a global operation decomposable into local tiles. for attention, it was online softmax. for sampling, it's Gumbel-Max. in both cases, a large intermediate tensor that seemed necessary turns out to be eliminable. if you can reduce data while it's still on SRAM, don't write it to HBM just to read it back.

link to paper in the comments.

author: Farhan A.
subtitle: Computer Engineer | LLMs | GPU Programming | Optimization | ML | AWS
content:
Many of us think that optimizing LLM inference is about better model architecture or better prompts. Whereas, in reality, a huge part of LLM performance is decided at the kernel level of the GPU hardware where every read/write on the SRAM needs to be optimized.

Every time you prompt an LLM like GPT-4 or Llama 3, thousands of matrix multiplication kernels fire off in milliseconds.

While writing my own matrix multiplication kernel in Triton, I ran into a lesson.

Instead of the naive approach in which we take one row from matrix A and one column from matrix B, I used tiling. Each program instance operates on a small tile (or chunk) of the matrices, defined by a block size and group size. This layout strategy, called as the group-wise ordering, really improves cache reuse and minimize the memory access.

So for this kernel, all the test cases passed but when I benchmarked it against the PyTorch's matmul (powered by NVIDIA cuBLAS) on a T4 GPU, I noticed that my kernel was achieving ~2 TFLOPs, while PyTorch's kernel was reaching 50–60 TFLOPs. Upon researching, I came to learn that the same Triton kernel does not execute the same way on every GPU.

I was running the kernel on a T4 GPU (via Colab). Turing Architecture T4 doesn't always automatically leverage its Tensor Cores for Triton's "tl.dot" function. If tile sizes aren’t tuned for Turing, the exceeds the register's capacity and Triton falls back to scalar FMA (slower execution) instead of (the faster) Tensor Core HMMA  high throughput instructions. 

That difference of execution path alone explains the massive performance gap.

This experience reinforced a core lesson for me: when you’re this close to the hardware, software abstractions alone are not enough but having an understanding of the data flow in the actual hardware memory is critical especially while working with the modern LLM inference engines.

author: Rahul Kumar
subtitle: Lead, Applied AI & Machine Learning | Ex PayPal | IITH
content:
Deciphering Phases of LLM Inference That Decide Performance

Under the hood, LLM inference is actually two completely different workloads fighting for the same GPU. If you want to make your AI application faster and cheaper, you have to understand the difference between the Prefill phase and the Decode phase.

1️⃣ The Prefill Phase (Processing the prompt)
What it does: Processes the entire input prompt via massive matrix math to build the KV Cache context map.
The Bottleneck: Compute (GPU FLOPs).
The Symptom: High Time To First Token (TTFT)—users stare at a loading screen.
The Optimizations:
✱  FlashAttention: Rewrites the attention algorithm to keep matrix math in the GPU’s ultra-fast SRAM, bypassing slow memory reads.
✱  Prompt Caching: Caches the KV Cache for repeated system prompts or RAG docs, dropping TTFT to near zero by skipping the compute entirely.

2️⃣ The Decode Phase (Generating text)
What it does: Generates the output autoregressively (token by token).
The Bottleneck: Memory Bandwidth. The GPU does minimal math but must fetch massive model weights and the growing KV Cache for every single token.
The Symptom: High Time Between Tokens (TBT)—the text generation stutters and lags.

The Optimizations:
✱  PagedAttention (vLLM): Manages KV Cache memory in non-contiguous "pages" (like an OS). This eliminates VRAM fragmentation, allowing massive increases in concurrent batch sizes.
✱  Speculative Decoding: Uses a tiny, fast "draft" model to guess the next 5 tokens, which the large model then verifies in one parallel step. It turns a memory-bound problem into a compute-bound one.
✱  KV Quantization : Compresses the context data (e.g., 16-bit to 8-bit) so the GPU can pull it through the memory bus twice as fast.

💡 The Insight:
You can’t just "buy a faster GPU" without knowing what is actually broken.
Slow to start answering? Optimize Compute (Prefill).
Slow to type out the answer? Optimize Memory (Decode).

author: Prashanth Velidandi
subtitle: AI Infra Researcher | Co-founder at @InferX, a Multi-Tenant Serverless Platform for Scalable Inference.- github.com/inferx-net/inferx
content:
A customer came to us recently after trying to benchmark Qwen3.5 on a B200 GPU on a different platform. 

Expected throughput was around 130 tokens per second.

Instead they were seeing about 16 tokens per second.

Nothing was wrong with the GPU.
Nothing was wrong with the model.

The issue was the environment.

The optimized CUDA kernels required for fast attention did not compile inside the container. When that happens, most inference stacks silently fall back to the PyTorch implementation.

Performance drops dramatically.

From the outside it looks like a model performance problem. In reality it is an infrastructure problem.

Modern LLM inference depends on a deep stack of CUDA kernels and optimized libraries. When those builds fail or time out, the system still runs but often at a fraction of expected performance.

A surprising amount of friction in AI deployment today is not the model itself.

It is the runtime environment underneath it.

author: Joydeep Bhattacharjee
subtitle: Lead ML Engineer @ Adobe | GenAI & Inference Optimization | Author of 2 ML Books
content:
Running an AI model involves much more than just writing high level PyTorch or JAX code. These libraries sit on top of a huge ecosystem of software stacks and each layer can impact the performance in both good and bad ways. 

First comes the hardware at the base. We have the physical GPU (A100, H100, RTX, etc.), with Linux distros (Ubuntu, RHEL, SUSE) or Windows sitting on top of it.

Above it sits the Linux GPU driver. Here the software talks to hardware. Ig includes components like the CUDA driver, NVLINK (for GPU-to-GPU communication), and NVML (monitoring). Video & Graphics covers rendering APIs (OpenGL, Optix) and video codecs. Deployment & Management includes DCGM (datacenter GPU manager) and orchestration tools like Kubernetes and Docker.

Above this is the CUDA Toolkit which is the heart. This is the parallel computing platform that enables the programmability of GPUs. It contains the CUDA compiler (nvcc), math libraries (cuBLAS, cuFFT), image processing, DevTools for profiling/debugging, and the CUDA runtime that manages GPU memory and kernel launches. Almost all GPU-accelerated software is built on this. Magnum IO sits alongside it for high-speed multi-GPU data movement (NCCL for collective ops, GPUDirect for direct NIC-to-GPU transfers).

On top of this we have the kernel libraries such as cuDNN, cutlass, OpenAI triton etc. The deep learning libraries such pytorch call these kernels to execute the actual computations. Then there are powerful inference libraries such as Triton Inference Server, vLLM, and SGLang that serve LLMs at scale.

author: Paul VanKoughnett, PhD
subtitle: Research Scientist at Colfax International
content:
Big day for us at Colfax International, with 3 new blog posts coming out on advances in GPU kernel design:

1. Jay Shah (joint with others including Vijay Thakkar and Tri Dao) has released FlashAttention-4, the most performant implementation of attention for Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. The authors show how to integrate Blackwell's new hardware features, notably its fully asynchronous MMA instruction with a dedicated memory region (Tensor Memory) and possibility for pair-CTA collaboration, into attention. Compared with Hopper, these features motivate a significant redesign of the algorithms, including polynomial approximation of the exponential function to avoid bottlenecking on softmax, use of Tensor Memory as an auxiliary shared memory during the backward pass, and longest-processing-time-first scheduling for better load balance during causal and variable-length attention.

And, for you script kiddies out there, this is in Python now, using CUTLASS's CuTeDSL framework to produce performant architecture-targeted GPU code via JIT compilation.

Blog post with paper link: https://lnkd.in/g9CgXg7Q
Code: https://lnkd.in/gE5HCa_S

2. Yuqing Lin, Ryo Asai, and myself have posted the final part of our series on Blackwell GEMM kernels, showing how to do GEMM using Blackwell's low-precision blockscaled data formats. These kernels involve some subtlety in terms of data layouts and memory movement that we elucidate here using CuTe layouts. We dig into the PTX backend so you don't have to, uncovering the new Tensor Memory access patterns required to write these kernels. Again, all in Python with CuTeDSL.

Blog post: https://lnkd.in/gANAQgdG

3. Over at the PyTorch blog, Reuben Stern, Jay, Tri, and others present their redesign of FlexAttention for FlashAttention-4 and CuTeDSL. FlexAttention is a set of hooks for attaching an attention backend to some caller-defined modifications, specifically a modification to the score function and a block-sparse mask.
