author: Pawan Kumar Raj
subtitle: AI Engineer | LLMs, RAG, Multi-Modal AI Agents | Python| Gemini, LlamaIndex, LangChain | Conversational AI & AI Agents
content:
How we optimized NVIDIA H100 GPU usage for LLM workloads

One of the biggest problems while deploying LLM inference systems is not model performance…
It's GPU utilization.

Even with powerful GPUs like NVIDIA H100, many teams end up using only 30–40% of the GPU capacity.

While building an LLM serving system with Ollama, we explored two different GPU sharing strategies:
• MIG (Multi-Instance GPU)
• Time Slicing

And the results were interesting.

Option 1 — MIG (Multi-Instance GPU)
MIG allows the GPU to be physically partitioned into smaller GPUs.
Each partition gets:
• Dedicated memory
 • Dedicated compute cores
 • Dedicated cache

This is great for multi-tenant environments where strict isolation is required.
But there is a catch.
Once the GPU is partitioned:
 • Memory becomes statically allocated
 • Idle partitions cannot share resources
 • Large LLM requests may run out of memory

For dynamic inference workloads, this can become inefficient.

Option 2 — Time Slicing
Instead of splitting the GPU physically, Time Slicing allows multiple processes to share the GPU over time.
Each workload gets a small time window to execute, and the GPU scheduler rotates between them.
Advantages:
• Full GPU memory available
• Better utilization for burst traffic
• Flexible resource allocation
• Works well for LLM serving workloads

This made a big difference when multiple users were sending requests simultaneously.

Adding an Nginx Layer for Load Handling
To scale the inference system, we placed Nginx in front of the Ollama server.
Architecture looked like this:
Client Requests
 ⬇
 Nginx Load Balancer
 ⬇
 Multiple Ollama Workers
 ⬇
 Shared NVIDIA H100 GPU

Nginx helped us:
• Queue incoming requests
• Distribute load across workers
• Prevent server overload
• Improve overall throughput

Where KV Cache Becomes Important
In transformer models, KV Cache memory stores attention states for previously generated tokens.
This avoids recomputing the entire sequence every time a new token is generated.

But here's the challenge:
KV Cache consumes a large portion of GPU memory.
With MIG, memory is already partitioned, so each instance gets a limited KV cache space.

With Time Slicing, the GPU memory pool stays flexible, allowing:
 • Larger KV cache usage
 • Higher token throughput
 • More efficient LLM serving

Final Insight
For LLM inference workloads:
🔹 MIG → Better isolation
🔹 Time Slicing → Better utilization

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
The world of Kernel Engineering is rife with acronyms so I’m going to create a few posts covering 10 acronyms each. How many of these do you know?

CUDA → Compute Unified Device Architecture

ROCm → Radeon Open Compute Platform (AMD’s equivalent of CUDA)

PTX → Parallel Thread Execution all CUDA programs are compiled to PTX which is the equivalent of assembly level language for NVIDIA GPUs. Further higher level DSL’s like Triton compile down to PTX too. Crucially the same 
PTX code can run on any NVIDIA family of GPUs i.e. there’s always forward compatibility.

SASS → Streaming/Shader Assembler is the low-level assembly language that compiles to binary microcode, which executes natively on NVIDIA GPU hardware.

NVCC → Nvidia Cuda Compiler a toolchain from NVIDIA for compiling CUDA C/C++ as well as PTX code.

NCCL → The NVIDIA Collective Communications Library is a library providing inter-GPU communication primitives.

SM → Streaming Multiprocessor, the fundamental compute unit of an NVIDIA GPU. An SM executes programs in groups of 32 threads called warps. All the threads in the warp execute the same instruction but on different pieces of data.

CC → Compute Capability, a version number of NVIDIA GPUs. Each version of GPUs have new hardware and software features. For e.g. the Hopper with a CC of 9.x introduced Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA)

GeMM → General Matrix Multiply, gemm actually also includes a translation and scaling factor. GeMM operations compute α·(A × B) + β·C. Where A,B,C are all matrices

FMA → Fused Multiply and Add computes a X b + c where a, b and c are all scalars. A GeMM is composed of a series of FMAs.

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
Pt 2 of acronyms that aspiring kernel engineers should know:

𝗰𝘂𝗕𝗟𝗔𝗦 → CUDA Basic Linear Algebra Subroutine library, containing efficient implementations of operations like dot product, gemm (matmul), imax (index of max) etc. cuBLAS is closed source and its implementation details are a black box.

𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀 → CUDA Templates for Linear Algebra Subroutines. An open source CUDA C++ library containing templates and abstractions that map onto their hardware for implementing custom CUDA kernels and GEMMs. 

𝗦𝗜𝗠𝗧 → Single Instruction Multiple Threads. The core working principle of GPUs, they have multiple threads running the same instruction at the same time on different pieces of data, parallelizing work.

𝗗𝗥𝗔𝗠 → Dynamic Random Access Memory, corresponds to the main/largest memory component of a GPU. 

𝗛𝗕𝗠 → High Bandwidth Memory also refers to the same thing as DRAM.

𝗦𝗥𝗔𝗠 → Static Random Access Memory, SRAM makes up registers, shared memory l1/l2 caches, the way it stores bits is different to DRAM.

𝗣𝗖𝗜𝗲 → Peripheral Component Interconnect Express is a high-speed serial computer expansion bus standard that’s used for connecting the GPU and CPU.

𝗖𝗧𝗔 → Co-operative Thread Array. This includes the groups of threads that are scheduled to run on a single SM. All the threads in a CTA have access to the same Shared Memory but each thread gets its own private registers. CTAs are divided into multiple warps, all the threads in the same warp execute at the same time i.e. in lock-step while the threads in other warps wait.

𝗠𝗠𝗔 → Matrix Multiply and Accumulate. Computes C += A @ B

𝗪𝗚𝗠𝗠𝗔 → Warp Group MMA. A warp group is composed of 4 warps. Supported from the Hopper family of GPUs, this allows us to perform matrix multiplications in an async manner and with work divided between 128 threads.

𝗧𝗠𝗔 → Tensor Memory Accelerator a new hardware unit introduced in Hopper that helps moving data between Global Memory and Shared Memory in an async manner. It doesn’t use any of the cuda cores or warps associated with a SM freeing them up to do other work.

Are there other's that I missed?

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
One of the challenges of the MoE architecture is dealing with variable length tensors i.e. ragged/jagged tensors. Let’s learn how Grouped GeMMs tackle it.

❓ What’s the problem
The MoE layer of a model has N experts, the router of an MoE layer takes a token and decides the top-k experts that a token is routed to.

Now suppose you have a batch of tokens of size B. Each of the B tokens can be routed to any of the N experts. This is problematic because it means that for a given expert the number of tokens that it needs to process can be anywhere between 0 to B.

🧐 Example

Say we have 3 experts, our batch size is 4 and each token is routed to the top-1 expert

Token 1 → Routed to expert 1
Token 2 → Routed to expert 1
Token 3 → Routed to expert 2
Token 4 → Routed to expert 1

In this scenario the weights of expert 1 need to be multiplied with a token matrix of shape [3, H] where H is the token embedding dim.

Expert 2 → [1, H] and Expert 3 → No tokens.
So we have matrix multiplications of various lengths/sizes.

❓ Why is this a problem?

If all experts were guaranteed to have the same number of tokens routed to them, all the matrix multiplications for all the experts could be grouped into one large batched GeMM kernel (general matrix mul operation).

However, with the variable routing lengths a naive solution would need to loop through each of the experts and perform one GeMM per expert sequentially despite the fact that the computation of each expert is independent of other experts.

Another issue is that the sizes of the matrices involved in the GeMMs are quite small so the actual gpu compute time for the GeMM itself is tiny and can be comparable to the amount of time it takes to launch the GeMM kernel.

💡Grouped GeMMs
This is where Grouped GeMM kernels come into the picture. A Grouped GeMM involves just one kernel launch and ensures that multiple GeMMs run in parallel.

🔑 Key takeaway
Grouped GeMMs increase the speed of MoE models by avoiding multiple GeMM kernel launches and parallelizing the GeMMs across experts. So if you ever find yourself dealing with ragged tensors make sure to use Grouped GeMMs.

For more read: https://lnkd.in/dq4KrpDn

Padding is one of those things in transformer inference that often goes unnoticed, but it can have a real impact on performance.

When embedding requests are batched together, sequences rarely have the same length. Standard batching pads everything to match the longest sequence, which means the GPU ends up processing many tokens that contain no real data.

Because transformer layers are token-parallel, those padded tokens still go through the full stack of projections and MLP layers.

Variable-length execution (varlen) addresses this by packing only real tokens together and tracking sequence boundaries, so the model processes actual tokens instead of padding.

Triggering a single Tensor Core instruction on a 16x8x16 micro-tile is great, but to compute large matrices, we need to tile the work.
In my latest visual CuTe tutorial, "The Global GEMM," I break down the structure behind every high-performance GPU GEMM.

The architecture runs like a factory shift:
Phase 1 (Loading Dock): TiledCopy moves data from Global Memory to Swizzled Shared Memory via async copies.
Phase 2 (Stamping Press): TiledMMA processes the data from Shared Memory into Registers and executes the MMA.
Phase 3 (Shipping): The accumulator writes the results back to Global Memory in the epilogue.

author: Lorenzo Bradanini
subtitle: Software Engineering & Systems Design Read by 15k+ engineers. I write about the deep structure of software: data engineering, computation, and the physical limits that shape technology. Author of The Software Frontier.
content:
Most CUDA engineers I know optimize the wrong layer.

They tune PTX, unroll loops, carefully balance register pressure. All legitimate work. But none of it is the first bottleneck.

Before a single warp executes, your kernel crosses a user-to-kernel privilege boundary, gets serialized into a command packet inside nvidia.ko, traverses the PCIe fabric via an MMIO doorbell write, and lands in the GigaThread Engine's pushbuffer. 

Only then does the hardware scheduler decide whether your blocks can even reside on an SM given current register and shared memory pressure.

The atomic unit of GPU performance is not the thread, the warp, or the kernel. It is the submission.

Part III of the series is out. 

This one covers the full execution path end to end: fat binaries and JIT compilation, pageable vs. page-locked memory, DMA copy engine orchestration, block residency constraints, and Unified Memory page migration semantics. 

Code and commands throughout, everything fact-checked against NVIDIA architecture documentation.

If you work with CUDA at any level of the stack, from ML infrastructure to HPC to GPU kernel development, this is the layer most people never reason about explicitly.

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
We see the term "cudagraphs" everywhere in LLM training and inference, but do you know what they are?

📖 Context
Deep Learning models are a series of kernels/functions that run on gpus. A forward pass through an entire model often involves calling the same kernels multiple times. For e.g. the attention kernel is called L times per forward pass where L is the number of layers.

However, kernels are usually launched (tell the GPU to run said function) by the CPU. Launching the kernels involves a bunch of overheads like validating arguments, the launch command moving from cpu to gpu, gpu scheduling the kernel etc.

All of these overheads add up and can amount to a significant fraction of the total run-time of the kernel itself.

If you zoom out and consider how many times each kernel is called in a training or inference environment, the overhead becomes quite substantive.

💡Cudagraphs
Cudagraphs eliminate the repeated kernel launch overheads by replacing it with a one time graph capture + launch overhead.

They do this by capturing all the kernel calls that your model makes and creating a graph, with edges between nodes that depend on each other. It can also nodes that have no deps and can run in parallel

Once the graph is captured it can be “replayed” multiple times. Which means that all kernels will be invoked with the same set of arguments that had been seen during the graph capture.

Since input tensors are passed as pointers to kernels, all we need to ensure is that the data that the pointer is associated with is updated when a kernel is invoked.

🎁 Wrap Up
The main limitation of cudagraphs, is that you shouldn’t have any dynamic arguments or dynamic control flows since only the shapes and flow-paths seen during graph capture will be supported by the replayed graphs.

In general enabling cudagraphs is always a good practice and is one of those easy wins for boosting run-time.

For more read: https://lnkd.in/dX2r-vpn

author: Emilio Andere
subtitle: Co-Founder and CEO at Wafer - Hardware Acceleration for AI
content:
LLM inference has become an OS problem. there's working sets, paging, fragmentation, eviction, swap, memory tiers, all happening inside GPU memory. here's how we got here:


the KV cache has become the central managed resource. every request claims memory and holds it until completion, exactly like a process claiming pages in RAM. for llama 3-70B at 128K context, one user's KV cache is 40 GB. 8 concurrent users = 320 GB, literally more than the model weights. 

before vLLM, systems pre-allocated contiguous memory for each request's max sequence length, which led to ~60-80% of KV cache memory being wasted. 

PagedAttention fixed this by borrowing straight from 1960s OS virtual memory: split the kv cache into fixed-size blocks, map them through a block table, allocate on demand. "think of blocks as pages, tokens as bytes, and requests as processes." waste dropped to under 4%, and throughput jumped 2-4x! 

but paging was just the start in the OS makeover of inference serving. when HBM fills up, something has to go, and the field reinvented OS page replacement. StreamingLLM found that first tokens absorb disproportionate attention regardless of content. evict them and inference crashes. these are pinned pages -- always resident and never evictable.

then came swap. HBM (3.35-8 TB/s) → CPU DRAM (~100 GB/s) → NVMe (~7 GB/s). 50x bandwidth drop per tier. vLLM swaps preempted requests' kv blocks to CPU DRAM.

sharing eventually showed up too. SGLang stores kv in a radix tree. requests sharing system prompts point to the same physical blocks. when one diverges, copy-on-write kicks in. this is basically fork() for inference.

scheduling maps just as cleanly. prefill is compute-bound, saturating tensor cores. decode is memory-bound, so it loads the entire kv cache for one token. continuous batching = time-sharing.

and now it's gone distributed. Mooncake pools kv cache across entire GPU clusters via RDMA at petabyte-scale. kv cache becomes network-attached memory. NVIDIA Dynamo routes requests to where kv data already lives, scheduling meets memory locality.

40 years of OS memory management:

paging → eviction → swap → distributed shared memory

recreated in 3 years inside HBM.

what OS concept will inference systems reinvent next?

author: Devansh Devansh
subtitle: Chocolate Milk Cult Leader| Machine Learning Engineer| Writer | AI Researcher| | Computational Math, Data Science, Software Engineering, Computer Science
content:
The attention mechanism in a standard Transformer is incredibly good at what it does: fetching highly specific information from anywhere in the prompt. The problem isn’t the attention operation itself; the problem is the storage bill it racks up.

The compute required for a standard Transformer layer (dense attention plus dense MLP) roughly scales as: 24nd² + 4n²d. At deep networks and very long contexts, this can ruin your finances. 

There are several ways to address this issue. One of the most interesting is  DeepSeek-V2’s Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). Instead of storing massive Key and Value tensors for every token, what if we just store a highly compressed “summary” vector?

In standard attention, you cache the Keys and Values. In MLA, you project the token’s information down into a much smaller latent vector. During the decode phase, the GPU only appends this tiny vector to the cache. When it needs to calculate attention, it rapidly “up-projects” or reconstructs the Keys and Values on the fly.

By replacing the large 2 * g * d_k term with a much smaller compressed dimension d_c, DeepSeek reported a staggering 93.3% reduction in KV cache size — “Compared with DeepSeek 67B, DeepSeek-V2 achieves significantly stronger performance, and meanwhile saves 42.5% of training costs, reduces the KV cache by 93.3%, and boosts the maximum generation throughput to 5.76 times.”

Unfortunately, this is not a free lunch. You are trading memory for compute. Reconstructing the keys and values requires an extra matrix multiplication. Furthermore, low-rank compression breaks traditional position embeddings like RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding). Applying RoPE to compressed keys increases their mathematical variance, degrading accuracy unless you implement careful “decoupled” RoPE strategies.

There are several other strategies to address the costs of Self Attention, which we will discuss soon.

author: Vinayak Gautam
subtitle: SDE II @ Walmart Global Tech | IIT Bombay
content:
Log 4: Learning GPU programming by building things

I wrote 5 CUDA kernels. 2 of them were slower than doing nothing.

Here's what learning GPU programming actually looks like:
I spent a week optimizing memory access patterns for 2D convolution. Shared memory tiling. Cached halos through L2. Textbook stuff.
One of them gave me 0.87x. That's right — slower than the naive version.
Then I stopped trying to be clever and just changed the math.
O(k²) → O(k). 59ms → 5ms. 11x faster.
3 things I learned the hard way:
→ The "laziest" optimization (3 lines of constant memory) was the most reliable
→ Two textbook optimizations hurt performance on modern hardware
→ At small input sizes, every optimization was slower. Same code, same GPU, opposite conclusion
Doing less work will always beat doing the same work faster.

content:
In-depth write-up on the RAG architecture in prod at Notion and how they scaled infra by 10x & reduced costs by 90% over 2 years. Some salient lessons👇:

1. keeping fresh time based indices using tenant IDs

"when a set of indexes approached capacity, we'd provision a new set and direct all new workspace onboarding there. Each set got a "generation" ID that determined where reads and writes would go. This kept us moving without stopping to do any re-shard operations."

2. using turbopuffer vector indices based on s3 object based storage 

"on top of object storage for performance and cost-efficiency. 60 percent cost reduction on search engine spend. 35 percent reduction in AWS EMR compute costs. p50 production query latency improved from 70-100ms to 50-70ms"

3. maintaining and keeping the index fresh efficiently 

"we chunk the page, get the previous state of the page from DynamoDB, and compare all the text hashes. We detect exactly which spans changed, and only re-embed and re-load those spans into our vector database."

4. maintaining text and metadata hashes

"We detect that all the text hashes are the same, but all the metadata hashes are different. This means we can skip embedding altogether, and just issue a PATCH command to our vector database to update the metadata, a much cheaper operation."

"70% reduction in data volume which saved money on both embeddings API costs and on vector DB write costs."

5. on the advantages of using open source embedding models + using embedding models for both batch and live query processing with Ray vs Spark

"Model flexibility: Ray lets us run open-source embedding models directly, without being gated by external providers. As new models are released, we can experiment and adopt them immediately"

"Unified compute: By consolidating preprocessing and inference onto a single compute layer, we eliminated the double-compute problem"

"GPU/CPU pipelining: Ray natively supports pipelining GPU-bound inference with CPU-bound preprocessing on the same machines, keeping utilization high"

"Developer productivity: Anyscale's integrated workspaces let our engineers write and test data pipelines from their favorite tools (Cursor, VSCode, etc.) without provisioning infrastructure"

"Lower query-time latency: Self-hosting embeddings removed a third-party API hop from the critical path, which materially reduced end-to-end latency for user-facing searches."

author: Florian Elio Mattana
subtitle: GPU Performance Engineer | CUDA
content:
I wrote a CUDA kernel that ran in 2.6 ms on a 4096×4096 matrix. cuBLAS took 9.7 ms. So I'd beaten the library?
No. My kernel was wrong.

Currently I'm preparing an article about GEMM. 
So to get all the element to share with you I am implementing GEMM kernels from scratch like naive, tiled, register tiling etc .... but that suspiciously fast tiled version wasn't loading the full shared memory tile.

With a 16×16 thread block and a 64×8 tile, only half the elements were loaded.

The rest stayed at zero.
The kernel did less work, so it ran faster and produced garbage.🥬

My best register-tiled kernel? 21 ms. Slower, but correct. I didnt optimize yet anyways and the story is not there.

The point is the only reason I caught this bug. CPU reference validation. 
A triple-loop GEMM on CPU, compared element by element against every GPU kernel output.

It takes a bit of time to write but it takes hours to debug without it.
Rule to always follow: no kernel gets benchmarked until it passes validation.

A fast wrong answer is worse than a slow right one.
You'll build every next optimisation on top of a lie.

If you're writing CUDA kernels and you don't have a CPU reference check, add one today. 
For instance when I worked at Airbus I spent more time checking the correctness of the result compare to the CPU than only focusing on the perf itself. Because the quality of the data you are producing is always top priority.

It's maybe the most boring code you'll write, and the most valuable.

author: Emilio Andere
subtitle: Co-Founder and CEO at Wafer - Hardware Acceleration for AI
content:
Together AI, Jump Trading, and Cursor are all running megakernels in production. instead of ~100 kernel launches per forward pass, they launch one. here's how megakernels actually work:


a standard Llama forward pass launches ~100 separate kernels per iteration. RMSNorm, QKV projection, RoPE, attention, SwiGLU, output projection, repeat per layer. each kernel reads weights from HBM, computes, and then writes results back. the CPU launches the next one, and you repeat this 100 times.

the cost isn't kernel launch overhead (5-10μs per launch does add up but is not the main bottleneck). the real cost is memory pipeline bubbles. every time a kernel finishes, the SM's memory pipeline drains completely before the next kernel can start loading data. 

Hazy Research measured this on H100: vLLM and SGLang achieve ~50% of available memory bandwidth. the other ~50% is the memory system sitting idle in the gaps between kernel launches.

what a megakernel will do is replace the CPU's kernel launch loop with an on-GPU interpreter. the model gets pre-compiled into typed instructions: loads weights from address X, compute matmul with tile size Y, apply RMSNorm to these registers. these would all get packed into per-SM instruction queues in device memory before launch.

one kernel launches, occupying all 132 SMs on an H100. each SM enters that persistent loop: fetch instruction from its queue, execute, signal a dependency counter, fetch the next one. the CPU never re-enters.

shared memory gets divided into pages with lightweight on-chip counters for dependency tracking. when a producer instruction finishes writing to a page, it increments the counter. the consumer instruction polls the counter before reading. no global barriers, and no CPU coordination.

the critical optimization is inter-instruction pipelining. while an SM computes the current instruction's matmul, it simultaneously loads the next instruction's weights into a different shared memory page.

megakernels pipeline work at three levels:

1. within each SM: next instruction's data loads while current instruction computes. CUDA Graphs can't do this; graphs just replay launches faster but still enforce full barriers between kernels.

2. across SMs: some SMs compute layer N's matmul while others handle layer N's RMSNorm concurrently. operations that would be serialized as separate kernels now run in parallel across SM groups.

3. across GPUs: dedicated "storer" warps handle NVLink allreduce in the background while compute warps work on the next matmul chunk. compute and communication overlap at warp granularity, not kernel granularity.

megakernels work for LLM inference because it's a static workload. every token follows the exact same path with near zero divergence. the interpreter loop is small, keeping register pressure low and the i-cache warm. and the bottleneck is memory bandwidth, not compute, exactly what pipeline bubble elimination optimizes for. 

so for LLM inference, megakernels are back!

author: Zen van Riel
subtitle: Member of Technical Staff at Apollo Research | Safer AI Engineering
content:
Finetuning a 7B model can require 56GB of GPU memory.
Most consumer GPUs max out at 24GB.

So you either pay for cloud compute or you don't finetune.

I was reading Chip Huyen's "AI Engineering" and she covers a workaround I hadn't thought much about: model merging.

You take two open source models that are already good at different things.
One handles code. One handles reasoning.
You combine their weights into a single model that does both.

No training loop. No GPU cluster. No cloud bill.

The approaches range from simple weight averaging to more advanced interpolation techniques.
But the core idea is the same: combine what already works.

This is how indie developers are competing on Hugging Face leaderboards against well-funded labs.
Goliath-120B was built by merging two Llama 2-70B variants. No massive training run required.

There's another cost benefit: inference.

If you need a model that does task A AND task B, you have two choices.
Run two separate models (2x the compute cost).
Or merge them into one model that handles both.

The catch: models need to share the same base architecture.
And merged models sometimes need light finetuning to smooth out rough edges.

But compared to training from scratch, merging is practically free.

author: Sifal Klioui
subtitle: ML Research Engineer
content:
Why did every major modern LLM quietly drop mean centering from their normalization layers? And how do they get away with it?

The standard answer is usually "it's computationally cheaper and empirically fine." But as someone who likes to know exactly how data moves through a network, I found that unsatisfying. If mean centering exists for a reason, removing it must have consequences. 

In my latest post, I strip away the indices and summations to visualize the hidden 3D geometry behind Layer Normalization. By building a simple 3D toy simulation, we can literally watch the data move: projecting onto planes, locking to hyperspheres, and stretching into ellipsoids.

We explore what actually happens when we drop the mean, how the epsilon parameter (you'll start to see its effect everywhere ahah) secretly traps your low-variance data, and I share a unified mathematical derivation that reframes RMSNorm not just as a cheaper approximation, but as a self-regulating system with a fascinating "directional collapse" failure mode.

While I owe a nod to the excellent geometric foundations laid by Andy Arditi and Paul M. Riechers, my goal here is to build a clear, visual intuition so you can close your eyes and see the shape of your activation space.

author: Emilio Andere
subtitle: Co-Founder and CEO at Wafer - Hardware Acceleration for AI
content:
nvidia just launched a first-party backend for triton. instead of fighting the portable DSL, they're making it compile better on nvidia. here's what changes:


in a previous post i broke down triton's 5 compilation stages: Python → TTIR → TTGIR → LLVM IR → PTX → cubin. in another post i broke down CUDA Tile IR,  nvidia's new virtual ISA for tile programming.

they just unexpectedly connected! nvidia released a CUDA Tile IR backend for triton. so naturally i had to write about it. 

but, what was the problem with the old path? 

triton writes tiles. you express operations on blocks of data: tl.dot(A, B), tl.load(block_ptr). but the compilation target, PTX, only understands threads.

the critical information loss happens at stage 3: TTGIR → LLVM IR. your tile-level tl.dot gets decomposed into per-thread wmma intrinsics. layout encodings get flattened into concrete index calculations. once in LLVM IR, the tensor abstraction is gone. ptxas then operates on thread-level SIMT code with zero understanding of your original tile structure.

triton's programming model is tile-based. its compilation target was thread-based. this was a fundamental mismatch that was leaving performance on the table.

the new path nvidia just launched

instead of TTIR → TTGIR → LLVM IR → PTX → SASS

triton now compiles: 

TTIR → CUDA Tile IR → SASS. 

and tile semantics are preserved end-to-end! 

the Tile IR compiler natively understands tile-granularity operations. it selects tensor core instructions, orchestrates TMA descriptors, allocates TMEM, and generates warp specialization automatically. all the blackwell-specific hardware complexity that you'd normally manage by hand in PTX,  the compiler now handles. 

activation is one env var: export ENABLE_TILE=1. you can select the backend per-kernel, and if Tile IR compilation fails it auto-falls back to PTX.

what will change in practice

the old triton pattern for loading data involves explicit pointer arithmetic. you compute offsets per element, build a tensor of pointers, and call tl.load. every thread calculates its own address.

the new TMA descriptor pattern replaces all of that with tl.make_tensor_descriptor. you pass the base pointer, shape, strides, and block shape. then desc.load([offset_m, 0]) handles address generation, bounds checking, and async copy in hardware. no per-thread pointer math.

this matters because tl.load (the tensor-of-pointer pattern) is actually 20% slower with the Tile IR backend than with PTX. TMA descriptors are the recommended path.

on B200 at 1000W, persistent matmul with Tile IR peaks 650 TFLOPS vs 574 TFLOPS with PTX. about ~13% faster.

nvidia is embracing triton's python DSL rather than fighting it, while managing to take control of the part of the stack they care about. triton's frontend stays portable across NVIDIA, AMD, Intel. but the optimized compilation path now goes through nvidia's Tile IR, which only targets nvidia hardware.

author: Parth Kalkar
subtitle: Builder | Full-Stack AI/ML Engineer | LLMs, Agentic Systems & On-Device Intelligence | ex AI @ BMW
content:
I just fine-tuned Llama-3B on my *phone*. (literally, on-device)

No, I didn't use LoRA. I used something weirder.

For a while now, we've accepted a false choice in fine-tuning:

1. MeBP (Standard Backprop): You get exact gradients, but your memory explodes. You need a data center to change a few weights.
2. MeZO (Zeroth-Order): You save memory, but your gradients are just educated guesses. You trade correctness for memory.

MeZO estimates gradients by perturbing weights and measuring the loss difference. It's clever, but it's also *blind*.

(and I just found out *why* it converges so slowly)

The Lesson:
I switched to a new technique called MeSP (Memory-efficient Structured Backpropagation) .

MeSP asks a simple question: "Why are we storing *anything*?"

The key realization is about LoRA. When you use LoRA, you have a low-rank projection: `h = xA`.

- In standard backprop, you store `h` to use when computing the gradient for `A`. 
- But since the rank `r` is tiny compared to the input dimension (`r << d_in`), **you can just... recompute it** on the fly during the backward pass. 

It's cheaper to redo the math than to hold onto the result .

The Result:
- Memory: 49% average reduction across Qwen2.5 models. For Qwen2.5-0.5B, peak memory drops from '361MB → 136MB' .
- Correctness: The gradients are *mathematically identical* to full backprop. You lose nothing.
- Freedom: You can now fine-tune on devices that fit in your pocket.

We've been so obsessed with approximating gradients that we forgot to check if the approximations were even pointing in the right direction.
 
(more like, If your compass is off by 90 degrees, you'll eventually get there, but you'll walk across the entire continent to do it.)

Stop guessing. Start recomputing!

#MachineLearning #LLMs #FineTuning #AIResearch

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🐎 New GLM-5 Technical Report

(Full training pipeline with sequential RL and DSA+MLA training)

The GLM-5 tech report just dropped, and it's one of the most detailed blueprints for building an agentic LLM I've read. I wrote a blog post about GLM-5 when it was released, but this report fills in a lot of gaps. Here are the most interesting additions:

→ They layer DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) on top of MLA via continued pre-training. They ablated sliding window, Gated DeltaNet, and SimpleGDN, but all failed on long-context retrieval. DSA's dynamic indexer achieves token-level sparsity without losing long-range dependencies, cutting attention compute by ~1.5-2x.

→ Pre-training data selection has been refined: a DCLM classifier on sentence embeddings for quality filtering, plus a "World Knowledge classifier" trained on Wikipedia + LLM labels to extract signal from otherwise low-quality data. They also refreshed their code corpus, gaining 28% more unique code tokens.

→ Post-training introduces three thinking modes: Interleaved (think before every response/tool call), Preserved (retain thinking blocks across turns to avoid re-deriving reasoning), and Turn-level (per-turn on/off for latency tradeoffs). They also mask erroneous segments in agent trajectories so the model learns error correction.

→ Their agentic RL is fully async with decoupled inference/training GPUs. A Multi-Task Rollout Orchestrator handles 1k+ concurrent rollouts. They tackle the off-policy problem with Double-sided Importance Sampling + token-level clipping, dropping stale samples that lag too far behind the current policy.

→ To prevent catastrophic forgetting across RL stages, they use On-Policy Cross-Stage Distillation: checkpoints from SFT, Reasoning RL, and General RL serve as teachers, with advantage signals computed from teacher-student logit gaps instead of sampled rewards.

I updated my blog post to reflect these additions (link in the comments).

The report is a goldmine for anyone building post-training pipelines. I'm curious about the choice of this cross-stage distillation approach to prevent forgetting. Model merging could be a much simpler and more flexible alternative, but isn't mentioned in the paper. What stood out to you in the GLM-5 tech report?

No sentience. No background “thinking.”

author: Emmanuel Alo
subtitle: AI/ML Engineer
content:
I recently finished a deep dive into GPU optimization by implementing a custom CUDA Megakernel to accelerate inference for the Qwen3-0.6B model.
Standard LLM pipelines often suffer from "kernel launch overhead",the time spent by the CPU telling the GPU to run hundreds of small, separate operations (like LayerNorm, Softmax, or GEMM) for every single token generated. By fusing these operations into a single, persistent "Megakernel," I was able to keep the workload entirely on the GPU, significantly reducing synchronization bottlenecks.
Key Technical Highlights:
Fused Transformer Operators: Integrated RMSNorm, SwiGLU, and Attention into a unified kernel to minimize global memory round-trips.
Warp-Level Primitives: Leveraged cooperative_groups and shuffles for high-speed reductions and synchronized data sharing across threads.
Zero-Sync Generation: Implemented a generate_nosync mode that allows for multi-token generation without returning control to the CPU until the sequence is complete.
Performance: Designed specifically to squeeze maximum performance out of consumer-grade hardware like the GTX 1650, achieving high token parity with the Hugging Face baseline.
The Hidden Trap: Memory Layout & Torch Alignment
One of the most prominent hiccups when writing raw CUDA kernels for PyTorch is managing Memory Layout and Alignment.
When we want maximum speed, we use 128-bit vectorized loads (using uint4 or float4). This allows a single instruction to grab 16 bytes of data. However, modern GPUs are extremely strict about this: if your pointer is not perfectly aligned to a 16-byte boundary, the kernel won't just run slowly, it will throw a "misaligned address" error and crash.
In this project, I had to implement Hardware Guards in the C++ extension to validate that the tensors passed from PyTorch were correctly aligned.
Why is this tricky? PyTorch tensors are often views or slices of larger memory blocks. Even if a tensor is "contiguous," its starting memory address might not be 16-byte aligned depending on how it was allocated or transposed. When building kernels for specific GPUs, you have to ensure that your Torch-side memory management aligns perfectly with your CUDA-side struct definitions. If your LDGLayerWeight struct expects a specific padding and the Python-side packing doesn't match, you end up with silent memory corruption.
While building kernels from scratch is an incredible learning experience, frameworks like SGLang and vLLM show the power of professional-grade CUDA optimization:  vLLM utilizes PagedAttention to manage KV cache memory like an operating system's virtual memory to eliminate fragmentation, while SGLang introduces RadixAttention to enable high-speed prefix caching and automatic KV cache sharing across multiple generation requests.

content:
While exploring LayerNorm triton kernels, found something elegant I hadn't come across before: 𝐖𝐞𝐥𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐝'𝐬 𝐚𝐥𝐠𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐦.

The naive variance formula (𝐄[𝐗²] - 𝐄[𝐗]²) can fail in floating-point arithmetic, sometimes returning wrong variance when variance << mean².

𝐄𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐖𝐞𝐥𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐝’𝐬 𝐀𝐥𝐠𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐦:
It’s an elegant, online, single-pass approach that maintains running statistics without ever storing individual data points. The key lies in the recurrence relation that updates the M2 (the sum of squares of differences from the mean) using the current and previous mean.

The elegance reminds me of the FlashAttention tiling trick-> update the "running" state incrementally!

For GPU kernels, this is crucial as it’s:
✅ Numerically stable (crucial for FP16/BF16)
✅ Memory efficient (single pass over the data)

I wrote a technical deep dive to better understand the intuition and I’m currently working on a Triton implementation of this kernel(WIP)

https://lnkd.in/eTeRGmYZ

Note:
I'm curious—for those working in Distributed Training, have you seen Welford's implemented in your custom kernels, or are you still sticking to the two-pass approach?

author: Saurav Pawar
subtitle: Machine Learning | ML Researcher | ML Engineer
content:
𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗣𝘆𝗧𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿

Sometimes performance improvements are not about changing your model…
They’re about changing one line (see the code snippet).

That's it.

🤔 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗼?
When you're training on a GPU (especially NVIDIA GPUs), PyTorch uses a library called cuDNN. cuDNN has multiple ways (algorithms) to perform operations like:
🔹 Convolutions
🔹 Matrix multiplications
🔹 Other deep learning math

When you enable benchmarking, PyTorch will:
Try different algorithms
Benchmark them
And pick the fastest one for your input size ⚡
So instead of guessing, it chooses the best-performing option.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽𝗳𝘂𝗹?
It works best when:
1.  Your input size stays the same
2.  For example: same image resolution, same batch size
In that case, PyTorch finds the best algorithm once…
and keeps using it.

Result?
👉 Faster training.

⚠️ 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴:
If your input size keeps changing (for example: variable image sizes), then:
1.  PyTorch keeps benchmarking again and again
2. This can actually slow things down

So this setting is powerful, but only when used correctly.

✨ 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆:
Sometimes performance optimization isn’t magic.
It’s just knowing which switch to turn on.

author: Arjun Jain
subtitle: Co-Creating Tomorrow’s AI | Research-as-a-Service | Founder, Fast Code AI | Dad to 8-year-old twins
content:
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 "𝗯𝘂𝗴" 𝗶𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲?
𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘔𝘰𝘯𝘰𝘵𝘰𝘯𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘔𝘺𝘵𝘩
Every textbook tells you activation functions 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 be monotonic. 

Monotonic → predictable gradients → stable training. Clean. Elegant. 𝗪𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴.

Your loss landscape is about as convex as a crumpled piece of paper. So why design activations like it is?

𝗦𝘄𝗶𝘀𝗵 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝗸𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘀.
A slight plunge into negative territory for 𝑥 < 0 before recovering. That "dip" isn't noise - it's 𝘯𝘦𝘨𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘥𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘧𝘭𝘰𝘸. Unlike ReLU, which zeros out negatives forever, non-monotonic activations preserve a small nonlinear signal. More expressivity. More gradient recovery.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗡𝗼𝗻-𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗰 𝗖𝗹𝘂𝗯:
🔸 𝗠𝗶𝘀𝗵 — 𝑥·tanh(ln(1+eˣ)). Smoother, deeper dip. Boosted YOLOv4 over ReLU. Diganta Misra's gift to CV. 
🔸 𝗚𝗘𝗟𝗨 — 𝑥·Φ(𝑥). You use this 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘥𝘢𝘺. Default in BERT, GPT, most Transformers. Non-monotonic 𝘢𝘯𝘥 probabilistic. 
🔸 𝗦𝗶𝗟𝗨 — 𝑥·σ(𝑥). Swish with β=1. Powers Stable Diffusion 3.5 and growing. 
🔸 𝗦𝗾𝘂𝗮𝘀𝗵 — Lesser-known, used in Hinton's capsule networks.

𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗮 𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝗽 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿?
A dip of -0.1 in one neuron? Negligible. Across 𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 of neurons, 𝘮𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 of times? It compounds into implicit regularization across the entire network. The dip preserves gradient flow where ReLU kills it. It creates small bumps in the loss surface that help optimizers escape sharp minima. GELU replacing ReLU in Transformers wasn't an accident. Mish in YOLOv4: ~1-2% mAP boost 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 from swapping the activation. At scale, that's enormous.

𝗡𝗼𝘄 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝘂𝗿𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗴𝗮𝗶𝗻.
Swish, Mish, GELU, SiLU - overlay them and they look 𝘢𝘭𝘮𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘭. Squint and you can't tell them apart. Yet each produces measurably different training dynamics, different generalization, different results.

That should stop you in your tracks.

Fractions of a decimal in a tiny region - and those fractions change what a billion-parameter model 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘯𝘴. The geometry of intelligence is sensitive at a scale we barely have language for.

And a deeper question: if these functions are all converging on nearly the same shape - a smooth, slightly non-monotonic curve with a gentle dip around 𝑥 ≈ -1 - 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘸𝘦 𝘩𝘪𝘵 𝘢 𝘭𝘰𝘤𝘢𝘭 𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘪𝘮𝘶𝘮 𝘪𝘯 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘧𝘶𝘯𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘴𝘱𝘢𝘤𝘦?

Are we circling the same attractor, each new activation a minor perturbation of the last? Or is there a fundamentally different shape - waiting to break the ceiling the way Swish first broke monotonicity?

𝗘𝗺𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗽.

author: Maziyar P.
subtitle: Building OpenMed | AI for Healthcare & Life Sciences | 3,500+ Open-Source Models | #1 on Hugging Face
content:
I spent weeks trying to make Anthropic's SAE steering generate valid JSON for PII extraction (think HIPAA/GDPR compliance).

You know that Golden Gate Bridge experiment? Where Anthropic's team used activation steering to make Claude obsess about the Golden Gate Bridge? I thought: if steering can control what a model talks about, maybe it can control how it formats output.

So I ran 6 experiments on Qwen2.5-0.5B using PII entity extraction as the task.

The results:

Untrained base model: 86.8% valid JSON Steering only: 24.4% valid JSON Fine-tuned model: 96.6% valid JSON, 91.2% F1 Fine-tuning + steering: 25-36 percentage points WORSE than fine-tuning alone

Steering didn't just fail to help. It actively broke things.

After weeks of dead ends, I built a custom FSM-based LogitsProcessor that tracks JSON state during generation and masks invalid tokens. 50 lines of Python. No external libraries. Result: 100% valid JSON on the first experiment.

The lesson is simple: steering works for semantic control (personality, safety, bias, topic focus). It fails for syntactic constraints (JSON validity, bracket matching, quote placement). Different problems need different tools.

I wrote up all 6 experiments with code, results, and a production-ready implementation on Hugging Face. Would be curious to hear from anyone who has tried steering for structured output.

author: Remus Kalathil
subtitle: AWS Community Builder (Containers) | Cloud & Platform Engineer | SRE | DevOps | Kubernetes & AI Infrastructure | Scalable Production Architectures | AWS & Terraform Certified | NVIDIA NCA-AIIO
content:
Understanding NCCL - The Backbone of GPU Communication in AI Workloads

While working deeper into AI infrastructure and distributed training systems, one component that keeps showing up is NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL)  and it’s worth understanding why it matters.

When we talk about scaling AI/ML workloads across multiple GPUs or nodes, raw compute power isn’t the only challenge  communication between GPUs becomes the bottleneck. This is where NCCL steps in.

What is NCCL?
NCCL is a high-performance library designed to optimize communication primitives between GPUs. It accelerates collective operations like:
• All-Reduce
• Broadcast
• Reduce
• Gather / Scatter
These operations are foundational for distributed deep learning frameworks like TensorFlow, PyTorch and many more.

In modern training pipelines:
GPU clusters (Kubernetes / bare metal / HPC fabrics) rely on fast synchronization of gradients and parameters. NCCL:
- Uses NVLink, PCIe, InfiniBand, and Ethernet efficiently
- Optimizes topology-aware routing
- Reduces latency during gradient synchronization
- Improves multi-node scaling efficiency

Without efficient communication, adding GPUs doesn’t scale performance linearly NCCL helps bridge that gap.

Where you’ll see it in practice
If you’re building or operating AI platforms, NCCL is typically under the hood in:
• Distributed LLM training
• Multi-GPU inference workloads
• HPC clusters for AI/ML
• Kubernetes GPU operator environments
• Ray / DeepSpeed / Horovod pipelines

 Architect takeaway
As infrastructure architects, we often focus on compute provisioning but network topology + communication libraries define real scalability.
Understanding components like NCCL helps when designing GPU clusters, choosing interconnects, or debugging performance bottlenecks.
I’m currently exploring this deeper as part of my AI infrastructure learning journey curious how others are optimizing GPU communication at scale.

author: Arpit Bhayani
subtitle: Principal Engineer II - Data x AI at Razorpay • databases • ex-Staff Engineer at GCP Memorystore and GCP Dataproc • creator of DiceDB • built and sold Profile.fyi • ex-Amazon Fast Data and DoE Unacademy
content:
In C, you can define two interesting macros - likely() and unlikely(). Here's what they would do and how they could make code performant...

These macros would wrap GCC's __builtin_expect() function to give hints to the compiler about which branch of a conditional statement is more probable. When you write if(likely(x > 0)), you're telling the compiler "this condition will almost always be true."

The compiler uses this hint for branch prediction optimization. It arranges the assembly code so the likely path executes without taking a jump instruction, keeping the processor pipeline flowing smoothly and improving cache locality.

The Linux kernel uses these extensively - likely() appears over 3,000 times and unlikely() over 14,000 times in the codebase. The Linux ftrace tracer saw up to 20% performance improvement by adding proper likely/unlikely hints.

In practice, you might see 5-15% performance improvement in hot paths where branches are predictable.

But modern CPUs are already pretty good at predicting branches on their own. If you guess wrong and mark something as likely when it's not, you can make performance worse.

So, we should not blindly add these everywhere for every single `if` in the code. They should be used in critical loops where you know the pattern and the branch happens millions of times per second.

Use them rarely, profile the code, and only apply it where the branch probability is genuinely skewed (90%+ in one direction).

Hope this helps.

author: Sameer Wadkar
subtitle: LLM Infrastructure · Training & Inference Systems · Distributed Compute · Cloud-Native AI Platforms
content:
🧪 Recently I ran a computer vision model on NVIDIA Triton Inference Server using ONNX Runtime (CUDA Execution Provider) as the execution backend. ONNX Runtime is attractive because it’s portable: the model remains a graph of operators that can be executed across different hardware backends with minimal friction.

❓That portability comes with a question: what does it cost at inference time?

🧭 To establish a baseline, I compared ONNX Runtime CUDA against TensorRT, which takes the opposite approach. TensorRT deliberately gives up portability and instead specializes aggressively for a specific GPU, precision, and input shape, compiling the model into a fixed execution plan.

🧠 I used TensorRT as the reference baseline here because it represents a last-mile performance extractor: most execution-time decisions (kernel selection, fusion, memory planning) are resolved at build time rather than deferred to runtime coordination. That makes it a useful anchor for understanding where overhead lives when performance is the primary objective.

I measured throughput along with host-side p50 and p99 latency on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070.

⚙️This repository starts in the easy regime:
- Static input shapes
- Image-style models (ResNet-50)
- FP32 and FP16 precision
- Fixed batch sizes of 1, 8, and 16
- TensorRT invoked via trtexec, not custom C++ or Python runtimes

🔍The results were instructive (see graphs). 

- ⚠️ As batch size increases, ONNX Runtime CUDA shows rising median latency and a widening p50–p99 gap. This pattern is consistent with increasing host-side coordination costs as batching grows, including scheduling, memory management, and synchronization that occur outside fused GPU kernels.

-  ⚡TensorRT behaves differently. Both FP16 and FP32 scale more predictably with batch size, and the p50–p99 gap remains comparatively tight. This suggests that more of the added work stays inside pre-compiled GPU execution paths rather than spilling into per-request runtime orchestration.

- 🚀 The throughput plot reinforces the same story. TensorRT FP16 converts larger batches directly into higher throughput, while ONNX Runtime saturates earlier. In practice, ONNX Runtime continues to pay coordination costs at execution time, whereas TensorRT amortizes much of that overhead during engine build by committing to a fixed execution plan.

ℹ️ This is an intentionally conservative baseline. Even in a friendly regime with static shapes and no dynamic behavior, the portability–specialization tradeoff is visible in both throughput and tail latency.

ℹ️ This baseline highlights a key rule: once tail latency and throughput both matter, where execution-time decisions live matters as much as the kernels themselves.

➡️The next steps are to relax these assumptions: dynamic shapes, optimization profiles, and quantization and observe where the gaps narrow, widen, or change character.

author: Shivani Gajulapalli
subtitle: Enterprise AI | Ex-Amazon | IIT Madras
content:
Day 2/30 of reading research papers in ML

Today: "A Neural Probabilistic Language Model" by Yoshua Bengio et al. (2003)

Before this paper, language models were basically giant lookup tables. You counted how often "the cat is" was followed by "sitting" in the training data. If a word combination wasn't in the data? model wouldn't work. No generalization.

Bengio's idea: give every word a learned numeric vector (what we now call "embeddings"), and train a neural network to predict the next word using those vectors. The beautiful part is that the model learns that "dog" and "cat" are similar because it needs to know that to predict the next word well. Meaning emerges as a byproduct of prediction.

One training sentence doesn't just teach the model that sentence. It teaches the model about an exponential number of similar sentences. That's how you fight the curse of dimensionality.

This was 2003. No GPUs for AI (CUDA came in ~2008). They trained on clusters of 32 dual-CPU machines for weeks. Manual backprop derivations. 

The results? 24% better perplexity than the best n-gram models at that time

This paper is the conceptual ancestor of Word2Vec, GloVe, and every modern LLM. The core idea, learn word meaning by predicting the next word, is still exactly what GPT does today.

author: Rishabh Misra
subtitle: Principal ML Lead - Generative Personalization | ML Book and Course Author | Researcher - LLMs & RecSys - 1k+ citations | Advisory @ Startups | Featured in TechCrunch, NBC, TheSun | AI Consultant
content:
I watched a senior engineer spend three weeks quantizing an LLM to 4-bit.

The P99 latency got worse.

The issue wasn’t the technique; it was treating quantization as a storage problem instead of a memory-bandwidth problem.

At Twitter, I spent a month debugging why our "optimized" models ran slower than the originals. The models were smaller. The math was correct. Yet latency regressed. The missing piece: the *unpacking tax*. 

Here’s the reality most benchmarks hide:
Time ≈ Total bytes moved / Memory bandwidth

On paper, moving from FP16 (16-bit) to INT4 (4-bit) means 4× less data moving across the memory bus per token. In a memory-bound regime, that translates to 3–4× higher throughput.

But there’s a catch.

GPUs don’t compute in 4-bit or 8-bit. Those weights are dequantized back to FP16/BF16 in the local cache before computation. 

That dequantization costs clock cycles and creates production surprises:
 → High batch sizes: Time saved on memory movement dominates = throughput improves
 → Batch size of 1: Unpacking overhead dominates = latency gets worse

Quantization is not a free win. It’s a tradeoff.

If you’re choosing a method, align it with your deployment reality:
 → GPTQ: Effective for static weights, but sensitive to outliers
 → AWQ: Preserves critical weights at higher precision for better quality
 → GGUF: Excellent for CPU/Metal inference, less relevant for H100/A100 clusters

This is Part 4 of a deep dive into inference optimization. Previous posts:

author: Daniel Svonava
subtitle: Self-host your inference, save $$$, own your AI | xYouTube
content:
Flash Attention 4 is coming. Everyone's hyped. 

Almost no one can explain why it's actually faster. 

"It's optimized for Blackwell" it's like saying "it's fast because it's new."

Here's what's actually going on:

1️⃣ They replaced GPU hardware with basic math (And it's faster)
GPUs have Special Function Units for exponentials. Dedicated silicon. Sounds fast.

Problem: way fewer SFUs than CUDA cores. Heavy attention load = waiting in line.

FA4's fix? A cubic polynomial approximation on CUDA cores.

Three fused multiply-adds beats the dedicated hardware queue. 🤯

2️⃣ They got lazy with rescaling (On purpose)
Standard attention rescales values every time you see a new maximum. Safe. Also wasteful.

FA4 only rescales when the change actually threatens numerical stability.

10x fewer rescaling ops. Same correctness. Pure computational fat trimmed.

3️⃣ They turned attention into an async pipeline.
FA3 had 2 stages. FA4 has 5 (load, MMA, softmax, correction, epilogue) running concurrently on specialized warps.

Think event loop on steroids.

The result? ~20% faster than FA3. First kernel to break the petaflop barrier.

FA4 isn't widely available yet (Blackwell only, forward pass only). But when it lands broadly, the "just throw more GPUs at it" crowd is in for a rude awakening.

Architecture eats hardware for breakfast.

Props to Tri Dao for pushing the boundaries again.

author: Kavishka Abeywardana
subtitle: Machine Learning & Signal Processing Researcher | Semantic Communication • Deep Learning • Optimization | AI Research Writer
content:
Linear attention scales beautifully, but it has always lagged behind softmax attention in performance.

The root cause is surprisingly simple: linear attention ignores query magnitude.

As a result, its attention distribution cannot adapt or sharpen during training, leading to overly smooth and weak locality.

Magnitude-Aware Linear Attention (MALA) fixes this by reintroducing query magnitude without sacrificing linear complexity.

It produces attention distributions that are neither too spiky like softmax nor too smooth like vanilla linear attention.

author: Pranay Tiwari
subtitle: Vice President, Data Science | Leading Enterprise-Wide AI/ML Transformation | Founding Member of AI CoE | Agentic AI & Scalable Recommender Systems | US Patent Holder
content:
Building an LLM - Concepts and Interview question series

Topic 16 - 5 LLM inference metrics your team needs to understand

Everyone talks about model output quality when it comes to LLMs. But the fact is users actually feel "serving quality". Hence look into these as you put your LLM use cases to prod.

1) TTFT (time to first token): Request -> first token; this will include queuing, prefill, and network, and longer prompts which will generally increase TTFT because the prompt must be processed to build the KV cache before decoding begins.

2) End-to-end latency: Request -> final token, often approximated as 
                                e2e = TTFT + generation time.

3) ITL / TPOT (inter-token latency): Average time per streamed output token during generation; this is the "mid-response snappiness" users perceive. Consistent ITL are a sign of efficient KV cache management and memory bandwidth - when it starts spiking, that's your diagnostic signal before throughput will visibly start degrading. (Post 15 of mine dealt with why KV cache is important) 

4) Total TPS (system throughput, token per sec): Output tokens/sec across concurrent requests; here definition matters too - GenAI-Perf and LLMPerf can differ because of how they treat benchmark overhead and warm-up/cool-down, and that can materially shift results (reported as ~33% in some single-concurrency cases).

5) Per-user TPS: A simple approximation is output_length / e2e_latency; system TPS can rise with concurrency while per-user TPS falls (which is the core tradeoff).

REMEMBER THIS - These metrics often move in opposite directions. So when you optimize for System TPS while ignoring TTFT, you will tank the UX for RAG workloads (where users are stuck waiting for that first chunk). Always benchmark to your SLOs, and not a leaderboard. 

The only link I will add is the NVIDIA blog which is one of the best here.

author: Emmanuel Alo

content:
Standard PyTorch is great, but when you're scaling LLMs, every millisecond counts. I just implementing a Fused SwiGLU kernel from scratch.
The Llama family popularized the use of SwiGLU. In their production environments, they use fused kernels (often via FlashAttention or vLLM) to ensure the MLP blocks don't become a bottleneck.
Google's internal XLA (Accelerated Linear Algebra) compiler automatically tries to "fuse" operations, but for their most critical models, they use hand-written Triton or CUDA kernels to squeeze out every millisecond.
The reason why they fuse SwiGLU?
The Problem with Standard pytorch require multiple VRAM "round-trips" like calculating gates, activations, and up-projections separately. This wastes memory bandwidth.
By fusing the linear projections and the SiLU activation into a single CUDA kernel, I reduced memory overhead by ~20%.
My implementation: 
- Written in raw CUDA C++ with PyBind11 integration. 
- Custom Autograd support for seamless training. 
- Handles BFloat16/Half precision for modern GPUs.

author: Arjun Jain
subtitle: Co-Creating Tomorrow’s AI | Research-as-a-Service | Founder, Fast Code AI | Dad to 8-year-old twins
content:
𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻. 𝗜𝘁’𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁.

At least, not anymore.

I keep seeing students, tutorials, and even some papers casually say “we add positional encoding to the token” as if that’s still how modern LLMs work. It was true in 2017. It hasn’t been true for years.

Here’s the shift nobody talks about clearly enough.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟳 𝗪𝗮𝘆: “𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻”

In the original Transformer, BERT, and early GPT - position was treated like a page number written directly onto the document.

📍 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲: The very bottom. Input layer. Once.
🔧 𝗛𝗼𝘄: Literally add a position vector to the word embedding.

𝘱𝘰𝘴_𝘦𝘮𝘣𝘦𝘥𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨 + 𝘵𝘰𝘬𝘦𝘯_𝘦𝘮𝘣𝘦𝘥𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨 → 𝘪𝘯𝘱𝘶𝘵

The problem? Once that token enters Layer 1, it’s 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘭𝘺 contaminated with position. The model now has to spend capacity disentangling “what this word means” from “where this word sits” — across every single layer. That’s wasted compute.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗼𝗣𝗘 𝗪𝗮𝘆: “𝗧𝘄𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗩𝗶𝗲𝘄”

Modern LLMs (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma) use Rotary Position Embeddings. The key insight: 𝘥𝘰𝘯’𝘵 𝘵𝘰𝘶𝘤𝘩 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘬𝘦𝘯 𝘢𝘵 𝘢𝘭𝘭.

📍 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲: Inside every attention head. Repeatedly.
🔧 𝗛𝗼𝘄: Apply a rotation matrix to Q and K 𝘢𝘧𝘵𝘦𝘳 projection.

Token (𝑥) → 𝘶𝘯𝘵𝘰𝘶𝘤𝘩𝘦𝘥
Query (Q) → 𝗥𝗼𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 → R_m · Q
Key (K)  → 𝗥𝗼𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 → R_n · K
Value (V) → 𝗡𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥 𝗧𝗢𝗨𝗖𝗛𝗘𝗗

This is the part people miss. The 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘵 (Value) stays pure - completely uncorrupted by position math. We only “twist” the search keys so they encode 𝘳𝘦𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘦 distance. When Q_m and K_n interact, the rotation difference (R_{m-n}) naturally encodes how far apart tokens m and n are.

No stamping. No contamination. Just geometry.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸:

🔹 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻. Absolute positions are fixed — you trained on 512 tokens, you’re stuck at 512. RoPE’s relative encoding is why modern models can extrapolate to longer sequences. It’s also why techniques like NTK-aware scaling and YaRN work — they manipulate the rotation frequencies, not the token.

🔹 𝗖𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗲𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀. Value vectors carry pure semantic content. The model doesn’t waste layers untangling meaning from position.

🔹 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘃𝘀. 𝗮𝗯𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝘂𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. You don’t read a sentence by thinking “the word at position 47.” You read it by understanding that 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 word is 3 words after 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 one. RoPE encodes language the way we actually process it.


𝗧𝗟;𝗗𝗥:

⬜ 2017 → Adds position to the 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 (token embedding). Once. At the bottom.
⬜ RoPE → Adds position to the 𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 (Q & K only). Every layer. Never touches the Value.

Next time someone says “positional encoding is added to the token,” ask them: 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘤𝘩 𝘺𝘦𝘢𝘳 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘪𝘯?

author: Parth Kalkar
subtitle: Builder | Full-Stack AI/ML Engineer | LLMs, Agentic Systems & On-Device Intelligence | ex AI @ BMW
content:
I paused chunking my documents before embedding them. (other ways exist)

And, I think there is a clear pattern in the pipeline, (`Chunk -> Embed -> Store`). 

For 3 years, we have built RAG pipelines the same way:
1. Split text into 512-token chunks.
2. Embed each chunk independently.
3. Pray.

At least this is what we have seen in 99% of the RAG tutorials. 

The Problem:
This approach breaks *Context*. (for example)

Chunk 1: "Apple announced a new device today."
Chunk 2: "It costs $3,500 and features spatial computing."

- If you search for *"What costs $3,500?"*, your Vector DB fails. 
- Why? Because the embedding for Chunk 2 only sees the word "It." 
- It doesn't know "It" = "Apple Vision Pro." 

The connection was severed by the knife.

This happens because, we usually assume that to fit text into a Vector Database, we must chop it up first.

The Lesson:
I switched to *Late Chunking*. This technique proves that chopping first destroys the meaning. 

You should Embed *first*, and Chunk *later*.

Instead of isolating the chunks, it leverages the massive 8k+ context window of modern embedding models (like `jina-embeddings-v3`).

1. The Pass: We feed the *entire* document (all 8,000 tokens) into the Transformer at once.
2. The Magic: Inside the model, the *Attention Mechanism* connects every token to every other token. The vector for "It" (token 500) mathematically absorbs the identity of "Apple" (token 10).
3. The Cut: *After* the model has encoded this global context, *then* we slice the vector array into chunks.

The Result:
• Context Preservation: The chunk "It costs $3,500" now effectively contains the semantic meaning of "The Apple Vision Pro costs $3,500."
• No Hallucinations: The retriever doesn't return random chunks about "It" (Stephen King's clown).
• Drop-in Upgrade: You don't need a new database (like ColBERT). You just change how you generate the vectors.

Stop cutting the wire before you send the signal.
(this way, the hallucinations can be reduced significantly)

author: Yash Satwani

content:
Your model is 50% smaller.
But inference time didn't change.
This is a mistake that happens constantly with unstructured pruning. Here's what actually matters:

The Hardware Reality:
Removing random weights (unstructured pruning) creates sparse matrices that LOOK efficient on paper. You've eliminated 50% of the parameters!

But modern GPUs are built for dense matrix operations. They can't skip individual zeros in a sparse matrix without special support.

Result: No real-world speedup despite the smaller model.

The Better Approach: Structured Pruning

Instead of removing random weights, remove entire structures:
- Complete attention heads
- Entire neurons
- Full layers

This gives you truly smaller, faster models because the hardware can actually optimize for the reduced operations.

Real Example: 2:4 Sparsity

NVIDIA A100 GPUs support a specific pattern: 2 out of every 4 consecutive weights are zero.

This isn't random - it's hardware-optimized. The GPU has special instructions to accelerate this exact pattern, giving you actual 2x speedups on supported operations.

According to NVIDIA's technical documentation, Sparse Tensor Cores achieve up to 2x throughput by processing only non-zero values while maintaining the same accuracy as dense models.

Actionable Framework:
Before implementing pruning:

✓ Check what your hardware supports (sparse operations? specific patterns?)
✓ Choose structured pruning over unstructured when possible
✓ Benchmark actual inference time, not just parameter count
✓ Consider 2:4 sparsity if using NVIDIA A100/H100

The Key Lesson:

Model optimization isn't just about mathematics - it's about understanding the hardware that runs your code.

LLMs rules differ than microservices on Kubernetes  

what we changed:

1-Scale LLM inference based on queue depth and concurrency instead of CPU, because GPU workloads do not reflect load through CPU or memory metrics.

2-Keep a small number of warm inference replicas and only mark pods ready after the model is fully loaded to avoid latency spikes caused by cold starts.

3-Standardize and isolate GPU capacity using consistent node configuration and workload separation so available GPUs are always schedulable and usable.

4-Use an inference optimized serving layer and cap per replica concurrency

The Hidden Problem with Scaling LLMs on Kubernetes?

Most teams scale LLMs the same way:

→ Add more GPUs
→ Hope latency stays within limits

It “works”… 

but it’s expensive, inefficient, and hard to operate in shared cloud clusters.


Why?
Because Prefill and Decode are treated as one big workload
even though they behave very differently.


The Fix?
Split the Work, Not Just the GPUs

This is where llm-d comes in.

llm-d is a Kubernetes-native way to split LLM serving into prefill and decode,

And scale each part independently, without breaking cloud or platform workflows.


What llm-d changes?
→  Prefill and decode run as separate services
→  Each scales based on own latency and throughput needs
→  Works in multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters
→  Supports different GPU types for different workloads
→  Uses standard K8s tools for routing, autoscaling, and failures


llm-d makes prefill–decode separation practical for real production systems, not just papers and prototypes.

This is where LLM infrastructure is heading.

content:
Found a solid learning path for vLLM that gets you productive in an afternoon.

Start with Aleksa Gordic's technical overview (https://lnkd.in/ef59_EJC). He explains vLLM's architecture clearly: how it serves LLMs efficiently, why it matters for production deployments, and what makes it different from naive inference approaches. The post walks through the core components without drowning you in unnecessary details.

Then dive into the two fundamental techniques that make vLLM work:

Hamza Elshafie breaks down Paged Attention from first principles (https://lnkd.in/eeSYtJzZ). The key insight: treating attention's key-value cache like virtual memory in operating systems. Instead of pre-allocating huge contiguous blocks, vLLM pages the KV cache dynamically. This eliminates memory fragmentation and lets you serve more requests with the same hardware.

The Hugging Face post on Continuous Batching shows why traditional batching fails for LLM inference (https://lnkd.in/eG4Fcp2X). Sequences finish at different times, leaving GPUs idle. Continuous batching processes new requests as soon as slots free up, keeping your expensive hardware saturated. Simple idea, massive throughput improvement.

These three articles build on each other naturally. You'll understand not just what vLLM does, but why these design choices matter when you're running models in production. Whether you're deploying on your own infrastructure or evaluating cloud options, this knowledge translates directly to making better engineering decisions.

Pro tip for code readers: Checkout nano-vllm (https://lnkd.in/errWD2Ju), a vllm implementation in ~1200 lines of Python.

Worth spending a few hours on this if you're serious about LLM deployment.

👩‍💻 Key Techniques for Efficient LLM Inference Serving ✨

Efficient LLM inference is as much about systems engineering as it is about the model itself. Small optimizations in scheduling, caching, and cluster orchestration can dramatically improve latency, throughput, and cost.

1️⃣ Instance-Level Techniques
🔸Model Placement & Parallelism: Distribute model parameters across GPUs or CPU-GPU combinations to fit memory budgets efficiently.
🔸Dynamic Request Scheduling: Prioritize and batch incoming requests intelligently to reduce latency.
🔸Decoding Length Prediction: Estimate output lengths in advance to optimize scheduling and throughput.
🔸Disaggregated Architectures: Separate prefill and decoding phases to reduce idle GPU time.

2️⃣ Cache Optimization
🔸KV Cache Management: Reuse and compress key-value caches to save memory and speed up inference.
🔸Semantic-Aware Reuse: Cache results based on similarity of inputs for repeated patterns.
🔸Memory-Efficient Storage: Optimize cache data structures to maximize hardware utilization.

3️⃣ Cluster-Level Techniques
🔸Heterogeneous Resource Management: Use GPUs, CPUs, and accelerators efficiently within a cluster.
🔸Load Balancing & Autoscaling: Distribute workloads dynamically to avoid bottlenecks and leverage cloud elasticity.
🔸Fault-Tolerance & Cold-Start Mitigation: Reduce latency spikes when nodes spin up or fail.

4️⃣ Emerging Techniques
🔸Long Contexts & RAG Pipelines: Optimize memory and scheduling for extended input sequences and retrieval-augmented generation.
🔸Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): Conditional execution of model experts to reduce compute per request.
🔸Speculative Decoding: Early output predictions to accelerate inference without sacrificing quality.
🔸Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (LoRA, adapters): Customize models with minimal compute overhead.

Curious to hear from the community: Which optimization technique has given you the most impact in production?
