author: Mohamed Hedi Turki
subtitle: Deep learning R&D engineer | LLM, Deep Learning, Computer Vision
content:
When deploying LLMs in production, choosing the right inference framework is very important. I ran a head-to-head comparison between SGLang and vLLM to see which one delivers better performance on accessible hardware.

What is SGLang?
SGLang is a high-performance serving framework for large language models and multimodal models, delivering low-latency and high-throughput inference from single GPUs to large distributed clusters.
 Key advantages:
▶️ RadixAttention for efficient prefix caching
▶️ Optimized for complex serving patterns
▶️ Python-based with minimal overhead
▶️ Excellent for conversational AI and agents

What is vLLM?
vLLM is a widely adopted inference engine built for high-throughput LLM serving at scale.
Key advantages:
▶️ PagedAttention for memory-efficient KV cache
▶️ Continuous batching for maximum GPU utilization
▶️ OpenAI-compatible API
▶️ V1 architecture with improved performance
▶️ Strong community support and broad model compatibility

I tested both inference frameworks using “Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct” on my NVIDIA RTX A2000 12GB. Both frameworks were tested with identical prompts and configurations. As a result, SGLang 🏆won across all metrics delivering faster responses, higher throughput, and better memory efficiency on this workload:
🔵 Throughput: 242.9 tok/s vs 206.4 tok/s (+17.7% faster)
🔵 Response Time: 1.22s vs 1.45s (19.2% improvement)
🔵 Memory: 9.8GB vs 12.0GB (2.2GB less, 18.6% more efficient)
🔵 Total Duration: 24.3s vs 29.0s (19% faster completion)

What I have learned:
▶️ Production inference frameworks pre-allocate large KV caches for scalability. Even a 0.5B model consumed 10-12GB due to production optimizations.
▶️ Without real-world testing, you won't know which framework suits your workload pattern and how much memory you exactly need. So, test before you deploy. Framework choice can impact cost, latency, and user experience significantly.

Both SGLang and vLLM are excellent tools. The "best" one depends on your specific use case. For my test workload on resource-constrained hardware, SGLang delivered superior performance.

author: Jino Rohit
subtitle: Deep Learning Engineer@ PiSchool | Former AI @AiCrowd | Kaggle Competitions Expert(Global Top 1%)
content:
understand vllm for beginners

ive been working on a minimal implementation for the paged attention in vllm, so lets try to understand from here.

why paged attention?

kv cache stores the key and values from past tokens so the model does not have to recompute them during attention at each step. but there are problems with this approach(yes, besides memory growing like a freak)

normal kv cache results in -

1. fragmented memory - requests have different sequence lengths. frequent allocation and deallocations results in memory being allocated weirdly and leaves gaps in between, those gaps basically become unusable.

2. over allocation - when you pre-allocate a certain GB VRAM, theyre often underutilized and results in wastage.

paged attention instead inspired from OS concepts, implements a paging based system where you breaks the sequences into smaller fixed size pages/blocks. during attention you iterate over all the pages and get the final result.

components

1. page - the page(often called as block) is the smallest allocation unit for the kv cache. it stores the kv for a fixed number of tokens defined by the page_size.

it also has a ref_count that tells you how many sequences are using this particular page. 
this enables two things -
> prefix sharing - a lot of the requests start with the same system prompt. it makes sense to not store duplicated kv cache for this each time. prefix sharing enables you to point to the same page if they share the same prefix tokens.
> decoding - for some of the decoding strategies like beam search etc requires starting from the same tokens but diverges as the generation moves forward in time. in this case, multiple sequences share the same initial kv pages but diverge in the future.

2. page_table - the page table keeps a mapping of the logical pages to the actual physical page in the GPU. each request maintains its own page table.
the page table gives the illusion of the pages being contiguous in memory, but the kv can live anywhere in the GPU.

3. sequence - the sequence represents the user's decoding request.  

each sequence has its own - 
> token ids
> status (WAITING/RUNNING/FINISHED)
> page table
> current position

4. block_manager - the block manager is the heart which handles and maintains the allocation and deallocation of pages for every sequence.

> handles allocation for the prefill stage
> does incremental allocation for the decoding phase.
> also does the reference counting for each page
> frees the pages when the sequence is finished.

author: Emilio Andere
subtitle: Co-Founder and CEO at Wafer - Hardware Acceleration for AI
content:
nvidia now releases its most optimized inference kernels through a PhD student's open-source project. here's a breakdown of FlashInfer:

FlashInfer is a GPU kernel library built specifically for LLM serving. it won Best Paper at MLSys 2025, powers both SGLang and vLLM, and NVIDIA now actively ships TensorRT-LLM kernels through it. the creator, Zihao Ye, built it during his PhD at UW and now works at NVIDIA full-time.

LLM serving has a combinatorial explosion of attention kernels. every combination of KV-cache layout (paged, radix tree, tree masks), attention variant (GQA, MLA, RoPE-fused, sliding window), and batch mode (prefill,
decode, append, shared prefix) needs a different kernel.

FlashInfer's insight was: all KV-cache layouts are special cases of block-sparse matrices. paged attention is just block-sparse with page_size as block width. radix tree? block-sparse. tree attention for speculative decoding? block-sparse. 

one abstraction can replace what used to be separate kernel implementations. then you get JIT compilation to handle the variant explosion, in the form of  CUDA/CUTLASS templates that get specialized at runtime

there's two other major innovations built on top of FlashInfer:

1. cascade attention

when multiple requests share a prefix (document QA, system prompts), FlashInfer decomposes attention into two stages: a multi-query kernel for the shared prefix (loaded once into SMEM, reused across all queries) and a
batch decode kernel for unique suffixes. results merge using an associative operator on partial attention states. 31x speedup over vLLM's PagedAttention for 32K-token shared prefixes at batch size 256.

2. plan/run scheduling for CUDAGraph

LLM serving has dynamic sequence lengths. CUDAGraphs need static configurations. FlashInfer solves this with a two-phase pattern: plan() inspects request shapes and computes balanced scheduling metadata, run() launches
kernels. you plan once per decode step, then replay across all transformer layers.

FlashInfer is an amazing project that i deeply respect, so also want to share some links for anyone that wants to go deeper: 
- paper (MLSys 2025 Best Paper): https://lnkd.in/gc_CTbnf
- github: https://lnkd.in/gwfQ8B72

author: Pranay Tiwari
subtitle: Vice President, Data Science | Leading Enterprise-Wide AI/ML Transformation | Founding Member of AI CoE | Agentic AI & Scalable Recommender Systems | US Patent Holder
content:
Building an LLM - Concepts and Interview question series

Topic 15 - KV caching is all you need (almost!)

Most teams are not using the single optimization that cuts their LLM inference costs by 80%!!

Back to basics, everytime a transformer generates a token, it recomputes attention over every previous token, growing quadratically with context length. KV caching stores the Key and Value matrices from prior tokens so the model has to compute attention ONLY for the new token.

Look at the numbers -
Generating 512 tokens from a 7B model on an A100 drops from ~8.2 seconds to ~1.4 seconds with KV cache - a 5.8x speedup. At 4K contexts, you're looking at 10-15x improvements.
But the real unlock most teams miss is prefix caching. If your system prompt or RAG context is shared across requests, frameworks like vLLM can cache those KV pairs across users leading to a 30-60% compute reduction for workloads where the first 1000+ tokens are identical. That describes nearly every production RAG pipeline.

Also, this isa game changer in Multi-turn conversations. Without KV caching, a 10-turn conversation reprocesses the entire history every turn. With session-level caching, each turn only processes the new message. For a chatbot handling 50K daily conversations averaging 8 turns, that is the difference between 40 GPUs and 8 GPUs.

So what is the catch? Memory. 

For a 70B model at FP16 with 8K context, KV cache runs ~2.5 GB per request. Multiply by concurrent users and you see why techniques like PagedAttention (treating KV cache like virtual memory, 2-4x throughput boost) and GQA (4-8x cache reduction, used in Llama 3 and Mistral) aren't optional - they're table stakes. (I have talked about Memory bottle neck in post 14 of this series, added in comments too) 

The takeaway for leaders building LLM products: KV caching isn't an optimization you get to later. The time is now!! It's a design decision that shapes your architecture, hardware budget, and unit economics from day one. The teams that treat inference efficiency as a first-class problem are the ones shipping AI products that actually make money.

author: Rishabh Misra
subtitle: Principal ML Lead - Generative Personalization | ML Book and Course Author | Researcher - LLMs & RecSys - 1k+ citations | Advisory @ Startups | Featured in TechCrunch, NBC, TheSun | AI Consultant
content:
You don't need more H100s. 

You need a better mental model for how GPU memory actually works.

Most teams routinely see north of 50% GPU memory go to waste because they treat memory like a physical bucket.

It's not. It's virtual. Here's the mental model: 
→ The traditional setup forces you to pre-allocate one contiguous GPU memory chunk per request. 
→ This makes your GPU memory look like a Swiss Cheese, leading to frequent OOMs even if free memory exists. 
→ PagedAttention (the core of vLLM) fixes this by breaking the KV cache into small, non-contiguous pages or blocks.
→ This allows your prompt’s data to be scattered across GPU memory. A Block Table maps it together at runtime. 

Same data, a fraction of the waste.

The real breakthrough isn't even fitting more data; it's how we can process it now. PagedAttention unlocks *Continuous Batching*
→ When a request finishes, its memory is freed instantly. 
→ A new request can be inserted into the batch immediately.
→ GPU cores stay at high utilization, processing a constant stream of tokens.

For your team, this logical mapping optimization of physical silicon can easily translate into 2–3× inference cost differences.

This is Part 3 of a deep dive into inference optimization. Next up: I will break down how we can cut the model, which is still 100GB+, by ~70% using Quantization to optimize the GPU memory further.

Curious: in your production inference stack, what breaks first - KV cache growth, memory fragmentation, or tail latency under load?

author: Eric Chung
subtitle: VP of AI Computing at NVIDIA
content:
I often get asked how NVFP4 differs from MXFP4, so here is a quick primer.

FP4 is defined as E2M1: 1 sign bit, 2 exponent bits, and 1 mantissa bit. That gives 15 unique values: ±0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, and 6.

On its own, that is very limited range and precision. So how does FP4 work at all for real tensor math?

The answer is that deep learning is surprisingly tolerant to approximation. Exact arithmetic is rarely required.

To use FP4, we quantize a higher-precision tensor, typically BF16 or FP32, by factoring it into two components: an E2M1 value x shared scale factor.

For example, take an FP32 block like [0, 12, 32, 48]. If we choose a scale factor of 8, the rescaled values become [0, 1.5, 4, 6], which fits cleanly into the E2M1 range. We then store the FP4 values plus one shared scale, achieving a large compression win. In practice the numbers are not this neat, so some rounding error is expected, but accuracy generally holds up well.

So what is the difference between MXFP4 and NVFP4?  In microscaled formats, the scale factor itself is quantized, which introduces another source of error.

MXFP4 uses a power-of-two scale. Values are reconstructed as E2M1 times 2 raised to an exponent. This is efficient in hardware, but it limits which scales can be represented.

NVFP4, first appearing in Blackwell GPUs, introduces a non power-of-two scale stored in FP8 (E4M3). Values are reconstructed as E2M1 times an FP8 scale, giving much finer control over scaling and significantly lower quantization error across blocks. The attached plot shows how this difference manifests as block amaxes move across the number line.

author: Victoria Slocum
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer @ Weaviate
content:
𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀 aren't an afterthought or extra credit anymore - they're core architectural patterns that determine whether your agentic system is safe to deploy.

So here are four different workflow patterns that we've seen implemented in production systems:

1️⃣ 𝗔𝗱𝗮𝗽𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗙𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗟𝗼𝗼𝗽𝘀
Worker agents execute tasks → Supervisor evaluates → Rewards Service updates policies → Guidelines adjust → Workers improve over time. This creates a continuous learning cycle where the system reinforces effective behaviors and discourages risky ones. It's reward-driven learning that improves with iteration.

2️⃣ 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
The centralized Supervisor assigns tasks, compares outputs against application guidelines, and if errors are detected, engages alternative workers. The best validated result gets returned. This prevents bad outputs from ever reaching users.

3️⃣ 𝗛𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗟𝗼𝗼𝗽
For sensitive domains (medical diagnosis, legal review, financial approvals), agents generate preliminary responses but humans validate before execution. The workflow automatically pauses for expert review, then resumes once approved.

4️⃣ 𝗘𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗽
Critical for high-risk environments like trading systems. Agent 1 collects market data → LLM processes signals → Agent 2 evaluates conditions → if anomalies or risks detected, execution halts immediately. Consider a trading bot with access to a volatility API showing VIX at 42 (extreme market stress). Even if the bot generates an aggressive trade recommendation, the evaluator independently verifies: "Given current volatility, does this make sense?" If not, it blocks the action entirely.

𝗕𝗲𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 is the underlying philosophy here - a three-step loop of scoring, feedback, and correction. The evaluator doesn't just measure performance after the fact. It actively intervenes: triggering rollbacks for bad transactions, halting workflows propagating incorrect data, or routing edge cases to human reviewers.

This is especially important when agents interact with volatile external states - market conditions, API health, system load. The evaluator provides a sanity check to ensure the model correctly interpreted the signals it was given, not just that it generated understandable text.

The goal isn't catching every possible failure upfront (impossible). It's building systems that detect problems as they happen, understand what went wrong, and automatically correct course before damage propagates.

author: Parth Kalkar
subtitle: Builder | Full-Stack AI/ML Engineer | LLMs, Agentic Systems & On-Device Intelligence | ex AI @ BMW
content:
I built a State-of-the-Art LLM this morning. (quite literally at 4 am)

I didn't use a GPU. I didn't write a training loop. I didn't spend a dollar.

I just *Merged* two existing models.
(yes, I call it the "Frankenstein" way of building models that anyone can build from their basements or attic)

- For years, we thought the only way to get a smarter model was to Train it (expensive) or Fine-tune it (still expensive).

- But if you try to simply "average" the weights of a Coding Model and a Chat Model, you usually get a brain-damaged model.

Why? "Interference".
If Model A wants a weight to go up (+5) and Model B wants it to go down (-5), averaging them gives you Zero. They cancel each other out, and the model forgets everything. 

(so this idea kinda failed, but I found something cooler)

The Lesson:
I used *TIES-Merging* (Trim, Elect Sign, Merge). It proves that it can be equal if you know how to handle the math.

It fixes the "Frankenstein" problem by treating weights like votes.

1. Trim: It ignores the bottom 70% of parameter changes (noise). It only cares about the "big moves."
2. Elect Sign: If Model A says "Left" and Model B says "Right," TIES doesn't compromise. It calculates the total magnitude and picks a *winner*. The loser is silenced.
3. Merge: It combines only the non-conflicting updates.

The Result:
• Skills: You get a single model that codes like DeepSeek *and* writes poetry like Llama-4.
• Cost: $0. It’s just matrix arithmetic on a CPU.
• Dominance: This is why the Open LLM Leaderboard is full of names like "Laser-Hermes" and "OpenMath-Mistral."

Stop training from scratch. Start composing. 

(this technique can truly give you the freedom to be a builder)

content:
AI inference has gone from an afterthought to a priority. In an industry dominated by training, this shift has created a whole new role: the AI performance engineer.

Though it's only been around a couple of years, the stack has already grown tremendously. Here's a breakdown of the parts at play:

Model Weights & Definition: These typically come from a model registry like Hugging Face. The definition is the architecture of the model, and the weights are the learned values.

Framework (PyTorch or Custom): Frameworks provide an API to turn a definition into a working model and handle moving weights to devices. Modern frameworks also include a graph compiler for operator fusion.

Engine (Max, VLLM, TensorRT):  Here is where LLM-specific optimizations take place. Many optimizations revolve around attention. Things like KV caching, custom attention kernels, and prefix caching are all focused on making attention less expensive.

Cloud Serving (Dynamo, Mammoth, BentoML): This layer manages the workloads the engine will handle. It handles routing, load balancing, and autoscaling, while also providing observability for future improvements.

With this growing complexity comes new roles and opportunities. Engineers are needed to manage every part of the stack, I myself am a kernel engineer, but roles exist for improving the engines, serving, compilers, etc. 

The field has truly blossomed into something expansive, and there's no better time to get involved than now!

I just published a deep-dive into CUDA occupancy that challenges this assumption. Here's what I discovered:
The Real Bottleneck: GPU Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) are constrained by FOUR resources simultaneously:
Thread slots
Warp slots
Register file
Shared memory
Maxing out one doesn't mean you can max out the others.
The Surprise: In my tiled matrix multiplication kernel, despite using 39 registers per thread (considered high), I achieved 98.18% occupancy. How?
Because warp availability, NOT register pressure, was the limiting factor.
Key Insight: High resource usage ≠ poor performance. Understanding WHICH resource is your bottleneck is what separates good CUDA code from great CUDA code.
In the article, I walk through: ✅ Complete tiled MatMul implementation with L2 cache optimization ✅ Nsight Compute profiling results ✅ Why occupancy is a multi-dimensional problem ✅ How to identify your actual performance limiter

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
Blockwise Quantization is the secret ingredient behind training and serving 8, 4 bit models. Let’s understand the fundamentals of how it works.

❓ Why do we need it?

The implication of a lower dtype is that the absolute number of unique values that we can represent goes down. A 4 bit format can only represent 16 unique numbers ( 2 raised to the power 4).

However, both the weights and activations of a model have a much larger range and precision of representable values. 

Quantization tries to preserve the range of values by computing a scaling factor. For e.g. say that I have a vector [24, 12, 3, 1.5] I want to represent it in FP4 (E2M1).

The unique set of values in FP4 are 0, ±0.5, ±1, ±1.5, ±2, ±3, ±4, ±6

Quantization Algo:

𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗲_𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 = 𝗺𝗮𝘅(𝘃𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿) / 𝗺𝗮𝘅_𝗳𝗽𝟰 = 𝟮𝟰 / 𝟲 = 𝟰

𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 = 𝗻𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁_𝗳𝗽𝟰(𝘃𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿/ 𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗲) = 𝗻𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁_𝗳𝗽𝟰([𝟲, 𝟯, 𝟬.𝟳𝟱, 𝟬.𝟯𝟳𝟱]) = [𝟲, 𝟯, 𝟭, 𝟬.𝟱]

𝗱𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 = 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 × 𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗲 = [𝟮𝟰, 𝟭𝟮, 𝟰, 𝟮]

Note that the scale factor is stored in a high precision format like FP32.

𝗤𝘂𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿 = [𝟬, 𝟬, 𝟭, 𝟬.𝟱]

The scale factor depends on the max value and if the max value is an outlier it can lead to large quantization errors.

🧱 Block Quantization

Instead of taking the max over the whole vector let’s say we break it down to two blocks

[24, 12] and [3, 1.5]

Block 1: [24, 12] → scale = 24/6 = 4  → fp4: [6, 3] → dequant: [24, 12] 
Block 2: [3, 1.5] → scale = 3/6 = 0.5 → fp4: [6, 3] → dequant: [3, 1.5] 

 Voilà we have no quantization error!

👇🏽 Implications

It’s well known that most LLMs have a few outlier weights/activations that have a massive impact on the performance of the model. By using block-wise quantization we preserve the locality of the outliers via the scale factors of the blocks they are located in, while alleviating the quantization error on weights/activations not in the block of the outlier.

Being able to represent weights and activations in lower precisions like FP8, FP4 etc. allows us to leverage NVIDIA’s FP8/FP4 tensor cores which have much higher throughput.

In practice block sizes tend to be 16/32.

If you think this is cool checkout NVFP4 which goes a step further and introduces two levels of quantization, can you guess what the second level is?

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🤔 Why do we need BOTH SFT and RL?

This paper analyzes why the SFT-then-RL recipe works so well, going beyond "accuracy went up". The main author is my colleague Kohsei Matsutani and it's going to ICLR. :)

Trajectory-level analysis:

→ RL reduces incorrect reasoning trajectories while SFT increases correct ones. When you apply RL from a base model, you dramatically reduce the diversity of wrong paths. SFT does the opposite: it teaches new correct solution strategies but keeps incorrect paths around.

→ The two-stage SFT→RL pipeline is not arbitrary. SFT first expands the set of correct paths (improving Pass@k), then RL prunes the incorrect ones (improving Pass@1).

Step-level analysis:

→ RL consolidates reasoning functionality into a few critical "hub" steps. It makes the model rely on a small number of important reasoning steps. SFT does the opposite, spreading functionality across many steps.

→ RL reduces correct trajectories too, which explains a known phenomenon. Yue et al. (https://lnkd.in/e_GSGpK4, 2025) showed that base models eventually catch up to RL models on Pass@k at large k. This paper provides the mechanistic reason: RL squeezes all trajectories, including correct ones. The base model's latent capabilities are still there; RL just concentrates probability mass on fewer paths.

It's a cool analysis that supports our intuition about how SFT and RL work. The step-level reasoning graph analysis goes even a step further and provides useful insights for RLVR.

author: Toviah Moldwin
subtitle: Computational neuroscience, Data Science, Machine Learning
content:
Lots of people (myself included) have trouble understanding why transformer architectures directly add token embeddings to the position embeddings. It's weird to just directly add the representation of the content - i.e. the token embeddings, with the representation of the content's position within its context. (Note: there are techniques like RoPE that try to get around this, however here I'll deal with the more basic strategy of addition.)

Together with Raneem Mahajne, we trained a small transformer on a simple next-token prediction task. We gave the transformer a sequence of random digits, occasionally interspersed with a + sign. Whenever the + sign appeared, the next number would have to be the same as the *most recent even number*. 

For example, if we have the sequence 3 1 2 7 5 +, the next number would have to be a 2. 

Because we used an embedding dimension of 2 for both the positions and the tokens, we can directly visualize the token embeddings, the position embeddings, and their sum, for every possible token and position combination.

In the token embedding space, the transformer learned to separate out the even numbers from the odd numbers, and it also learned to separate the + sign from everything else. Interestingly, the model also decided to smush all the odd numbers together, while maintaining some space between each even digit, presumably because once a + sign appears, it becomes necessary to predict a specific even number. 

In the position embedding space, the transformer learned to correctly order the positions along a curve. Position ordering is important for this task, because in order to know what the "most recent" even number is, you need to have a sense of ordering.

When the token and position information are summed, the structure of *both* the token embedding space and position embedding space are preserved. The even numbers remain separated from each other and the odd numbers, the odd numbers remained smushed together, and the "+" token occupies its own area of space. But now, for each token, we see a local structure based on the curve of ordered positions. 

Part of the reason why this occurs is because the magnitudes of the token embeddings along one of th axes are ~10x larger than the magnitudes of the position embeddings, allowing the 'macro' structure to be dominated by the tokens, while the 'micro' structure is determined by the positions.

In other words, summing the position information and token information doesn't just mix things haphazardly, it actually retains the geometric structure of both by using a different scale to encode 'what' and 'where'.

author: Lyudmil Pelov
subtitle: Senior Principal Product Manager | Generative AI & Agents
content:
Never trust LLM structured output. ✅🤖
 …even when you think you do.

My app was working perfectly for weeks structured JSON, streaming responses, everything smooth.

Until one day, the client suddenly failed parsing one of the responses.

The reason?

A tiny malformed generation in the structured output from the LLM (see screenshot 👇). Nothing dramatic. Not common. But enough to break the flow.

Lesson learned:
Even if you enforce structured outputs and schemas, you should still assume you'll get occasional malformed generations from the LLM.

In my case, the best solution was client-side guardrails:
- detect parse failures
- recover gracefully (retry / fallback / sanitize)

Why not fix it fully in the backend?
Because doing heavy validation / repair server-side adds:
- compute overhead
- extra latency
... and it gets more complex with structured streaming.

You learn something every day 🙂

Curious: how do you handle malformed structured outputs in production? Do you validate server-side, client-side, or both?

author: Emilio Andere
subtitle: Co-Founder and CEO at Wafer - Hardware Acceleration for AI
content:
what if you could bring up a complete PyTorch backend for a new chip overnight?

Meta recently published TritorX - a system that generates functionally correct Triton kernels for their custom ASIC (MTIA). they get LLMs to write kernels, but optimize for coverage instead of performance.

to give a bit of context:

enabling a new PyTorch backend is non-trivial. PyTorch supports roughly 3,500+ operators, and new accelerators must implement/lower a large subset of these (often hundreds of kernels) before common models can run with basic functional parity. this can make backend bring-up a multi-month to multi-year engineering effort. 

TritorX attacks this bottleneck by using an FSM-based agent (Finite State Machine-based agent) instead of the usual free-form tool calling. the LLM iterates through a state machine: generate kernel → lint → compile → test → debug → repeat. they explicitly chose FSM over fully agentic because it's more predictable and debuggable in production.

they also don't just feed the LLM all available MTIA documentation. they just feed it PyTorch docstrings. surprisingly, the model learns hardware quirks (32-byte alignment, scatter store restrictions) autonomously by only using compiler errors and crash dumps.

TritorX generated 481 ATen operators at 84.7% coverage, passing 20,000+ OpInfo tests. a full sweep takes about 2 hours on 200 MTIA devices. 80%+ of required operators worked out of the box. 

they also ran it on simulation for future hardware and hit 73% coverage on chips that don't exist yet!

importantly, TritorX isn’t validated only on unit tests: Meta decomposes real production models (NanoGPT, DLRM, and large-scale recommendation systems) into their individual operator invocations and feeds these real model inputs directly into the validation loop. this not only enables backend bring-up without full end-to-end model support, but also matures previously generated kernels to specific production workloads, refining general operators to reliably support the exact shapes, dtypes, and argument patterns that the real production models exercise.

this is an exciting early update for alternative hardware accelerators. more cost efficient bring-up gives more opportunity for alternative accelerators to compete with NVIDIA.

author: Emilio Andere
subtitle: Co-Founder and CEO at Wafer - Hardware Acceleration for AI
content:
Triton compiles your Python kernel through 5 stages before it hits the GPU. this is what happens at each step:

stage 1: Python AST → Triton IR (TTIR)

the @triton.jit decorator triggers a walk of your function's abstract syntax tree. this produces Triton IR, an MLIR-based representation that's machine-independent. your tl.load becomes tt.load, your tl.store becomes tt.store. TTIR captures the tile-level semantics but knows nothing about the target GPU.

stage 2: Triton IR → Triton GPU IR (TTGIR)

this is where hardware awareness comes in. TTGIR adds layout encodings that describe how tensor elements map to threads and memory. the key layouts are:

 - blocked: each warp owns a contiguous chunk of the tensor
 - shared: data lives in GPU shared memory (LDS on AMD)
 - dot_op: optimized arrangement for feeding tensor cores
 - nvidia_mma / amd_mfma: output layouts from matrix units

TTGIR also carries metadata like compute capability, warps per CTA, and threads per warp. this stage runs the critical optimization passes: loop pipelining (overlapping memory and compute across iterations), memory coalescing (reordering accesses), prefetching (inserting async copies), and layout propagation (minimizing expensive layout conversions).

stage 3: TTGIR → LLVM IR

the GPU-aware representation gets lowered to LLVM's intermediate representation. tensor operations become loops over vector operations. memory loads become inline assembly calling the appropriate hardware instructions. pointer arithmetic gets explicit. this is still portable across backends.

stage 4: LLVM IR → device assembly

for NVIDIA: LLVM IR compiles to PTX, NVIDIA's virtual ISA. PTX is text-based and human-readable. for AMD: LLVM IR compiles to AMDGCN, AMD's GPU assembly format.

 stage 5: assembly → binary

for NVIDIA: ptxas compiles PTX to cubin, the actual GPU binary. for AMD: lld links AMDGCN into hsaco. these binaries get cached so recompilation only happens when kernel parameters change.

if you want to go deeper:
- PyTorch blog on compilation stages: https://lnkd.in/ei3H359t
- Triton MLIR dialects docs: https://lnkd.in/erC6EKWY
- AMD's Triton optimization guide: https://lnkd.in/eCDS2nWY
- IBM's "Anatomy of a Triton Attention Kernel": https://lnkd.in/e8TNTJze

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
Replacing the up-projection layer in the MLP of Transformers with an Embedding Layer 🤯. If you’re interested in arch changes this post is for you!

📘 Background Context
The FFN/MLP of a Transformer layer consists of two linear layers and an activation function. The W_up linear layer up-projects the hidden state from size H to size I, where H > 1.

The shape of W_up is [H, I], so has H * I params per layer.

🥼 Scaling Transformers with Embedding Modules (STEM)

In STEM the authors replace W_up with an I sized vector T_i for each input token. 

T_i is obtained by mapping the token id T to an embedding layer of shape [Vocab size, I].

Since we know the token ids that need to be looked up before the start of a forward pass, rather than loading the whole embedding layer into GPU memory, the embeddings for each token can be lazily loaded based on the input token ids.

😌 Benefits

Lazy asynchronous loading/prefetching, coupled with LRU caching leveraging the Zipfian distribution of tokens/words results in STEM consuming less VRAM.

We also reduce FLOPs since multiplications with W_up (shape [H, I]) are replaced with multiplications with a single embedding of shape [1, I] for a given token.

Simpler to enforce token steering, by substituting the embedding lookup of token T with that of the steering token S.

No complexities of token routing, expert-to-expert communication and data transfers etc.

Improved downstream task performance.

🎁 Wrap Up
The main downside of the paper is that they only tested their approach on models between 350M and 1B params, so we don’t know how well it scales to larger models.

author: Pere Martra
subtitle: AI Research Engineer | Structured Pruning & LLM Efficiency | Fairness-Aware Optimization | Author “Rearchitecting LLMs” @Manning | 2K GitHub ⭐
content:
Thanks to a post by Sophia Yang, Ph.D. I came across the paper where Mistral AI presents how they created their Ministral 3 model family. 

I started reading it a few days ago with caution and ended up really excited. The process that Mistral followed is essentially the same one I've been detailing in Tailoring LLM Architectures. 

The main approach of both methods is to create models through Pruning + Knowledge Distillation.

But there are some differences that I want to detail.

🔶 Depth Pruning. To decide which layers to remove, we use a dynamic method that requires only one forward pass; we use different metrics.
    ▪️ Mistral: Norm ratio. They measure the magnitude of change that the layer introduces (||output|| / ||input||).
    ▪️ TLM: Cosine similarity. I measure the direction of change. Even if there's a lot of change in magnitude, if the semantic direction doesn't change significantly, I can discard the layer.
    ▪️Differences: I think both methods will give very similar results, especially on large and varied datasets. The biggest differences can occur when adapting models to a very specific domain or task, but Mistral doesn't deal with that and I do.

 🔷  Width Pruning MLP. We both work with GLU structures, the one Mistral uses and almost all current transformers. However, there are differences in how we measure which parts of the model to preserve.
    ▪️Mistral: Purely activation-based method. They calculate the absolute value of activations in the two layers that modulate information input (gate and up) and remove the corresponding dimensions in the output layer (down_proj).
    ▪️TLM: I use hybrid approach: static Peak-to-Peak magnitude to preserve the structural importance of all three layers and multiply it by the L2 norm of activations at the down_proj input.
    ▪️Difference: Mistral's method is designed to work with representative calibration datasets, while mine may works better with small specialized datasets, by introducing structural preservation that prevents catastrophic model degradation when removing neurons that don't activate in specific tasks.

I'll talk more about the KD process later, but we also have many similarities.
In summary. 

‼️ I'm really happy to see that the way of working in Mistral's labs has many similarities with what I'm teaching in TLM. ‼️

P.S. The paper leaves me with a list of future work that honestly I don't think I'll be able to do in the short term! But I'd love to be able to make comparisons of both methods, especially the width pruning one. Maybe I'll implement it in OptiFair so you can prepare your models using the same implementation as Mistral.

I'll leave links to TLM and OptiFair in the comments.

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🌍 TranslateGemma: 4B, 12B, 27B translation models with OCR

Google introduces TranslateGemma, a family of open-weight translation models (4B, 12B, 27B) that distill Gemini's translation capabilities into the Gemma 3 architecture through a two-stage SFT + RL pipeline.

→ The 12B model outperforms the 27B Gemma 3 baseline on WMT24++. This 2x efficiency gain comes from fine-tuning Gemma 3 for this specific task. Another good sign for small language models!

→ Synthetic data generation uses Gemini to translate MADLAD-400, generating up to 10K examples per language pair. The training mixture includes 30% general instruction data to maintain chatbot capabilities.

→ The RL reward combines MetricX-QE (learned regression metric), AutoMQM (span-level error predictor), ChrF (character n-gram overlap), a naturalness autorater using the policy model as LLM-as-judge, and a generalist reward model to prevent capability regression. Token-level and sequence-level rewards are combined during advantage computation.

→ Human evaluation on WMT25 confirms the automatic metrics for most directions, but Japanese→English shows a regression due to named entity errors. This is a classic failure mode when optimizing for learned metrics that do not penalize proper noun mistakes heavily enough.

→ Multimodal translation survives the specialization process. Performance on the Vistra image translation benchmark actually improves without any multimodal-specific fine-tuning, suggesting the text translation improvements transfer to OCR-style tasks.

It's a well-executed distillation recipe with an interesting reward ensemble design that addresses a known weakness of pure MQM optimization. Note that it doesn't seem perfect yet, since the Japanese→English regression suggests blind spots for named entities. I would've liked comparisons with recent strong baselines and bigger models to showcase the efficiency of this specialization. Finally, it's too bad the model is English-centric and uses this language as the main pivot. Probably a data-related issue, but it would've been neat to leverage the latent representations to perform any-to-any translations.

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
A simple normalization trick on your reward scores can boost the performance of your reasoning model. GDPO > GRPO.

❓ What's the problem?
When you use multiple reward functions to train an RL model, GRPO sums up the rewards from each function before normalizing them to compute the Advantage Scores.

However, summing up the rewards fudges the signal of individual rewards leading to missed nuance. This is because each reward function can have a different mean/std compared to the aggregated reward.

This is illustrated in the top-half of the image shown below. Say, you have two rollouts r1 and r2, with their total rewards represented as (rollout 1 total reward, rollout 2 total reward). GRPO will only have two unique sets of advantage scores post-normalization.

💡 GDPO
GDPO's simple solution is to:

1. Normalize each of the rewards from each reward function individually. (group-level normalization)
2. Sum up the normalized reward scores for each rollout.
3. Obtain the advantage scores by normalizing the summed up rewards using batch mean and batch std.

This is shown in the second half of the image.

🎁 Wrap Up
This simple solution leads to having more distinct advantage scores and yields improvements in RL training across a range of tasks.

GDPO has also been implemented by the authors and HF team in TRL. To use it all you need to do is set the multi_objective_aggregation flag to "normalize_then_sum".

For more read: https://lnkd.in/dr84H3Vb

author: Elie Bakouch
subtitle: Research at Prime Intellect, prev: Hugging Face
content:
Mistral just dropped the Ministral 3 tech report, and it's a great example of how you don't need massive compute to build competitive small models. they trained their 3B/8B/14B models on only 1-3 trillion tokens. the trick? smart pruning + distillation

the approach is pretty clean: start with their 24B model, progressively prune it down to smaller sizes, then use the original model as a teacher to recover performance through distillation. each smaller model is initialized from the pruned weights of the previous one, but they all learn from the same 24B instruct teacher

the pruning itself is interesting. they prune depth, hidden dim and ffn dim, each with a different method. for layers they look at how much each layer transforms its input (output/input norm ratio). for hidden dimensions they use PCA to find the important directions since features aren't axis-aligned, then prune the low variance ones. for FFN they look at the gated activation score since in SwiGLU a high value can still be killed by a low gate

they have some cool ablations too. using an instruct model as teacher works better than base for STEM tasks. and they show a capacity gap effect where a bigger teacher can actually hurt, Medium 3 (larger model but size is not public) as teacher performed worse than Small 3.1 for pretraining but better for post-training

solid paper with good ablations, bravo Mistral AI!

🚨One of the first things I learned when starting to optimize LLMs is that the starting point matters a lot. 

When you make an LLM smaller by removing Transformer blocks, it's crucial to know which ones contribute the least to your use case or data.

An example with Gemma-270M, same goal (remove 4 layers), dramatically different results:
📊 Data-Driven Strategy: Layers [9,8,14,16] → +840% perplexity 
📊 Last 4 layers: Layers [14-17] → +1,835% perplexity 
📊 Last 4 protecting final ones: Layers [12-15] → +3,402% perplexity 
📊 Data-driven consecutive central block: +3,507% perplexity

The difference: 4.2x more degradation = extra training days in KD

The analysis process with your own dataset is one line of code using optipfair and needs just a single forward pass through your data (fast).

That translates to:
⚡ Fewer KD epochs needed
💰 Fewer GPU hours
🎯 Better final model
🚀 Faster time-to-production

The lesson:
Not all layers contribute equally. A data-driven analysis can save you days of training and hundreds/thousands or millions of Euros in GPU.

author: Sriram Bharadwaj
subtitle: Making RL go Brr || Dissecting AI ||
content:
Importance of Hardware aware optimization:- Why does a "small" SOTA model crash where a "big" dumb one succeeds on on-device hardware?

In deploying deep learning models to the edge, specifically on the Imagination Technologies PowerVR DXT GPU architecture (Pixel 10 Pro), I encountered a counter-intuitive bottleneck where "smaller" models fail while "larger" models succeed. 

This phenomenon is not driven by total parameter count or aggregate VRAM availability, but by the specific limitations of the Uniform Buffer Object (UBO) size, which is capped at 16KB on this hardware. ( A100 has a cap of 64KB for instance)

MobileNet V3, despite being optimized for FLOPs, utilizes complex, deep layer structures with fused operations (e.g., Squeeze-and-Excitation blocks). These fused layers frequently require a constant set exceeding the 4,096-float capacity of the UBO for a single dispatch. This necessitates a fallback to Shader Storage Buffer Objects (SSBOs), incurring a significant latency penalty due to global memory access, or results in a VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_DEVICE_MEMORY failure if not properly managed.

Conversely, architectures with higher parameter counts but simpler, uniform layer definitions (such as VGG-style blocks) fit within the L1-adjacent UBO cache, allowing for uninterrupted, high throughput execution.

Conclusion: Efficient edge inference requires a departure from minimizing parameter counts in isolation. It demands a hardware-aware optimization strategy that respects the physical constraints of the instruction pipeline and memory hierarchy specifically the limitations of on-chip SRAM versus global DRAM.

author: Pere Martra
subtitle: AI Research Engineer | Structured Pruning & LLM Efficiency | Fairness-Aware Optimization | Author “Rearchitecting LLMs” @Manning | 2K GitHub ⭐
content:
L2 norm vs Peak-to-Peak Magnitude for width pruning in GLU architectures.
Spoiler: There's no comparison.

I just integrated L2 norm (the academic standard) into OptiPFair for neuron selection in static width pruning. 

The results on Llama-3.2-1B are conclusive:
With 10% pruning: 
→ PPM: +54% degradation in perplexity ✅ 
→ L2: +10,067% degradation in perplexity ❌

What's happening?
L2 norm measures the Euclidean magnitude of weights - the standard metric in pruning papers. But in GLU architectures (Llama, QWen, Gemma...), where you have multiplicative gate mechanisms, L2 produces total model collapse.

PPM (Peak-to-Peak Magnitude) measures the dynamic range of weights: it identifies which neurons have the largest outliers and greatest potential to produce strong activations. Preserving neurons that, when activated, are crucial for model coherence.

Result: 
→ PPM preserves critical model capabilities while allowing aggressive pruning. 
→ L2 eliminates neurons critical for coherence.

This is exactly why OptiPFair is specialized in modern GLU architectures. Not all metrics are equivalent when your goal is maintaining production performance.

Reproducible experiments in the Llama-3.2 expansion analysis paper notebook.

optipfair library: https://lnkd.in/dgiJjiAQ

Notebook with comparision: https://lnkd.in/dyUk56s2

author: Vikas Rajpurohit
subtitle: AI/ML Engineer | GenAI @ Nomura
content:
“5 𝗚𝗣𝗨 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 > 𝗯𝘂𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗚𝗣𝗨.”

𝗟𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 5 (𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘁 2): 𝗚𝗣𝗨𝘀
Once you understand GPUs, you hit reality:
𝗠𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗚𝗣𝗨𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗻’𝘁 𝘀𝗹𝗼𝘄 — 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆’𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴.

The Roofline Model shows a hard limit: performance depends on compute per byte moved. Low operational intensity → 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆-𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱. More FLOPs won’t help.

𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹 𝗱𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 worsens this.
GPUs execute threads in warps (SIMT). If threads branch differently, the GPU runs both paths sequentially. No errors. Just 𝗹𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗺 and more waiting.

Fast GPU code favors uniform, high-intensity computation.
🔹 𝗟𝗼𝘄 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀𝗻’𝘁 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆 — 𝗶𝘁’𝘀 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗯𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘄𝗶𝗱𝘁𝗵
Modern GPUs are built for 𝗺𝗶𝘅𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻.
FP16 / BF16 handle matrix multiplies and most pointwise ops.
FP32 is reserved for reductions (softmax, normalization, loss) to avoid numerical drift.
Lower precision → smaller tensors, less memory traffic, faster execution.
Precision is a 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻, not just a numerical one.

🔹 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻: 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵
Every kernel launch reads from global memory, computes, and writes back.
sin²(x) + cos²(x) naively launches 5 kernels.
𝗙𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗱? One kernel. 𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗽.
That’s why operator fusion matters — and why tools like torch.compile exist.
Not to be clever. But to 𝗰𝘂𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰.

🔹 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴
Storing activations is expensive. Reading them back is worse.
Stacking 3 sigmoids naively causes 8 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘀/𝘄𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀 across forward + backward.
Recompute activations during backward instead of storing them.
Same math. Far less memory traffic.
On GPUs, recomputing is often cheaper than remembering.

🔹 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗮𝗹𝗲𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴: 𝗗𝗥𝗔𝗠 𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗺𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀
Global memory is read in 𝗯𝘂𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 (typically ≥128 bytes).
If all 32 threads in a warp access the same burst → 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗗𝗥𝗔𝗠 𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁.
If not → many requests.
That’s memory coalescing.
This is why access patterns matter more than intuition.
Matrix multiplies live or die by this detail.

🔹 𝗧𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴: 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗯𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗚𝗣𝗨 𝗮𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺𝘀
Tiling cuts large tensors into small blocks, loads them into fast shared memory, and reuses them before touching global memory again.
𝗡𝗼𝗻-𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗺𝘂𝗹 reads each element 𝗡 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲𝘀.
𝗧𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗺𝘂𝗹 reads each element 𝗡/𝗧 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲𝘀 — a 𝗧× 𝗿𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 in memory traffic.
The catch?
Tile size, alignment, and coalescing decide performance.

This is where performance engineering becomes 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭 engineering.
📺 Lecture link: https://lnkd.in/dNq-4fpg

author: Tom Aarsen
subtitle: 🤗 Sentence Transformers & NLTK maintainer, MLE @ Hugging Face
content:
You can perform 200ms search over 40 million texts using just a CPU server, 8GB of RAM, and 40GB of disk space. The trick: Binary search with int8 rescoring. Details:

This is the inference strategy:
1. Embed your query using a dense embedding model into a 'standard' fp32 embedding
2. Quantize the fp32 embedding to binary: 32x smaller
3. Use an approximate (or exact) binary index to retrieve e.g. 40 documents (~20x faster than a fp32 index)
4. Load int8 embeddings for the 40 top binary documents from disk.
5. Rescore the top 40 documents using the fp32 query embedding and the 40 int8 embeddings
6. Sort the 40 documents based on the new scores, grab the top 10
7. Load the titles/texts of the top 10 documents

This requires:
- Embedding all of your documents once, and using those embeddings for:
- A binary index, I used a IndexBinaryFlat for exact and IndexBinaryIVF for approximate
- A int8 "view", i.e. a way to load the int8 embeddings from disk efficiently given a document ID

Instead of having to store fp32 embeddings, you only store binary index (32x smaller) and int8 embeddings (4x smaller). Beyond that, you only keep the binary index in memory, so you're also saving 32x on memory compared to a fp32 search index.

By loading e.g. 4x as many documents with the binary index and rescoring those with int8, you restore ~99% of the performance of the fp32 search, compared to ~97% when using purely the binary index: https://lnkd.in/edc9yM6W

I've created a demo that allows you to test this technique on 40 million texts from Wikipedia! Give it a try here: https://lnkd.in/ebNSHA4y

It would be simple to add a sparse component here as well: e.g. bm25s for a BM25 variant or an inference-free SparseEncoder with e.g. 'splade-index'. 
In short: your retrieval doesn't need to be so expensive!

get faster moe inference in transformers by changing how the matmuls are executed

· batched_mm is faster than eager because it parallelizes work
· faster for small inputs because it doesn't generate enough work to offset extra overhead of grouping tokens
· grouped_mm is better for large inputs because it is faster to consolidate 100 tokens into 1 matmul versus doing 100 smaller matmuls
· uses gpu more efficiently and lower memory bandwidth because W is loaded once and shared

author: Ilyas Moutawwakil
subtitle: Optimisation | GPU | PyTorch | ML | Kernels, Engineer @HuggingFace 🤗
content:
TL;DR: one MoE backend isn’t enough, but combining them gets you up to 12× faster end-to-end generation 🚀

In my last post, I showed how the new torch._grouped_mm is a very strong kernel for MoEs, delivering excellent performance in many settings. However, it’s still suboptimal in some scenarios, especially for small inputs and very sparse MoEs, where batched_mm can better exploit the memory-boundness and low compute utilization by duplicating expert weights and trading memory for faster execution.

I had my doubts about whether this would hold in real workloads, so I rewrote the benchmarks to look at prefill, decode, and end-to-end generation latency. The numbers were exactly what I expected: using either grouped_mm or batched_mm does improve generation, but a closer look shows that each one exceled at a different stage 🤔

So I went ahead and opened a new PR in Transformers to use different expert implementations at different stages of inference:
👉 grouped_mm for prefill
 👉 batched_mm for decode

The result? A consistent best-of-both-worlds approach with highly optimized inference, reaching up to 12× end-to-end speedup compared to the previous all-eager implementation 🤯

Why and how this works ?
- Prefill benefits from grouped_mm, which scales extremely well with prompt size.
- Decode benefits from batched_mm, which shines on small, sparse workloads and is extremely tensor-pure and Dynamo-friendly.
- Because batched_mm has no graph breaks or custom operators, we can enable optimizations that were previously unavailable: static cache, fullgraph, max-autotune, and CUDA graphs ⚒️

If you’re running MoEs in production or optimizing for inference efficiency, this setup gets you close to peak hardware utilization while preserving the flexibility and accessibility of Transformers.

Benchmarks, micro-benchmarks, and PR/repro scripts are in the first comment 👇

author: Pere Martra
subtitle: AI Research Engineer | Structured Pruning & LLM Efficiency | Fairness-Aware Optimization | Author “Rearchitecting LLMs” @Manning | 2K GitHub ⭐
content:
"What are you doing now?" 

That's the question my former colleagues from the bank ask me the most.
 
And honestly, it's not easy to explain. I don't do RAG. I don't implement agent frameworks (with nuances, I'm starting Open Source agent migration projects). 

I create specialized model families from LLMs. 

📅 This morning I started with a client who has a classic dilemma: they have a fine-tuned model that works well, but... 
→ They need it to respond faster 
→ They want a version that runs on edge devices 
→ They can't lose quality My job: turn THEIR model into a FAMILY of models adapted to the same domain and task. 

Today I spent the ENTIRE day playing with toy models and synthetic data generated by the base model. Why? Because before touching the client's model (which is 20x larger), I need to validate the complete process. 

Take a small model. Remove 30% of its transformer blocks (depth pruning). Test different knowledge recovery methods The numbers don't lie (see image): 
→ Without recovery: the model collapses (perplexity of 881) 
→ With my KD approach: 95.2% recovery in 30 minutes 
→ Only 3 training epochs 

What's interesting here is that NOT all methods work the same:
Uniform + Logits-only: 92.6% recovery
Last-Layer + Logits: 92.6% recovery
Last-Layer + Features (Cosine) 92.5 (sor
Advanced KD (Skew KLD + FDD): 95.2% recovery 

Now it's time to create the adapted base model for the client. 

The real process will be: 

→ Analyze which layers the model uses less in THEIR specific task 
→ Specific vs empirical pruning (contrast both) 
→ Minimum target: 98% capacity recovery. 

What follows will be days of  work: Most on this project, and the rest  I'm trying to document the ENTIRE process in my project : "Tailoring LLM Architectures". (https://lnkd.in/ehBpz7KQ)

These experiments with small models are fundamental. 

30 minutes of KD here = validation of a process that will cost hours (or days) with the client's real model. 

Each number you see in that table is an architecture decision. Each method tested is a technical hypothesis validated or discarded.

author: Anshuman Mishra
subtitle: ML @ Zomato
content:
LoRA sounds simple:

1. Add low-rank matrices
2. Train with less memory
3. Get same results

Reality:
- Learning rate needs 10x adjustment
- Layer selection changes everything
- Batch size tolerance is different
The "low-regret regime" nobody talks about:

Most teams follow the original LoRA paper:

- Attention layers only
- Rank 64
- Same hyperparameters as full fine-tuning

Thinking Machines ran 1000+ experiments across 14 models.

Every single one of these is wrong.
Finding #1: Attention-only LoRA is leaving performance on the table.

They tested:
- Attention-only (rank 256)
- MLP-only (rank 128) 
- All layers (rank 256)

MLP-only matched all-layer performance.
Attention-only underperformed despite 2x the parameters.

Why?

The MLP/MoE layers contain most of your model's parameters.
When you skip them, you're ignoring the layers that dominate the empirical neural tangent kernel.
It's like trying to steer a ship by only touching the rudder.

get my post in your inbox daily:
https://lnkd.in/g8ZJGsWj 

Finding #2: Your learning rate is probably 10x too low.

Across every model tested (Llama 3, Qwen 3):
- Optimal FullFT LR: ~2e-5
- Optimal LoRA LR: ~2e-4

The 10x ratio held constant regardless of model size.

This isn't a bug. It's the math.
The 1/r scaling factor in LoRA makes optimal LR nearly independent of rank.

Weird consequence:
Learning curves for rank 1, 16, 64, 256 are IDENTICAL for the first ~100 steps.

We thought it was a bug. It's not. It's what the math predicts.


Finding #3: Batch size kills LoRA performance differently than FullFT.

At batch size 32: LoRA ≈ FullFT
At batch size 512: LoRA falls behind

The gap grows with batch size, independent of rank.

It's a property of the BA parametrization, not capacity.
But here's the good news:

When you get these 3 things right:
1. Train ALL layers (especially MLPs)
2. Use 10x higher learning rate
3. Keep batch sizes reasonable

LoRA matches full fine-tuning performance at 67% of the compute cost.

The "low-regret regime":

LoRA works when:
- LoRA parameters > dataset information content
- Applied to all layers
- Proper hyperparameters

For typical post-training:
- Instruction tuning: ✅
- Reasoning datasets: ✅  
- RL with policy gradients: ✅ (even at rank 1!)
RL is especially interesting.

Policy gradient RL provides ~1 bit of information per episode.
Even rank-1 LoRA has 3M+ parameters for Llama-3.1-8B.

Result: LoRA matches FullFT for RL even at rank 1.

DeepSeek-R1's 5.3M episodes? Totally replicable with LoRA.
Practical takeaways:

Don't:
- Train attention-only
- Use FullFT learning rates
- Assume higher rank = better

Do:
- Train all layers (MLP + attention)
- 10x your learning rate
- Start with rank 256
- Keep batch sizes under 256


LoRA isn't "good enough."
Done right, it's equivalent.

author: Jayant Anand
subtitle: Software Engineer | Distributed Systems | C++ | IIT Dhanbad
content:
What really changes when you run your AI model with TensorRT instead of PyTorch

When you run a model in PyTorch, you’re running Python code.
That’s great for:
- experimenting
- changing models quickly
- debugging
But Python makes a lot of decisions while the model is running.

When you export the model to ONNX, something important changes:
- the model becomes a fixed graph
- the order of operations is known
- shapes are mostly fixed
In short, the model stops behaving like a script and starts behaving like a plan.

TensorRT takes this plan and prepares it before inference runs:
- it merges layers where possible
- picks the fastest GPU kernels
- decides memory usage in advance
- uses lower precision (FP16 / INT8) when allowed

At inference time, Python is out of the picture and the GPU simply executes a pre-built plan. That’s why TensorRT inference is often much faster than "plain" PyTorch.

It’s not magic!
It’s just doing the work earlier instead of at runtime.

Excited to share that my PR on optimizing the experts implementation for MoEs just got merged into 🤗 Hugging Face Transformers.

We added a new API for MoEs, with two new optimized paths to choose from: *grouped_mm* and *batched_mm*. These paths achieve substantial inference speedups compared to the previous eager implementation and behave much better under PyTorch compilation.

author: Sifal Klioui
subtitle: ML Research Engineer
content:
Why 256 + 1 = 256 (And where low-precision bites)

We often talk about float32 vs bfloat16 in terms of memory bandwidth/capacity, but we rarely visualize the "step size" trap that comes with lower precision accumulation.

Here is a quick intuition check:
In bfloat16, if you try to calculate 256 + 1, the answer is 256.

The 1 just vanishes.

Why does this happen?
It comes down to Absolute Precision vs. Relative Precision.
Floating point numbers don't have a uniform grid. The "step size" (the gap between adjacent representable numbers, formally known as Unit in the last place (ULP)) grows as the numbers get larger.

In bfloat16 (7 mantissa bits):

- Around 1, the step size is ≈ 2^7 ≈ 0.0078  
- Around 256 (= 2^8), the step size is 2

This means any number between 256 and 258 literally *cannot exist* in this format. Any update smaller than 2 is rounded away.

"But my weights are small (often normal/Laplacian distributed with a mean close to 0, and a small std), so I'm safe, right?"

Not exactly. While your weights start small, the "Vanishing Update" problem is about the ratio between the Weight and the Gradient Update.

In mixed precision training, your updates (learning_rate x gradient) are often magnitudes smaller than the weights themselves.
If your weight is 1 (step size ~0.0078) and your update is 0.001, that update is lost. Your model effectively stops learning, even though the gradients are nonzero.

The Solution: FP32 optimizer state (and sometimes master weights) ensure updates aren't lost.

This is why we use the Master Weight pattern in mixed precision training (like AMP):
1. Forward/Backward: Cast weights to bfloat16 for fast matrix multiplication.
2. Update Step: Cast gradients *up* to float32 and apply them to a FP32 Master Copy of the weights.
3. The Magic: The high precision master copy *can* represent 256.5. It accumulates the tiny changes that would otherwise be rounded to zero.

So if you see this in your code... this is why!

You'll often see specific Transformer operations cast to float32 even in a "full" bfloat16 pipeline:

- Softmax (in Attention): The exponentials in exp(x) amplify differences rapidly. In bfloat16, the limited precision (only 7 mantissa bits) causes smaller values to vanish during the summation, breaking the probability distribution.
-LayerNorm / RMSNorm: These layers compute variance (sum((x - mean)**2)). Squaring values in lower precision amplifies errors, so we cast to float32 to calculate stable statistics before casting back.

export VLLM_TORCH_PROFILER_DIR=/tmp/vllm_traces
export VLLM_RPC_TIMEOUT=1800000 # 30 min

llm.start_profile()
outputs = llm.generate(["Your prompt"])

SGLang:
# Set on BOTH server and client
export SGLANG_TORCH_PROFILER_DIR=/tmp/sglang_traces

python -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang \
  --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --num-prompts 10 --profile

Method 2: Nsight Systems (deeper)

nsys profile \
  --trace-fork-before-exec=true \
  --cuda-graph-trace=node \
  python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
   --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct # insert your model

Visualizing: Open https://ui.perfetto.dev and drag in your .json trace.

Look for the gap between prefill and decode phases. Pink slices = GPU work. White gaps = GPU idle, waiting for CPU.

author: Anshuman Mishra
subtitle: ML @ Zomato
content:
"Just use Vector Database"

Until you need:
- 100M+ vectors indexed
- <10ms p95 search latency
- $50/month (not $500/month)

Then you build your own vector database.

Here's what that actually means:

Most engineers think vector DB = 
- Install FAISS
- Wrap with Flask
- Add some metadata filtering
- Done

Reality hits around 10M vectors.

You're not building a system to search ONE index for ONE user.

You're building a system that handles THOUSANDS of concurrent searches, with filters, hybrid search, and real-time updates.

Completely different beast.

What you actually need:

> HNSW index builder that doesn't block writes
> Metadata filtering that scales with cardinality
> Distributed sharding across index size
> Real-time upsert pipeline without rebuild

And that's just the foundation.

get my posts in your inbox daily (for free) by subscribing:
https://lnkd.in/g8ZJGsWj 
now back to post -

Your <10ms p95 search breaks down as:

- Network: 2-3ms (fixed)
- Metadata pre-filter: 1-3ms (explodes with complex filters)
- ANN search: 3-8ms (depends on ef_search)
- Post-filtering: 1-2ms

You have 0-2ms buffer. "Just scale horizontally" doesn't work.

Index memory is the silent killer.
- 100M vectors × 768 dims × 4 bytes = 307GB just for vectors.
- HNSW graph adds 2-3x that.
- You're at 900GB memory for ONE index.

And you have 20 different embedding models.

"We need hybrid search with BM25 + vector + metadata filters"

Now your platform needs:
- Inverted index alongside HNSW
- Score fusion that doesn't kill latency
- Query planning for filter pushdown
- Cross-encoder reranking in <5ms

This is where 80% of custom vector DBs fail.

Use Managed DB when you're under 10M vectors, using standard embeddings, can tolerate 50ms+ latency, and cost per query is 100x raw compute.

Build your own when you have 50M+ vectors, custom embeddings, need sub-15ms p95, or when you're spending $500+/month.

Let's do the math:

> Managed DB at $70/million vectors/month + $0.10 per 1K queries:
> 100M vectors + 10M queries/month = $7,000 + $1,000 = $8,000

Your self-hosted setup with 2TB RAM machine at $1,000/month:
= $1,000 compute

But add $80K engineering, $5K/month maintenance, 8 month break-even.

Production vector DBs have four layers:

> Query parsing (filter optimization, query planning, type checking).
> Search execution (HNSW navigator, hybrid fusion, distributed scatter-gather).
> Index management (real-time updates, compaction, shard rebalancing).
> Observability (latency per component, recall metrics, memory pressure).

Most build layer 2 only.

That's it.

Building a vector db is a 8-month project with memory costs everywhere.

But at 100M+ vectors? Pays for itself in 3 months.

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
KernelEvolve is Claude Code but specializes in creating highly performant kernels. The generated kernels are being used by Meta to power their Recommendation Engines.

❓ What’s the problem?
There’s a growing number of AI chips NVIDIA, AMD, Inferentia etc. each chipmaker has their own design philosophy further different families of chips within the same maker have their own advances and properties.

Further custom model architectures and operations don’t have the benefit of highly efficient open sourced kernels like Flash Attention.

Pre-processing operations that operate on the raw input data stream which serves as input to a model are often run on CPU but have their own computational budget.

All of this leads to the need for custom kernels that are specialized to the underlying hardware and use-case, but there’s a shortage of good kernel engineers and the process is tedious.

💡 Kernel Evolve
The Meta team built their own Multi-Agent Kernel generation stack. The system creates triton kernels, since triton can execute on any hardware. These are the key features that makes this system work:

1️⃣ Graph Based Progressive Kernel Refinement: A graph keeps track of all the attempts at generating a kernel. Each node in the graph represents a generated kernel, all metadata associated, a fitness score, numerical accuracy etc.

2️⃣ Fitness Score: A scores computed as the ratio between time taken to execute a raw pytorch implementation vs the generated kernel in triton. The higher the score the better.

3️⃣ Retrieval Agents: They use Agentic RAG for retrieving metadata from ancestor nodes, instructions from documented best practices, similar error logs encountered in the past, hardware specifications, constraints etc.

4️⃣ Claude Skills Style File System: All the information listed in step 3 is either located in a database or in a navigable file system arranged similar to claude skills. An MCP server provides all the tools needed for the agents to search through these information banks.

5️⃣ Real-time Instructions for Code Generation: The retrieval agents structure all the retrieved information and pass it on as a message to the LLM that actually generates the kernel. The dynamic nature of this ensures that we aren’t stuck with a static prompt that tries to cover all failure modes or optimization techniques.

6️⃣ Evaluation Harness: The generated code is then plugged into their internal evaluation harness that executes the code and profiles them on any hardware device. The combine multiple profile tools together to create a super-comprehensive profiling of the performance.

🎁 Wrap Up
In their evaluations they note significant speed-ups on a number of ops that they use during pre-processing and their custom model architectures.

author: Sagar Desai
subtitle: Senior Solutions Architect | NVIDIA
content:
The Silent Scalability Killer in Python LLM Apps: Thread Pool Starvation


In building high-concurrency GenAI gateways, we often obsess over GPU VRAM and token latency. But there is a silent bottleneck in the application layer that can freeze your system long before the GPU is saturated: Thread Pool Starvation.

Here is the technical breakdown of why it happens and how to mitigate it.

🔹 The Mechanism
Python’s asyncio handles thousands of connections efficiently. However, many vendor SDKs (speech-to-text, vector DBs) still rely on blocking synchronous I/O.
To avoid freezing the event loop, we wrap these calls: loop.run_in_executor(None, blocking_func).

🔹 The Trap: Default Limits
The None argument uses the default ThreadPoolExecutor.
Formula: min(32, os.cpu_count() + 4)
The Container Reality: In a K8s pod with 8 vCPUs, this defaults to just 12 threads.

🔹 The Bottleneck
Assumption: Your pipeline requires 1 blocking thread per active user (e.g., waiting on a streaming gRPC response).
Scenario: You deploy a pod to handle 50 concurrent users.
Result: The first 12 users get serviced. The 13th user is queued by the Python runtime—even if your GPU is idle and CPU is at 5%.

🔹 The "Parking Lot" Analogy
It doesn’t matter if the heavy lifting happens on the GPU. The Python thread must sit idle, blocked, waiting for the response. Even an empty car takes up a parking spot. Once the spots (threads) are full, new traffic stops.

🔹 Mitigation Strategies
Explicit Configuration: Never trust defaults in containers. Initialize a dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=N) where N matches your target concurrency, not your CPU count.

Horizontal Scaling: Use K8s HPA with custom metrics. Scale pods based on active_connections to ensure you hit pod limits before thread limits.

Observability: Monitor executor._work_queue.qsize(). If this is > 0, you are starving.

Efficiency isn't just about faster models; it's about ensuring your application layer has the capacity to wait for them.

author: Manu Mishra
subtitle: AI/Software Dev | Crafting Smart Software Systems | Applied AI Research |
content:
KV Cache : The Real Reason LLM Inference Hits GPU Memory Limit💽

When long conversations cause LLM inference to hit GPU OOM errors, the problem is often misdiagnosed. The bottleneck is rarely the model size or parameter count.

The real issue is "KV (Key–Value) cache" growth. 
During inference, GPU memory is consumed by:
GPU Memory = Model Weights + KV Cache

Model weights remain static, but KV cache grows linearly with every generated token. For long contexts, KV cache can consume significantly more memory than the model itself.

Example
  - 7B model with 8K context → ~4 GB used only by KV cache
  - At 32K context, memory usage increases dramatically

The hidden inefficiency
In multi-turn applications, KV cache often sits idle in GPU memory between user interactions. Even when users pause, their cache continues occupying expensive GPU memory blocking new requests and reducing overall throughput.

How this appears in production
Typical signs of a KV cache bottleneck:
  - High GPU utilization but low throughput
  - OOM errors on long contexts
  - Idle sessions holding GPU memory
  - Repeated recomputation of the same context

The correct fix: KV cache offloading
Instead of truncating context or scaling GPUs, production systems use tiered KV cache offloading:
  - GPU for active tokens
  - CPU RAM for paused sessions (fast resume)
  - SSD or distributed storage for inactive sessions

This enables cache reuse instead of recomputation. NVIDIA benchmarks show up to 14× faster Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) when reusing offloaded KV cache compared to recomputing it.

Core principle 🧷
Offload when: transfer cost < recomputation cost.

Efficient LLM inference is about memory hierarchy and cache management not just bigger GPUs.

author: Khushiyant Chauhan
subtitle: Senior MLE | Production ML & Low Latency Systems | Research @ CERN, LBNL, NTNU
content:
>> Good just got better, I am talking about Tenso

For months, the journey with Tenso has been focused on a single mission: reclaiming every microsecond lost to the serialization bottleneck that plagues modern machine learning infrastructure. I have been sharing the progress of this project for a while now, and today marks a major turning point in how we handle tensor transport. It started with the frustrating realization that even industry-standard tools like gRPC were struggling when tasked with moving 4MB tensors because standard Protobuf was getting bogged down in the overhead of parsing millions of individual floats. I watched as systems hit resource limits and latencies spiked, proving that a general-purpose highway simply was not enough for specialized high-performance workloads.

The breakthrough came when I decided to stop trying to fit tensors into traditional data structures and instead treated them as what they actually are: SIMD-aligned binary blobs. By integrating Tenso directly into the gRPC layer as a raw byte payload, the result was a staggering 13.3x speedup over standard gRPC implementations. We moved from 47 milliseconds per operation down to just 3.53 milliseconds. This shift is not just a numbers game; it is about freeing up the CPU so that inference servers can focus entirely on running models rather than wasting over 40% of their cycles just trying to parse the data arriving at their doorstep.

This latest update also brings Tenso closer to full production readiness by adding several critical features I have been working on. I have implemented LZ4 compression to handle sparse data efficiently and integrated ultra-fast XXH3 64-bit checksums to ensure data integrity across the wire. 

Furthermore, the project’s release pipeline has been updated to automatically generate gRPC stubs, ensuring a seamless experience for anyone integrating these tools into their stack. It has been a long road of refining zero-copy memory mapping and hardware alignment, but seeing the protocol now outperform Apache Arrow by 12.6x and standard gRPC by over 13x confirms that Tenso is evolving into a foundational piece of infrastructure for the ML community.

author: Sameer Wadkar
subtitle: LLM Infrastructure · Training & Inference Systems · Distributed Compute · Cloud-Native AI Platforms
content:
🚀 KV Cache is the first memory management optimization. Managing KV head count with MQA and GQA builds on it. The goal is to reduce memory requirements without compromising accuracy.

In Transformer inference, queries Q attend over cached keys and values KV from previous tokens. The number of KV heads you keep makes a massive difference.
- MHA (Multi-Head Attention) : Each Q head has its own KV head. Best quality. Maximum KV memory.
- GQA (Grouped-Query Attention) : Multiple Q heads share a smaller set of KV heads. Large memory savings with minimal quality loss.
- MQA (Multi-Query Attention) : All Q heads share one KV head. Smallest KV cache. Highest efficiency.

🛠️ Modern production models like LLaMA, GPT-4–class architectures, PaLM, and Qwen rely on GQA or MQA variants to make long-context, batched inference economically viable. 

After adding KV cache support to nanoGPT, I added another control knob: the number of KV heads. This makes it possible to experiment with MHA, GQA, and MQA variants while keeping the model size and training data fixed, and to collect clean, comparable benchmarks.

💡 Memory pressure shows up before compute pressure. At small batch sizes everything looks fine. At batch = 32 with long context:
- MHA decode latency bends upward quickly
- GQA tracks close to MQA
- MQA remains the flattest, with only a modest advantage over low-KV GQA

💡 Peak decode memory scales linearly with context length, and the slope is determined by the number of KV heads.
For the same prompt length, MHA consumes roughly 3× the KV memory of MQA.

💡 Model quality still matters, measured here using perplexity:
- MHA performs best (Expected)
- MQA shows a noticeable drop
- GQA lands very close to MHA with about 50% lower KV memory (Key insight)

🧠 Takeaway: GQA delivers near-MHA quality while cutting KV memory roughly in half. MQA is more memory-efficient, with a larger quality tradeoff.

🔥🔥 One key reason KV heads can be reduced while query heads cannot:
Query heads define attention diversity and model capacity, so reducing them directly impacts accuracy. KV heads mainly drive decode-time memory and bandwidth, and sharing them is far less damaging.

Another way to view this is through the projections themselves. Small changes to Wq significantly alter how attention behaves. Comparable changes to Wk or Wv have a much smaller effect. This is why models keep high representational power in queries while sharing heads across keys and values (core idea behind GQA and MQA)

author: Mayur Jain
subtitle: Writing about ML concepts, trends, & tools
content:
🔥Memory Coalescing In GPU

Consider a CUDA program where the input data is stored in two different formats on the DRAM (Global Memory).

1. Stride Access Pattern / Non-Contiguous Access Pattern
Assume the data is stored on a memory space (ms) in a strided access pattern, 

A[ms]=d1, A[ms+5]=d2, A[ms+10]=d3...so on. Now, for the program to fetch this data from different non-continuous memory locations, the GPU has to execute many separate memory transactions, which is very slow in GPUs.

2. Contiguous Access Pattern
If the data is stored in A[ms]=d1, A[ms+1]=d2, A[ms+2]=d3...so on, in an adjacent memory location. Now, to read this data, the GPU at the hardware level combines the multiple memory requests from threads within a single warp (a group of 32 threads) into the fewest possible number of physical memory transactions, making it extremely fast!

The hardware recognizes this sequential pattern in the memory space and issues a single wide transaction to fetch the whole block of data. This is called Memory Coalescing.

Usually, when data is stored in a strided access pattern, it is moved to shared memory, and then the data is transformed to perform memory coalescing.
