author: Hongliang Liu
subtitle: AI Research
content:
The cat's approach to understand DeepSeek's new paper https://lnkd.in/gVV5ZNZh "mHC: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections"

While hyper-connections hold promise for enhancing information flow in deep networks, existing implementations often rely on rigid linear projections that tend to neglect the complex underlying geometry of evolving feature spaces. To address this limitation, this DeepSeek paper introduces Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), a novel formulation that explicitly models non-adjacent layer connectivity as paths along learnable manifolds. By imposing these geometric inductive biases, mHC guides the network toward learning more compact and robust representations, effectively reducing noise associated with dense connectivity. 

In short, replacing standard linear hyper-connections with geodesic paths on a learnable manifold ensures that feature aggregation respects the underlying non-Euclidean geometry of the representation space rather than distorting it with linear projections.

🚀 Writing CUDA kernels from scratch? Take tinyCUDA with you!

While going through CUDA tutorial examples recently, I realized how much boilerplate is needed just to launch a simple kernel. cudaMalloc, two cudaMemcpys, and cudaFree quickly make the code noisy and hard to read. Things get even worse once you add error checking and profiling.

So I built tinyCUDA: a small, header-only C++ library that keeps CUDA kernel code clean and focused. The Buffer class follows RAII principles and uses C++17 move semantics, making device memory ownership explicit, safe, and easy to pass across functions and lambdas without worrying about leaks or double frees. PyTorch-style to_cpu() and to_gpu() APIs let you focus on kernel development rather than memory transfers. Designed for following CUDA tutorials and teaching, with an emphasis on readability and reduced boilerplate. 

What tinyCUDA provides:

🧠 A lightweight Buffer class to wrap device memory management
⏱️ A simple kernel profiler for runtime measurement
✅ Minimal, explicit CUDA error checking

That’s it! No heavy abstractions, just enough structure to reduce friction and let you focus on the kernel itself. It’s a header-only library. Just include tinycuda.hpp in your .cu file, and you’re ready to go!

subtitle: Research @ Netflix
content:
I published 154,434 words (~1.5 books) across 16 newsletters that were read by ~300,000 people in 2025. None of these words were written by an LLM. Here’s why…

LLM research moves quickly. It seems that every few months the field completely reinvents itself. In order to keep pace, researchers (including me) must constantly evolve their skill sets. 

Due to this fast pace, I set a goal to prioritize skill acquisition at the beginning of the year. As my career has gotten busier, this goal has become more difficult. However, I set strict deadlines for publishing my newsletter that force me to allocate time to learning.  

Strict deadlines cause a lot of mental friction. I’ve had many 60 to 80 hour work weeks turned into 100+ hour work weeks as I try to finish my newsletter on nights / weekends. “He’s trying to finish his newsletter” has become a sarcastic trope among my family.

Despite the process being difficult, the newsletter has deepened my understanding of so many different topics (e.g., RL, MoEs, VLMs, agents, new models, recent trends in post-training, etc.). Gaining this level of understanding without going through the process of planning and writing each newsletter would be impossible.

Given the time I’ve invested and the quality bar I’ve upheld, I am very proud of the newsletter and its reach, but I am most proud of what I have learned. The newsletter has allowed me to improve as a researcher, engineer and teacher.

Going into 2026, I’m primarily motivated by what I don’t know. As I continue writing, I’ll barely scratch the surface of our collective and expanding understanding of AI research. I look forward to learning new things and remaining curious!

content:
DeepSeek AI dropped a banger yesterday about scaling Hyper-Connections using a 1967s algorithm.

A little background, Hyper-Connections were introduced as new variants of Residual connection but as depth increases the residual stream becomes noisy and identity mapping is lost(lots of jargon here, but bear with me).

Residual networks on the other hand preserve the identity mapping and provide training stability.

To overcome this, DeepSeek use 1967's Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm to project H_res into Birkhoff polytope. Tl;dr The resulting operation is a convex combination of input features, minimizing exploding gradients while the signal propagates from shallow layers to deeper layers.

subtitle: ML/AI research engineer. Author of Build a Large Language Model From Scratch (amzn.to/4fqvn0D) and Ahead of AI (magazine.sebastianraschka.com), on how LLMs work and the latest developments in the field.
content:
Efficiency and performance tweaks in the transformer architecture usually focus(ed) on the normalization, attention, and FFN modules. 
For instance:

Normalization: LayerNorm -> RMSNorm -> Dynamic TanH

Attention: Grouped-query attention, sliding window, multi-head latent attention, sparse attention

FFN: GeLU -> SiLU, SiLU -> SwiGLU, Mixture of Experts.

Well, I just saw the New Year’s gift from DeepSeek, which includes some improvements to the residual path. 

In short, it’s built on the hyper-connections (HC) approach, which generalizes the regular (identity) residual connection into a learned one by widening the residual stream via multiple parallel ones and allowing information to mix across those parallel layers.

They then take the HC idea a step further and propose mHC, which constrains the residual mixing to lie on a structured, norm-preserving manifold. They found that this "m"-modification improves training stability.
This adds a small amount of overhead, but they get much better training stability and convergence.

author: Gabriele Berton
subtitle: Training Vision Language Models
content:
How distillation will save Waymo and why HD maps and lidar are not a problem

Waymo famously has HD 3D maps of areas it drives. Many people think Waymo will fail because 3D mapping the world doesn't scale (it's very expensive to collect and maintain HD 3D maps). Here is what they're missing:

Imagine an expensive, huge neural network that is very good at driving, and that requires lots of data as input (e.g. 3D maps + lidar). You deploy it and still potentially lose money because the input data (up-to-date 3D maps) is so expensive.

Luckily, there is distillation. A common pattern in distillation is to have a teacher that produces the most accurate predictions you can get, regardless of the cost. You can then use these predictions to train a student model that is lighter and takes less input data. 

Realistically, you can have a huge teacher that uses 3D maps/lidar/radar/RGB/IMU inputs, and train a lighter student that uses only RGB/IMU/radar. I would bet that in the future even with low-res RGB images we will achieve super-human driving capabilities, using a strong teacher.

Note that this means you only need to collect HD 3D maps of few areas to train the teacher + student, and then the student will drive anywhere without 3D data. It won't be necessary to actually map the whole world as some claim.

This concept is known as "privileged teacher distillation" or "Learning using privileged information" (LUPI), link to paper in comments. It is very common in teacher/student paradigms. An example is in DINOv3, where the Gram teacher uses 2x larger images than the student.

Also, this is not specifically to Waymo, but to any self-driving car company (or any tech in general) that uses temporary crutches. With standard old-school software it would be a nightmare to get rid of such crutches later on once the software is deployed, but deep learning makes it easy

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
My latest contribution to TRL adds the Soft Adaptive Policy Optimization (SAPO) loss function introduced by the Qwen team.

📖 Background Context
Most RLVR loss functions like GRPO, GSPO, DAPO etc. clip the magnitudes of the token losses based on hyper-params. This is often implemented as:

𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘤𝘩.𝘤𝘭𝘢𝘮𝘱(𝘱𝘦𝘳_𝘵𝘰𝘬𝘦𝘯_𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘴, 𝘮𝘪𝘯_𝘷𝘢𝘭, 𝘮𝘢𝘹_𝘷𝘢𝘭)

💡SAPO
SAPO gets rid of clamping by introducing a gating function leveraging the sigmoid activation to adaptively set the per token loss.

Additionally it introduces a couple of hyper-parameters that are dubbed “temperature” to scale the per token loss. The purpose of these hyper-params is to treat tokens corresponding to incorrect responses differently from the ones corresponding to the correct responses.

🥼 Experiments
When compared with GRPO and GSPO, SAPO led to more stable training and better final performance on mathematical reasoning and multimodal (vision + text) tasks.

Study hints for deliberate practice in LLM training during holidays:

1. Stanford CS 336 Language Modeling from Scratch - really good videos and exercises from people that do pre-train and post-train quite large LLMs and talk to a lot of people in the industry.

2. The TPU book ("How To Scale Your Model") - teaches not just how TPUs are used to do efficient matmuls for transformer training, but all the transformer math, parallelism methods, strategies for effective inference, etc.

3. "Interview Prep: The ML Grind" by Jenya - lots of interesting little tasks to implement in pure NumPy to deepen the understanding of the matmul flow, activation flow, and gradient flow.

4. "Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction" book by Sutton and Barto. It's not exactly about RLHF and RLVF, but has all the important fundamentals.

How to practice deliberately? Take an interesting piece you want to improve on, copy-paste the relevant material into your favorite LLM and ask it to formulate you some problems to solve in JAX, NumPy, PyTorch. Try to write in Google Colab or your favourite editor as much code on you own as possible and only go to the LLM for hints when truly stuck. Send the partial and full solution to your chatbot and ask for the review/critique, ask how it could be improved, what needs to be changed for it to work at the big labs scale.

author: Sameer Wadkar
subtitle: LLM Infrastructure · Training & Inference Systems · Distributed Compute · Cloud-Native AI Platforms
content:
Following Karpathy's famous video where he builds GPT from scratch (https://lnkd.in/e8euRmSV) led me to NanoGPT (https://lnkd.in/es5cZf3p) where he publishes the code. 

Realized it does not implement KV Caching. So decided to add that (https://lnkd.in/ex864Hhb) to get a sense for how KV caches are actually implemented in practice.  Then ran some benchmarks on my RTX 5070 GPU machine. They are attached below.

The additions are-
- optional KV cache support
- an inference-only benchmarking harness
- controlled sweeps over prompt length and batch size
- per-token decode latency + peak GPU allocation tracking

The figures below illustrate-
1.  Decode latency vs prompt length (KV cache = False)
- Decode cost explodes with prompt length
- At batch size 8, long prompts become catastrophically slow
- This is the textbook O(T^2) attention cost during decode

2.  Decode latency vs prompt length (KV cache = True)
- KV cache flattens decode latency dramatically
- But only up to a point: batch size and memory pressure still matter
- Decode becomes linear in new tokens, not full context

3. Peak GPU memory vs prompt length (KV cache = False)
- Memory grows linearly with prompt length and batch size

4. Peak GPU memory vs prompt length (KV cache = True)
- Memory still grows linearly but now it’s KV cache growth
- You’re trading recompute for persistent memory
- This is where serving systems hit VRAM ceilings

What KV cache actually does:
- converts a compute-bound decode loop
- into a memory-bandwidth-bound one

That’s a win only when:
- sequences are long (Impact visible only when I use 1024-2048 length)
- generations are long
- you have headroom in VRAM
- memory bandwidth isn’t already saturated

The codebase also illustrates how major frameworks vLLM, Transformers, TensorRT-LLM, Dynamo,  treat KV cache as a serving-layer concern, not a model property.

The model doesn’t "have KV cache". The serving framework decides:
- when to allocate it
- how to shard it
- when to evict it
- how to batch around it

Methodology:
- Base model: nanoGPT (minimal transformer)
- Precision: bf16
- Single-GPU runs
- Fixed model weights
-Sweeps over:
   - prompt length
   - batch size
   - KV cache on/off
- Metrics:
   - decode ms/token
   - peak allocated GPU memory

Full code base - https://lnkd.in/ex864Hhb
Additional docs - https://lnkd.in/eRdn47hU
Detailed metrics of sweeps - https://lnkd.in/e4g2Xhpz

Next up: KV caching is only the first step. Next I intend to extend this same benchmarking harness to add Multi Query Attention (MQA) and Group Query Attention (GQA) to further reduce inference costs by sharing KV across multiple query heads. This shrinks the KV-cache memory and bandwidth during decode - trade off "better attention" for more efficient memory utilization.

We built "intelligent" agents that forgot your name between sentences and called it "stateless architecture." While it was just bad memory.


But this recipe fixes that by giving agents persistent memory across sessions using LlamaIndex + Weaviate + Google AI for Developers

At a high level, LlamaIndex orchestrates memory with three blocks:

- 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆𝗕𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸 for fixed facts (like "User's name is ABC")
- 𝗙𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗘𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆𝗕𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸 that auto-extracts key details ("vegetarian," "loves potatoes")
- 𝗩𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆𝗕𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸 that stores conversation chunks in Weaviate for retrieval

Why this is great for the users:

- They don’t have to repeat themselves
- Recommendations improve instead of resetting
- Conversations feel continuous, not stateless

Under the hood: When token limits hit, conversation chunks get embedded with Gemini embeddings and stored in Weaviate by session_id. Later queries retrieve relevant chunks and inject them back into context.

So now, when a user says, "I want something different than last time," the agent already knows what "last time" was and adjusts automatically!

author: Hrithick Sen
subtitle: Data Scientist @Ford | NLP, LLMs
content:
Hey guys! If you look at the below loss curve, you’ll notice that the model trained with RoPE embeddings (rotary) achieves lower loss compared to the model trained with absolute positional embeddings - often this is the case when training GPT-like models. That’s why RoPE is used in almost all modern LLM architectures like LLaMA, Mistral, Deepseek and others.

So let’s understand the main intuition behind RoPE.

Traditionally, transformers add positional information directly to the token embeddings and this mixes positional information with token embedding semantics in the same space. So in a way we are kind of polluting the token embedding space as we are also changing the magnitude of the embeddings.

RoPE takes a different approach. It does not modify the token embeddings at all. Instead, it injects positional information directly into the attention mechanism by rotating the query and key vectors.

So how does this work?

Let’s say we have a query (q) and a key (k). The attention score between them is:
q · k = |q||k| · cos(theta)
Here, theta is the angle between the vectors q and k.

RoPE works by manipulating this angle. Intuitively, it rotates the query and key vectors in a position-dependent way, which makes the attention score depend on relative position.

Let’s see this more clearly.
We can think of q and k in polar coordinates:
- q has magnitude Lq and angle theta_q
- k has magnitude Lk and angle theta_k

So the attention score becomes:
q · k = Lq · Lk · cos(theta_q − theta_k)

At this point, there is no positional information, the score only measures how similar q and k are. Now we define a fixed rotation step theta so If a token is at position m, we rotate it's query by m · theta and If a token is at position n, we rotate its key by n · theta.

So the new angles become:
- angle of q = theta_q + m · theta
- angle of k = theta_k + n · theta

The difference between the new angles is:
(theta_q − theta_k) + (m − n) · theta

And the new attention score becomes:
q · k = Lq · Lk · cos((theta_q − theta_k) + (m − n) · theta)

Now the attention score explicitly depends on (m − n), which is the relative position between the query and the key. That’s the core intuition behind RoPE.

(In practice, this rotation is applied across multiple dimension pairs with different frequencies, but this simplified view captures the main idea - we will see how RoPE exactly does it in the next post)

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
Think you know pytorch well? Here are some must-know torch functions and how they are used in building deep learning models.


⭐ 𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗹→ Creates a lower triangular matrix with all the upper triangle values of the matrix set to 0. Used for creating causal language modeling masks.


⭐ 𝗰𝘂𝗺𝘀𝘂𝗺 → Computes the cumulative sum of a tensor. Used to produce positional ids when using packed datasets.


⭐ 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘂𝘁𝗲 → Transposes the axes of a tensor. Used for reshaping operations most popular use case is in self-attention to run batched matrix multiplications across attention heads.


⭐ 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗼𝘂𝘀 → Returns a tensor where all the elements are contiguously located (in accordance with their stride layout) in memory, ensures efficient reads and writes on a GPU. Often used after reshaping operations of tensors.


⭐ 𝗱𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗵 → Detaches a tensor from the computational graph, all subsequent operations using the detached tensor will not track gradients and not affect the computational graph. Used commonly in loss functions.


⭐ 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁 → Automatically determines the right precision level for an operation. Used in mixed-precision training.


⭐ 𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗹𝗶 → Creates a tensor drawn from a bernoulli distribution. Used in dropout and creating masks in masked language modeling.


⭐ 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗮𝗹 → Creates a tensor drawn from a multinomial distribution. Used in decoding algorithms like greedy, top-k, top-p etc.


⭐ 𝗻𝗻.𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿 → Creates a contiguous tensor that is added to the computational graph and accumulates gradients. Used for setting learnable parameters like a mixing weight of different losses, initializing MoE weights etc.


⭐ 𝗿𝗲𝗴𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿_*_𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗸 → Registers a function that needs to be called immediately before/after a module. Often used to patch an existing torch module to alter default behavior like in vector steering or up-casting default dtypes.

author: Sameer Wadkar
subtitle: LLM Infrastructure · Training & Inference Systems · Distributed Compute · Cloud-Native AI Platforms
content:
🔥 Reposting this because one idea really clicked for me while reading it. Training a multi-trillion model in days instead of months is a scale-out, not scale-up, problem. The number of GPUs you need is in the 50k–100k GPU range. At that point, the problem is the network.
(https://lnkd.in/e2zQjhj3)

Scale-up solutions like NVLink and NVSwitch are incredible, but they are node-bound. They make a small number of GPUs behave like one big GPU. Once you leave the node, you are back in datacenter networking land: NICs and switches.

The traditional workaround is hierarchy.
• You group GPUs.
• You optimize communication within the group.
• You accept slower communication across groups.

You are baking workload assumptions into the topology itself. Change the communication pattern and performance falls apart.

What OCI is doing with multi-planar networking is fundamentally different. The key realization for me was this:
• Planes don’t partition GPUs.
• Planes partition bandwidth.

Each plane is a complete, cluster-wide network that can reach every GPU.

🧠 You don’t assign GPUs to planes. You assign traffic to planes.

Concretely, for collectives like all-reduce:
• Tensor chunks are assigned to planes up front
• Each chunk is fully reduced inside exactly one plane
• No chunk is ever reduced across planes
• All-gather then replicates results, again within the same plane (to all GPUs across the network)

Yes, all-gather means all data reaches all GPUs. But it does not mean plane-to-plane merging. Each plane independently delivers its assigned data to all GPUs. Traffic is striped across parallel networks to the same endpoints.

NVSwitch cannot solve this problem. NVSwitch creates a single, fast GPU island inside a node. Trying to build one global NVSwitch-like fabric across tens of thousands of GPUs just recreates the same scaling wall.

Multi-planar avoids that by keeping each network well-behaved and scaling total bandwidth by replication, not by enlarging one fabric.

🔥 One last distinction that really needs to click:

There is no single NIC that all GPUs connect to.
There are many NICs, one per node. Each NIC is connected to all planes and has queues for them. Software like NCCL decides which plane traffic belongs to. The NIC injects traffic into the right network and switches move packets.

⚡️ The core idea at the logical level is:
• GPUs are not partitioned into planes.
• Bandwidth is partitioned into planes.
• All planes see all GPUs.

⚡️ The other core idea at the physical level is:
• A NIC belongs to a node and serves the GPUs in that node.
• A NIC is aware of multiple queues, one per plane.
• There are many switches per plane. Each switch belongs to exactly one plane. Planes do not share switches. A queue at the NIC level is the local representation of a plane.

author: Kavishka Abeywardana
subtitle: Machine Learning & Signal Processing Researcher | Semantic Communication • Deep Learning • Optimization | AI Research Writer
content:
Vision Transformer (ViT) 📸 

After the success of the Transformer architecture in natural language processing, researchers spent years trying to adapt the same idea to machine vision. The breakthrough came with the Vision Transformer (ViT).

The core idea is surprisingly simple. An image is divided into fixed-size patches. Each patch is flattened and passed through a linear layer to obtain a patch embedding. 

These embeddings are then fed into a standard Transformer encoder, together with positional embeddings that preserve spatial information.

In addition, a special class token is introduced. This token acts as a global information aggregator, collecting context from all patches through self-attention. 

A similar mechanism was previously used in BERT for sentence-level representation learning.

 After the Transformer layers, the output corresponding to this class token is used for image classification.

With sufficient data and proper training, ViT has demonstrated performance that rivals and often surpasses traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs), marking a major shift in how visual representations can be learned.

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
You’re not in a Sr. Inference Engineer interview with OpenAI, but you’d still like to know what makes serving multimodal models harder than text-only models because learning shouldn't need a reason. 😆

Multimodal models often have modality specific encoders. For e.g. image and video (VLMs) use a ViT encoder to produce features that are passed onto the transformer block of the model.

ViT’s themselves can be a few billion parameters in size. This makes them a bottleneck.

🖼️ Scenario
You have a request coming in with two images attached to the user’s query. Before the VLM can process any textual tokens or produce outputs, it needs 
to pass the images through the vision encoder.

The language modeling block of the model is essentially blocked until all the images are processed.

Further the distribution of requests with images vs purely-text tokens is going to be quite different making it hard to scale up resources for just one scenario if the Visual encoder + Language modeling transformer are on the same serving instance.
💡Solution: Disaggregated Image Token Processing

The solution is to have a completely different GPU/service that runs the vision encoder.

The Visual service, can process image tokens independently and store the results in a cache. Once the vision cache is populated for a specific request, an orchestrator notifies the instances running the language block to pick up those visual tokens and start processing the user’s query.

The language instances can avoid stalling by processing other requests which do not need any visual tokens.

🎁 Wrap Up
The vLLM team have a nice blog on this and run experiments showing how metrics like time to first token and time per output token and effective QPS benefit from a disaggregated serving approach.

author: Shamsher Ansari
subtitle: Group Product Manager | LLM Inference | GPU Cloud | AI Infrastructure @ NeevCloud
content:
The Multi-GPU Inference Problem

LLMs have become too big to fit on a single GPU.

Eg. Llama 3.1 has 405 billion parameters which needs around 405 GB of memory, even in a compressed FP8 format.

NVIDIA H100 has only 80 GB, so the model must be split across multiple GPUs just to run.

But memory size isn’t the only problem.

AI inference actually has two very different steps

When an AI answers a question, it does:

Prefill
→ Reads your input
→ Builds internal memory
→ Heavy on memory, light on compute

Decode
→ Generates the answer word by word
→ Heavy on compute
→ Very sensitive to delays


These two steps behave very differently.

Most systems treat inference as one single task.

That leads to:

→ GPUs waiting idle while memory work is happening
→ Large chunks of memory reserved but never used
→ Up to 60–80% memory waste due to fragmentation
→ Extra slowdown because GPUs need to constantly talk to each other.


Which means 
Inference isn’t one problem,

It’s two very different problems forced into one system.

If we don’t design systems with this in mind,
we waste GPUs, memory, money, and time.

Luckily vLLM and llm-d are solving these challenges in very interesting way.

author: Jatin Singh Sagoi
subtitle: Associate AI Engineer @Techolution || Knight @Leetcode (Top 2%) || Specialist @Codeforces || Ex ML Intern @Culinda
content:
What if we treated experts in MoE LLMs like a dynamic cache?

Take Kimi 2, Instead of loading all 384 experts into memory, what if we kept only ~10 - 25% experts (the “hot” ones) and loaded others on demand kind of like how operating systems manage memory? 

🔹 We could dramatically reduce GPU memory requirements. No need to pin every expert in VRAM all the time 
🔹This could let powerful MoE models (like Kimi K2, DeepSeek, Qwen 3 MoE variants, and LLaMA 4 heard) run on far smaller hardware 

Kimi K2 a SOTA Mixture-of-Experts model with 1 trillion total parameters and 32 billion active parameters have 384 experts. MoE models don’t use all experts at once, they use only a small number of experts per token, which means many experts remain unused for large parts of a single query. Even so, today the system still needs to hold all expert weights somewhere. 

If we could track which experts are frequently used or recently used and keep just those in memory, we could reduce peak memory costs significantly. This kind of dynamic expert loader could work like:
🔹 Hot experts stay in GPU memory
🔹 Cold experts live in CPU RAM (or even on NVMe)
🔹 Load on demand when a new token triggers a “cold” expert 

In many real-world scenarios, a slight hit in latency is a fair trade for accessibility and democratization of SOTA AI

Of course, this would need thorough testing especially to figure out how many experts should live in VRAM, which largely depends on the average number of unique experts used per user query. That number can vary a lot, but understanding it is key to making this practical

author: Marcos Heidemann
subtitle: Principal Data Scientist | AI Architect | ML Ops | Machine Learning Engineer
content:
Your GPU is sitting idle 80% of the time during LLM inference.

Not because it's slow. The problem is that autoregressive generation is memory-bound, not compute-bound. Each token requires a full forward pass, reading the entire model weights. GPUs can do hundreds of trillions of operations per second, but memory bandwidth is only trillions of bytes per second. That's a HUGE gap.

Speculative decoding fixes this by doing something clever: use a small, fast "draft" model to guess multiple tokens ahead, then have the big model verify them ALL in a single parallel pass.

The mechanics:
- Draft model (10-50x smaller than target) generates 3-12 candidate tokens
- Target model verifies all candidates in ONE forward pass
- Accept correct predictions, resample only rejections
- Rinse and repeat

The BEST part? Output quality is MATHEMATICALLY IDENTICAL to standard decoding. Not "almost as good". Actually identical. The rejection sampling algorithm guarantees the same probability distribution as if you ran the big model alone.

Real numbers from production:
- Google's original paper: 2-3x speedup
- NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM: 3-3.6x on Llama 3.3 70B
- Mirror-SD (2025): 3.8x on Qwen3-32B
- Speculative Diffusion: up to 7.2x in experimental setups

Google currently uses speculative decoding in Search AI Overviews. Together.ai, Fireworks.ai, Baseten, and Replicate all use it for cost-efficient inference. IBM reports 2-3x speedup on Granite models.

Where it shines:
- Code generation: 2.5-4x (highly predictable patterns)
- Summarization: 2-2.8x (output overlaps with input)
- Translation: 2-3x (structural patterns)

Where it struggles:
- Creative writing: only 1.2-1.5x (less predictable)
- Batch size >16: benefits disappear or reverse
- Memory-constrained devices: must load BOTH models in VRAM

The catch is real. You need identical tokenizers between draft and target. Implementation complexity is non-trivial. And at high batch sizes, speculative decoding can actually be SLOWER than standard decoding because the overhead doesn't pay off.

But for latency-sensitive, single-user applications? This is probably the most impactful inference optimization available today that doesn't sacrifice quality.

The evolution is interesting too. Medusa adds multiple prediction heads to the target model itself. Prompt lookup decoding is completely training-free, just using n-gram matching against the input. EAGLE-3 extracts features from internal model layers for drafting.

For anyone running local LLMs or building inference APIs, understanding speculative decoding is becoming essential. The technique is mature, well-documented, and supported in vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and Hugging Face Transformers.

author: Niloufar G.
subtitle: Technical AI Product Manager| LLM Specialist | AI-Driven Solutions | Scalable SaaS & Platform Innovation | Customer & Developer Advocate
content:
🧠 LLM Memory Is Missing Its “Kernel” Layer
Why do we treat GPU OOM, KV cache thrashing, and retry storms as application-level problems, when they are clearly operating-system problems?
In today’s LLM platforms, memory is still managed implicitly:
prompts are converted to tensors,
tensors are pushed into GPU memory,
and when memory runs out, CUDA throws an exception and the system retries.
This is the equivalent of building a computer where applications directly malloc() physical memory and hope the OS doesn’t crash.
Where current solutions stop
After studying Tokencake and LMCache, the gap becomes obvious — they solve complementary halves of the problem.
Tokencake
Brings policy and scheduling to LLM serving
Space / Time schedulers prevent idle KV cache during agent tool calls
❌ But it lacks a production-grade, low-latency KV offload & transfer substrate
❌ Limited support for cross-engine KV reuse and persistence
LMCache
Excels at moving, storing, pinning, and reusing KV caches
GPU ↔ CPU ↔ Disk, async I/O, compression
❌ Engine-agnostic by design
❌ Not agent-aware; no admission control or fairness logic
The missing abstraction
💡 What we really need is an “LLM memory kernel”:
admission control before GPU allocation
virtualized KV address space
fair scheduling across agents and tenants
explicit KV residency accounting
predictable backpressure instead of OOM retries
Tokencake-style scheduling + LMCache-style KV infrastructure is the closest thing we have today to that kernel layer.

Tokens are just a billing unit.
The real scarce resource is GPU memory residency over time.
The next step in LLM platforms won’t be bigger models —
it will be kernel-level thinking applied to inference systems.

In a world where GPU performance is as unpredictable as a cat on a hot tin roof, this white paper attempts to solve the age-old problem of resource management in GPU-centric systems. The authors have bravely ventured into the murky waters of user-space runtimes and OS kernel modifications, highlighting the trade-offs that every developer has faced at 2 AM while trying to optimize performance. Their big idea? The GPU driver and device layer should become an extensible OS policy interface. Bold choice, considering we are all just trying to keep our GPUs from having existential crises.

Enter gpu_ext, their knight in shining armor, which claims to seamlessly integrate eBPF into GPU management without tossing safety and efficiency into the lava pit. With promises of throughput improvements up to 4.8x and tail latency halved—all while keeping applications blissfully unaware of the chaos in the background—it looks interesting on paper (as these things often do). The real test, of course, will be if this "coherent, application-transparent policy" can withstand the harsh realities of diverse workloads without collapsing under the pressure. It’s a captivating read, but will it deliver when the chips are down? Time will tell.

author: Mayank Mishra
subtitle: PhD at UC Berkeley
content:
🚀SonicMoE🚀: a blazingly-fast MoE implementation optimized for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. SonicMoE reduces activation memory by 45% and is 1.86x faster on H100 than previous SOTA😃

Paper: https://lnkd.in/guyBPtXS
Work with Wentao Guo, Xinle Cheng, Ion Stoica, Tri Dao

We open-source all our code: https://lnkd.in/gRXP6TND. We welcome feedback and contributions! Our future roadmap includes adding support for Blackwell GPUs, fused expert-parallelism, and FP8.

The activation memory usage is the same as a dense model with equal activated parameters (minimum activation memory required for backward computation without doing activation recomputation with GEMM). SonicMoE’s activation memory usage is also independent of expert granularity.

SonicMoE achieves 50%+ speedup compared to existing baselines for a single MoE layer with open-source MoE configurations from 7B to 685B. For 7B MoE model with FSDP-2, SonicMoE on 64 H100s gets 213B tokens/day while ScatterMoE (previous SOTA) on 96 H100s gets 225B tokens/day.

For highly-sparse MoEs, the FLOPs wasted by Grouped GEMM tile-based computation (due to padding) linearly scales w.r.t. expert activation ratio. We introduce a token rounding routing algorithm that rounds the per-expert token count to avoid wasted FLOPs. The token rounding routing eliminates padding waste in grouped GEMM and can achieve 16% relative speedup over TC top-K on kernel computation time while delivering robust token-choice accuracy even under highly sparse MoE training regimes.

1️⃣ Tailoring: Because the future isn't "one-size-fits-all." It's about adapting the architecture to a specific domain or task. Sometimes you don't adapt a model to a domain, but you're looking for it to be good at following instructions.

2️⃣ Surgical: Because pruning neurons and layers requires a precision that standard Fine-Tuning doesn't offer.

3️⃣ Beyond Fine-Tuning: Because to truly optimize, you have to go beyond weights; you have to intervene in the structure. Reducing latency and inference costs that Fine-Tuning alone can't touch.

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
Ever wondered why commonly used Reinforcement Learning Objectives for training reasoning models include a clipping term? 🤔

A naive answer might be “to scale the loss to stay within a manageable range”. However, that’s a superficial response that fails to capture the true mechanics, which is revealed when you take a look at the gradient of the loss.

📖 Background Context

In PPO/GRPO and derivatives of those objectives the loss includes a term that looks like

𝗰𝗹𝗶𝗽(𝗿_𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗮, 𝗹𝗼𝘄=𝟭-𝗲𝗽𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗼𝗻, 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵=𝟭+𝗲𝗽𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗼𝗻) * 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲_𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲

In the expression 𝗿_𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗮 corresponds to the ratio of probability scores between the policy model and rollout model for a given token.

Note that 𝗿_𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗮 is obtained from operations 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 i.e. the model being trained.

The 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲_𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲 results from a 𝘳𝘦𝘸𝘢𝘳𝘥 𝘮𝘰𝘥𝘦𝘭 𝘰𝘳 𝘯𝘰𝘯-𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘢𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘳𝘪𝘤 𝘳𝘦𝘸𝘢𝘳𝘥 𝘧𝘶𝘯𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘤𝘩 𝘢𝘳𝘦𝘯’𝘵 𝘣𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘥.

📈 Gradients

Let’s consider the case of 𝘳_𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘵𝘢 > 1+𝘦𝘱𝘴𝘪𝘭𝘰𝘯.

In this scenario the 𝗹𝗼𝘀𝘀 = (𝟭 + 𝗲𝗽𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗼𝗻) * 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲_𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲

The gradient of the loss wrt. to the parameters of the policy model is 0 because neither the term (𝟭+𝗲𝗽𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗼𝗻) nor the term 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲_𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲 are functions of the policy model.

The same case holds for 1-epsilon.

🧩 Putting it all together.

The actual loss formula includes taking the min between 𝗿_𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗮 * 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲_𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲 and the clipped term listed above, that combination ensures that tokens corresponding to

𝗿_𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗮 > 𝟭+𝗲𝗽𝘀𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 & 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲_𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲 > 0 or 
< 𝟭 - 𝗲𝗽𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗼𝗻 & 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲_𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲 < 0 

do not contribute to training i.e. gradient = 0

Why do we do this? The intuition is to limit to the exploratory space of the model to avoid it drifting too far from the old policy at any given step of training when the model is already doing a good job at picking good or avoiding bad tokens.

content:
I just finished reading DeepSeek 3.2's paper to keep up with the trends. The key innovation it brings up is 'DeepSeek Sparse Attention'.

LLMs are all built on the “attention” mechanism introduced in Google's “Attention is All You Need” paper, where the cost of full attention grows quadratically with the context length.

Recently released, DeepSeek 3.2 implements dynamic sparse attention, using an indexer to reduce attention to only on the most relevant tokens, unlike current Llama's dense or Mistral's fixed sliding window approaches.

This reduces the core complexity of attention from quadratic to linear, reducing significantly the computation requirement for long contexts - perfect for Agentic and RAG applications.

This new version also includes other innovations on the reinforcement learning reward model, and on the self-verification of reasoning.

subtitle: Founder | YC (x26) | Agents | Graphs | RL | 4× Founding Engineer | Winner of 10+ Hackathons
content:
𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗣𝗢𝗖𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘆. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹.

For agentic systems, one overlooked area is threat modeling. These systems make autonomous decisions, chain together unpredictably, and invoke external tools. Traditional security frameworks weren't built for this.

I've been studying and applying threat modeling to major agentic architectures. In my latest blog, I break down the supervisor-agent pattern using the MAESTRO framework.

Here's the 5-step process I follow:

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟭: 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Map your architecture to MAESTRO's 7 layers — from foundation models to the agent ecosystem.

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟮: 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗜𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Identify layer-specific threats (prompt injection, data poisoning, tool misuse) and cross-layer attack chains.

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟯: 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗸 𝗔𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
Score each threat by likelihood and impact. Prioritize ruthlessly.

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟰: 𝗠𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴
Define concrete defenses — sandboxed tool execution, memory access controls, agent authentication.

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟱: 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 & 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿
Deploy controls. Baseline agent behavior. Alert on deviations. Iterate.

Key insight from this exercise: cross-layer attacks are the real danger. A compromised tool can poison an agent, which corrupts memory, which affects every future decision. You can't secure these systems by looking at one component in isolation.

If you're moving agentic AI to production, threat modeling isn't optional. Start early, update often.

author: Andriy Burkov
subtitle: PhD in AI, author of 📖 The Hundred-Page Language Models Book and 📖 The Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book
content:
This is the Outstanding Paper Award at ICLR 2025, and this is exactly the kind of research on LLMs we need, not those quasi-psychological studies of the form "we asked the same question to these 3 models and see which one is more sycophant."

As you might already know, when finetuning language models, researchers first perform supervised learning on good examples, then apply preference optimization—training the model to distinguish preferred responses from rejected ones using algorithms like Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). This two-stage process improves model behavior, but prior work observed a curious phenomenon: during the preference stage, the model's predicted probability of generating responses (measured by log-likelihood) decreases for nearly all responses, including the preferred ones the training is supposed to encourage.

This paper provides a mathematical framework explaining why this happens by decomposing each gradient update into three components: how the model currently predicts, how training on one example affects similar examples, and the direction of the gradient signal.

The analysis reveals a "squeezing effect": when you apply negative gradients to push down the probability of bad responses, the probability mass doesn't get redistributed evenly—it concentrates on whichever token has the highest probability at each position. This makes the model's predictions increasingly peaked. The effect becomes severe when the negative gradient targets responses that already have very low probability, which commonly occurs when using pre-collected datasets where the rejected responses were generated by a different model.

The framework explains why methods that generate new response pairs from the current model at each training step outperform methods using fixed pre-collected pairs—they avoid applying large negative gradients to responses in low-probability regions.

The insight leads to a simple improvement: including both preferred and rejected responses during supervised fine-tuning before preference optimization demonstrably improves alignment by reducing the harmful squeezing effect.

Let the paper talk to you and answer your questions on ChapterPal: https://lnkd.in/eRt4yyVP

author: Daniel van Strien
subtitle: Machine Learning Librarian at Hugging Face 🤗 | Making AI work for libraries, archives, and their communities
content:
We all know about being GPU poor, but many of us are also disk poor 😢

AI datasets are getting larger, with multi-TB datasets becoming more common. There are great tools to avoid loading everything into RAM, but this doesn't help if you don't have TBs of disk available first.

But what if you skip the download entirely?

Polars can stream directly from Hugging Face Hub using the hf:// protocol. Point it at a dataset path, and it reads what it needs overthe network - no massive local storage required!

Why this works so well:

- Parquet is a columnar format. If you only need 3 columns out of 50, Polars only fetches those 3. The rest never touches your network.

- Predicate pushdown takes it further. Filter for `language == "en"`? Polars pushes that filter down to the scan level. Combined with Parquet's row group statistics, it can skip entire chunks of data without reading them.

For datasets stored on the Hub, this means:

- No download step
- No large amount of disk space needed
- Filters reduce network transfer, not just memory
- Works with datasets far larger than your storage

I tested this on HuggingFaceFW/finepdfs-edu: ~736GB, 50M rows of educational PDF metadata spanning 12 years of CommonCrawl dumps (2013-2025).

The question: Is the web getting more educational over time?
The answer: Yes - high-quality educational content is up ~22% (take this with a pinch of salt...) 

The setup:
- Single Astral UV script with inline dependencies (runs anywhere with `uv run`)
- Ran on Hugging Face Jobs (CPU instance, no GPU needed)
- ~14 minutes for the full 50M rows
- A few seconds when filtering to a single language
- Results upload directly to Hub with an auto-generated dataset card

Disk poor shouldn't mean data poor. I focused mostly on doing an analysis-type run here. This can also be very useful for filtering a large dataset into a smaller subset for training/evaluation, etc. 

Try it yourself:

- Results: https://lnkd.in/eE46J6wS

author: Ashish Patel 🇮🇳
subtitle: Sr Principal AI Architect at Oracle | Generative AI Expert & Strategist | xIBMer | Author: Hands-on
content:
DeepSeek cuts LLMs' costs by 70% and is 62.5× faster with one math trick: turning L² into L*k. 

👉 Here’s what that actually means — and let’s calculate it.

Most LLMs models use full attention, where every token looks at every other token.

Plain math:
✔️ Work = L × L = L²

If you double L, the cost becomes 4 times higher. That’s why long context is expensive.

📐 DeepSeek’s DSA changes the rule by allowing each token to compare only k important tokens.

New math:
✔️ Work = L × k

If k stays fixed, the cost grows slowly instead of exploding.

The Lightning Indexer scores all tokens and grabs the top 2,048.
So full attention runs on 2,048 tokens instead of the entire 128,000.

❓ HOW? LET’S CALCULATE

1. Dense attention cost:
128,000 × 128,000 = 16,384,000,000 operations

2. Sparse attention cost:
128,000 × 2,048 = 262,144,000 operations

3. Speedup:
128,000 / 2,048 = 62.5× faster

📤RESULT:
This single shift — from L² to L*k — is why DeepSeek can run long-context inference at a fraction of the cost without losing accuracy.

author: Ronald Yu
subtitle: Cartesia.ai
content:
The speculative decoding algorithm, which powers Google’s AI overviews, speeds up LLM auto-regressive inference by leveraging two observations—one more philosophical and one more practical:

1) Not all tokens are equally difficult to predict. Easier tokens can be predicted by weaker models to save on compute.
2) Auto-regressive LLM inference for transformers is often memory-bound rather than compute-bound, meaning that the latency is bottlenecked not by the computation per se but by readingthe KV cache from the GPU’s high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to the SRAM, where the computation actually occurs.

It does so by having a cheap, weak model that proposes multiple tokens at once and an expensive, strong model that verifies that the weak model correctly proposed easy tokens and then overrides the weak model on the hard tokens. One of the challenges in speculative decoding is how to cheaply increase the capacity of the weak proposal model by “borrowing” capacity from the expensive, strong model.

Masked text diffusion models are a class of typically compute-bound models that offer a method for large models to potentially cheaply perform inference via parallel generation, but they perform worse than standard auto-regressive models, becoming weaker as they become more parallel and efficient.

Nvidia’s recent paper “TiDAR: Think in Diffusion, Talk in Autoregression” proposes to train one big base model capable of both auto-regression and masked text diffusion and to use the diffusion setting as the weak proposal model and the auto-regressive setting as the strong verifier model for powerful and efficient inference. This results in an improved speculative decoding algorithm that pushes the frontier of the efficiency vs quality trade-off. My NBA comparison for this paper is: Paolo Banchero.

author: Youssef El Manssouri
subtitle: Co-Founder & CEO at Sesterce - first principles, small teams, simple systems.
content:
Kubernetes is the default for orchestrating containers.

It's not the default for training large AI models.

OpenAI scaled Kubernetes to 7,500 nodes. They wrote multiple blog posts about the pain. etcd bottlenecks. API server overload. N² scaling problems with endpoint watches.

The core issue is that Kubernetes was designed for web services, not distributed training.

Web services are stateless. They scale horizontally. Individual pods are replaceable.

Training jobs are the opposite. They need synchronized execution across hundreds of GPUs. They're sensitive to network topology. A single node failure can crash the entire job.

Kubernetes adds overhead at every layer. Pod networking introduces latency. The container runtime consumes memory that could go to model weights. Resource abstraction means you're not getting bare metal performance.

At scale, these overheads compound. Communication latency between pods affects gradient synchronization. Every millisecond of added latency multiplies across thousands of GPUs and millions of training steps.

Kubernetes doesn't understand GPU topology. It doesn't know which GPUs share NVLink. It can't optimize placement for InfiniBand fabrics. It treats GPUs as generic resources.

The industry is building better tools. Meta open-sourced NCCLX in October 2025. It's their production-tested collective communication library that powered Llama 3 and Llama 4 training. Scales to 100,000+ GPUs.

NCCLX provides host-initiated and device-initiated APIs with lower latency than baseline NCCL. Works with CTran, Meta's custom transport layer supporting NVLink, InfiniBand, and RoCE backends.

This is why Slurm still dominates large-scale training.

Slurm was built for HPC. It understands hardware topology. It can allocate nodes so data transfer passes through the fewest switches. It handles coordinated multi-node execution natively.

Over half the Top 500 supercomputers run Slurm. Most frontier model training does too.

The industry is converging on hybrid approaches. CoreWeave built SUNK to run Slurm on Kubernetes. Best of both worlds. Kubernetes for inference and deployment. Slurm for training.

If you're running inference at scale, Kubernetes works.

If you're training models across thousands of GPUs, you need something that understands the hardware.

That gap is where the next generation of AI infrastructure companies are building.

author: Anshuman Mishra
subtitle: ML @ Zomato
content:
Google investing in TPUs 10 years back was a 1000 IQ move. 

Here's a deep dive into TPU architecture 🧵 

The problem: von Neumann bottleneck.

CPUs load values from memory → compute → store back to memory. For EVERY calculation.

Memory access is orders of magnitude slower than computation. This bottleneck kills throughput in ML workloads that need billions of operations.


GPUs solved this with massive parallelism - 2,500 to 5,000 ALUs running simultaneously.

Great for neural networks! But GPUs are still general-purpose. Those thousands of ALUs still need to constantly read/write from registers and shared memory for every operation.


Enter TPUs: Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) that ONLY do matrix operations.

No word processing. No rocket engines. Just matrix multiply-accumulate operations at insane speeds.

The key? Systolic array architecture.

NOTE - btw subscribe to my newsletter to get this in your inbox daily:

https://lnkd.in/gCPD6fUz

now back to the post:

A systolic array is thousands of multiply-accumulators directly connected to each other in a physical matrix.

Cloud TPU v3: 128 x 128 ALUs per systolic array, 2 arrays per chip.
TPU v6e/v7: 256 x 256 ALUs.

That's 16K multiply-accumulate ops per cycle, per unit.


Here's the magic:

TPU loads parameters from memory into the Matrix Multiplication Unit once. Then loads data. As each multiplication executes, the result passes DIRECTLY to the next multiply-accumulator.

No memory access during matrix multiplication. Zero.


TPU system hierarchy:

• TensorCore = MXUs + vector unit + scalar unit
• Chip = 1+ TensorCores  
• Slice = chips connected by high-speed ICI (inter-chip interconnect)
• Pod = collection of slices
• Multislice = multiple slices using datacenter network

Scale from single chip to thousands.


TPU v5p and v6e also include SparseCores - specialized processors for sparse operations.

Perfect for recommendation models that rely heavily on embeddings. 4 SparseCores per chip on v5p, 2 per chip on v6e.

Hardware acceleration for the entire ML stack.


TPU VM architecture gives you direct SSH access to the VM connected to TPU hardware.

Root access. Full compiler logs. Real debugging. No gRPC middleware.

(TPU Node architecture is deprecated as of April 2025 - migrate to TPU VMs if you haven't already)


The trade-off?

CPUs: flexible, general-purpose
GPUs: parallel, gaming + ML
TPUs: specialized matrix processors for neural networks only

But for training and inference on transformers and neural nets? TPUs achieve computational throughput that GPUs can't match.

That's the power of purpose-built silicon.

author: Hao Hoang
subtitle: I share daily insights on AI agents, LLMs, Data Science, Machine Learning | I help AI engineers crack top-tier interviews | 56K+ community | LLM System Design, RAG, Agents
content:
You're in a Senior ML Interview at OpenAI. The interviewer points to a Transformer diagram and sets the trap:

"How do we use the Attention mechanism's weights to measure the model's uncertainty?"

90% of candidates walk right into the trap.

"Easy. The Attention scores pass through a Softmax. They sum to 1.0. Therefore, they represent a probability distribution. If the attention is peaked on one token, the model is confident. If the distribution is flat (high entropy), the model is uncertain."

This answer sounds intuitive. It is also mathematically invalid.

They just confused a 𝐌𝐢𝐱𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐖𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 with a 𝐑𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐨𝐦 𝐕𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞.

In a standard Transformer (during inference), the attention mechanism is 100% deterministic.
- You do not sample from it.
- You do not roll dice.
- You strictly calculate a weighted average of Value vectors.

Because the process is deterministic, the "entropy" of the attention weights is a measure of information dispersal, not probabilistic confidence. A model can have extremely "peaked" attention (looking at one specific token) and still be completely "hallucinating" or wrong about the output.

Relying on this for safety-critical uncertainty estimation is a recipe for silent failure.

-----
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: To pass the interview, you need to identify 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐆𝐚𝐩.

Real uncertainty requires a source of randomness (stochasticity) to measure the variance of outcomes. Since standard attention is fixed, you must introduce external noise to measure confidence.

You have two production-grade options:
- 𝐌𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐨 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐨𝐮𝐭: Keep Dropout turned on during inference. Run the forward pass 10 times. Measure the variance in the attention outputs. That variance is your uncertainty.
- 𝐋𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐕𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐬 (𝐕𝐀𝐄𝐬): Introduce a true latent variable z (sampled from a Gaussian prior). The variance of the posterior q(z|x) gives you the actual epistemic uncertainty.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐆𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐘𝐨𝐮 𝐇𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐝
"Attention weights sum to 1, but they are deterministic mixing coefficients, not probabilities. To measure uncertainty, I would not look at the weights themselves. I would measure the variance of the weights across multiple stochastic forward passes (MC Dropout) or use a VAE architecture."

author: Sourav Verma
subtitle: Lead Applied AI Scientist at Bayer | AI | Agents | NLP | ML/DL | Engineering
content:
You’re in a Google AI Engineer interview.

Interviewer: "How does speculative decoding speed up LLM inference?"

This is how you respond...

You: "It uses a smaller draft model to predict multiple tokens ahead. The main model verifies predictions in parallel. Correct predictions allow skipping full forward passes for several tokens."

Interviewer: "What if the draft predictions fail?"

You:
 - Rollback triggers recomputation for mismatched tokens
 - KV cache partial updates must be recomputed -> memory and compute spike
 - Kernel-level synchronization adds latency

Interviewer: "Can you quantify the benefits?"

You: Sure - 
 - For a 30B parameter model, context 4,096 tokens, batch 64
 - Draft predicts 4 tokens ahead, 80% match -> 3,200 tokens skipped per batch
 - Latency drops ~400 ms -> ~180 ms (~2.2x speedup)
 - 20% mismatch adds ~50 ms -> net gain remains significant

Interviewer: "Memory implications?"

You:
 - Main KV cache ~28 GB FP16
 - Draft model cache adds ~2–3 GB
 - Total ~30 GB -> fits comfortably on 80GB GPU
 - Freed memory allows larger batch size or longer context

Interviewer: "How do you optimize speculative decoding?"

You:
 1. Asynchronous verification kernels -> reduce idle GPU cycles
 2. Dynamic speculation window -> adjust ahead-predict size based on draft entropy
 3. Chunked KV updates -> minimize recomputation memory overhead
 4. Mixed precision draft -> FP16 or INT8 to reduce memory footprint

Interviewer: "Any trade-offs to watch?"

You:
 - High mismatch rates can negate gains
 - Extra kernels may increase code complexity
 - Need careful memory orchestration to avoid exceeding GPU capacity

Speculative decoding is risk-managed acceleration. Proper KV cache handling, prediction verification, and kernel orchestration are key to real-world throughput gains while maintaining memory efficiency.

author: Hao Hoang
subtitle: I share daily insights on AI agents, LLMs, Data Science, Machine Learning | I help AI engineers crack top-tier interviews | 56K+ community | LLM System Design, RAG, Agents
content:
You're in a Senior ML Interview at NVIDIA. The interviewer sets a trap:

"You attach a new, random linear head to a pre-trained Transformer. Do you unfreeze all layers and start backprop immediately?"

90% of candidates walk right into the trap.

Their answer is: "Of course. End-to-end training allows the backbone to adapt to the new task immediately. If we have the compute, why artificially restrict the model by freezing layers?"

It feels efficient. It works in the tutorials.
-----
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲: They aren't accounting for 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐒𝐡𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐰𝐚𝐯𝐞.

Their classification head is initialized with random noise. This means their initial loss is high, and their initial gradients are mathematical garbage.

When they backpropagate this "noise" through their perfectly pre-trained backbone, they aren't adapting the features. They are shattering them.

The backbone features (which were already robust) are forced to move aggressively to accommodate a random, untrained head. You destroy the pre-trained structure before the head even learns which way is up.

-----
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: You must respect the initialization gap. The fix is executing "𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐞-𝐓𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠" 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐨𝐥

- 𝘗𝘩𝘢𝘴𝘦 1 (𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘚𝘩𝘪𝘦𝘭𝘥): Freeze the backbone parameters. Train only the new linear head. Since the features are fixed, this is effectively a convex optimization problem. It converges rapidly.
- 𝘗𝘩𝘢𝘴𝘦 2 (𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘙𝘦𝘧𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵): Once the head is sensible, unfreeze the backbone.
- 𝘗𝘩𝘢𝘴𝘦 3 (𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘋𝘳𝘪𝘧𝘵): Lower your learning rate (e.g., from 1e-3 to 1e-5) and fine-tune the full model to adapt the features slightly for the specific task.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐆𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐘𝐨𝐮 𝐇𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐝: "Never fine-tune a backbone against a random head. We must align the head to the existing feature space before we allow the feature space to shift."

author: Benjamin Marie
subtitle: Ph.D in Computer Science, Researcher
content:
Quantizing Olmo 3 7B for local deployment (vLLM-compatible):

- FP8 is by far the most token-efficient format overall. It preserves almost all of the original model’s accuracy while significantly improving latency.
- NVFP4 is the fastest per token on a Blackwell GPU… …but it also tends to generate the most tokens, which actually makes it a poor choice from an end-to-end efficiency standpoint.
- All quantized variants have similar PASS@k, meaning that with multiple samples, they can still “find” as many correct answers as the FP16 baseline.
- Where things diverge is single-shot quality: average and best accuracies show that NVFP4 and GPTQ are less likely to give a correct answer on the first try, especially for Math tasks.

What quantized format to choose (order of preference)?
- FP8: If you have Hopper or Blackwell GPUs
- INT8 (W8A8 SmoothQuant): If you have older GPUs
- AWQ: If you want a model that consumes less memory

content:
🚀Optimizing Long-Context + Large-Batch Inference with NVFP4 KV Cache

We have released a deep dive into a deceptively simple but extremely high-leverage optimization: NVFP4 KV-cache quantization.

KV cache is one of the largest bottlenecks in large-scale inference-driving HBM usage, decode-phase bandwidth pressure, cache-miss recompute stalls, and, ultimately, user-facing latency.

With NVFP4, we cut KV-cache footprint by ~50% vs FP8, effectively doubling the on-device context budget. In practice that means:
⚡ Fewer evictions → higher hit rates
⚡ Up to 3× lower TTFT on Blackwell
⚡ Larger batches, longer sequences, higher concurrency
⚡ <1% accuracy deltas across coding, knowledge, and long-context workloads
⚡ Cleaner stacking effects with NVLink, Wide-EP, and optimized kernels

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🧑‍🍳 Transform LLMs into diffusion models!

The creator of dLLM (Zhanhui Zhou) has shared an open-source recipe for turning an autoregressive LLM into a diffusion LLM. This means parallel generation and infilling for fast inference.

→ The conversion is surprisingly simple: swap the causal mask for bidirectional attention, then train on randomly masked sequences to predict missing tokens. Light SFT is often enough to get a working diffusion model from an AR base.

→ Your base AR model quality matters more than adaptation compute. Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct significantly outperforms Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B after identical A2D adaptation.

→ Block diffusion (BD3LM) beats vanilla masked diffusion (MDLM) consistently, especially on math and coding tasks. BD3LM combines AR-style sequential block generation with diffusion within each block, getting the best of both worlds.

→ The resulting Qwen3-0.6B diffusion models are the smallest working diffusion LLMs to date and perform on par with Qwen2.5-0.5B on several benchmarks, though they still lag behind their AR parents.

The conversion still degrades performance quite a bit, but that's expected in this setting. The cool thing is there's still plenty of work to be done in terms of data, training, and algorithms to match the quality of autoregressive models. It's a really refreshing library, and I encourage you to give it a try if you're into diffusion! :)

author: Dakshi Goel
subtitle: MS DS @UMD || Bachelors in EE and CS @IIT Jammu’24 || GenAI + CV
content:
Training a deep learning model, but don't know about DDP ! 

I wish someone had taught me about it in my university courses. When my friend and I were discussing how increasing the number of GPUs helped me reduce the training time, BUT NOT HIM, that is when I got to know the difference between Data Parallel and Distributed Data Parallel. 

So that's why I’ll tell you all about Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), so you can save up your time and utilize the resources to the fullest. 

Why do you need to know about it? 

  • Single GPU = under-utilized hardware 
  • Speed near-linear scaling:  4 GPUs ≈ 4× faster training (or close to it).
  • DP (DataParallel) is slow + outdated: DP overloads one GPU and scatters work inefficiently. DDP avoids this by giving each GPU its own process.
  • Modern pipelines assume it : Most production training workflows (vision, ASR, diffusion, mid-size NLP) expect DDP by default.
  • Parallelized backward pass: Backward pass + gradient computation becomes parallelized.

How does it work? 

The fundamental thing DDP does is to copy the model to multiple (let K) GPUs, gather the gradients from them, average the gradients to update the model, and then synchronize the model over all K processes  (Gradient Synchronization).

Key components to know about : 

DDP is built on top of PyTorch Distributed, and PyTorch Distributed uses NCCL(NVIDIA Collective Communication Library) as its communication backend for GPU operations.
    • init_process_group :  Initializes the distributed communication framework for multi-GPU training.
    • DistributedSampler : Splits the dataset so each GPU processes a unique subset.
    • DistributedDataParallel : Wraps the model to parallelize forward and backward passes across GPUs.
    • NCCL ops (all_reduce, broadcast, reduce_scatter) : Efficient GPU-to- 
       GPU communication primitives for synchronizing gradients and data.

Let me know if it was helpful 😁 ! This blog helped me learn about the implementation : 

https://lnkd.in/ew2WZFFw

Next up FSDP !

author: Sachin Dixit

content:
I created my LLM from ground up, you should too

As an AI Architect with production-level experience with AI/Neural Networks and regular reading of various research papers in the field, the arrival of ChatGPT didn’t stun my circle of technologists as much as it did to rest of the sector. 

The Cambrian explosion of LLMs

By the time 2024 ended, the default choice for GenAI projects wasn’t always OpenAI. There were many LLM companies that shipped many versions of LLMs with different architectural designs and sometimes shipped an internal mix of experts. In the larger field of LLMs, the scientist would still discard such differences as more differences of the same thing. But if one is crafting solutions around LLMs one has to account for differences in modality, reasoning, pure chatbots and so on.

For my learning style, I wanted to be guided by someone who could take the learning from a blank slate and build on it, like how the LLM state-of-the-art was built. My approach is also to type along, run, experiment. This is where Sebastian Raschka, PhD’s material on LLMs worked best for me.

Building the Actual, not so Large Language Model

Building from scratch approach meant that I had to literally start with understanding transformers, choose text and convert it into embeddings, code attention and then move on to multi-head attention while experiencing the why of it, normalize the layers and code my own GPT model. This version just allowed me to chat around the text I trained it for. But the real intention was to see how everything I did leads up to and affects the output rather than saying look, here is my LLMs”.There were 2-3 variations of my model that I fine-tuned for classification and also generating my riddle version of output (remember 4th standard kids inventing their own riddle/cryptic languages for speaking, that thing).My most fun moments were experiencing the epochs and watching the output of the print command on the model object(this is real fun, do it).

author: Narendiran Chembu
subtitle: Staff ML Engineer | UvA | IITM
content:
"Attention is All You Need"... but that says nothing about how we handle fast inference for insanely large trillion-parameter models.

GPT-5 is rumoured to have ~1.5 trillion parameters. How does it still give you really fast answers?

Over the last eight years, transformers have emerged as a dominant force in text, vision, speech, and other modalities. But as models got bigger, we quietly hit a wall:

❌ Compute exploded
❌ Latency became painful
❌ Inference costs are unforgivable
❌ Dense models gave us diminishing returns

So what do we do? We take a shortcut. More precisely, we route.

Only the right parameters fire for the right token. Enter Mixture of Experts (MoE), the unsung hero behind every modern “efficient at scale” LLM.

MoE lets you build trillion-parameter models while keeping inference costs roughly the same as a 10B or 20B model. Sounds amazing, right? But MoE comes with its own dragons: router collapse, expert capacity bottlenecks, load balancing headaches. But there are a dozen clever fixes from the research community.

If you’ve ever wondered how modern frontier LLMs actually scale, or why companies like Google, DeepSeek, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta keep investing in MoE, you might want to read this blog: 👇

author: Atharva Ingle
subtitle: AI Engineer @E2E Cloud (Building Jarvislabs.ai), Kaggle 4x Expert, Ambassador @Weights & Biases
content:
𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝘁'𝘀 𝘀𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹. 𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻, 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀, 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲𝘀.

EAGLE-3 breaks this pattern. You train a tiny draft head that predicts multiple tokens ahead. The target model verifies them all in parallel in one forward pass. Same output quality, just faster (lossless speedup).

Spent the last few days going deep on this and understanding what makes EAGLE-3 different from older speculative decoding approaches:

→ The draft head is just 1 transformer layer (not a separate model)
→ It fuses features from multiple layers of the target model (not just the top layer)
→ A technique called "training-time testing" simulates actual inference conditions during training

𝗪𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗟𝗹𝗮𝗺𝗮-𝟯.𝟭-𝟴𝗕 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗯𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝘁. 𝗚𝗼𝘁 𝟮.𝟯𝘅 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗽. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘀 𝟰-𝟲𝘅 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝟳𝟬𝗕 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀.

Why do larger models see even better speedups? They're more memory-bandwidth bound (so reducing forward passes helps more), and the draft head overhead becomes negligible. It's under 1% of a 70B model's parameters.

The post covers the full pipeline: architecture deep-dive, GPU setup on E2E Cloud, data preparation, training your own draft head with SpecForge, and deploying for inference with SGLang.

If you're running inference at scale, this is one of the most practical optimizations you can apply.

author: Norman Paulsen
subtitle: Published AI/LLM Researcher & Architect | Delivering Value from AI, Digital Transformation, Service Improvement | AI & Data Background
content:
Google's Titans architecture rewrites the rules for how AI systems store and process information over extended timeframes.

The Titans framework introduces a neural memory module that departs from static transformer approaches by enabling AI systems to learn and update their memory during inference, a capability that mirrors biological memory consolidation more closely than previous architectures. This shift from purely training-time learning to continuous test-time adaptation represents a meaningful architectural evolution.

Benchmarks demonstrate substantial performance gains, with Titans outperforming GPT-4 and Llama3 + RAG variants on long-context reasoning tasks, particularly in the BABILong benchmark designed to stress test extended reasoning chains. The architecture scales to contexts exceeding 2 million tokens without accuracy degradation, a threshold that positions it well beyond current mainstream model capabilities.

Practical applications span diverse domains, from maintaining coherence across long contexts to preserving interaction history in customer service systems with measurable fidelity improvements. The MIRAS framework compounds these gains by enabling faster computation and more efficient memory utilization, reducing the computational overhead typically associated with extended context processing.

The incorporation of a "surprise metric" that weights learning based on information novelty introduces a principled approach to memory prioritization, effectively filtering signal from noise in streaming data scenarios. This mechanism prevents information overflow while preserving model adaptability, addressing a core limitation in systems that treat all inputs uniformly.

From the paper:
Low surprise: If the new word is "cat" and the model's memory state already expects an animal word, the gradient (surprise) is low. It can safely skip memorizing the word "cat" in its permanent long-term state.

High surprise: If the model's memory state is summarizing a serious financial report, and the new input is a picture of a banana peel (the unexpected event), the gradient (surprise) will be very high. This signals that the new input is important or anomalous, and it must be prioritized for permanent storage in the long-term memory module.

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🔧 Why Your RL Training Keeps Crashing (And How to Fix It)

Another cool paper from Qwen about RL! It explains why token-level optimization in RL for LLMs actually works, and provides practical recipes for stable training with MoE models.

→ The mismatch between sequence-level rewards and token-level optimization isn't a bug. The paper shows that token-level objectives are a valid first-order approximation to the true sequence-level reward, but only when two conditions hold: minimal training-inference discrepancy and low policy staleness. Break either condition and your training collapses.

→ Importance sampling (IS) correction isn't optional. Removing the IS weight for training-inference discrepancy causes immediate training collapse and entropy death. Length normalization (used in GRPO and CISPO) biases the objective and leads to suboptimal performance. The basic REINFORCE with IS correction beats fancier algorithms.

→ MoE models are especially fragile because expert routing amplifies both sources of instability. About 10% of routers select different experts between training and inference engines, and 94% of tokens hit a different expert in at least one layer. This makes the first-order approximation much more likely to break.

→ Routing Replay fixes MoE instability but introduces bias. R2 (replay training engine routes) works better with low off-policiness, R3 (replay inference engine routes) becomes necessary when you split batches into many mini-batches. Neither is strictly superior.

→ Cold-start initialization doesn't matter much if you train long enough. Models initialized from Qwen3-Max, DeepSeek-R1, and GPT distillation all converged to similar performance with stable RL.

I like how this paper elegantly reconciles token- and sequence-level rewards. The MiniRL algorithm it introduces also feels credible. However, experiments are only focused on math reasoning with binary rewards (the easiest RL setup). The claim that cold-start doesn't matter is based on just three initializations trained on the same prompt set, which feels too narrow to make strong conclusions.

author: Mahammad Iqbal Shaik
subtitle: AI Engineer | Building & Optimizing Generative AI Applications with Foundation Models, RAG & Prompt Engineering | Driving Innovation & Efficiency | Modeling & Optimization | MLOps | LLMOps
content:
Part 2 of my 'Back to Square One' series, rebuilding deep learning foundations through systematic experiments. In the age of Agents and GenAI, you can't innovate on what you don't truly understand.

After visualizing how Batch Normalization acts as a "computational superhighway" preventing signal attenuation, I wanted to revisit the other half of the equation: activation functions. 

Ever wondered why your 50+ layer network converges to garbage while your friend’s identical architecture trains perfectly? The answer lies in a single function you probably never think about: your activation function.

So I deliberately killed 100% of neurons in a neural network, then resurrected them with a 0.01 mathematical tweak. 

Performance gap? 54x. 

The experiments revealed: 
- Why Sigmoid's 0.25 max derivative mathematically guarantees failure in deep networks (0.25^50 ≈ 0) 
- How ReLU permanently kills 33% of neurons even with perfect initialization and they can never recover 
- Why GELU enables Transformers to train reliably at 100+ layers (smooth derivatives = stable optimization) 

The smoking gun: gradient flow visualization across 5, 20, and 50-layer networks. Sigmoid collapses catastrophically. ReLU stays stable. GELU stays smooth. 

Checkout Activation functions deep dive: https://lnkd.in/gYufE9iX

This explains decades of AI history in three charts: 
 1980s-2000s: Deep learning "impossible" (Sigmoid decay) 
 2010s: CNN revolution (ReLU stability) 
 Now: Transformer dominance (GELU smoothness)

author: Sheng Zhang
subtitle: Principal Researcher at Microsoft Research
content:
#DeepSeek has released some of the best OSS LLMs. But they’re blind! 
What if we could turn any text-only LLM into a competitive multimodal reasoner without modifying its parameters? (Fig 1)

Excited to introduce #BeMyEyes: a modular multi-agent framework that extends LLMs to new modalities by letting them collaborate with lightweight vision perceivers.

Core idea💡: decouple perception from reasoning. (Fig 2)
▸A lightweight VLM acts as the eyes: it inspects images and sends textual evidence.
▸A powerful frozen LLM acts as the brain: it reasons over that evidence.
They talk via natural-language multi-turn conversation, so the LLM can ask follow-ups and the perceiver replies with targeted visual details.

✓ No joint multimodal training. No architecture changes. Just agents collaborating through text, and you can swap in better eyes/brains anytime.

1️⃣Results (Table 1): equipping DeepSeek-R1 with a small perceiver (e.g., #Qwen2.5-VL-7B) unlocks strong multimodal reasoning. BeMyEyes + DeepSeek-R1 reaches #MMMU-Pro 57.2, #MathVista 72.7, #MathVision 48.5, which are competitive with, and often surpassing, large proprietary VLMs like GPT-4o on knowledge-intensive benchmarks.

2️⃣BeMyEyes generalizes to different model families. (Table 2)
Beside DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen-VL, we consider different model families: #InternVL3-8B as the eyes, and #GPT-4, a large proprietary LLM, as the brain. Our BeMyEyes framework also shows very strong results.

3️⃣BeMyEyes generalizes to specialized domains. (Table 3)
With a medical perceiver (Lingshu-7B), the same framework stays competitive on multimodal medical reasoning benchmarks, without needing to rebuild or retrain a giant medical VLM from scratch.

⭐Takeaway: multimodality doesn’t have to mean a monolithic unified model. A scalable alternative is agent collaboration through language: small, adaptable “eyes” + strong “brains,” improving independently over time.

author: Berk Gökden
subtitle: AI/ML & Data Engineer | Data Infrastructure · RAG · Agentic · Multi-Agent AI · Vector Search | Python, Go
content:
Make llama.cpp models behave
I released a small library that adds strict constrained generation to any model running on llama.cpp.
 No retraining.
 No think tokens.
 All control happens at generation time.
The library enforces structure at the token level.
 Invalid tokens are blocked immediately.
 This reduces hallucination, keeps outputs in a known format, and lets you inject signals during generation, not just in the prompt.
I focus on XML-style tags because they send clearer structural signals to LLMs.
 Tags define where reasoning happens and where final output is allowed.
 Even smaller models start to act more predictable under these constraints.
The example below (in the screenshot) shows a forced-thinking loop:
The system prompt defines <think> for reasoning and <output> for the final answer.
For the first two steps, the code forces <think>.
After that, the model must select between <think> and <output> using llm.select({"<think>", "<output>"}).
llm.generate(...) is constrained to stop at </think> or </output>, so reasoning never leaks into the final answer.
This pattern gives you:
Controlled multi-step reasoning
Lower hallucination
Stronger guarantees on where and how the model can respond
Repo: https://lnkd.in/eBDiD986
If you are building agents or automation on llama.cpp and need predictable behavior, constrained generation will give you more control than another size jump in model weights.
