content:
Production LLM Deployment: From Model to Scale in 10 Steps

Deploying Large Language Models to production is fundamentally different from traditional ML. Here's a practical roadmap based on real-world constraints. 🚀

The LLM Reality Check

Models are 10-100GB+. Updates are expensive. Your product metrics: p95 latency < 1s and cost per 1,000 tokens. Inputs are free-form text prompts.

Step 1: Optimize the Model 🔧

Before deployment, compress aggressively:
- 4-bit quantization (NF4): Cuts VRAM by 75%
- LoRA adapters: Fine-tune without touching base weights
- KV-cache optimization: Reuse attention computations

Choose your format (GGUF/Safetensors) and engine (vLLM, TGI) based on GPU architecture.

Step 2: Package as Artifact 📦

Build a Docker image with compressed model weights, CUDA dependencies + vLLM runtime. Keep image < 300MB using multi-stage builds.

Step 3: Deploy with Kubernetes ☸️

Standard K8s Deployment + Service for fault tolerance. Use HPA/VPA to autoscale on GPU utilization, RPS, and token throughput.

Step 4: Monitor What Matters 📊

Track via Prometheus + Grafana:
- p95 latency: User experience threshold
- Tokens/sec: Throughput measure
- GPU utilization: Resource efficiency
- VRAM usage: Avoid OOM kills

Use DCGM-exporter for GPU metrics. Log prompts to Elastic/Loki for debugging.

Step 5: Build MLOps Infrastructure 🏗️

- Model Registry: Version weights, LoRA diffs, checkpoints
- Prompt Store: Template library with A/B test history
- CI/CD pipeline: Static analysis → unit tests → Docker build → GitOps deployment

Step 6: Smart Load Balancing ⚖️

Implement Token-Aware Load Balancing: Route requests based on prompt length. Long prompts block GPUs longer—distribute intelligently.

Step 7: Close the Feedback Loop 🔄

Production data fuels improvement:
- Collect bad responses (LLM feedback + user signals)
- Build datasets for fine-tuning or RLHF
- Calculate offline metrics (BLEU, Rouge, Hallucination Rate)

Step 8: Manage Costs 💰

Calculate per-environment: GPU hours + networking + checkpoint storage. Autoscale down during off-hours. Use Spot/Preemptible GPUs for batch jobs.

Step 9: Plan for Incidents 🚨

Set SLOs: p95 < 800ms, error rate < 1%

Alert on latency spikes, GPU OOM events, throughput drops. Maintain runbooks for pod restarts and rollbacks.

Step 10: Iterate 🔁

LLM production is a cycle, not a destination. Monitor → optimize → deploy → repeat.

Key Takeaway: Production LLMs demand different thinking than traditional ML. Focus on latency, cost per token, and continuous feedback loops. ✨

The last few days reminded me of something important: in AI, timing matters as much as action.

Back in August, I was preparing a talk for PyCon on “Beyond Transformers: Exploring State Space Models (Mamba) for Next-Gen LLM Architectures.”
But three months ago, hardly anyone outside research circles cared about SSMs. Agentic AI was the hot topic, and I switched my talk to Observability in Agentic Systems because that’s what the audience needed at the time.

Looking back, I wish I had still spoken about SSMs.

Because now after Google’s new paper on Nested Learning suddenly the entire industry is talking about State Space Models, Mamba2, Titans, Hope, long-context architectures, and the broader beyond-Transformers movement.

The Google team literally benchmarks their new architecture against Mamba2, and overnight SSMs have gone from “interesting research” to “everyone should know this.”

Three months ago, most people didn’t even understand why Mamba was such a big deal.
Today, everyone is sharing threads, explainers, and analyses.

I missed being early on that conversation.

And it’s a good reminder:
In AI, if something feels ahead of the curve talk about it anyway. By the time the world catches up, it’s already late.

But the upside?
This whole wave Mamba, Titans/Hope, Nested Learning is showing the same direction:
we’re officially moving beyond Transformers, toward architectures that can learn continuously, remember longer, and act more like real intelligent systems.

LLMs & AI orchestration toolkits compared: Choosing the right stack

Since OpenAI’s GPT‑4o set the multimodal pace last year, Google has rolled out Gemini 2.5 Pro with a million‑token context window, Anthropic has boosted reasoning depth with Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and Meta’s open‑source Llama 4 Maverick has arrived to prove permissive licences no longer mean second‑tier quality. Even the cost curve is bending as Mistral Medium 3 now undercuts the big names at roughly $0.40 per million input tokens.

However, selecting a model is only half the engineering puzzle. Real-world systems must still meet strict latency budgets, stay within a cloud-GPU budget, respect corporate safety requirements, account for contextual limitations, and leave room for rapid iteration and deployment.

To address these challenges, cluster-scale orchestration frameworks such as Kubeflow and Ray play a pivotal role in managing training runs and enabling effective rollouts. Furthermore, agent toolkits such as LangChain, Semantic Kernel, CrewAI, and AutoGen enhance capabilities like retrieval, memory, observability, and multi-agent coordination. Complementing these, purpose-built vector databases and monitoring dashboards are crucial for maintaining pipeline health long after the initial demo.

This article examines three pillars of the stack: the trade-offs between proprietary and open-source model families; the architectural patterns—retrieval-augmented generation, chain-of-thought prompting, and agentic workflows—that govern model behavior in production; and the surrounding ecosystem of orchestration layers, storage engines, and evaluation tools that turn raw potential into a dependable product.

author: Hao Hoang
subtitle: I share daily insights on AI agents, LLMs, Data Science, Machine Learning | I help AI engineers crack top-tier interviews | 56K+ community | LLM System Design, RAG, Agents
content:
You're in a Senior ML System Interview at Meta. The interviewer sets a trap:

"We need to adapt Llama-3 70B to the highly technical Medical domain. We are GPU-constrained, so we can't do full fine-tuning. How do we proceed?"

95% of candidates walk right into the trap.

Most candidates say...
"Easy. We use standard 𝐋𝐨𝐑𝐀 (𝐋𝐨𝐰-𝐑𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐀𝐝𝐚𝐩𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧). It freezes the backbone, injects low-rank matrices, and saves us 70%+ VRAM. It’s the industry standard."

The interviewer nods, notes "𝘒𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘭𝘦𝘥𝘨𝘦 𝘎𝘢𝘱," and moves on.

Why? The candidate thinks they're teaching the model deep medical knowledge (𝐒𝐮𝐛𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞), but standard LoRA mostly just teaches it to write like a doctor (𝐒𝐭𝐲𝐥𝐞).

Standard LoRA is fantastic for 𝘐𝘯𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘛𝘶𝘯𝘪𝘯𝘨 (teaching a model to chat, summarize, or follow rules). But for 𝘊𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘶𝘢𝘭 𝘗𝘳𝘦-𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘪𝘯𝘨 (injecting new, complex domain knowledge like oncology or case law), vanilla LoRA fails.

Recent research ("LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less - 
arXiv:2405.09673 ") proves that standard LoRA updates are mathematically insufficient to capture high-rank data shifts. The model doesn't learn the medicine, it just mimics the doctor's tone.

-----
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧:
To match Full Fine-Tuning performance on a LoRA budget, you need to implement 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐇𝐲𝐩𝐞𝐫-𝐀𝐝𝐚𝐩𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐚.

You don't just "𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵 𝘱𝘦𝘧𝘵." You engineer the adaptation:

1. 𝘙𝘢𝘯𝘬-𝘚𝘵𝘢𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘻𝘦𝘥 𝘓𝘰𝘙𝘈 (𝘙𝘚-𝘓𝘰𝘙𝘈): Standard LoRA scales adapters by 1/r. This collapses learning as you increase rank. You must switch to scaling by 1/sqrt(r) to stabilize gradients at higher ranks (e.g., r=256).

2. 𝘓𝘰𝘧𝘵𝘘 𝘐𝘯𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯: Random initialization of adapters is inefficient. Use LoftQ to quantize the backbone and initialize adapters to minimize the approximation error immediately.

3. 𝘋𝘪𝘧𝘧𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘯𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘙𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘴: Not all layers learn at the same speed. You must apply a lower LR to embedding layers (to retain vocabulary stability) and a higher LR to the projection layers.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐆𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐘𝐨𝐮 𝐇𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐝:

"Standard LoRA is for changing behavior. The Trifecta is for acquiring knowledge. To match full fine-tuning performance on a budget, I don't increase compute; I increase mathematical efficiency using RS-LoRA and Differential Learning Rates."

content:
🔥 Agent fine-tuning is back— an 8B orchestrator carries GPT-5, hitting 37.1 on HLE
Over the past year, we’ve seen an explosion of “AI agents” built by chaining tools, APIs, and LLMs together — with ever-more-sophisticated routing logic and workflows.
But here’s the problem:
Wiring components together ≠ intelligence.
Workflows alone don’t learn, don’t adapt, and don’t optimize.

At some point, agents have to learn how to reason, not just be told when to call a model or how to retrieve a document. 
That’s where fine-tuning comes back — this time, reinvented through reinforcement learning (RL).
🧠 From orchestration to optimization
We at NVIDIA Research introduced ToolOrchestra, a framework that uses long-horizon RL to train small models (“orchestrators”) to manage big ones.
Instead of hand-coded heuristics or fixed workflows, the Orchestrator learns through RL how to decide:
→ Which model to use including powerful ones (GPT-5, Claude, etc.)
→ When to invoke a tool (search, code interpreter, API call)
→ How long to reason before acting

The orchestrator is rewarded not just for accuracy, but also for efficiency: balancing accuracy, latency, and cost.
This makes it a truly adaptive controller, not just a scripted pipeline.
⚙️ RL optimizing your workflow
This is a direction the community has barely explored: reinforcement learning applied to orchestration itself.
It’s long-horizon, multi-objective RL — optimizing workflows, not just single-step predictions.
And the results are striking.
Our Orchestrator-8B outperforms frontier LLMs like GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1, and Llama-3.3-70B on hard reasoning benchmarks (Humanity’s Last Exam, FRAMES, τ²-Bench) while being cheaper and faster. It outperforms GPT-5 on HLE (37.1% v.s. 35.1%) while being 2.5× faster and 70% cheaper.

💡 “Fine-tuning is dead”? Think again.
There’s been a popular narrative lately — that fine-tuning is over, and that prompt engineering or workflow composition are enough.
Our work proves that fine-tuning didn’t die — it evolved. 
Now it’s RL-based, multi-objective, and long-horizon.

ToolOrchestra marks a shift from “monolithic LLMs” to compound AI systems — modular, adaptive, and self-optimizing.

🚀 The rise of compound AI systems
We’re entering a new phase of AI system design:
→ From monolithic LLMs to compound AI systems — modular, adaptive, and self-optimizing.
→ From static workflows to RL-trained orchestration.
→ From brute-force scale to intelligent coordination.
Orchestration is no longer just a systems problem — it’s a learning problem.

author: Pranay Tiwari
subtitle: Vice President, Data Science | Leading Enterprise-Wide AI/ML Transformation | Founding Member of AI CoE | Agentic AI & Scalable Recommender Systems | US Patent Holder
content:
Building an LLM - concepts and interview question series

Topic 5 – Quantization: PTQ vs. QAT

When asked, “How do you optimize a 70B parameter model for inference?” many candidates jump to “Quantization.” But very few can explain how we get from FP16 down to INT8 or INT4 without turning the model into gibberish.
The bridge between massive weights and limited GPU VRAM is carefully engineered quantization.

So to control the trade-off between perplexity (accuracy) and latency, you must distinguish between two paradigms:

Post Training Quantization (PTQ) - This is like a quick win. You take a pre-trained Llama-3 or Mistral checkpoint and calibrate it after training.

Mechanics: Uses a small dataset to fix activation ranges.
Used - Flows like load_in_8bit or GGUF fall here. (for more see bitsandbytes package documentation)
Reason it works: Large models have parameter redundancy. They can "eat" the precision loss with <1% perplexity degradation.

Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) – So here you inject fake quantization nodes during a fine-tuning stage. The model “sees” the rounding noise during the forward pass and adapts its weights to survive it. (Fake it till you make it for LLMs :))
Used: Critical for INT4 (and below) or on-device SLMs.
Reason it works: At 4-bit precision, naive PTQ often breaks reasoning capabilities. QAT recovers that lost signal.

Why this matters for LLMs: A 7B model in FP16 needs ~14GB VRAM. In INT8, it needs ~7GB. This isn't just about saving space; it is about Memory Bandwidth. Since inference is memory-bound, moving 50% less data per token directly translates to higher tokens-per-second.

Real-World Example: Meta’s DLRM Recommender systems at scale (like Meta’s) are often bottlenecked by fetching massive Embedding Tables from memory, not by the CPU compute. By applying QAT to these embeddings, they compress Terabyte-scale tables by 4x. This frees up memory bandwidth, allowing the model to run drastically faster in production without losing the nuances about user preferences. 

My Rule of Thumb: Start with a solid PTQ process. If perplexity degrades beyond tolerance (especially at 4-bits)—pay the compute cost for QAT.

content:
Major release from DeepSeek.

And a big deal for open-source LLMs.

DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale is on par with Gemini-3-Pro on the 2025 International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) and the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI).

It even surpasses the Gemini 3 Pro on several benchmarks.

DeepSeek identifies three critical bottlenecks: 

> vanilla attention mechanisms that choke on long sequences, 
> insufficient post-training compute, 
> and weak generalization in agentic scenarios.

They introduce DeepSeek-V3.2, a model that tackles all three problems simultaneously.

One key innovation is DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), which reduces attention complexity from O(L²) to O(Lk) where k is far smaller than the sequence length. A lightweight "lightning indexer" scores which tokens matter, then only those top-k tokens get full attention. 

The result: significant speedups on long contexts without sacrificing performance.

But architecture alone isn't enough. DeepSeek allocates post-training compute exceeding 10% of the pre-training cost, a massive RL investment that directly translates to reasoning capability.

For agentic tasks, they built an automatic environment-synthesis pipeline generating 1,827 distinct task environments and 85,000+ complex prompts. Code agents, search agents, and general planning tasks (all synthesized at scale for RL training)

The numbers: On AIME 2025, DeepSeek-V3.2 hits 93.1% (GPT-5-High: 94.6%). On SWE-Verified, 73.1% resolved. On HLE text-only, 25.1% compared to GPT-5's 26.3%.

Their high-compute variant, DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale, goes further, achieving gold medals in IMO 2025 (35/42 points), IOI 2025 (492/600), and ICPC World Finals 2025 (10/12 problems solved). 

This is the first open model to credibly compete with frontier proprietary systems across reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks.

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
ToolOrchestra is such a cool work from NVIDIA

This paper shows that an 8B parameter model trained with RL can coordinate larger LLMs and tools to outperform frontier models like GPT-5 on hard benchmarks, while being 2.5x cheaper. It's a great demo of what frontier SLMs will be about in 2026.

→ Off-the-shelf LLMs are not good orchestrators. When prompted to coordinate tools, GPT-5 over-relies on GPT-5-mini (98% of calls) and Qwen3-8B defaults to GPT-5 (73% of calls). RL training eliminates these biases and produces balanced tool selection that actually works.

→ The reward design is the secret sauce. They combine three signals: correctness (did you solve it?), efficiency (how much did it cost?), and user preference (did you respect constraints like "be cost efficient"?). This multi-objective RL setup is what makes the orchestrator actually useful in practice.

→ Orchestrator-8B beats GPT-5 on Humanity's Last Exam (37.1% vs 35.1%) while using 30% of the cost (but note that it uses tools!). It also dominates on FRAMES (76.3% vs 74.0%) and Tau2-Bench (80.2% vs 77.7%).

→ Generalization to unseen tools is surprisingly strong. Even when swapped to completely different models not seen during training, Orchestrator-8B still outperforms all baselines.

→ They built a synthetic data pipeline (ToolScale) to generate verifiable multi-turn tool-use trajectories across 10 domains. This is crucial since real agentic training data is scarce and hard to verify.

We're definitely moving in the direction of small orchestrators that excel at using tools. When that happens, the cost of agentic pipelines will plummet because they will no longer rely on costly, cloud frontier models. I hope we can see more of this!

author: Emmanouil Antonios Platanios
subtitle: VP of Research at Scaled Cognition | ex-Microsoft, CMU
content:
Check out our new blog post “Prompt Trees: Training-time Prefix Caching,” by the research team at Scaled Cognition.

https://lnkd.in/dDYF2VXz 

TL;DR: Training speedups of up to 70x on tree-structured data. Not 70%. _70x_.

How do we do this? Let's consider the case of RL rollouts for a conversational agent (this is just one possible example of many). You typically have many rollouts at each turn - this is a tree.

In standard transformer training, you need to duplicate the prompt prefix for each rollout, compute gradients, and take a step (e.g., trl does this). That's a lot of duplicate encoding, especially for long conversations or many rollouts.

How do we remove the duplicate encoding? The key insight is that token encoding only depends on other tokens by means of the position IDs and attention mask - if we can set those appropriately for a tree structure, we can use standard transformers to encode trees.

It turns out you can use pytorch's flex attention to construct a tree-structured attention mask for a prompt tree. It's very efficient if you use a binary encoding of a node's path to compute whether one token is in the prompt prefix of another token.

With this attention mask and correctly-offset position ids, the encodings that you get (and gradients that you compute) are _exactly_ the same as if you had encoded each path through the tree as a separate linear prompt (modulo numerical stability).

How well does this work? That depends on a lot of things, but the biggest factor is how dense your prompt trees are. If your data is intentionally constructed to make good use of prompt trees, the speedup can be very large.

We ran timing experiments on our cluster, measuring the relative speedup as a function of how dense the prompt tree is. The speedup is roughly linear in the proportion of duplicated tokens in the tree, with empirical speedups of up to 70x.

It's not exactly linear, for various reasons we discuss in the post, but it's empirically nearly so. Note that this is a speedup for the gradient computation only, and it's one that potentially changes optimization dynamics (e.g., you're packing more information into each batch)

As we're coming out of stealth, we're excited to be sharing more with the community! (We'll be starting with projects which are at the periphery of our tech for now and saving our core agentic modeling tech for later.) We'll be at NeurIPS, happy to chat, and we're hiring 🙂

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🎯 SAPO: Qwen's new RL training algorithm

SAPO is a new policy optimization algorithm introduced by Qwen that replaces hard clipping with smooth, temperature-controlled gating to make RL training of LLMs more stable (especially for MoE models).

→ Token-level importance ratios in RL have high variance, which gets worse in MoE models due to routing heterogeneity. GRPO and GSPO use hard clipping to fix this, but it creates a brittle tradeoff: too tight and you lose learning signal, too loose and gradients get noisy.

→ SAPO uses a sigmoid-shaped soft gate centered at the on-policy point. Near on-policy, gradients flow normally; as deviation grows, they decay smoothly instead of getting cut to zero. This keeps useful signal from moderately off-policy tokens.

→ SAPO uses asymmetric temperatures for positive vs negative tokens, with negative tokens getting faster decay. The reasoning: negative gradients raise logits for many unsampled tokens in a huge vocabulary, spreading instability, while positive gradients only boost one token.

→ Under typical conditions (small on-policy steps, low variance in token ratios), SAPO's token-level gates average out to a sequence-level gate, so it behaves like GSPO. But when outlier tokens appear, SAPO selectively down-weights just those instead of killing the whole sequence's gradient.

→ Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B show SAPO trains longer before instability kicks in and hits higher Pass@1 on math benchmarks (AIME25, HMMT25, BeyondAIME). It also doesn't need the "Routing Replay" hack that GRPO requires for MoE stability.

Cool, clean contribution from Qwen. Soft gating is an elegant middle ground between GRPO's aggressive token clipping and GSPO's approach. Note that SAPO delays instability but doesn't eliminate it, and the benchmarks are limited to math reasoning on Qwen models.

author: Anshuman Mishra
subtitle: ML @ Zomato
content:
"Just use KV cache for inference"

Until you need:
- Same 5000-token system prompt for every request
- 10M+ requests/day burning $50k on redundant compute
- RAG pipelines reprocessing the same docs 1000x/day

Then you implement prefix caching.

You know why basic KV cache isn't enough?

A typical ChatGPT-style app:
- System prompt: 2000 tokens (same for every user)
- RAG context: 3000 tokens (same docs retrieved repeatedly)  
- User query: 100 tokens (unique)
- Generated response: 500 tokens

Without prefix caching:
- Process 5000 tokens EVERY request (prefill)
- 1M requests = 5 BILLION redundant token computations
- You're paying to reprocess "You are a helpful assistant..." 1 million times

NOTE - Subscribe to my email newsletter to get my free posts daily -

https://lnkd.in/g8ZJGsWj 

Prefill (prompt processing) is DETERMINISTIC. Same input tokens → same KV cache, always.

> Traditional KV cache: Stores within a single conversation
> Prefix caching: Stores ACROSS conversations, keyed by exact token sequence

If 10,000 users all start with the same system prompt, you compute it ONCE and serve 10,000x from cache. The prompt tokens become free after the first hit.

When to use prefix caching?

✓ Same system prompts across all users (chatbots, agents)
✓ RAG with frequently accessed documents (customer support, docs search)
✓ Multi-turn conversations (context grows but prefix stays same)
✓ Code assistants (same repo/file context)
✓ Few-shot prompting (same examples for every request)

Basically: ANY repetitive context at inference time.

How to design cache key though?

> Naive: Hash the entire prompt string
> Problem: One character change = full cache miss

> Better: Hash the TOKEN SEQUENCE  
> Why: Same text → same tokens → cache hit

> Best: Longest prefix matching
> Example: "You are a helpful..." (cached) + "Answer this: [new]" (compute)

Only the UNIQUE suffix needs prefill. vLLM and SGLang do this automatically.

Common mistakes that kill your hit rate:

❌ Dynamic timestamps in prompts ("Current time: 2:35pm")
❌ Random request IDs in system message  
❌ User-specific info in prefix ("Hello, John!")
❌ Non-deterministic formatting

✓ Move dynamic content to suffix
✓ Standardize system prompts across users
✓ Use template prompts with fixed prefixes
✓ Monitor cache hit rates in production

A 95% hit rate vs 50% hit rate is 2x cost difference.

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🗼 SAE Reloaded: steer LLMs at inference time

Excellent blog post from David Louapre (who's also my favorite science YouTuber) to reproduce Anthropic's famous Golden Gate Claude experiment. It uses Llama 3.1 8B and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to create a model obsessed with the Eiffel Tower instead.

It features AxBench (by Zhengxuan Wu, Aryaman Arora, et al.), my favorite paper in mechanistic interpretability. AxBench is quite bearish on the effectiveness of SAEs, but this recipe seems more successful. Here are the highlights:

→ Steering is delicate: if it's too low, nothing happens, and if it's too high, the model outputs gibberish. Even worse, the steering strength is prompt-dependent, making it hard to generalize. The sweet spot seems to be around half the layer's typical activation magnitude.

→ Clamping activations at a fixed value works better than simply adding steering vectors, which contradicts AxBench's findings on Gemma models but aligns with what Anthropic did for Golden Gate Claude.

→ Steering multiple Eiffel Tower features across layers barely helps compared to using a single well-chosen feature - the features seem redundant rather than complementary.

→ Simple prompting still crushes SAE steering: prompted model scores 1.67 on the harmonic mean vs 0.44 for the steered model, with much better fluency and instruction following.

→ Repetition penalty and lower temperature during generation significantly reduce the gibberish problem that plagues SAE steering, improving fluency without hurting concept inclusion.

I'm a fan of the recipe approach, trying different methods (like clamping) to improve the trade-off between concept inclusion and outputting gibberish. It's disappointing that the multi-feature steering didn't pan out. Not sure why features are redundant rather than complementary. It's a really cool blog post that goes in the right direction but, to be clear, SAE steering is still more of a research curiosity than a practical technique. And it's perfectly fine that way since it's a great tool to understand the inner workings of LLMs better. :)

author: Pascal Biese
subtitle: AI Lead at PwC <​/​> Daily AI highlights for 80k+ experts 📲🤗
content:
AI agents are forgetting what they shouldn't - and it's a design flaw, not a capacity problem.

Most AI agent memory systems today follow an "Ahead-of-Time" approach: they compress historical information into lightweight memory structures before requests arrive. This seems efficient, but there's a fundamental issue - compression always means information loss.

Researchers from the Beijing Academy of AI propose General Agentic Memory (GAM), a system that flips this paradigm using "Just-in-Time compilation." Instead of compressing everything upfront, GAM maintains complete historical information in a page-store while creating a lightweight navigational memory. When a request comes in, it performs "deep research" - iteratively planning, searching, and reflecting across the full history to retrieve exactly what's needed.

The architecture consists of two modules: a Memorizer that indexes history with searchable abstracts, and a Researcher that conducts multi-step information gathering at runtime. This design leverages the agentic capabilities of frontier LLMs and benefits from test-time scaling—more compute at inference leads to better results.

GAM demonstrates substantial improvements across memory benchmarks like LoCoMo and long-context tasks like HotpotQA, with accuracy gains of 6+ percentage points from the architecture itself. On top of that, the framework is optimizable end-to-end through reinforcement learning, allowing it to improve with deployment experience.

The takeaway? GAM shows us that search might be a critical component of agent memory systems.

author: Aanchal Karamchandani
subtitle: Senior ML Engineer | LLM Inference & Serving | Production AI Infrastructure
content:
𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐘𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐋𝐋𝐌 𝐆𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐓𝐨𝐤𝐞𝐧 ⏳
𝐀𝐧𝐝 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐊𝐕 𝐂𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐀𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐅𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐬 𝐈𝐭
Anyone who has profiled LLM inference has seen this pattern.
The model begins generating quickly, then each new token becomes slower than the one before.

The hardware is strong, yet latency keeps growing.

So why does this happen?

Transformers generate text one token at a time.
Each token relies on the entire sequence so far.
As the context grows, the model has more history to process.

Inside attention, every new token creates a Query vector.
That Query must compare itself with all past Keys and then gather the associated Values to form the next state.

Here is the key detail.
Keys and Values for earlier tokens never change.
But without KV caching, the model rebuilds them for every new token.

This repeated work is the main reason decoding slows down.

KV caching removes that redundancy.

The model stores the Key and Value projections as soon as they are created.
Then each new token only computes:
• The new Query
• The new Key
• The new Value

Everything else is pulled directly from the cache.

This eliminates the quadratic computation that would otherwise appear.

There is an important nuance.
Even with KV caching, the model still performs O(N) attention because the new Query must compare against N cached Keys.
For very long contexts, this memory access becomes the bottleneck.
This is also why GPUs can appear underutilized.
They are not waiting for compute tasks.
They are waiting for data, since the KV cache requires heavy memory bandwidth.

And the familiar behavior remains.
The first token always takes the longest because the full prompt must be processed in the prefill stage to build the initial cache.

Once that is done, decoding becomes significantly faster.

If you are working on LLM inference, KV caching is essential.
It removes repeated projections, reduces computational load, and shifts the challenge toward managing memory bandwidth.

Curious how you handle KV cache scaling in your systems.

#AIEngineering #LLMs #Inference #Transformers #MachineLearning #GenAI

author: Jui Shah
subtitle: MLE @ Samsung Ads | Ex - LinkedIn
content:
Key-Value (KV) caching is a foundational optimization for Large Language Model (LLM) inference. Production systems like vLLM add layers of complexity - continuous batching, PagedAttention, prefix caching, quantized KV cache - but they all start with this core idea: don't recompute what you already know.

Sebastian Raschka, PhD's breakdown of it was excellent, and I wanted to understand it by implementing it on Andrej Karpathy's nanoGPT (GPT-2).

When GPT generates text, it's autoregressive - one token at a time. The naive way: at each step, recompute attention over ALL previous tokens. That's O(N²). Watch the red line in the graph - latency grows with every new token.
KV caching caches the Key and Value matrices from past tokens. Now you only compute attention for the NEW token. O(N²) → O(N). The blue line stays flat.

I forked Karpathy's nanoGPT and implemented it from scratch. The results on GPT-2 (124M): → 2.7x speedup for batch size 1
→ Time per token: constant vs. linearly growing 
→ Trade-off: memory grows linearly (no free lunch)

Three things I learned:
1. The first token (TTFT) is always slow - you must process the entire prompt. The cache only speeds up decoding. [I'm using the same prompt across batches so that helps speed-up the blue cache line a little bit]
2. Warm-up runs matter. My initial benchmarks had spikes until I realized CPU clocks and PyTorch kernels need stabilization.
3. Prompt length matters: To truly see the performance gap, the sequence length must be sufficient. With no cache, latency grows linearly with every token. With KV cache, it stays constant.

Production means handling edge cases: context limits (1024 tokens), cache truncation, batch processing. I built visualizations to see exactly how attention flows - the animated dashboard shows which past tokens the model "attends to" at each step. 

Github repo: https://lnkd.in/dD6NSg7N

author: Igor Gitman
subtitle: Engineer at NVIDIA
content:
What do we need to win IMO gold with open-weight LLMs next year? If we want to do it in natural language (like OpenAI and DeepMind did), we most likely need the following 3 components.

1. A scalable way to evaluate correctness of LLM-written proofs.
2. A massive test-time compute to generate, refine and verify proof candidates.
3. A large-scale RL run combining (1) and (2) to produce proofs for hardest training problems and reinforce correct reasoning.

We published a paper "Scaling Generative Verifiers For Natural Language Mathematical Proof Verification And Selection" exploring (1) and (2). Here are a few highlights.


How reliable are LLMs at evaluating mathematical proofs? To answer this question, we need a judge benchmark, i.e. a set of proofs with correct/incorrect labels. But does high accuracy on such a benchmark always mean an LLM judge has a good understanding of mathematical rigor? Not necessarily! 

We take a recently released OpenProofCorpus dataset as a case study and show that a simple linear classifier on top of problem-proof embeddings gets 75.3% (higher than Claude-Sonnet-4). An even simpler baseline that predicts "incorrect" if a word "triangle" is in a problem (geometry is hard!) and "correct" if a string "---" is in a proof (o3 does that a lot) gets 65.1% (higher than GPT-4.1).

To partially alleviate the bias from such spurious correlations, we augment proof-judge eval set with a specially constructed final-answer benchmark. If we see that our judge improves significantly on the proof benchmarks but still judges many incorrect final-answer solutions as correct, then we are likely overfitting to these superficial stylistic clues.


We use this new setup to investigate a few different aspects of how to improve the accuracy of a proof judge.

- Should we use rubrics or not? ⇒ We should, but the gains aren't that big.
- Should we ensemble multiple models or scale inference compute for a single judge? ⇒ Scaling single judge works best in most cases.
- Should we split proof into parts and judge each individually? ⇒ We weren't able to get consistent gains from this approach.
- What prompt should we use? ⇒ Models are very sensitive to the exact instructions, but a little bit of targeted RL helps to avoid heavy prompt engineering.


We use the best identified judge setup to scale up test-time compute for generating and selecting proofs from gpt-oss-120b. We pick a set of 19 most challenging problems from recent math competitions and show strong improvements. 47.1 pass@1 --> 82.2 maj@512 --> 92.1 GenSelect tournament --> 96.1 with a combination of GenSelect and LLM-as-a-judge. 


We will present this work at MathAI workshop at Neurips. If you're interested, come talk to us!

subtitle: MLE @ 🤗 Hugging Face
content:
Flux.2 is a BIG BOI! 🐘
The inference takes more than 80GB VRAM
A small post on how one can run it on a NVIDIA L4 (22 GBs of VRAM)? 😉

The text encoder is Mistral AI's "Small-3.2-24B". It has 24B bf16 parameters which occupies 24*2=48 GBs VRAM.

We can simply host it as an endpoint and delegate the encoding to our remote endpoint. This frees up 48 GBs worth of local VRAM 

One would quickly notice that text encoding here is a little nuanced, than input text, output hidden states.

This calls for some custom logic and wrapping it as an API for people to use.

I have built an end 2 end tutorial on just this.

> custom text-encoding function
> serve it with FastAPI
> package it as a Docker container
> deploy it on 🤗 Inference Endpoints

Did you know, with the help of remote text encoding, cpu offloading, and quantization, you can now run Flux.2 in a colab notebook?

Happy Flux Day to one and all!

PS: Thanks to Sayak Paul and Erik Kaunismäki for all the guidance and help for this project.

author: Philip Vollet
subtitle: VP Developer Relations & Growth @ Weaviate - Building memory
content:
4× compression. 42% faster queries. BETTER accuracy.

Sounds impossible right? Compression is supposed to be a tradeoff BUT 8-bit Rotational Quantization breaks the rules.

What makes this absolutely wild:

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝘆𝗽𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆: You compress vectors to save memory, you lose some quality, maybe you gain some speed. Pick your poison.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗤 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆: 4x compression + 2.3x faster distance computation + 98-99% recall (basically perfect) + 15-50% higher throughput MIND BLOWN

How does this even work? Two steps:

𝗙𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝘀𝗲𝘂𝗱𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗺 𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 using the Walsh-Hadamard Transform that redistributes your vector's information evenly across all dimensions (this is the clever part that makes everything else possible)

𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗿 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 to 8-bit integers with the quantization interval defined by each vector's min/max values

The rotation is doing something beautiful here - it's making EVERY vector universally well-suited for quantization regardless of structure or position in your dataset. No training needed, no cluster centers, just pure mathematical elegance.

We went DEEP on the technical implementation in the full blog post. The engineering to make this production-ready is genuinely impressive 💙


This is now available in Weaviate 1.32+ and we see it as a better default than uncompressed vectors for most use cases.

content:
Google just tested the largest Kubernetes cluster with 130,000 nodes 🤯, and all this because AI is pushing the boundaries!

The GKE setup was able to scale to 130,000 Pods in just 3 minutes and 40 seconds. During this test, there was a sustained Pod throughput of 1,000 Pods per second.

What's driving this need for scale? A single NVIDIA GB200 GPU requires 2,700W of power. When you're running tens of thousands of these chips, you're looking at hundreds of megawatts for a single cluster. Looks like we're shifting from being limited by chip supply to being limited by electrical power.

To handle this, Google rebuilt core Kubernetes systems. They used a Spanner-based storage backend that processed 13,000 queries per second required for lease updates. The cluster managed over 1 million objects (k8s metadata) while keeping the API server (central hub of k8s) latency stable.

Key design decisions:

- Snapshottable API server cache 
- Consistent reads from the API server cache instead of hitting the DB
- Spanner-based storage for handling massive metadata query load
- GCS FUSE with parallel downloads and caching for efficient data access

Yes. It was all about caching :) and caching things well.

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
It’s been a while since my last blog post, so here’s a new one breaking down the simple math behind online softmax. one of the key components of Flash Attention.

Flash Attention is a kernel (function that runs on a GPU) that makes self-attention run faster than a cheetah. It does this by:

1. Carefully tuning i/o operations between GPU HBM and SRAM to reduce the number of reads/writes between them.
2. Computing the Softmax operation in an online manner.

Given the limited size of SRAM (a few MBs) we can only load chunks of the Q, K, V tensors involved in self-attention at a time.

Online softmax reformulates the Softmax function using very simple high school math tricks that allows for computing the softmax operation in chunks. i.e. break the Q, K tensors into blocks/chunks along the sequence dimension without any loss in accuracy.

This lets GPUs compute the softmax in a parallel manner by loading different chunks onto different SMs.

In this blog, I walk you through the Math and show how all of this can be implemented in under 20 lines of torch code.

Link to the blog: https://lnkd.in/ead67Wws

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🧬 Train your LLMs with low-rank noise!

Evolution Strategies (ES) can optimize neural networks without backpropagation, but they've been limited to small models because generating parameter perturbations for each population member is prohibitively expensive at scale.

→ EGGROLL makes ES practical for billion-parameter models by borrowing the LoRA trick: instead of perturbing all parameters, it only samples two small matrices A and B, achieving 100x speedup over standard ES.

→ The method produces full-rank updates despite using low-rank perturbations because the final update averages across hundreds of thousands of population members (meaning even rank-1 perturbations work well).

→ On LLM fine-tuning, EGGROLL outperformed gradient-based GRPO on **specific** reasoning tasks. It processed 1024 parallel generations per GPU versus only 32 for GRPO, achieving 35% vs. 23% validation accuracy on the Countdown task (same hardware and time budget).

It's a very elegant idea, and I'm surprised I've never seen this kind of LoRA ES before. I'm more skeptical about the comparison with GRPO on artificial tasks: it'd be nice to see how it performs on math and code, for example. The RL results show EGGROLL only matching or slightly beating standard ES on 14/16 tasks, which suggests the low-rank approximation might limit exploration in some settings.

subtitle: ML/AI research engineer. Author of Build a Large Language Model From Scratch (amzn.to/4fqvn0D) and Ahead of AI (magazine.sebastianraschka.com), on how LLMs work and the latest developments in the field.
content:
There have been lots of interesting LLM releases last week. My favorite was actually the Olmo 3 release. Olmo models are always a highlight since they are fully transparent (including training methods and datasets) and come with very detailed technical reports. 

I am sure I'll talk more about the interesting training-related aspects from that 100-pager in the upcoming days and weeks.

In the meantime, here's the side-by-side architecture comparison with Qwen3: 

1) As we can see, the Olmo 3 architecture is relatively similar to Qwen3. However, it's worth noting that this is essentially likely inspired by the Olmo 2 predecessor, not Qwen3. 

2) Similar to Olmo 2, Olmo 3 still uses a post-norm flavor instead of pre-norm, as they found in the Olmo 2 paper that it stabilizes the training.

3) Interestingly, the 7B model still uses multi-head attention similar to Olmo 2. 
However, to make things more efficient and reduce the KV cache size, they now use sliding-window attention (e.g., similar to Gemma 3).

Next, the 32B model (the figure is not shown here due to space reasons, but you can find it in my "The Big LLM Architecture Comparison" article or my Olmo 3 from-scratch notebook):

4) Overall, it's the same architecture but just scaled up. Also, the proportions (e.g., going from the input to the intermediate size in the feed-forward layer, and so on) roughly match the ones in Qwen3. 

5) My guess is the architecture was initially somewhat smaller than Qwen3 due to the smaller vocabulary, and they then scaled up the intermediate size expansion from 5x in Qwen3 to 5.4 in Olmo 3 to have a 32B model for a direct comparison. 

6) Also, note that the 32B model (finally!) uses grouped query attention.


And yes, I also did a from-scratch implementation. It was still a lot of work, but since I had already implemented Qwen3 from scratch, as well as Gemma 3 (for the sliding-window attention component), it wasn't too bad!

If you are a coder, looking at the from-scratch implementation, it's probably the easiest way to understand the architecture: https://lnkd.in/gQgxtVUu

author: Jay Gala
subtitle: Researcher at Microsoft Research | Prev life: Intel, CVSSP Lab, IIT Patna | I’m into LLMs, Efficient AI, Indic AI, Open Source
content:
Why You Should Write Your Own GPU Kernels (and why 95% of people should never touch this stuff)

When You Genuinely SHOULD Write Custom Kernels

1. You're bottlenecked by something no library implements efficiently

All major ML breakthroughs in the last five years came from custom kernels: FlashAttention-1/2/3, Flash-Decoding, MQA/GQA, DeepSeek-MoE routing, and more. Each started when standard ops were 5-20× too slow. If your paper claims >2× speedup over SOTA without a custom kernel, expect skepticism.

2. Kernel fusion is your biggest optimization lever

Modern GPUs are so fast at math that memory bandwidth is the real bottleneck. Fusing 4-8 PyTorch ops into one kernel routinely delivers 2-5× speedup even when individual ops already hit 90% of peak.

3. You need hardware-specific tricks libraries won't expose

Cutting-edge optimizations include tensor-core scheduling quirks, persistent warps with grid-level register sharing on Blackwell, and double/triple buffering. NVIDIA's libraries often avoid bleeding-edge tricks for compatibility reasons. To extract every last TFLOP from H100/H200/Blackwell, you need custom code.

4. Independence matters for your business or research

Relying entirely on closed-source cuDNN creates business risk. NVIDIA has changed licensing, deprioritized features, and quietly slowed certain paths before. Custom kernels (or Triton code you control) = you own your destiny.

When You Should NEVER Write Custom Kernels

1. You need standard operations

For matmul, convolution, layernorm, softmax, or standard attention, cuBLAS/cuDNN and torch.compile are already within 5-15% of theoretical peak. Spending weeks for 8% gain is rarely worth it.

2. You lack expert GPU knowledge and profiling discipline

Writing a correct kernel is easy. Writing a fast one requires deep expertise in GPU architecture, profiling tools, and low-level optimization techniques. Most non-expert custom kernels are 2-10× slower than cuBLAS, not faster.

3. You're a solo developer or small team

Production-grade kernels take 2-8 weeks plus ongoing maintenance across CUDA versions and architectures. That's time not spent on models, data, or product.

4. You need multi-backend support

One CUDA kernel = great on NVIDIA but porting to other backends / hardware could take 3-12 more months. Use Triton or torch.compile instead.

5. The kernel is <5-10% of total runtime

Optimize the hot path first. If your custom op takes 3ms of a 500ms forward pass, you'll never notice the difference.

Bottom Line. Write custom kernels only when:

1. You've measured (not guessed) that existing solutions are >2× slower than physically possible
2. You're publishing/shipping a new primitive that doesn't exist yet
3. Kernel fusion gives you a clear 2×+ end-to-end wall-time win

Everyone else: Use torch.compile, FlashAttention-2, TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, or Triton templates and go build something that actually matters. Your time is worth more than another 7% of theoretical FLOPs.

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🍲 Create your LLM soup

Model merging is a cheap way to boost performance by combining the weights of multiple checkpoints without retraining. The most straightforward technique is a linear average, also called "model soup". Meta released a new paper that describes how to pick the weights for your soup!

→ Most models excel at different things, even within the same benchmark. The paper exploits these "category experts" by finding models that are weak on correlated tasks and combining them with optimized weights (instead of 50-50 blends).

→ The method achieves SOTA on Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard with 80.68% accuracy (70B models) by averaging just 3-4 models. This is 2.7% than the previous best and significantly higher than uniform averaging.

→ Model soups are also more consistent across tasks: performance correlations between categories jump significantly, meaning you're less likely to get a model that's great at tool calling but terrible at multi-turn conversations.

→ The approach scales beyond function calling: gains appear on multilingual math (MGSM) and long-context tasks (∞-Bench), though benefits are not as clear when benchmarks lack clear "expert" candidates or show high correlation between categories.

The core idea is nothing new (already done many times in the open-source community), but the results are pretty compelling. It's also interesting to see that it doesn't work for FLORES-36 translation, where all models perform similarly across languages. Have fun merging models!

author: BIREN PATEL
subtitle: Principal AI Architect @Oracle | IBM| IQVIA | IIIT | Conga | Generative AI, Quantum computing, Mentor
content:
🐢 5 Advanced RAG Debugging Problems (and How to Actually Fix Them)

Building a RAG system is easy.
Getting it to work reliably in production is a completely different game.

Here are 5 complex but incredibly powerful RAG debugging areas every AI/ML engineer should master — along with the exact solutions we use in real systems:

---

1️⃣ Embedding Space Drift & Misalignment

Problem: Queries and documents don’t “live in the same semantic world.”
Fix:

Use a single unified embedding model

Re-embed corpus when models update

Add cross-encoder rerankers (ColBERT / BGE)

Monitor cluster cohesion & drift metrics



---

2️⃣ Chunk Boundary Leakage & Context Toxicity

Problem: Chunking cuts concepts or drags irrelevant info → hallucination risk.
Fix:

Semantic chunking (sentence-coherent segmentation)

Domain-sized chunk windows

Dynamic overlaps

Relevance filtering before passing context to the LLM



---

3️⃣ Retrieval Top-k Noise & Rank Collapse

Problem: Too many irrelevant chunks in top-k → LLM answers poorly.
Fix:

Adaptive top-k (based on query specificity)

Hybrid retrieval (BM25 + embeddings)

ColBERT / cross-encoders for reranking

MMR for diversity + noise reduction



---

4️⃣ Grounding Loss Inside the LLM

Problem: LLM hallucinates even with correct context available.
Fix:

Strict answer-from-context prompts

Mandatory citations (chunk IDs / evidence sentences)

Multi-step verification chains

DPO/finetuning to penalize unsupported answers



---

5️⃣ Weak Query Transformation

Problem: LLM rewrites the query incorrectly → misses relevant documents.
Fix:

Multi-query expansion (3–10 variants)

HyDE retrieval (hypothetical answer embeddings)

Query broadening/narrowing classifiers

Keyword boosting inside Elasticsearch



---

💡 Takeaway

RAG failures rarely come from “the LLM.”
They come from broken retrieval pipelines, poor chunking, or misaligned embeddings.

If you fix these 5 areas, your RAG system will go from “sometimes works” to enterprise-grade reliable.

author: Sreedath Panat
subtitle: MIT PhD | IITM | 100K+ LinkedIn | Co-founder Vizuara & Videsh | Making AI accessible for all
content:
When we look at Vision Transformers practically, the first issue that stands out is how quickly the attention cost grows with image resolution, because the model is operating on tokens and not directly on pixels. 

Even a simple increase from an 80 by 80 image to a 160 by 160 image multiplies the number of patches from 25 to 100 (assuming each patch is 16x16), which means the attention operations jump from 625 to 10000. 

This quadratic growth makes the model extremely expensive to scale for real-world images and tasks like segmentation, where higher resolution is usually necessary.

This challenge naturally pushes us to think about whether we really need every token to attend to every other token in the entire image, or whether there is a more structured way to capture local patterns without exploding the compute. 

This is exactly where the Swin Transformer becomes important, because it introduces the idea of dividing the image into small non-overlapping windows and performing attention only inside these windows, which immediately brings down the complexity to a manageable level since the size of each window remains fixed regardless of the image size.

The second clever idea in Swin is the shifting of these windows between layers, which allows tokens to gradually communicate across different regions of the image without paying the full quadratic cost at any stage. 

This combination of local attention and window shifting creates a hierarchical representation that feels closer to the way CNNs process images, while still maintaining the flexibility and expressiveness of transformer-based modelling. 

I feel this simple structural change is the main reason Swin Transformer became such an important milestone in vision models, especially for tasks that demand high resolution inputs like detection, segmentation and dense prediction.

If we understand this idea clearly, the entire architecture of Swin starts making intuitive sense, because the model is not trying to force global attention everywhere, but rather building global understanding gradually through small, efficient, and predictable computation blocks. This is why Swin remains one of the most practical transformer-based designs for computer vision, and why many modern vision systems still rely on these core ideas when scaling to larger images.

In this week's lecture on Transformers for Vision Bootcamp, we will be working on Swin transformers. You can get access to all material here: https://lnkd.in/ghhPr2G2

author: Nathan Lambert
subtitle: Building Open Language Models @ Allen Institute for AI
content:
We present Olmo 3, our next family of fully open, leading language models. 
This family of 7B and 32B models represents:

1. The best 32B base model.
2. The best 7B Western thinking & instruct models.
3. The first 32B (or larger) fully open reasoning model.

This is a big milestone for Ai2 and the Olmo project. These aren’t huge models, but it’s crucial for the viability of fully open-source models that they are competitive on performance – not just replications of models that came out 6 to 12 months ago. As always, all of our models come with full training data, code, intermediate checkpoints, training logs, and a detailed technical report. 

2025 has marked a year where the entire industry rebuilt their training stack to focus on reasoning and agentic tasks, but some established base model sizes haven’t seen a new leading model since Qwen 2.5 in 2024. The Olmo 3 32B base model could be our most impactful artifact here, as Qwen3 did not release their 32B base model. We show that our 7B recipe competes with Qwen 3, and the 32B size enables a starting point for strong reasoning models or specialized agents. Our base model’s performance is in the same ballpark as Qwen 2.5, surpassing the likes of Stanford’s Marin and Gemma 3, but with pretraining data and code available, it should be more accessible to the community to learn how to finetune it. 

With these strong base models, we’ve created a variety of post-training checkpoints to showcase the many ways post-training can be done to suit different needs. We’re calling this a “Model Flow.” For post-training, we’re releasing Instruct versions – short, snappy, intelligent, and useful especially for synthetic data en masse, Think versions – thoughtful reasoners with the performance you expect from a leading thinking model on math, code, etc. and RL Zero versions – controlled experiments for researchers understanding how to build post-training recipes that start with large-scale RL on the base model.

This is the biggest project we’ve ever taken on at Ai2, with 60+ authors and numerous other support staff. 

In building and observing “thinking” and “instruct” models coming today, it is clear to us that there’s a very wide variety of models that fall into both of these buckets. The way we view it is that thinking and instruct characteristics are on a spectrum, as measured by the number of tokens used per evaluation task. In the future we’re excited to view this thinking budget as a trade-off, and build models that serve different use-cases based on latency/throughput needs.

We thank you for all your support of our work at Ai2. We’re going to be hunting for top talent at NeurIPS to help us scale up our Olmo team in 2026.

author: Stian Dyrnes

content:
Today I learned you can save 90% on your OpenAI bill, by adding a single line of code.

I might be late to the party on this one, but I stumbled upon a small detail which makes a huge difference, and thought I'd share in case anyone else has also missed this.

Many of us rely on OpenAI’s input caching to lower costs and speed up responses. But in production, it’s not always easy to structure prompts so they consistently hit the cache. Parallel flows can land on different nodes, breaking the caching chain and eliminating the savings.

However, by adding a simple "prompt_cache_key" to your requests, OpenAI lets you control the routing so related requests will hit the same node. This gives you full input-cache utilization even when you are running several workflows in parallel. 

Simply dedicate a unique "prompt_cache_key" to each workflow, and you will get max utilization of each input cache, even when multiple flows are running at the same time.

If you have also been missing out on cache hits despite careful prompt design, this small change might be the fix you need.

Do you know any other OpenAI or LLM life-hacks I might have missed? Feel free to drop them in the comments.

author: Angkul P.
subtitle: LLMs, reasoning, mechanistic interpretability, robotics
content:
publishing the work i did for the MATS program. Unfortunately, I wasn't selected this year. But it was a great learning experience :)

I tried to explore why SLMs hallucinates with simple instructions via mech interp. This is also my first work in mech interp  :)

I found that SLMs like Qwen0.5-B answer correctly for simple factual question when prompted to "Think step by step"(CoT) but hallucinates in case of "Give answer in one word"(GAOW).

To study this behaviour in SLMs, I applied the mech interp techniques such as logit lens, attention patterns. I also applied the path patching to fix this behaviour, but it makes the performance worse. GAOW introduces a global state change in the model.
Heuristic mode: a computationally cheap, globally consistent, and stable processing state that is triggered by simple instructions. Its a shortcut for the model.

𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐲𝐬:
1. To know where does the model go wrong, I ran the logit lens analysis for the prompt "What is the capital of america" with GAOW and CoT instructions. During the analysis, I found that qwen-0.5B show divergence in the mid-layers.
2. In the next step, I plot the attention pattern bar charts which helped in identifying the positive heads and negative heads in the model.
3. I ran the path patching experiment, where I patched a clean signal from CoT into the corrupted GAOW run. But instead of fixing it, it makes the model performance worse, activating more negative heads. Path patching results show that GAOW prompt induces a global, self-consistent "heuristic mode." The fact-retrieval heads are conditioned on being in "reasoning mode" and get confused by isolated, conflicting signals.
4. I also isolate the "heuristic mode" and "heuristic direction". Adding this vector to a successful CoT run induces the hallucination. But subtracting it is not enough to fix the GAOW run, suggesting the heuristic mode is a very stable state.
5. Takeaway: simple instruction or any instruction can trigger global, competing computational states in SLMs which can lead to failure.

You can read about my experiments in detail in my blog post. Do give feedback and suggestions or if you have any question, pls reach out :)

author: Pascal Biese
subtitle: AI Lead at PwC <​/​> Daily AI highlights for 80k+ experts 📲🤗
content:
NVIDIA did it again - 5-6x faster generation than the current standard.

TiDAR from NVIDIA is a new hybrid architecture that achieves what seemed impossible: 5-6× faster generation than standard autoregressive models while maintaining the same output quality.

The fundamental challenge with current LLMs is computational efficiency. Autoregressive models like GPT generate one token at a time, leaving GPU compute largely underutilized in a memory-bound regime. Diffusion language models can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but this comes at a steep cost - quality degrades significantly when attempting to decode more than one token per step.

TiDAR resolves this tension through a dual-mode architecture. The model "thinks" in diffusion by drafting multiple tokens in parallel, then "talks" in autoregression by sampling final outputs through rejection sampling - all within a single forward pass. 

The key innovation is a carefully designed attention mask that enables both causal and bidirectional attention patterns simultaneously. This allows the model to leverage what the researchers call "free token slots" - additional computation that incurs minimal latency cost in the memory-bound regime.

TiDAR generates 7-8 tokens per forward pass, translating to 4.71x to 5.91x throughput improvements measured in tokens per second. Most importantly, it's the first architecture to close the quality gap with pure autoregressive models while delivering these speedups. The method even outperforms EAGLE-3, currently the leading speculative decoding approach, in both throughput and quality metrics across coding, math, and reasoning tasks.

This could lead to a fundamental shift in LLM inference optimization. Rather than choosing between quality and speed, or relying on separate draft models with limited capacity, TiDAR shows we can achieve both by intelligently combining complementary sampling strategies within a unified architecture.

author: Pascal Biese
subtitle: AI Lead at PwC <​/​> Daily AI highlights for 80k+ experts 📲🤗
content:
LLMs tend to fail catastrophically after a few hundred steps. 

A new approach just solved a task with over 1 million steps perfectly - according to the authors.

Even state-of-the-art reasoning models inevitably make errors when chaining their capabilities into extended processes. Recent experiments showed that after a few hundred steps, the process becomes derailed. This fundamental reliability problem has been blocking LLMs from executing the kind of large-scale tasks that organizations and societies routinely perform.

Researchers at Cognizant AI Lab and UT Austin just demonstrated MAKER, a system that successfully completed over one million LLM steps with zero errors. Their approach might sound counterintuitive: instead of relying on increasingly intelligent base models, they achieve reliability through extreme decomposition and error correction.

MAKER breaks tasks into minimal subtasks - each handled by a focused microagent - and applies multi-agent voting at each step. This modular approach enables effective error correction that scales logarithmically with task length. 

The team provides formal scaling laws showing why this works: under maximal decomposition, the system scales log-linearly (Θ(s log s)) rather than exponentially failing like traditional approaches. Relatively small non-reasoning models like GPT-4.1-mini prove more cost-effective than advanced reasoning models for this architecture. When each agent focuses on a single tiny step, raw reasoning power matters less than reliability and cost efficiency.

This might open an alternative path to AI scaling beyond building ever-larger models. By decomposing intelligence into millions of coordinated pieces, we might build systems that are not just more capable, but fundamentally more reliable and controllable.

subtitle: AI researcher on LLM pretraining, tokenization and safety at Pleias & KU Leuven - Prev: Apple, Aleph Alpha, MilaNLP, PhD from KU Leuven
content:
There's a gap between using LLM APIs, running models locally with vLLM or Hugging Face's .generate(), and understanding what actually goes into an inference engine. I spent a year as an LLM inference engineer at Aleph Alpha, but I had never implemented fundamental techniques like KV caching from scratch.

I believe implementing from scratch is the best way to really understand a topic, so I built an inference engine starting with Andrej Karpathy's nanoGPT (a simple ~300 line GPT2 implementation). I've been sharing this in a blog series covering the optimizations that make the difference between a research demo and a profitable service.

The series progresses from a baseline with a few hundred tokens/sec to 10k tokens/sec by implementing:
• KV caching: eliminates recomputing attention, enables batch parallelism
• Fused sampling kernels: removes expensive sorting for top-p  
• CUDA graphs: reduces kernel launch overhead
• Tensor parallelism: splits models across multiple GPUs
• And more to come in the future (MoE, expert parallelism, speculative decoding,...)

While understanding these trade-offs is the difference between a profitable service and a loss-making one, I think it is also a good example of how software engineering and state-of-the-art research can come together. So part of this codebase, I prepared for a course on LLM inference at KU Leuven.

author: Parth Chokhra
subtitle: AI Forward Deployed Engineer @Databricks
content:
Here is a trick question 🤔: Does the computational complexity of a language model decrease if we increase the number of attention heads?

You might assume “yes” because the dimensions of Q, K, and V per head shrink when you add more heads.
But the subtle and often misunderstood trade-off in multi-head attention is this:
When you increase the number of heads, each head gets a smaller subspace (dₖ = d_model / h).
So, yes, each head becomes cheaper individually. 💡
But you also have more heads running in parallel, and when you multiply that out, the total cost becomes:

                                                    h⋅n2⋅dk​=n2⋅dmodel​

So, the overall computational complexity remains roughly the same.
You don’t get a speed-up, you get something far more valuable.

🚀 So why does multi-head attention actually help?
Because multiple smaller heads can learn different types of relationships at the same time:
🔍 One head learns positional patterns
🔗 Another captures long-range dependencies
🧩 Another model's syntax
🎯 Another focuses on entities or interactions
Instead of one big attention mechanism doing everything, you get a team of specialists, each focusing on its own view of the data.

The result?
 ✨ Richer representations
 ✨ Better contextual understanding
 ✨ Stronger model performance
All without increasing computational cost.

author: Jiajun Li
subtitle: RL & Inference @ Radixark.ai, We are hiring
content:
💡 Problem & Solution

Speculative Decoding is well-known as a clever inference acceleration technique, and is particularly effective under limited decoding parallelism, like long-tail RL rollouts.

In a typical RL training loop, we freeze the draft model’s weights. However, as the target model (the main policy) continues to improve, the frozen draft model drifts away, reducing the accept rate and weakening the speedup.

Our solution is to apply an online SFT cross-entropy loss to the MTP layer and train it jointly with the main model. This keeps the draft model’s predictions high-fidelity and yields stable long-term performance gains.

📈 Results: Stable & Significant Throughput Boost

We tested on an H200 cluster using the Mimo-7B-RL model with the DAPO-Math-17k dataset. The results demonstrate the clear advantage:

✅ Long-Term gains: The throughput advantage over the Frozen Spec baseline grows over time, starting at 14% and reaching 25% in later training stages, directly correlating with a steadily rising accept length and declining MTP loss.
✅ Minimal Overhead: The additional training cost is minor (< 5%) comparing to the significant positive speedup.
✅ Model Integrity: As theoretically expected, introducing speculative decoding does not impact the main policy's sampling or training effects.

🛠️ Engineering Highlights

Implementing this required solving several complex engineering challenges, especially for integration with Megatron:

1. Sequence Packing + CP: We support training the MTP layer in Megatron under sequence packing + context parallel (CP) configurations.
2. Loss Mask Alignment: We add proper loss mask edge-case handling for MTP training to ensure the MTP layer receives correct SFT loss signals.
3. Gradient isolation: We add gradient blocking for the main model’s LM head and embedding to prevent MTP loss gradients from flowing back into the main model.
4. Weight flow: We support Megatron↔SGLang weight syncing for the MTP layer.

This feature is now merged into the main branch of slime https://lnkd.in/gUwkKb_S and is available for out-of-the-box use!

- Technical guidance: Zilin Zhu, Shenggui Li, Tom

- Collaborative development: Yuzhen Zhou, Mao cheng, Ruiguo Yang, Ji Li, Qiaolin Yu, Kangrui Du, Jin Pan, Xinyuan Tong, Ethan Su

author: Akshay Kumar Hegde
subtitle: Programming Polyglot 👾 • GenAI Dev 🤖 • Researcher 👨‍🔬
content:
I spent some time trying to replicate the "3x free speedup" from LLM Speculative Decoding, inspired by a post from Jay Gala.
I benchmarked it across three different systems: an M2 Mac, an NVIDIA T4, and a new RTX 6000 (Blackwell-class).
The results were... not what I expected. On all three platforms, it was significantly slower. (See my attached benchmark screenshots).

After a lot of debugging, I finally understood why:
1. Where it should be used: Speculative decoding is only for Memory-Bound systems (e.g., a 70B model on an A100 GPU) where the "chef" (compute) is bored and waiting for the "waiter" (memory).
2. Why my tests failed: My systems were all Compute-Bound. The T4's "chef" was overworked. The new RTX 6000's "waiter" was so fast (like a teleporter) that the "chef" was still the bottleneck. In all my tests, I just added more work to an already-busy GPU.

It was a fantastic lesson, this "magic" speedup only works on specific older, high-end hardware.
For a full analysis and all the (many) scripts I used to figure this out, check out the GitHub Repo: https://lnkd.in/g4kFxGRW

I was working on a technique proposed by WebLeaper for one of my enterprise projects. Our customer service automation needed to gather product specifications from multiple vendor databases. Traditional agents took 20+ steps per query with 60% accuracy.

We implemented their three-stage approach: Basic tasks for single-source retrieval, Union for cross-vendor queries, and Reverse-Union for deductive reasoning. The ISR/ISE metrics guided our SFT curation, filtering only efficient trajectories. The Hybrid Reward RL further optimized our agent.

At Eka Care, we're tackling a fundamental challenge in Indian healthcare digitization: understanding medical information across Indic languages and mixed scripts while maintaining semantic accuracy.

The Problem: 
When a doctor says: "Patient ko sugar aur thyroid dono hai, dose adjust karna padega. Hb kam hai, iron tablet start kiya, diet mein palak aur beetroot add karne bola." But Medical systems need standardized information which can be codified using an international standard for exchanging healthcare information electronically (ex. SNOMED CT). We demonstrate bitwise consistent on-policy RL with TorchTitan (training) + vLLM (inference) — the first open-source run where training and inference numerics match exactly.

content:
I was in San Francisco✈️ this weekend and got the opportunity to review the codebase of a very early-stage startup🔥. It was interesting to see how products built on LLM wrappers actually run in real environments. 

As someone who works in LLM systems, I always assumed things like KV-cache, prefilling, and TTFT were widely understood. But many teams, especially early-stage ones, don’t always think deeply about these details, even though they make a big difference in performance. ⚙️🚀

One example I saw was passing the full conversation history to the model on every request. It works, but it forces the model to recompute everything from scratch, adding unnecessary latency.

If you're using inference APIs, reusing the 𝐊𝐕 𝐜𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞 from previous requests can give you a huge boost. With OpenAI, this is done through 𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐬, which creates a session on their side where your KV cache is stored. This reduces prefilling time and also cuts down network overhead because you're sending less data each time. ⏱️📉

I believe many of you are already using this. If not, I recommend reading about 𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐬 and 𝐊𝐕 𝐜𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞 reuse, it’s a small change that can make your system much faster. 📚💡

And if you rely heavily on inference and latency is becoming a pain point, I’d be happy to look at your implementation and share suggestions to the best of my knowledge. 🤝🚀

author: Pascal Biese
subtitle: AI Lead at PwC <​/​> Daily AI highlights for 80k+ experts 📲🤗
content:
Kimi K2 is great - but have you heard of Kimi Linear?

For years, we've accepted a hard trade-off: either you use standard attention and pay the quadratic complexity cost, or you switch to linear attention and sacrifice quality. This dilemma has become increasingly painful as models scale to million-token contexts for agentic applications.

At the core of Moonshot AI's new Kimi Linear architecture is Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), which introduces channel-wise gating that gives each feature dimension its own forgetting rate - enabling more precise control over what the model remembers and discards. Think of it as upgrading from a coarse volume knob to a full equalizer.

The team validated their approach at scale with a 3B-parameter model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens using identical recipes to full-attention baselines. The results are striking: Kimi Linear matches or exceeds full attention quality across short-context benchmarks, long-context retrieval tasks, and reinforcement learning scenarios - while reducing KV cache usage by 75% and achieving 6x faster decoding at 1M context length.

But traditional attentions isn't completely out of the picture: their hybrid architecture design interleaves KDA layers with periodic full attention in a 3:1 ratio. This gives you the efficiency of linear attention for most operations while preserving global information flow where it matters most.

The team open-sourced their KDA kernels with vLLM integration and released both pre-trained and instruction-tuned checkpoints. Link in the comments below.

author: Anshuman Mishra
subtitle: ML @ Zomato
content:
"Just use OpenAI's API"  Until you need:

- Custom fine-tuned models
- <50ms p99 latency  
- $0.001/1K tokens (not $1.25/1K input)

Then you build your own inference platform.

Most engineers think "build your own" means:
- Rent some GPUs
- Load model with vLLM
- Wrap it in FastAPI
- Ship it

The complexity hits you around week 2. 

Remember, You're not building a system to serve one model to one user. You're building a system that handles hundreds of concurrent requests, across multiple models, with wildly different latency requirements.

btw get this kinda content in your inbox daily - 
https://lnkd.in/gCPD6fUz
now back to the post - 

That's a fundamentally different problem.

What you actually need is 
> A request router that understands model capabilities. 
> A dynamic batcher that groups requests without killing latency. 
> A KV cache manager that doesn't OOM your GPUs.
> A model instance pool that handles traffic spikes.

And that's just the core components.

Your <50ms p99 requirement breaks down as:

- Network overhead: 10-15ms (you can't fix this)
- Queueing delay: 5-20ms (if you batch wrong, this explodes)
- First token latency: 20-40ms (model dependent)
- Per-token generation: 10-50ms (grows with context length)

You have maybe 5ms of slack. This is why "just throw H100s at it" fails.

The first principle of inference platforms:

"Continuous batching ≠ Static batching"

Static batching waits for 8 requests, then processes them together. Continuous batching processes 8 requests and adds request #9 mid-generation.

vLLM does this. TensorRT-LLM does this. Your FastAPI wrapper doesn't.

This single difference is 3-5x throughput.

"We have 20 fine-tuned models for different tasks"

Now your platform needs model routing based on user intent. Dynamic loading and unloading so you don't keep 20 models in memory. Shared KV cache across similar base models. LoRA adapter swapping in <100ms.

This is where 90% of DIY inference platforms die.

> Use OpenAI API when you're under 100K requests/month, using standard models, can tolerate 500ms+ latency, and cost per request is 10x higher than raw compute.

> Build your own when you have custom models, doing 500K+ requests/month, need sub-100ms p99, or when cost optimization actually matters.

The break-even is usually around $5-10K/month in API spend.

Production inference platforms have four layers:

> Request handling (load balancer, rate limiter, queue). 
> Orchestration (model router, dynamic batcher, priority scheduler). 
> Inference engine (vLLM/TRT-LLM, KV cache manager, multi-GPU coordinator). > Observability (per-component latency, GPU utilization, cost per token).

Most engineers build layer 1 and 3, then wonder why production breaks.

I spent weeks searching for a clear explanation of sparse attention and hybrid attention patterns. Frustrated by the lack of accessible resources, I decided to write one myself.

The Problem: Traditional transformers need O(n²) computations — processing 10,000 tokens requires 100 million attention operations. That's why GPT-3 was limited to 2,048 tokens.

The Solution: Sparse attention strategically chooses *which* tokens talk to which tokens, not everyone to everyone.

Three Fundamental Patterns:
1. Local Attention — Tokens focus on neighbors (like classroom conversations)
2. Global Attention — Special hub tokens connect everyone (like a CEO knowing everyone)
3. Random Attention — Shortcuts across sequences (like social network connections)

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗰: 𝗛𝘆𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗱 𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗯𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲, 𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴:
- 10-100x speedup
- 100-1000x less memory
- Process 100K tokens instead of 4K
- 95-98% performance with minimal loss

After reading this, you'll understand end-to-end how sparse attention powers long-context AI — from BigBird to Longformer to modern LLMs.

author: Pascal Biese
subtitle: AI Lead at PwC <​/​> Daily AI highlights for 80k+ experts 📲🤗
content:
Google ❤️ small LLMs

When trying to teach 7B models challenging reasoning tasks, researchers face a dilemma: Supervised Fine-Tuning overfits to demonstrations through rigid token-by-token imitation, while Reinforcement Learning fails when the model can't find correct solutions even after hundreds of attempts.

This gap becomes problematic as we push towards more complex, multi-step reasoning tasks where a single wrong intermediate step derails the entire solution chain. For these "hard" problems, both approaches leave performance on the table.

Google researchers now introduced what they call Supervised Reinforcement Learning (SRL), which reformulates problem-solving as a sequence of logical actions rather than a monolithic solution. 

Their key insight is this: decompose expert demonstrations into intermediate steps and provide dense rewards based on similarity between the model's actions and expert actions at each step - not just final answer correctness.

This step-wise supervision offers richer learning signals even when all attempts are incorrect, while still allowing the model flexibility to develop its own internal reasoning patterns. SRL achieves a 3% improvement over RLVR on challenging math benchmarks using just 1,000 training examples, and when combined sequentially (SRL then RLVR), reaches 3.7% gains.

The best part? The approach generalizes beyond math to software engineering tasks, achieving 74% relative improvement over strong SFT baselines on SWE-Bench. SRL offers a promising path for training smaller models on problems that previously seemed out of reach.
