author: Nicolai van der Smagt
subtitle: Senior Anthropic Specialist Solutions Architect @ AWS | LLM Strategy & Implementation | Curious builder
content:
The French AI lab pleias released a tiny reasoning SLM they call Baguettotron (😂). The 321 million parameter model beats much larger models on reasoning benchmarks. They built it on just 16 H100s with a small team.

Baguettotron has an unusual architecture: 80 layers, which is extremely deep for this parameter count (hence the name). They trained it on just 200 billion tokens from a synthetic reasoning dataset they created (with Wikipedia as the anchor) called SYNTH. Their tokenizer is optimized for European languages, and everything is open source.

 What's interesting is the synthetic data angle. It turns out that training on high quality synthetic data is much more efficient than using scraped data and prevents the previously feared model collapse - and it also mitigates the legal concerns around fair use of public, scraped data.

If this holds up at larger scales, it changes the training economics a lot. Smaller teams can compete with frontier labs. You don't need to scrape the entire internet. You don't need thousands of GPUs. Training costs drop. Your models can be deployed in more places. Etc.

I hope other labs will replicate this. The dataset and model are both open, so we should find out quickly if the results hold.

Vive le baguettotron 🥖!

author: Leonie Monigatti
subtitle: Sr. Developer Advocate @ Elastic | I help devs build search agents
content:
Multi-vector embeddings (e.g., ColBERT) are powerful but expensive to scale.

𝗠𝗨𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗔 cuts their memory costs by 70%.

MUVERA (Multi-Vector Retrieval via Fixed Dimensional Encodings) is an interesting approach by Google Research. It transforms multi-vector representations into single fixed-size vectors (Fixed dimensional encodings).

MUVERA uses a 4-step process:
1. Space partitioning (using k-means or LSH)
2. Dimensionality reduction via linear projections
3. Multiple repetitions for accuracy
4. Final projection

MUVERA works well in our experiments (LoTTE dataset tests):
• Memory footprint reduced by ~70%
• Import time reduced by ~70-85%
• HNSW graph size: Reduced by ~99%

Yes, there's some loss in recall quality. But you can mitigate this by increasing the HNSW ef parameter value during search.

Learn more about MUVERA, how it performed in our experiments, and whether it might be worth exploring for your use case: https://lnkd.in/esK2vhNX

The Lab That Quietly Built the Future of AI

There are places that don’t just teach — they transform.

Long before “artificial intelligence” became the world’s favorite buzzword, a small lab at Stanford was already defining what the future would look like.

The Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (SAIL), founded in 1963 by John McCarthy, has been home to some of the brightest minds to ever work in AI.

It’s where early experiments in computer vision, natural language processing, and robotics weren’t just academic exercises — they were the foundations of what we now call “AI.”

And decades later, look at the alumni list:

Andrew Ng – Co-founder of Coursera  & DeepLearning.AI, one of the world’s leading AI educators

Fei-Fei Li  – Former Director of SAIL; a visionary in human-centered AI and computer vision

Christopher D. Manning – Current SAIL Director; driving NLP research shaping ChatGPT-era breakthroughs

Yang Diyi  – Rising leader in human-centered NLP and computational social science

Larry Tesler – Early SAIL researcher who transformed human-computer interaction

One lab.
Decades ago.
And yet, the people leading AI at Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and beyond trace their roots back to this same place.

Can that really be a coincidence?

Maybe not.

Maybe it’s proof that environments that nurture curiosity, encourage collaboration, and allow people to fail fast — are the ones that end up building the future.

And for anyone navigating their career journey — that’s the real lesson.
It’s not just about being in the right industry; it’s about being in the right environment.

✨ As someone who helps students and professionals discover where their potential meets purpose, I often think about what “your SAIL” looks like — that one place, mentor, or project that will quietly shape your future.

Because every generation has its SAIL. The only question is — are you in yours?

author: Mohsen Fayyaz
subtitle: Senior Researcher at Microsoft | Computer vision | Machine Learning
content:
Do Multimodal LLMs really understand temporal dynamics in a video? 
In our #NeurIPS2025 paper, we show that current Video-LLMs have critical limitations in temporal understanding. To address this, we proposed Stacked Temporal Attention in Vision Encoders: STAVE.

📜 Paper: https://lnkd.in/eFiD3nGn

In our experiments, we found that while current video-LLMs excel at understanding simple actions (like the example on the left), they fail at temporally challenging actions (like the one on the right).

To better understand the root cause, we created a temporally challenging subset of the SSv2 dataset that represents pairwise counterparts regarding their temporal characteristics, where accurate action recognition depends on modeling the sequence and progression of visual elements across frames. We assessed the performance of video-LLMs by both zero-shot and ICL on our challenging subset.

Since zero-shot and ICL performance was poor, we also assessed SFT finetuning on our training subset, which also performed poorly. Based on these empirical findings, we found that the vision encoder architecture of current video LLMs are incapable of proper temporal modelling. To this end, we proposed Stacked Temporal Attention for Vision Encoders (STAVE).

Building upon our findings in the limitations of current STA models, we propose STAVEQ2, an enhanced Video-LLM that introduces stacked temporal attention modules directly within the vision encoder.  Our results show that this approach significantly improves temporal reasoning and outperforms existing models in video question answering tasks, specifically in action recognition. We improve on benchmarks including VITATECS, MVBench, and Video-MME by up to +5.5%.


See you at NeurIPS 2025 in Mexico City!

By: Ali Rasekh, Erfan Bagheri Soula, Omid Daliran, Simon Gottschalk, and me.

subtitle: ML/AI research engineer. Author of Build a Large Language Model From Scratch (amzn.to/4fqvn0D) and Ahead of AI (magazine.sebastianraschka.com), on how LLMs work and the latest developments in the field.
content:
My "The Building Blocks of Today’s and Tomorrow’s Language Models" talk at the PyTorch Conference is now up on YouTube, where I discuss the main developments: https://lnkd.in/gunhUS7C

If you have 25 min this weekend, it's a whirlwind tour to catch you up on the key LLM architecture design considerations in popular LLMs this year (plus, an overview of alternative architecture designs).

(The silver lining of my late arrival and rescheduling: Since there was no talk after mine, it's followed by a 30 min Q&A instead of just the usual 5 min :))

To summarize what's covered, here are the main key topics and takeaways:

- Grouped Query Attention (GQA) and Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA): both reduce KV-cache memory, with MLA offering better modeling performance for similar savings.

- Sliding Window Attention: limits the model’s context slice size to reduce compute and KV-cache memory. it's often used together with GQA.

- Mixture of Experts (MoE): increases capacity while keeping inference costs low(er) by activating only a subset of experts per token.

- Discussion beyond autoregressive transformers: I also briefly discuss emerging ideas like Hierarchical Reasoning Models, Code World Models, and Text Diffusion Models

author: Siddhant Rai
subtitle: Philomath 📚| Tech Expert - ML@Siemens | Applied Research@OpenMined | ✍️@vizuara
content:
💡Kimi-Linear: An Expressive, Efficient Attention Architecture〽️

This week I came across a really interesting paper that probably will pave the way forward for the next gen linear time attention systems named as Kimi-linear by Moonshot AI.

Quadratic compute bottleneck has been a persistent problem in development of attention modules at scale. Since the very first realisation of this, methods like Linformer, Longformer, SSSM(MAMBA), had been trying to tackle this from multiple angles.
Eventually Gated Delta Networks came pretty close to the linear time attention module, but, due to fixed state space and discrete global steps lost a lot of expressivity. This issue of expressivity is solved by Kimi-linear through a channel wise attention in something they refer to as KDA (kimi Delta Attention), which basically is a sort of recurrent architecture but with channel attention.
But, the parallelization issue triggers in as you go ahead with recurrent systems, but, Kimi-linear solved this by making their matrix GPU friendly using DPLR transformation. Also, thanks to the recursive assumption in KDA, there is an inherent inductive bias of time. They also mix global and local expressivity by using a 3:1 KDA to full attention  module ratio.

In summary, Kimi-linear brings in
1. NoPE : No positional Embeddings, as sequence is a function of architecture
2. KDA : kimi-delta Attention, insipired from GDN, sort of like SSM, with a memory state across time, but, there is a delta value which works as positional bias (NoPE) + soft attention filter
3. Thanks for the memory/state matrix the memory requirement also dips down significantly for KV caching (checkout the complexity analysis section of article below) 👇 
4. DPLR based matrix factorization to make S (state/memory matrix) a sparse triangular matrix.
5. An interleaved attention module, with an empirical 3:1 ratio of KDA to full attention.
6. Thanks to all the optimizations, they not only achieved a 1.16x higher computational efficiency, but also, beat full attention (MHA) architectures across multiple benchmarks (both on synthetic and real benchmarks).

I wrote a detailed blog on Vizuara Substack, covering the previous attempts, their issues, what needs to be fixed and how Kimi-linear did it (methodology). There is a seperate section on what and why of DPLR transformation as well. (check out the Table of contents below 👇 for better reference to topics, though their much subtle yet important sub-sections as well, not reflected in TOC).

📝Find the entire article here : https://lnkd.in/gUQGi3PR

subtitle: ML/AI research engineer. Author of Build a Large Language Model From Scratch (amzn.to/4fqvn0D) and Ahead of AI (magazine.sebastianraschka.com), on how LLMs work and the latest developments in the field.
content:
I just saw the Kimi K2 Thinking release. With this new release, it seems like open-weight LLMs are pulling ahead of proprietary ones, for now, according to their benchmarks.

Kimi K2 is based on the DeepSeek V3/R1 architecture, and here's a side-by-side comparison.

- 2× fewer attention heads (64 vs. 128)
- ~1.5× more experts per MoE layer (384 vs. 256)
- Bigger vocabulary (160k vs. 129k)
- K2 activates ~32B parameters per token (vs. 37B in DeepSeek R1)
- Fewer dense FFN blocks before MoE

In short, Kimi K2 is a slightly scaled DeepSeek V3/R1. And the gains are in the data and training recipes. Hopefully, we will see some details on those soon, too.

Note: It would have been interesting to include the DeepSeek R1 numbers in the benchmark they shared to see the progress from January 2025 to today.

And yes, there's not a week without something exciting about LLMs to report 😅.

author: Elvis S.
subtitle: Founder at DAIR.AI | Angel Investor | Advisor | Prev: Meta AI, Galactica LLM, Elastic, Ph.D. | Serving 7M+ learners around the world
content:
Anthropic just posted another banger guide.

This one is on building more efficient agents to handle more tools and efficient token usage. 

This is a must-read for AI devs!

(bookmark it)

It helps with three major issues in AI agent tool calling: token costs, latency, and tool composition.

How? It combines code executions with MCP, where it turns MCP servers into code APIs rather than direct tool calls.

Here is all you need to know: 

1. Token Efficiency Problem: Loading all MCP tool definitions upfront and passing intermediate results through the context window creates massive token overhead, sometimes 150,000+ tokens for complex multi-tool workflows.

2. Code-as-API Approach: Instead of direct tool calls, present MCP servers as code APIs (e.g., TypeScript modules) that agents can import and call programmatically, reducing the example workflow from 150k to 2k tokens (98.7% savings).

3. Progressive Tool Discovery: Use filesystem exploration or search_tools functions to load only the tool definitions needed for the current task, rather than loading everything upfront into context. This solves so many context rot and token overload problems. 

4. In-Environment Data Processing: Filter, transform, and aggregate data within the code execution environment before passing results to the model. E.g., filter 10,000 spreadsheet rows down to 5 relevant ones.

5. Better Control Flow: Implement loops, conditionals, and error handling with native code constructs rather than chaining individual tool calls through the agent, reducing latency and token consumption.

6. Privacy: Sensitive data can flow through workflows without entering the model's context; only explicitly logged/returned values are visible, with optional automatic PII tokenization.

7. State Persistence: Agents can save intermediate results to files and resume work later, enabling long-running tasks and incremental progress tracking.

8. Reusable Skills: Agents can save working code as reusable functions (with SKILL .MD documentation), building a library of higher-level capabilities over time.

This approach is complex and it's not perfect, but it should enhance the efficiency and accuracy of your AI agents across the board.

I visualised the full information flow within a Vision Language Model (VLM). The goal was to improve understanding of the vision encoders and language decoders. I used toy dimensions in my illustrations. In addition, I incorporated current research about VLMs, such as difficulties with spatial reasoning, large L2 norms, attention allocation. Here is a small summary:

- Full information flow, from pixels to autoregressive token prediction is visualised .
- Earlier layers within CLIP seem to respond to colors, middle layers to structures, and the later layers to objects and natural elements.
- Vision tokens seem to have large L2 norms, which reduces sensitivity to position encodings, increasing "bag-of-words" behavior.
- Attention seems to be more focused on text tokens rather than vision tokens, which might be due to the large L2 norms in vision tokens.
- In later layers of the language decoder, vision tokens start to represent the language concept of the dominant object present in that patch.

author: Sebastian Raschka, PhD
subtitle: ML/AI research engineer. Author of Build a Large Language Model From Scratch (amzn.to/4fqvn0D) and Ahead of AI (magazine.sebastianraschka.com), on how LLMs work and the latest developments in the field.
content:
I just saw the benchmarks of the new open-weight MiniMax-M2 LLM, and the performance is too good to ignore. So, I just amended my "The Big LLM Architecture Comparison" with entry number 13! Below is a summary of the architecture.

1️⃣ Full attention modules:

As shown in the overview figure below, I grouped MiniMax-M2 with the other decoder-style transformer LLMs as it does not use the efficient lightning attention variant proposed in MiniMax-M1. Instead, the developers went back to using full attention, likely to improve modeling (and benchmark) performance.   

2️⃣ Per-layer QK-Norm:

Overall, MiniMax-M2 is surprisingly similar to Qwen3. Besides changing the number of layers, sizes, etc., it uses the same components overall. Perhaps the one noteworthy highlight here is that MiniMax-M2 uses a so-called “per_layer” QK-Norm instead of the regular QK-Norm. A closer look at the code reveals the "per_layer" means that the RMSNorm (used for QK-Norm as explained earlier) is defined in each transformer block (as in regular QK-Norm), but, in addition, instead of reusing it across attention heads, it's a unique QK-Norm for each attention head.

3️⃣ Sliding-window attention:

The model configuration file also includes a sliding-window attention setting (similar to Gemma 3), but, as in Mistral 3.1, it is disabled by default.

Otherwise, besides the per-layer QK-Norm, the architecture is very similar to Qwen3, as shown in the figure below.

4️⃣ MoE sparsity:

A perhaps interesting tidbit, as shown in the figure below, includes the fact that they don't use a shared expert (similar to Qwen3 but unlike Qwen3-Next). As mentioned earlier, in my opinion, shared experts are useful because they reduce redundancy among the other experts.

Also, as apparent from the figure above, MiniMax-M2 is twice as "sparse" as Qwen3. I.e., at roughly the same size as Qwen3 235B-A22B, MiniMax-M2 has only 10B instead of 22B active experts per token (that is, 4.37% of the parameters are used in each inference step in MiniMax-M2, whereas Qwen3 uses 9.36% active tokens).

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🎓 On-Policy Distillation

New blog post from Thinking Machines Lab discussing on-policy distillation for LLM post-training. This consists of training a student model on its own generated outputs with dense token-level feedback from a teacher. It combines RL's on-policy relevance with distillation's compute efficiency.

→ RL provides sparse feedback that doesn't pinpoint where mistakes happened. On the other hand, traditional distillation trains on teacher trajectories the student will rarely encounter. This work combines these approaches by having teachers grade each token the student actually generates.

→ The method achieves similar performance to RL with dramatically fewer training steps because distillation shortcuts the expensive search process.

→ On-policy distillation naturally handles continual learning better than SFT because the student converges toward a fixed teacher's behavior without the drift that happens when training on finite batches of its own outputs.

→ The experiments show you can match teacher performance on math reasoning (AIME problems) by training on a single prompt for 20 consecutive steps. This is extreme overfitting by normal standards, but the dense supervision extracts the semantic strategy efficiently.

My take: on-policy distillation is not new, but this blog post has a lost of interesting results and an elegant framework to introduce it. They also have end-to-end examples with models, parameters, and datasets for reproducibility. It's a great read if you're interested in post-training.

author: Eduardo Alvarez
subtitle: Sr. Technical Lead | Inference at Scale @ NVIDIA
content:
⚖️ Expert load balancing - DevOps meets MoE Architectures 

Large scale expert parallelism, the distribution of experts across a wide pool of GPUs, introduces potential challenges in workload balance and compute utilization. Because of how MoE models are trained and deployed, some experts naturally become more “popular” than others, leaving GPUs hosting less-frequented experts underutilized 🧩

TensorRT-LLM Wide-EP helps solve this with the Expert Parallel Load Balancer (EPLB). The EPLB can operate in either static or online mode, which allows it to pre-define optimal expert allocation ahead of time or dynamically re-allocate experts based on real-time request characteristics ⚙️

Much like traditional load balancers, the EPLB applies a balancing algorithm to identify hot and cold workers across the GPU pool. When the online balancer detects an imbalance, it triggers a weight update process supported by a containerized design that allows experts to move fluidly in and out of container allocations without breaking the CUDA graph.

Read more about the EPLB in our latest blog: https://lnkd.in/e2rpVE2K

subtitle: Sr. Technical Lead | Inference at Scale @ NVIDIA
content:
🚀 Effectively scaling large MoEs means going beyond single node systems

Large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models are forcing us to think differently about inference and how we scale these applications to millions of users. This requires thoughtful deployments built on extreme software–hardware co-design principles 📐

Why is this important? At each transformer MoE block, tokens must be dynamically routed to their activated experts and then aggregated back. This is incredibly taxing on memory bandwidth, introduces significant communication overhead, and can cause serious compute utilization challenges ⚙️

Rack-scale helps but these systems are only as effective as their ability to maintain a coherent memory domain and pair it with efficient expert management at the system and kernel levels.

The GB200 and GB300 NVL72 rack-scale systems leverage up to 130 TB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth to ensure distributed experts don’t become a bottleneck... allowing compute parallelization to deliver real performance and price/perf gains.

In this article, we take that analysis much further, exploring the innovations across both the hardware and software layers that make large-scale expert inference practical, efficient, and scalable.

author: Sebastian Raschka, PhD
subtitle: ML/AI research engineer. Author of Build a Large Language Model From Scratch (amzn.to/4fqvn0D) and Ahead of AI (magazine.sebastianraschka.com), on how LLMs work and the latest developments in the field.
content:
DeepSeek finally released a new model and paper. And because this DeepSeek-OCR release is a bit different from what everyone expected, and DeepSeek releases are generally a big deal, I wanted to do a brief explainer of what it is all about.

In short, they explore how vision encoders can improve the efficiency of LLMs in processing and compressing textual information. And the takeaway is that rendering text as images and feeding that to the model results in more efficient compression than working with text directly. 

My first intuition was that this sounds very inefficient and shouldn't work as well as using text tokenizers (or alternatives like Byte Latent Transformer) to prepare the input. It actually reminded me of the line of research I saw years ago, where researchers represented 3D molecules as 3D inputs or 2D images for ConvNets instead of using graph neural nets. This shouldn't work well and should be prone to overfitting.

In the case of DeepSeek-OCR, why even try such an approach? I imagine it started as a curiosity, but then it may have turned into an interesting idea for long-context scaling in LLMs and how to make it cheaper by using vision tokens and representations. (An image can say more than a thousand words, but who would have thought that an image of text can say 1000 words more efficiently!)

In any case, this DeepSeek-OCR approach turns out to be surprisingly efficient. In particular, they found that at a fixed precision of 97% for long-context decoding (i.e., how well the model can compress information into a latent representation and reconstruct it), the OCR version needed 10 times fewer visual tokens than text tokens. In other words, the OCRed version can compress information 10x better than the text version.

However, I don't think that visual representations of text will solve the limitations of LLMs. Also, while it is popular to dislike text tokenizers like BPE, image representations are messy as well (one has to deal with aspect ratios, resolutions, croppings, color intensity variations, brightness levels, etc.). Still, it’s an interesting idea. Also, if this approach is more efficient than regular black&white text, I am curious to see compression ratios when we add syntax color to code.

Regarding code, this may be an interesting alternative for storing contextual information, as spacing and subword tokenization remain challenges in traditional tokenizers. (Especially when working with code that uses many custom variable names that may not be represented in vocabularies and that have to be broken down into many individual subword tokens.) 
Overall, it’s still such an esoteric concept to encode text in images that I am (still) surprised it could do well (and may it would only make sense for very long documents or special domains like OCR or code, not general language modeling).

author: hitesh ram
subtitle: Jr Artificial Intelligence Engineer at ContinuServe
content:
What is Sliding Window Attention 🚀

Ever wondered how modern Transformers read long documents without burning your GPU? 🔥
👉Let’s talk about a game-changer — Sliding Window Attention 🧠

🧩 What is it?
In standard Transformers, every token attends to every other token — meaning if you have 10,000 words, you’re calculating 100 million attention scores! 😵‍💫

👉 Sliding Window Attention changes the rule:
Each token only looks at its neighbors — say, 256 tokens before and after.
Just like how your eyes focus on a few words at a time while reading. 👀

💡 Why do we need it?
Because full self-attention is O(n²) in memory and computation. 
That’s fine for short sequences, but for long text, audio, or DNA data — it’s painfully expensive. ⚙️

With a sliding window, we reduce it to O(n × w) — where w = window size (much smaller than n).
💥 Faster. Leaner. Scalable.

⚙️ How does it work?
Imagine reading a long paragraph. You don’t need to remember every word — just the last few sentences to stay coherent.
Sliding window attention works the same way:

📘 For each token:
- Look left 🔙 (previous tokens)
- Look right 🔜 (next tokens)
- Ignore distant ones 🚫
As we move along the text, this window slides, maintaining local context efficiently.

author: Sreedath Panat
subtitle: MIT PhD | IITM | 100K+ LinkedIn | Co-founder Vizuara & Videsh | Making AI accessible for all
content:
Why do we transform inputs into Q, K, and V and why do we need multiple heads?

When we look at the architecture of the Transformer, the attention mechanism seems quite straightforward at first glance - take the dot product between tokens, find which ones are similar, and assign attention weights accordingly. But if we think carefully, this simple idea does not work well when applied directly to raw input embeddings.

Each word or patch embedding 𝑋 in the model carries rich but entangled information. If we simply took dot products of these raw vectors, we would be comparing them in the same untransformed space, without any specialization. One token might contain information about position, context, and content all mixed together, and the model would have no control over which of these aspects should influence attention.

This is why we introduce three learnable transformations  the weight matrices 𝑊𝑞, 𝑊𝑘, and 𝑊𝑣. These matrices project the same input 
𝑋 into three different spaces:

Q (Queries) represent what each token is trying to find or focus on.
K (Keys) represent what each token offers as potential information.
V (Values) represent the actual content to be transferred if attention is given.

The dot product between Q and K does not happen in the raw embedding space but in these specialized subspaces. This separation allows the model to learn what features to query and what features to offer during attention. Over time, the network learns optimal projections. For example, in a vision transformer, one head might learn to query edges while another might query textures or object boundaries.

Now, why stop at one head?

If we used only a single set of Q, K, and V transformations, all tokens would attend to each other using one kind of similarity measure. This would force the model to capture all possible relationships through a single narrow lens. But natural data (whether text or images) is inherently multi-faceted. In an image, different regions relate to each other in many ways: shape, color, texture, and spatial context. Similarly, in language, relationships may be syntactic, semantic, or positional.

By introducing multiple heads, the Transformer allows several attention mechanisms to operate in parallel, each with its own learned Q, K, and V transformations. Each head sees the same input through a different learned subspace and captures different kinds of dependencies. When we concatenate these outputs, we get a richer, more complete understanding of the input sequence.

This is what gives multi-head attention great expressive power.

In our Transformers for Vision Bootcamp at Vizuara, we visualize this process exactly like the figure above, showing how inputsare  split into multiple attention heads, how queries and keys interact, and how each head learns to focus on a different part of the image. When learners see this visually, the concept clicks instantly. You can join here: https://lnkd.in/gpmpR2at

author: Zachary Mueller
subtitle: Head of Developer Relations @ Lambda; prev Hugging Face
content:
torch(.)distributed(.)gather

There are a few reasons why it's critical to grab tensors from other GPUs and centralize them on a singular one.

Averaging your loss between all ranks. Gathering data to ensure your metrics align. Getting information that exists on all other GPUs and centralizing it for a singular GPU to print out.

We do so using the gather operation.

A singular process creates an empty list of tensors (that are the same dtype, shape, etc) which is large enough to contain all the data from tensors across ranks.

Then, rank0 will request the data from all other ranks, which then send their data to rank0, filling in the slots in that earlier list.

content:
Gated Attention by the Qwen team lessens the severity of the “attention sink” phenomenon but what makes it different from standard self-attention?

Here’s the step-by-step break down:

1. Introduce a new linear layer with num_attn_heads * head_dim number of parameters. Let’s call this L_g.

2. Our input X is passed through this linear layer. Q_g = x @ L_g.

3. The query Q, key K and value V tensors are obtained as usual by passing X 
through q,k, v specific linear/projection layers.

4. Apply Standard Dot Product Attention i.e. the infamous self-attention operation
attention_output = softmax(Q @ K_T/ scaling_factor) @ V.

5. This is the new step that introduces gating. 
gated_attention = attention_output * sigmoid (Q_g).

6. final_output = gated_attention @ O

Gated attention yields increased sparsity, better scaling to long context tasks and even lower perplexity scores.

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
🪲 Bug Alert! If you’re training an LLM using an on-policy RL algorithm like GRPO, DPO, PPO etc. you should be aware of this bug!

📖 Context
Most RL algorithms like GRPO require an LLM to generate completions also called rollouts/trajectories for a given prompt. Most RL libraries leverage inference engines like vLLM or sgLang to compute these rollouts.

However when you’re training a model the model whose weights are being updated run on distributed training frameworks like FSDP, DeepSpeed or Nemotron.

🔴 Logit Score Mismatches
This discrepancy between training time vs rollout generation time environments has a serious consequence because differences in implementations of different kernels lead to a mismatch in the logit scores of the same set of tokens in a sequence.

🧐 Example
So say you have the prompt “Write me a poem about rocks”?
Let’s say that the inference engine (vLLM) generates the text “Silent keepers of the earth, …” with some probability/logit scores [P1, P2 P3, P4, P5, ….] for those tokens.

Those same tokens for the same prompt will have different prob/logit scores when the model is run outside of vLLM!!

👉🏽 Implications
This matters because it means that we would obtain different sets of completions for the same prompt, with a fixed random seed based on which environment the model was running on to obtain the completions.

This makes algorithms like GRPO/PPO become slightly off-policy. i.e.. the data that’s used to compute the loss and update the weights is no longer strictly based on the weights of the model being updated!

🔧 Solutions
While the ultimate solution is making sure the logit scores of inference engines and train time environments are the same this is a very hard problem to solve.
A workaround is importance sampling where you assign a weight to the loss coming from each completion by the ratio between the prob scores obtained in the non-inference env vs inference env.

🎁 Wrap Up
Truncated Importance Sampling has recently been implemented by the HF team in TRL to support GRPO.

Link to trl docs to enable Importance sampling when ussing vllm: https://lnkd.in/eBH_2Y9t

author: Anshuman Mishra
subtitle: ML @ Zomato
content:
Research Scientist interview at Google.

Interviewer: "You need to quantize a model from FP16 to INT8. Walk me through how you'd do it without destroying quality."

Your answer: "I'll just convert all weights to INT8 format"

❌ Rejected.

Here's the critical mistake:

Don't say: "Quantization reduces precision" or "Use 8 bits instead of 16."
Too surface-level.
The real answer is the outlier feature problem.
INT8 quantization fails because 0.01% of activation values are 100× larger than the rest. Your quantization range is wasted on outliers.

You're compressing a skyscraper and a house with the same ruler.

Here's why naive quantization destroys quality:

FP16 weights → Scale to [-127, 127] → Store as INT8 → 2× memory reduction
Problem: Activation outliers exist at specific feature dimensions.

6,000 features: Normal distribution (-0.5 to +0.5)
144 features: Outliers (100× larger, -50 to +50)
Those 144 features control 90% of model quality.

btw subscribe to my newsletter to get these posts for free - https://lnkd.in/gCPD6fUz

The outlier math is brutal:

- Quantization range: [-127, 127] = 254 values
- One outlier at value=50: Forces scale = 50/127 = 0.39
- Normal value 0.3: Quantized to round(0.3/0.39) = 1
- Actual range used: 2 out of 254 values
- Precision loss: 99.2%

You're using a bathroom scale to weigh an ant and an elephant together.

Remember: Outliers are dimension-specific, not token-specific:

- Feature dim 2,145: Always outlier (±40 to ±60)
- Feature dim 891: Always normal (±0.2 to ±0.5)
- Pattern stable across ALL prompts, ALL batches
- Position-independent, dimension-dependent

This changes everything.

> Bad approach:
Single quantization scale per tensor
Convert all weights uniformly
Model perplexity: 12.3 → 2,847 (destroyed)

> Good approach (LLM.int8()):
Identify outlier feature dimensions (top 0.5%)
Keep outliers in FP16 (144 dims)
Quantize normal features to INT8 (5,856 dims)
Model perplexity: 12.3 → 12.6 (preserved)

The difference is mixed precision, not uniform precision.

Memory bandwidth bottleneck:

- FP16: Load 140GB from VRAM per forward pass
- INT8: Load 70GB from VRAM per forward pass
- Throughput: 1.8× higher
- Quality: 98% maintained

Cost reduction:

FP16: 70B model needs 4× A100 GPUs
INT8: 70B model fits 2× A100 GPUs
Cost: Cut in half

author: Pablo Montalvo
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer @ 🤗
content:
Code is the product.

How do you prevent a 1M+ LoC Python library, built by thousands of contributors, from collapsing under its own weight?

In transformers, we do it with a set of explicit software engineering tenets. With Lysandre Debut, Pedro Cuenca and Yoni Gozlan, we just published a deep dive on the principles that keep our codebase hackable at scale.

What’s inside:

– The Tenets We Enforce: From One Model, One File to Standardize, Don't Abstract, these are the rules that guide every PR.

– "Modular Transformers": How we used visible inheritance to cut our effective maintenance surface by ~15× while keeping modeling code readable from top to bottom.

– Pluggable Performance: A standard attention interface and config-driven tensor parallelism mean semantics stay in the model while speed (FlashAttention, community kernels, TP sharding) is a configurable add-on, not a code rewrite.

This matters for anyone shipping models, contributing to OSS, or managing large-scale engineering projects. It’s how we ensure a contribution to transformers is immediately reusable across the ecosystem (vLLM, SGLang, etc.).

Did Tencent just overcome model training?

One of the most expensive and frustrating parts of deploying AI has historically been the need to fine-tune models for specific tasks - a process that can cost over $10,000 and requires maintaining separate specialized models for each use case.

A new paper from the Youtu-Agent team tries to overcome this: Instead of changing the model's parameters through costly training, they propose something simpler: let the model learn from experience by building a dynamic library of lessons learned, which gets injected into prompts as "experiential knowledge." 

Think of it as giving the AI a notebook where it writes down what worked and what didn't, then consulting that notebook on future problems. This Training-Free GRPO method applied to DeepSeek-V3.1 outperformed models that underwent expensive fine-tuning, achieving 82.7% accuracy on challenging math problems compared to 67% for traditionally trained models. 

The best part? It cost just $18 in API calls versus $10,000+ for parameter tuning, using only 100 training examples instead of thousands. When the model tries to solve a problem multiple times, it compares successful and failed attempts within each group, extracting semantic insights about what strategies worked. 

These insights become refined experiences like "When solving geometry problems with intersections, validate solutions lie within bounded regions or segments, not on extensions" - the kind of meta-knowledge that transfers across similar problems.

Instead of maintaining fleets of specialized models, organizations could use powerful general models that adapt through experience, dramatically reducing costs while maintaining flexibility.

author: Sebastian Raschka, PhD
subtitle: ML/AI research engineer. Author of Build a Large Language Model From Scratch (amzn.to/4fqvn0D) and Ahead of AI (magazine.sebastianraschka.com), on how LLMs work and the latest developments in the field.
content:
Multi-Head Attention (MHA) is the engine of LLMs. But over the years, we have added several tweaks to make it more efficient for long-context settings, especially when using KV caching during inference.

I implemented the most common variants from scratch:

1) Grouped-Query Attention (GQA):
Instead of having a unique key and value for each query head, multiple queries share the same key and value. As long as the sharing ratio is not too extreme, this has minimal impact on model quality. It is the most widely used variant today and found in almost every modern LLM including Llama 2-4, GPT-OSS, Gemma 3, Qwen 3, GLM 4.6, and many others.

2) Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA):
This variant introduces a compressed latent representation for the keys and values that are stored in the KV cache. During inference, these latent keys and values are up-projected back to the full dimension. The extra projection adds a small computational cost, but the memory savings make it worth it. This approach is currently used by DeepSeek V3 and Kimi K2.

3) Sliding-Window Attention (SWA):
SWA restricts each token’s attention span to a fixed local window, which reduces memory needs by shrinking the KV cache in long-context regimes. It is usually applied selectively, for example every other layer, or in Gemma 3's case, five SWA layers for each full-attention layer. While less common today, it remains an important optimization, notably in Gemma 3.

All three variants, GQA, MLA, and SWA, can also be combined freely within the same model.

content:
One of the most important concept in Audio Language models is 𝗡𝗲𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗼 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗰𝘀.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘁?

Neural audio codecs are revolutionizing how AI agents handle voice by using deep learning to compress audio at 3 kbps while maintaining quality that traditional codecs like Opus struggle to achieve even at 16 kbps. By training encoders, quantizers, and decoders end-to-end with adversarial losses, these systems learn perceptual representations directly from data—enabling real-time conversational AI, edge-deployed voice assistants, and bandwidth-efficient multimodal agents that would be impossible with legacy compression techniques.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱: Traditional codecs (MP3, Opus, AAC) relied on handcrafted psychoacoustic models and fixed transforms, but failed at ultra-low bitrates, couldn't adapt to diverse audio types, and required separate models for different compression levels.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Architectures like SoundStream, EnCodec, and Lyra learn optimal compression strategies directly from data, achieve remarkable quality at 1.5-6 kbps, support bitrate scalability from a single model, and can jointly compress and enhance audio—all while running in real-time on edge devices.

𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲: Neural codecs consist of three jointly-trained components: 

(1) an encoder network that maps raw audio to compressed latent representations,
(2) a vector quantizer (typically Residual Vector Quantization) that converts continuous latents to discrete codes for efficient transmission, and
(3) a decoder network that reconstructs high-quality audio from quantized codes—all optimized end-to-end with adversarial losses for perceptual realism.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀:
✅ 10x Bandwidth Efficiency - Deliver natural-sounding audio at 3 kbps vs 32+ kbps required by traditional codecs, enabling AI agents to operate over constrained networks and edge devices
✅ Real-Time Performance - Streaming architectures with <25ms latency make conversational AI feel instantaneous, even on mobile CPUs without GPU acceleration
✅ Multi-Task Intelligence - Simultaneously compress and enhance audio (denoise, bandwidth extension) in a single forward pass, eliminating separate preprocessing pipelines that add complexity and latency

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
Why aren’t more people talking about Qwen3-Next? This MoE model includes a number of architectural changes to make training cheaper and inference throughput to sky rocket 🚀

💡Highlights of the model

1. Total 80B params but just 3B activated.

2. 25% of the layers use dense self-attention and 75% of layers use linear attention.

3. Self-attention layers adopt Gated Attention, which helps eliminate issues like Attention Sink and Massive Activation

4. Self-attention layers adopt partial rope to only the first 25% of position dimensions

5. Linear Attention is implemented via a Gated Delta Net

6. 512 total experts out-of-which 10 are activated via routing and 1 shared expert.

7. Zero-centered RMSNorm as the normalization function, with weight decay applied to the weights of RMSNorm.

8. Router weights go through normalization immediately after initialization to account for any biases that affect routing.

9. Also trained on Multi-token prediction instead of just predicting the next token.

The combination of linear and dense self-attention leads to impressive increases in throughput with the model being nearly 2.5 times faster than Qwen3-30B-3B i.e. same number of activated params but much faster with almost no difference in performance. 🏃‍♀️‍➡️ 

We’ve seen quite a few models use alternating self and local/sliding window attention layers, this is the first model that I’ve come across that uses linear attention instead of local attention.

In the coming days I’ll also dive deeper into what Gated Attention is and also how Gated Delta Net implements Linear attention, stay tuned 🤓.

author: Pascal Biese
subtitle: AI Lead at PwC <​/​> Daily AI highlights for 80k+ experts 📲🤗
content:
More performance for 10,000 times less parameters. This is NOT a typo.

While the industry races to build ever-larger models, a new paper from Samsung's AI lab shows that a tiny 7 million parameter network can outperform models 10,000 times its size on certain tasks.

The paper introduces Tiny Recursive Model (TRM), which beats GPT-4 and even some of the newest reasoning models on difficult puzzles like Sudoku, maze-solving, and the ARC-AGI benchmark - a test specifically designed to measure genuine intelligence rather than pattern matching.

Instead of throwing more parameters at the problem, TRM uses a clever recursive approach. The model takes its initial answer and repeatedly refines it, using its previous reasoning as context for the next iteration. Think of it like a student checking their work multiple times, each pass building on insights from the last.

On ARC-AGI, a benchmark where even frontier models struggle, this 7M parameter model achieves 45% accuracy - higher than models with billions of parameters. On extremely hard Sudoku puzzles, it reaches 87% accuracy where even the most advanced LLMs score 0%.

What makes this work stand out is not only the performance but also the simplicity: the researchers stripped away unnecessary complexity from previous approaches, removing biological justifications and complex mathematical theorems. 

They discovered that a single 2-layer network, recursively applied, could outperform much larger architectures. Less really was more.

This challenges our current trajectory in AI development. Yes, models are much more efficient now than they were just two years ago, but the core mechanisms have - on average - become more complex. 

From standard token generation to two phases (reasoning and final generation) to more complex reasoning patterns to... a much simpler recursive approach?

For practitioners, this suggests we might be over-engineering our solutions. For researchers, it hints at unexplored paths to artificial general intelligence that don't require planet-scale computing resources. And for all of us watching AI's trajectory, it's a reminder that the next breakthrough might come from thinking differently, not larger.

The field is moving so fast that our assumptions barely have time to solidify before they're overturned. That's both thrilling and humbling.

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
If you’re into LLMOps/Distributed Training you should know about Context Parallelism.

❓ What’s the problem?
Today’s LLMs are not just huge in the number of parameters that they have but also in the max context window that they support. However, supporting long context windows means that your KV-cache starts consuming a lot of memory which can lead to OOM errors, when all the KV tokens reside on just one GPU.

🤓 Context Parallelism
The goal of context parallelism is to split the computation of self-attention on a batch of sequences to multiple GPUs as efficiently as possible.
Today’s post covers how Context Parallelism works in the prefill stage.

1️⃣ Ring Pass KV During Pre-filling
Pre-filling is when the entire prompt (system+user) is loaded into an LLM. In this phase we need to compute attention of all tokens against every other token. For simplicity we’ll assume a batch size of 1, sequence length L=2 and total number of GPUs to be N=2.

a. Each GPU is assigned L//N contiguous indices. These indices correspond to the indices of the Query, Key,Value Tensors that’ll reside on the device. So if we have a sequence length of 2 and 2 gpus, the Query tensors for indices 0 will reside on GPU-0 and 1 will reside on GPU-1.

b. Initially GPU-0 will contain KV-Tensors at index[0] and GPU-1 the other index.

c. We now perform ring-attention (as shown in the image below). GPU-0 computes attention of Q[0] against (K[0],V[0]) and GPU-1 computes attention of Q[1] against (K[1], V[1]).

d. Notice that at this point we only have partial results of self-attention. Since Q[0] hasn’t attended to (K[1], V[1]) yet!

e. As the GPUs start computing attention they also simultaneously send their K,V tensors to the other GPU. GPU-0 sends (K[0],V[0]) GPU-1 and GPU-1 does the same for its KV tensors.

f. On receiving the KV-tensors from another GPU they start computing attention on the newly received KV-tensors. This happens N-1 times in a ring pattern, so each GPU processes KV tensors from all other GPUs.

g. At the end GPU-0 has all the attention results it needs (Q[0], K[0], V[0]) and (Q[0], K[1],V[1]) and GPU-1 has a similar set of results for Q[1].

h. Since we computed attention in chunks, each chunk has its own local max/sum for softmax. Online softmax (merge attention) is used to combine these partial results correctly, accounting for the different normalization constants.

🤔 Why rotate KV instead of Q during prefill?
For models that use Grouped Query Attention or Multi-Query Attention the memory consumed by KV-tensors is far less than Query Tensors after a certain sequence length.

As a reminder in GQA if we have a sequence of length L, Number of Query Heads Q_H and Hidden Size of Heads H

Query Tensors have a size of L * Q_H * H

Whereas KV-Tensors have a size of 2 * L * G * H
Where G is the number of Groups and G < Q_H, In MQA G=1.

🎁 Wrap Up
Stay tuned for Context Parallelism at the decode stage.
For more read: https://lnkd.in/eJrzUYg2

content:
REFRAG from Meta Superintelligence Labs is a SUPER exciting breakthrough that may spark the second summer of Vector Databases! REFRAG illustrates how Database Systems are becoming even more integral to LLM inference!

By making clever use of how context vectors are integrated with LLM decoding, REFRAG is able to make TTFT (Time-to-First-Token) 31X faster and TTIT (Time-to-Iterative-Token) 3X faster, overall improving LLM throughput by 7x!! Most of the RAG systems today that are built with Vector Databases, such as Weaviate, throw away the associated vector with retrieved search results, only making use of the text content. REFRAG instead passes these vectors to the LLM, instead of the text content! 

This is further enhanced with a fine-grained chunk encoding strategy, and a 4-stage training algorithm that includes a selective chunk expansion policy trained with GRPO / PPO.

author: Sebastian Raschka, PhD
subtitle: ML/AI research engineer. Author of Build a Large Language Model From Scratch (amzn.to/4fqvn0D) and Ahead of AI (magazine.sebastianraschka.com), on how LLMs work and the latest developments in the field.
content:
From the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) to a new Tiny Recursive Model (TRM).

A few months ago, the HRM made big waves in the AI research community as it showed really good performance on the ARC challenge despite its small 27M size. (That's about 22x smaller than the smallest Qwen3 0.6B model.) 

Now, the new "Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks" paper proposes Tiny Recursive Model (TRM), which a simpler and even smaller model (7M, 4× smaller than HRM) that performs even better on the ARC challenge. 


🔹 What does recursion mean here?

TRM refines its answer in two steps:
1. It updates a latent (reasoning) state from the current question and answer.
2. Then it updates the answer based on that latent state.

Training runs for up to 16 refinement steps per batch. Each step does several no-grad loops to improve the answer, followed by one gradient loop that learns from the full reasoning process. 

By the way, the question and the answer are grids of discrete tokens, not text. (E.g., 9×9 Sudoku and up to 30×30 ARC and Maze.)

🔹 And how does it differ from HRM?

In short, HRM recurses multiple times through two small neural nets with 4 transformer blocks each (high and low frequency). TRM is much smaller (i.e., 4x) and only a single network with 2 transformer blocks. 

TRM backpropagates through the full recursion once per step, whereas HRM only backpropagates through the final few steps. And TRM also removes HRM's extra forward pass for halting and instead uses a simple binary cross-entropy loss to learn when to stop iterating.

🔹 Surprising tidbits

1. The author found that adding layers decreased generalization due to overfitting. And going from 4 to 2 layers improved the model from 79.5% to 87.4% on Sudoku. 

2. Replacing the self-attention layer with an MLP layer also improved accuracy (74.7% -> 87.4% on Sudoku); however, note that this only make sense here since we have a fixed-length, small context to work with.


🔹 Bigger picture

My personal caveat: comparing this method (or HRMs) to LLMs feels a bit unfair since HRMs/TRM are specialized models trained for specific tasks (here: ARC, Sudoku, and Maze pathfinding) while LLMs are generalists. It’s like comparing a pocket calculator to a laptop. Both serve a purpose, just in different contexts.

That said, HRMs and the recursive model proposed here are fascinating proof‑of‑concepts that show what’s possible with relatively small and efficient architectures. I'm still curious what the real‑world use case will look like. Maybe they could serve as reasoning or planning modules within a larger tool‑calling system.

In practice, we often start by throwing LLMs at a problem, which makes sense for quick prototyping and establishing a baseline. But I can see a point where someone sits down afterward and trains a focused model like this to solve the same task more efficiently.

Anyways, the paper is a fun and refreshing read: https://lnkd.in/gPNJRvhq

author: Pramodith B.
subtitle: ML Engineer | Ex’s shall not be named
content:
The 6 parallelism strategies you must know about if you’re looking to train LLMs. 👇🏽

💽 Data Parallel
Parallelism along the batch dimension. Given N GPUs, each GPU gets a unique batch of size B. Each GPU computes the gradients corresponding to its batch. Before updating the weights, all N GPUs share their gradients via an all-reduce (mean) and then proceed to update the weights. The all-reduce operation ensures that all the GPUs have the exact same copy of the model weights before the next batch of data.

0️⃣ Zero-3 
In standard Data Parallel, each GPU stores a complete copy of all weights, gradients, and optimizer states (running mean and variance of gradients). This redundancy can lead to OOM errors.

Zero works by sharding i.e. breaking the model weights, gradients and optimizer states and distributing them between the N GPUs.

➗ Tensor Parallel
Key difference from Zero-3 is that TP can also be applied to activations i.e. the intermediate outputs after each layer/sub-module of an LLM.

TP splits both weight and activation matrices along rows or columns. For e.g. if you had a Matrix of shape [R, C]. Depending on what degree you set for Tensor parallelism (T), the matrix can be broken down as [R/T, C] or [R, C/T]

🔧 Pipeline Parallel
Focuses on distributing the weights of the model between GPUs by breaking the model along the layer dimension. So if you have L layers and N GPUs (L > N) each GPU is assigned L/N layers. Naive distribution of the layers can lead to a lot of idle GPU time, since each GPU needs to wait for the results from prior layers before they can start their forward pass.

Researchers have come up with a bunch of clever ways to distribute layers and order forward and backward passes to drastically cut down on idle time.

📏 Sequence Parallel and Context Parallel
Parallelism along the sequence dimension, used in operations like layer norm, dropout and self-attention. Sequence Parallel distributes the S tokens between the N GPUs, since layer norm can be calculated on each token independently from the other we can run layer norm in parallel with any repercussions.

Context Parallel focuses on reducing memory consumed by self-attention by distributing KV-cache tokens between the N GPUs and using Ring Attention, last week’s post dove deep into this.

🤓 Expert Parallel
Relevant for Mixture-of-Expert Models, where all the E experts are distributed between the N GPUs

🎁 Wrap Up
The beauty of these strategies is that most of them are complementary with each other meaning that you can mix them all up to create a highly distributed and efficient training cluster.
However, finding the right balance between communication overhead and the right configuration of distribution strategies depends on the specs of your GPU cluster, model architecture etc.

For more read this brilliant blog by HF: https://lnkd.in/eYS-WB3q

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🎛️ How to match full fine-tuning quality with LoRA!

A new blog post from Thinking Machines Lab investigates when Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) performs as well as full fine-tuning for language models. It provides practical guidance for efficient post-training!

First, two well-known facts in the fine-tuning community:

→ LoRA matches full fine-tuning on typical post-training datasets when applied to ALL layers (especially MLPs), not just attention layers like the original paper suggested.

→ The optimal learning rate for LoRA is consistently 10x higher than for full fine-tuning across models and tasks. This ratio is empirically robust but still lacks a complete theoretical explanation.

Now, some less obvious facts:

→ LoRA works exceptionally well for reinforcement learning, matching full fine-tuning even at rank=1. Policy gradient methods only absorb ~1 bit of information per episode, so even tiny LoRA adapters have enough capacity.

→ Large batch sizes hurt LoRA more than full fine-tuning, creating a persistent performance gap.

→ The 1/r scaling factor in LoRA's parametrization makes optimal learning rates nearly independent of rank, which simplifies hyperparameter tuning significantly.

I enjoy the systematic approach in this paper, testing across multiple model families and parameters. It's a good reminder that high batch sizes can negatively impact evals (speaking from experience), but this parameter is usually blindly maxxed instead. The information-theoretic analysis for RL is interesting but assumes REINFORCE-style algorithms. Still, this is the most comprehensive LoRA analysis to date and should become required reading for anyone doing LLM fine-tuning.

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🧮 Why LLMs can't multiply (and how to fix it)

Multiplication seems trivial for humans, but it is still surprisingly hard for LLMs. Even current frontier models sometimes fail at 4×4 digit multiplication if no tool is provided. The authors trained a small model to perform exactly this task.

→ Standard fine-tuning with gradient descent and autoregressive loss gets stuck in a local optimum where the model learns early and late digits correctly, but completely fails on middle digits 🚮

→ Successful models trained with implicit chain-of-thought build sparse "attention trees" that cache partial products (like a2×b0) at earlier timesteps and retrieve them later, essentially constructing a directed acyclic graph across the sequence.

→ The working model represents digits using Fourier bases forming a pentagonal prism geometry and computes digit-wise multiplication through Minkowski sums. These elegant mathematical structures were never discovered by the failed model.

→ Adding an auxiliary loss that predicts intermediate "running sums" via linear probes provides the right inductive bias, allowing even a 2-layer model to achieve 99% accuracy without any chain-of-thought supervision (!!).

Overall, it's a very impressive paper. Prior work (https://lnkd.in/e5YRCDiP) has shown transformers struggle with compositional tasks and long-range dependencies, but this paper provides concrete mechanistic evidence of why: gradient descent simply doesn't push models toward the sparse, structured attention patterns multiplication requires.

However, the proposed fix (auxiliary loss for running sums) is admittedly task-specific and feels like a band-aid. The real question the paper doesn't answer is whether there's a general architectural or training modification that could help transformers discover these long-range structures naturally.

author: Anshuman Mishra
subtitle: ML @ Zomato
content:
You’re in a Machine Learning interview at Meta, and the interviewer asks:

Why is scaling context length so hard? What’s the fundamental bottleneck?’

Here’s how you answer:

Don’t say: ‘Memory limitations’ or ‘GPU constraints.’ 
Wrong framing. 
The real answer is the O(n²) complexity of self-attention. Every token must attend to every other token. 
Double your context? You 4x your compute. It’s not linear scaling - it’s exponential pain.

NOTE - if you want to read this kinda content daily, consider subscribing my free newsletter - https://lnkd.in/gCPD6fUz

Here’s the math that breaks everything: 

→ 8K context = 64M attention computations. 
→ 128K context = 16B computations
→ 1M context = 1T computations. 

Your compute cost doesn’t grow with n, it grows with n². This is why throwing money at the problem doesn’t solve it.

The architectural constraint everyone misses:
- Full attention means an 8×8 matrix for 8 tokens, 128K×128K matrix for 128K tokens.
- Memory isn’t just storing tokens - it’s storing every possible token relationship.
- At 1M tokens, you need to materialize a 1M×1M attention matrix. That’s 1 trillion float values.

This is why context length is the great divider:

- GPT-4, Llama = 128-200K max (hitting the O(n²) wall) 
- Claude, Gemini 1M = Heavy optimization + unknown architecture tricks + $$$
- Most open source = 32K or less (the practical ceiling) 
- Startups = Can’t afford to compete on context

‘So how do you actually scale past 128K?’ Interviewer leans forward.

This is where Sliding Window Attention (SWA) can help. 

> Instead of every token attending to every token, each token only attends to a fixed window around it. 
> Complexity drops from O(n²) to O(n×w). Suddenly 1M tokens becomes feasible.

The clever part: local attention + deep layers = global understanding.

Token 1 doesn’t directly see token 100K, but through 32 layers of propagation, information flows across the entire sequence. 
Like how CNNs build from edges to objects - each layer has local receptive field but stacks create global vision.
The implementation trick that makes it work: Split Q and K into overlapping chunks (size 2w, overlap w). 

Do attention within chunks only. 
One PyTorch matmul operation. 
Yes, you compute 2x more than theoretically optimal. 
But you go from “impossible” to “runs on one GPU.” That’s the tradeoff that matters.


The answer that gets you hired: 
‘Scaling context is hard because attention is fundamentally O(n²). Full attention at 1M tokens is computationally intractable for most. The solution isn’t more hardware - it’s architectural changes like SWA that break the quadratic bottleneck. Gemini likely uses SWA variants + massive optimization. The math dictates the limits.’

The follow-up that makes you stand out: ‘The interesting question isn’t “how do we get 1M context” - it’s “do we need it?”

author: Pascal Biese
subtitle: AI Lead at PwC <​/​> Daily AI highlights for 80k+ experts 📲🤗
content:
The AI hype train just won't stop - back to big news almost daily!

AI Coding + World Models = 🧡 

Meta just released something that could fundamentally change how we build coding AI: they're teaching models to understand what code actually does, not just what it looks like.

The challenge with current Large Language Models for code is that they treat programming the same as any other text - predicting line by line based on patterns. But any developer knows that writing good code requires understanding execution: how variables change, how functions interact, what happens when your code actually runs. This gap between syntax and semantics has been a persistent limitation in AI-powered coding tools.

Instead of just training on static code repositories, they trained their new Code World Model (CWM) on millions of execution traces - actual step-by-step recordings of what happens when Python code runs. 

The model learns to predict not just the next line of code, but the state of variables, the flow of execution, and the outcomes of running programs. They even trained it on agentic interactions with Docker environments, teaching it how real developers debug and fix code in practice.

With great success: CWM achieves 65.8% on SWE-bench Verified, matching or beating models many times its size. More impressively, it can simulate Python execution in its "mind" - predicting what will happen when code runs without actually executing it. It seems to have learned a "mental model" of what the code is doing.

This is a shift from teaching AI to mimic developers to teaching it to think like one. As software development becomes increasingly AI-assisted, models that truly understand code execution - not just syntax - will be the ones that can handle complex debugging, optimization, and architectural decisions. The fact that Meta is releasing this as open-weights means researchers everywhere can build on this foundation.

Can't wait for the first frontier models that utilize this. GPT-5.1-codex-world, anyone?

author: Sameer Wadkar
subtitle: LLM Infrastructure · Training & Inference Systems · Distributed Compute · Cloud-Native AI Platforms
content:
🚀 Speculative Decoding: Faster LLM Inference, Not Less Compute

Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference. A smaller, faster draft model generates a block of candidate tokens (say 8) and passes them to a larger, more accurate model. The large model checks all 8 together in one forward pass. If it agrees, those tokens are accepted. If not, the disagreed tokens are recomputed. For example, if it agrees on 6 but not 7, tokens 7 and 8 are recalculated.

⚡ People often think speculative decoding reduces compute. Not quite. The savings are in time, not FLOPs.

Here is how it works in detail:

- A small draft model proposes 8 candidate tokens.
- A large target model runs once on the sequence of 30 past tokens plus the 8 candidates.
- That means a 38×38 attention mask (fully computed on the large model, no FLOPs saved here).
- Token 31 attends to the first 30.
- Token 32 attends up to 31.
- This continues until token 38 attends up to 37.
- All 8 logits come out in one forward pass, with masks ensuring each token only sees what it should.

Normally those 8 tokens would take 8 separate forward passes:
30×30 → 31×31 → … → 37×37.
Speculative decoding batches this into one bigger step, 38×38.

📌 Key points:

- FLOPs do not drop. They rise slightly because some tokens get recomputed when the draft and target disagree.
- The speedup comes from fewer sequential steps. GPUs do better with one larger matrix multiply than with many small ones.
- If the draft and target agree often, you advance multiple tokens per step. If they diverge, you fall back, but overall generation is still faster.

💡 The key point here is - Speculative decoding is only valuable if the draft and target agree often. If they disagree often, it will be slower. 

It works best for the following use-cases:
- Chatbot workloads - Customer service bot answering account balance or shipping status questions. The draft model is good enough at predicting common continuations (“Your order is…”, “The balance is…”), so the target agrees most of the time.

- Draft/target pairs from the same family (high agreement) - For example, a 7B distilled model drafting for a 70B base model. Shared training data and architecture mean the smaller model’s guesses often mirror the larger one’s, leading to high acceptance rates.

It tends to be less effective for creative or open-ended tasks, where the draft and target models disagree more often which reduces or eliminates the speedup.

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
🧑‍🏫  Can LLMs learn reasoning shortcuts?

This paper from AI at Meta tackles a major inefficiency where LLMs waste tokens re-deriving the same mathematical steps repeatedly. The authors propose a system that extracts reusable "behaviors" from reasoning traces to cut redundancy.

→ LLMs constantly rediscover the same intermediate steps like geometric series formulas or inclusion-exclusion principles, inflating token usage and squeezing context windows that could be used for actual exploration

→ The three-step metacognitive pipeline works by having models solve problems, reflect on their solutions, then extract named behaviors like "behavior_systematic_counting" with specific instructions for future reuse

→ Providing relevant behaviors as context during inference cuts reasoning tokens by up to 46% while matching or improving accuracy

→ Fine-tuning on behavior-conditioned traces creates models that internalize these procedural shortcuts, making non-reasoning models significantly better at math

→ The approach works across different model sizes and enables self-improvement where models use behaviors extracted from their own failed attempts to solve problems better on retry

This work tackles a real inefficiency in current LLM reasoning but is very focused on math problems, showing that it probably doesn't generalize very well. The embedding-based retrieval for behaviors is something that could be improved, especially compared to the extraction process. This is quite a nice approach though, which could be useful for task-specific models with reasoning.

author: Sameer Wadkar
subtitle: LLM Infrastructure · Training & Inference Systems · Distributed Compute · Cloud-Native AI Platforms
content:
🔥 Bandwidth, Not FLOPs: The Real Constraint in LLM Inference

📌  This new development from NVIDIA underscores a principle battle-tested in high-performance computing. At scale, the true limiter is not raw compute, it is moving data. Whether it is memory feeding a single GPU, training across a cluster, or SQL on Spark, throughput only rises when bandwidth improves.

⚡ LLM inference follows the same story. The wall is not FLOPs but bandwidth. Not all quadratic costs in attention hurt equally. Some are compute bound. Others choke on I/O.

Take a huge query such as giving a model a full codebase to refactor:
- Prefill crunches all tokens once to build the KV cache. Compute heavy.
- Decode generates tokens one by one, streaming the cache from memory each step. Bandwidth heavy.

📌 CPX and Rubin

NVIDIA is now splitting hardware along this line:

- #CPX targets prefill with large GDDR7 (higher capacity and lower $/GB, still fast but less bandwidth dense).
- #Rubin targets decode with HBM close to cores and NVLink for scale-out (smaller memory, blazing bandwidth density).

Serving frameworks such as TensorRT-LLM and Dynamo already let you route workloads across pools. A policy like “prefill on CPX, decode on Rubin” maps work to the right hardware. 

The practical split looks like this:

- CPX lowers time to first token.
- Rubin drives higher throughput.


📌 The Catch

Rubin is built for inference, where the KV cache dominates. HBM sits right next to the cores, NVLink ties GPUs together, and decode runs fast as long as everything fits inside HBM. But HBM does not scale. Contexts keep growing (agentic AI, million plus tokens). Sooner or later the cache spills out, and performance goes with it.

⚡ Enfabrica: The Missing Tier

NVIDIA’s $900M+ move to bring Enfabrica’s tech and leadership in-house plugs the memory gap Rubin leaves open.

- NVLink shares the memory you already have
- Enfabrica + CXL adds memory you never had

Instead of stranding GPUs as memory donors, you bolt on racks of DRAM over CXL fabric. Terabytes of cheaper capacity, close enough to keep decode running at speed.

Rubin plus Enfabrica extend the hierarchy: NVLink moves cache between GPUs, CXL stretches the memory tier itself.

📌 What You Can Do Today

On AWS you can already split pools:

- Use compute rich GPUs with large GDDR for prefill
- Use NVLink or NVSwitch instances (p4d, p5, p5e) for decode

Frameworks like TensorRT-LLM and Dynamo let you steer workloads across these pools (with lots of planning and design).

What you cannot do yet is the fabric piece. There is no way in the cloud today to bolt on pooled DRAM with CXL. That is the gap Enfabrica fills.

🔥 Takeaway: The real efficiency gains in GenAI will come less from chasing FLOPs and more from managing bandwidth now and adding fabric memory when it arrives.

#LLMInference #GenAI #CXL #Rubin #Enfabrica

author: Ita Zaporozhets
subtitle: ML/AI Software Engineer
content:
🚀 BLT (Byte Latent Transformer) in 🤗 Transformers
I’ve been working on integrating BLT (Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens, https://lnkd.in/g-V--24c, FAIR @ Meta) into the Hugging Face Transformers library! 

TL;DR: A tokenizer-free transformer that efficiently groups bytes into entropy-based patches, enabling competitive inference compared to traditional token-based approaches.

⚡ Key Highlights⚡

Tokenizer-free: robust to noisy, multilingual, or mixed-script inputs without tokenization. No more dealing with tokenizer pipelines or OOV handling.

Entropy-based patching: dynamically groups bytes into patches, scanning until an entropy threshold is reached. Low-entropy regions form larger patches, high-entropy regions form smaller patches.

Hash n-gram embeddings: preserves context from neighboring bytes by constructing n-grams and mapping these to embedding vectors using hash functions.

Efficiency: avoids slow byte-by-byte processing of prior byte-level approaches (ByT5, CANINE, etc.), making scaling much more practical.


⚡ Impact⚡

Simpler pipelines: robust to noisy, multilingual, or mixed-script inputs without tokenization.

Character-level tasks: significant performance improvements on character level tasks like spelling and character searching (try it out on this character-level benchmark( CUTE: https://lnkd.in/ggeJJQTR) 

Better scaling: patches allow large portions of predictable bytes to be processed efficiently, reducing FLOPs.

Flexible architecture: Local Encoder → Latent Global Transformer → Local Decoder + separate Entropy Model


⚡ Checkout the Integration⚡

Patch-byte attention ≈ multi-modal attention: The way BLT attends between patches and bytes is analogous to vision-text attention in multi-modal models like Mllama (checkout the modular file to see where blt is similar to mllama). Interesting to consider what other techniques from multi-modal models could be transferrable to tokenizer-free methods!

Entropy model (BltPatcher) is modular: the entropy model (patcher) is its own model, separate from BltModel and can be plugged into other models in Transformers.

Checkpoints: 1B and 7B parameters available, lightweight enough for MPS.
Modality potential: So far only trained on text input, but the flexible architecture allows for training other modalities.


⚡ Limitations⚡

Text-focused training: BLT is trained exclusively on text data, so its performance on other modalities is untested. Processing audio or image bytes is much slower than text

Character-level understanding: Even though BLT operates at the byte level, the 1B model isn't inherently good at character-level analysis, such as counting specific characters in a word. Without careful prompting, BLT does not answer “How many 'r's are in "strawberry"? correctly, showing tokenizer-free approaches still requires some work.

Check it out here: https://lnkd.in/gwMkQBcM

content:
You're in a ML Engineer interview at Meta, and the interviewer asks:

"Your LLM inference is running out of GPU memory with long conversations. How do you solve this without losing performance?"

Here's how you answer:

Most candidates say "buy more GPUs" or "truncate context."

Wrong approach.

The real bottleneck isn't model size - it's KV cache memory that grows linearly with every token.

Smart engineers offload, don't truncate.

btw if you want to receive these bites daily, subscribe my newsletter, and you'll have it in your inbox - https://lnkd.in/gCPD6fUz

now back to post -

Remember, GPU Memory = Model Weights + KV Cache.

As context grows, KV cache can consume 10x more memory than the model itself.


A 7B model with 8K context? That's ~4GB just for KV cache storage.
The problem everyone misses:

Your KV cache sits idle in expensive GPU memory between user interactions. User types a message, pauses for 30 seconds, types again. Meanwhile, their 2GB cache is blocking new requests from being served.

You need to remember -
- High GPU utilization + Low throughput = KV cache memory bottleneck
- OOM errors on long contexts = Need offloading strategy
- Idle sessions consuming memory = Wasted GPU resources
- Recomputing same context = Missing cache reuse opportunities

The metric that separates juniors from seniors: 
Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) with cache reuse. NVIDIA reports 14x faster TTFT when reusing offloaded cache vs recomputing from scratch. Cache transfer < recomputation cost.

"Our model handles 4K context fine!"

Interviewer: "What's your KV cache size at 32K tokens? How do you handle multi-user sessions? Where do you store inactive caches?"

No offloading strategy = You don't understand production inference.

The memory hierarchy that gets you promoted:

Junior: Keep everything in GPU memory until OOM
Senior: GPU → CPU RAM → SSD → Network storage based on access patterns
Principal: Predictive offloading with usage analytics

Know your offloading targets by use case:

- Multi-turn conversations: Offload to CPU RAM (fast resume)
- Document analysis: Shared cache in distributed storage
- Code assistance: Local SSD for IDE sessions
- Batch inference: Aggressive disk offloading

The brutal production reality:
- Perfect model + no cache strategy = OOM crashes 
- Smart offloading + slow storage = Latency spikes Great hardware + poor cache management = Wasted money

You need tiered storage, not just bigger GPUs.

Pro tip for the interview:
Mention LMCache integration "I'd implement tiered KV cache offloading with tools like LMCache.

Benchmark transfer costs vs recomputation, optimize for access patterns, monitor cache hit rates."

Understanding memory hierarchy > buying bigger GPUs

That's it for today! 

Scaling LLM inference is 80% memory management, 20% compute optimization. 

Offload smart, serve more. 

See ya tomorrow!
