author: Rajat Dandekar
subtitle: Making AI accessible for all | Solving AI problems for Industries | Co-founder at Vizuara, First Principle Labs and Videsh | IIT Madras and Purdue
content:
PPO and GRPO are reinforcement learning algorithms which are the backbone of reasoning models like o1, o3 and DeepSeek. ChatGPT would not have been possible without PPO which is instrumental in the RLHF Step.

Both PPO and GRPO, come under a class of methods are called as Policy Gradient Methods.

Now, Policy Gradient Methods build upon a pivotal theorem called "Policy Gradient Theorem".  Interestingly, two sets of researchers came up with this theorem at the same time. One with a 12-page proof and one with a half page proof.

The half page proof came from Richard Sutton's group, which he also includes in his famous book on RL. I wanted to teach this proof to scratch as a part of my course "Reasoning LLMs from Scratch". But the proof is so compact that many stages in-between are missed, making it really hard to understand.

So, I spend an entire day to expand this proof fully and make detailed notes without anything omitted. After all, this proof is responsible for the modern applications of RL including ChatGPT and reasoning LLMs.

Below are my notes for the proof. I have made this available for everyone here: https://lnkd.in/duefHvRV

HELM—the Holistic Evaluation of Language Models—Published by Stanford's Center for Research on Foundation Models, is your compass through the maze of the complex LLM Evaluation.

Here’s why it matters:

✸ HELM evaluates 30 prominent LLMs across 42 scenarios and 7 essential metrics, covering accuracy, fairness, robustness, and more.

✸ It reveals blind spots and trade-offs across models and scenarios, ensuring you make informed choices.

✸ All evaluation data is public—empowering the community to dive deeper and innovate further.

﹌﹌﹌﹌﹌﹌﹌﹌﹌

》 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝗛𝗘𝗟𝗠 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗱?

✸ Broad Coverage: Imagine exploring 16 core scenarios like question answering, summarization, sentiment analysis, and toxicity detection. HELM doesn’t stop there; it also dives into 7 targeted evaluations (e.g., reasoning and bias).

✸ Multi-Metric Evaluation: Accuracy isn’t the sole ruler here. HELM assesses LLMs using:

☆ Calibration: How confident is the model in its predictions?
☆ Robustness: Does it handle typos and dialects gracefully?
☆ Fairness: Are all groups treated equitably?

✸ Standardization: HELM levels the playing field. All 30 models, from OpenAI’s GPT series to Meta’s OPT, are benchmarked under consistent conditions.

﹌﹌﹌﹌﹌﹌﹌﹌﹌

》 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗟𝗼𝘄𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀

✸ Instruction-Tuning Rules: Models like OpenAI’s text-davinci-002 excel in accuracy and fairness. Why? Their training prioritizes user-friendly instructions.

✸ Closed vs. Open Models: Closed models generally outperform open ones, but open models like BLOOM are rapidly closing the gap.

✸ Trade-offs Everywhere: Improving one metric often sacrifices another. For example:


》 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗙𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗗𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

✸ Dynamic Benchmarks

✸ Scalability

✸ Ethical Considerations

author: Meri Nova
subtitle: ML/AI Engineer | Community Builder | Founder @Break Into Data | ADHD + C-PTSD advocate
content:
If you want to get a job as an AI engineer, don’t start with the hottest agent frameworks like CrewAI, LangGraph or Autogen. 

Sure, you’ve probably heard everyone talking about them like they're the secret sauce to success… but here’s the truth nobody tells you.  

Frameworks change. Core engineering fundamentals don’t.
Agents that actually work in production are built by people who understand what’s going on under the hood, not just what to plug in.


Focus on these first:

🔑 Programming Fundamentals
You need to be confident with OOP, functions, classes, and working with APIs. If you’re building full-stack agentic systems, knowing TypeScript is a huge plus.
Start here: https://realpython.com for Python or https://lnkd.in/gZ9e4jgd for TypeScript 

🔑 Prompt Engineering for Agents
 Learn how to structure prompts to guide reasoning, decision-making, and tool use. This is what makes or breaks your agent.
Start here: https://lnkd.in/geHd_uf5

🔑 Tool & API Integration
Agents don’t just respond, they act. That means wrapping real tools: APIs, calculators, scrapers, databases. Learn how to expose them cleanly so the agent knows how to use them. Only then try using MCP.  
Start here: https://lnkd.in/gx8Qfsx2

🔑 Agentic System Design 
Build simple linear workflows before diving into multi-agent systems. 
Study the most common design patterns and try to implement them with Python only, before using any frameworks.
Start here: https://lnkd.in/g8jBUVKn

🔑 Evals 
 You can’t improve what you don’t measure. Set up tracing for your agents. Choose 3-5 metrics you care about. Build an LLM as a judge. And continuously improve.

author: Mark Worrall
subtitle: Helping humans learn, adapt, and create in the age of AI | Founder @ nodeledge.ai
content:
Apple just dropped a new paper on LRMs and it’s not pretty. 🙈 

Paper title: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity.

Some highlights:

🧩 Using controlled puzzle environments (e.g. Tower of Hanoi), the authors show that frontier LRMs like Claude 3.7 and DeepSeek-R1 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗽𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝟬% 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆 beyond a certain complexity threshold.

⚠️ Surprisingly, giving these models the 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺 doesn't help. They still fail to execute logical steps correctly - exposing severe limits in symbolic reasoning and step-by-step verification.

📉 Even worse, as problems get harder, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝙡𝙚𝙨𝙨 - using fewer tokens despite having available budget. This suggests a compute scaling limit 𝘯𝘰𝘵 caused by external constraints, but internal brittleness.

🤖 They exhibit “overthinking”: generating correct answers early, then undermining them by exploring incorrect paths. And as complexity increases, the models stop finding correct answers altogether.

𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀?

To me all this is consistent with the fact that current LRMs don’t “reason” in any robust or generalisable sense. They simulate reasoning through pattern-matching - and once the patterns break down so does their ability to reason.

Mistaking examples of reasoning for actual reasoning is a logical fallacy. Don't fall for it.

author: Ross Wightman
subtitle: AI, Computer Vision, Technology Dreamer, Angel Investor
content:
I just merged the initial version of a new, very flexible Vision Transformer model into the timm library, called *NaFlexVit*. It combines ideas from FlexiViT, NaViT, and NaFlex. The model supports:
• variable aspect/size images of NaFlex (see SigLip-2 paper)
• factorized and fractional pos embed w/ scaling that covers NaFlex and most interesting NaViT modes
• on-the-fly patch resizing of FlexiViT w/ a re-written, fast torch native impl
• loading of existing vit weights in vision_transformer.py (add use_naflex=True in model factory) in NaFlexVit (can try with existing validate script and any vit model today)

The bulk of the code was not in the model, that was relatively quick. The data pipeline was the time sink. There's now a NaFlex data pipe that supports patchified outputs and allows switching sequence length and patch size per batch (also scaling batch size per batch). This includes a special impl of Mixup/Cutmix for variable aspect images, RandomErasing for patchified images. All of this is orchestrated by a dataset wrapper to handle all of the sampling, transform, collation details (cannot rely on the usual loader + collate fn combo with an isolated dataset due to worker process boundary complications). 

Hopefully the various bits prove useful, at least as a reference for use in other contexts, especially multi-modal / document use cases. I have a partially completed integration with OpenCLIP (still need to finish the iterable dataset wrapper), but the basic eval of the 2 NaFlex models was verified. #ai #computervision #visiontransformer

We NimbleEdge are excited to share Sparse Transformers: Fused operator kernels for structured sparsity in PyTorch. 

The team worked hard to bring the latest research in sparsity to unlock bigger models on tighter budgets!

In LLMs, only 10-20% of the weights actually get activated during a single token prediction. Rest all get zeroed out by the activation functions. This is a massive compute cost we bear unnecessarily. 

The result? For #llama 3.2, 5x faster MLP layer performance in transformers with 50-70% lesser memory. 

We are building on-device AI with efficiency as the key driving force for us but it cannot come at the cost of quality. You can find the code at https://lnkd.in/gJFnNSBS.

subtitle: AI/ML Researcher | Data Science | Data Analytics | GenAI | LLMs | On a Mission to Spread Tech Literacy
content:
Post #8: Building LLM from Scratch

𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝗔𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗠𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗺 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗪𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 - 𝗕𝗲𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗰𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘀

The 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗺 that we discussed in Post #6 works like a rule-book --> 𝗳𝗶𝘅𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗱𝗮𝗽𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲.

But in real life, we don't just follow rules we learn who to listen to based on our past experience. 
That is what trainable weights add to simplified self attention mechanism. 

With 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀, the model no longer just compares words but it 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝘀 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 that which relationship matters the most. 

Imagine you are in a group of friends, each person shares three facts. Instead of treating equally, you would learn who is most helpful and adjust your understanding accordingly. 
That's exactly what the model does with 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝗿𝘆, 𝗸𝗲𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲 discussed in 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝘁 #𝟳. 

Inspired by Sebastian Raschka's "Building Large Language Models from Scratch", I've created a minimal working example in PyTorch and explained each line in layman terms. Please find the implementation attached to this post. Hope it helps!

Please do not hesitate to reach out in case of any doubt or suggestion.

4 cases when NOT to use Random Forest

(that'll save you 50% of ML modeling time)

🔥 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗟 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗺𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS

🟢 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗮𝗿
In this case, Random Forest will barely outperform Linear or Logistic Regression.

👉 Linear models:
↳ Train faster
↳ Are easier to tune
↳ Are more interpretable

🟢 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝗶𝘀𝘆, 𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘀𝗲, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝘃𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆
Random Forest likes when:
↳ Data having many distinct feature values
↳Low noise levels

For noisy and sparse data, simpler models (e.g., Linear Regression) often perform just as well.

🟢 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁
Random Forest doesn’t extrapolate well.

👉 Use smooth non-linear models instead:
↳ Neural Networks
↳ Gaussian Processes

🟢 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Random Forest’s piecewise constant structure makes optimization gradients noisy and unstable.

👉 In this case, use smooth non-linear models:
↳ Neural Networks
↳ Gaussian Processes
↳ Splines

🔥 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗟 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗺𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲: https://lnkd.in/emb4cFCS

IBM open-sourced a powerful document processing toolkit that makes enterprise data usable for language models, without the usual OCR headaches.

Docling is an open-source Python library designed to convert complex documents such as PDFs, DOCX, PPTX, HTML, and images into structured, AI-ready formats like JSON and Markdown. It’s built for developers working on RAG pipelines, agentic workflows, and fine-tuning LLMs on proprietary data.

Key features:
(1) Advanced PDF understanding - powered by IBM’s DocLayNet and TableFormer models, Docling handles layout parsing, reading order, tables, code blocks, and formulas with high accuracy.

(2) Unified document representation - outputs a richly structured DoclingDocument object, exportable to Markdown, HTML, or lossless JSON.

(3) Seamless integrations - works out-of-the-box with LangChain, LlamaIndex, Crew AI, and Haystack.

(4) Local execution - runs efficiently on standard hardware, making it suitable for resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive environments.

If you’re building AI systems that need to understand real-world documents, from financial reports to technical manuals, Docling is the missing link between raw files and structured knowledge.

author: Shantanu Ladhwe
subtitle: Head of AI ML | 145k+ Linkedin & Substack | AI Agents, RAG, NLP, Recommenders, Search & MLOps
content:
You’ll think I’m crazy 😄
But this is how RAG is really built in production.
You should check it out 👇

It’s not just plugging in OpenAI + a vector DB.
Here’s the real flow I’ve seen from messy docs to a shipped feature:👇

1️⃣ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗰𝘀
→ What’s the user problem?
→ What’s the feature we’re enabling?
→ Do we really need RAG? Rules or IR might work better.

2️⃣ 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗔𝘂𝗱𝗶𝘁
→ Do we have the right documents?
→ Are they structured or unstructured? Clean? Complete?
→ Do we need extraction like HTML parsing or OCR?

3️⃣ 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴
→ Chunking strategy → fixed, semantic, overlap?
→ Extract metadata, HTML clean-up, language detection
→ NER or Classification to filter/query data
→ Choose between vector retrieval / hybrid / keyword / rule-based

4️⃣ 𝗥𝗮𝗽𝗶𝗱 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗼𝘁𝘆𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗯𝗼𝗼𝗸
→ Try embeddings + vector search (OpenAI, BGE, E5)
→ Store locally (FAISS) or use pgvector for quick validation
→ Evaluate retrieval manually with query–chunk pairs
→ Start small → get 10–20 examples right

5️⃣ 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹 𝗟𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰
→ Try different similarity techniques (cosine, HNSW, hybrid)
→ Add business logic to boost or suppress results
→ Consider cost vs latency vs quality
→ Use bi-encoders or cross-encoders (re-rankers) if needed
→ Using custom models? Now you need MLOps too!

6️⃣ 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻
→ Pick a model (OpenAI, Claude, Mistral)
→ Design prompts, add guardrails
→ Handle hallucinations, cost, and context limits

7️⃣ 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁!)
→ Build Golden dataset
→ Use RAGAS, LLM-judge, human evals
→ Metrics: Recall@k, MRR, helpfulness

8️⃣ 𝗜𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 & 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
→ Try OCR tweaks → breaks chunking? fix again
→ Change embedding model → update backfill pipeline
→ Add filters, rerankers, fallback mechanisms

9️⃣ 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗡𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗯𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝘁𝗼 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮
→ Build the data pipeline if needed
→ Set up Vector DB / SQL DB / hybrid system
→ Dockerize, CI/CD, push to cloud (ECR, Lambda, ECS, Vertex, etc.)
→ Add monitoring (token usage, latency, failure rate)
→ Setup dashboards (Grafana, Prometheus, DataDog, etc.)

🔟 𝗥𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘂𝘁 & 𝗙𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗟𝗼𝗼𝗽
→ Add logs → retrieval candidates + selected context
→ Enable user feedback logging 
→ AB test against product KPIs (CTR, time-on-task, bounce rate)
→ Use structured feedback to retrain ranking models

🔁 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘂𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
→ Fine-tune embeddings
→ Use cross-encoders
→ Add fallback strategies
→ New OCR? New docs? Repeat pre-processing 😅

🧠 𝗕𝗼𝗻𝘂𝘀 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀
→ Requirements will change
→ Legal/GDPR will knock
→ Stakeholders want analytics
→ You’ll need to explain retrieval logic to non-tech teams
→ Didn’t even cover LLMOps or Agentic RAG yet…

The process never ends and that’s the point.
It’s system design.

author: Sumit Vaise
subtitle: Sr. Machine Learning Engineer @Fidelity Investments | Building Production GenAI & RAG Systems | GCP · AWS · LangChain · MLOps | vLLM | Open to Senior/Lead AI Roles.
content:
MP4 files replacing Vector db for AI memory.

Store millions of text chunks in MP4 files instead of expensive vector databases with lightning-fast semantic search.

Under the hood:

- This just stores text as images in the video file. It has a separate FAISS lookup for the vector similarity
- FAISS is still a vector db
- The video is just the QR code of text
- The mp4 trick may give you some basic video compression and is fine for portability
- Ultimately a dedicated text encoder like gzip is going to be much higher compression of raw text

No database needed. 100% Opensource.


Why this could be a gamechanger?

Mermvid could be a gamechanger due to its cost-effectiveness, eliminating the need for pricey vector databases like Pinecone, and its 10x storage efficiency using MP4 files. Its offline functionality and open-source nature make it highly accessible, especially for smaller teams or remote settings. 

However, its unconventional use of video files raises concerns about data integrity and query complexity, potentially limiting adoption. The approach is novel, but skepticism remains about its suitability for complex AI tasks compared to traditional databases. Further testing is needed to confirm its scalability and reliability.

author: Borys Semerenko
subtitle: Solutions Architect
content:
One topic I find particularly interesting is how to handle concurrent user requests to large language models (LLMs).


Think of an LLM as a function: 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗽𝘂𝘁 = 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹(𝗶𝗻𝗽𝘂𝘁). It accepts an input vector and returns an output vector.

We can’t simply call the model function simultaneously from multiple threads - each thread causes the model weights to be loaded into memory separately (which, for large models, can be tens of terabytes), quickly leading to out-of-memory errors.

The proper way to handle this is to batch user inputs and process them together 💪.

This is one of the strengths of transformer-based models: they can process a batch of inputs nearly as fast as a single one, thanks to how GPUs handle matrix operations.

Internally, the model multiplies input token vectors by weight matrices - a task GPUs are good at due to optimized general matrix multiplication (GEMM). Whether it's a 𝟭 × 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹-𝘀𝗶𝘇𝗲 matrix or a 𝗯𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵_𝘀𝗶𝘇𝗲 × 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹-𝘀𝗶𝘇𝗲 matrix, the GPU performs essentially the same operation.

Batching is more efficient because fetching weights from memory is expensive, and doing it once for a large batch is better than repeating it for individual requests.

This leads to an important question: what's the right batch size?

Since LLM inference is often memory-bound, the batch size should be calculated based on the available GPU memory. Check the following guide on how to do that - https://lnkd.in/eucD9z6B

This batching logic is typically handled by the inference server - a layer that sits between the model and the rest of your system. Rather than implementing batching from scratch, I recommend using libraries like vLLM, which automatically batch incoming requests and apply many other optimizations. But, if you still want to customize batching behavior, you can use the --𝗺𝗮𝘅-𝗻𝘂𝗺-𝘀𝗲𝗾𝘀 flag to control the maximum batch size.

author: Philip Vollet
subtitle: VP Developer Relations & Growth @ Weaviate - Building memory
content:
Have you ever wondered why your vector search sometimes misses nuanced matches? You're going to fall in love with multi-vector embeddings.

Traditional embeddings compress your entire text into a single vector - like trying to describe a movie with just one word. But what if we could capture 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗹 instead?

Multi-vector embeddings (think ColBERT, ColPali, ColQwen) represent each object using multiple vectors instead of just one. It's like having a team of specialists each focusing on different aspects of your documents rather than one generalist trying to do it all.

Here's the magic: "late interaction" 
• Each part of your query finds its best match in the document
• Token-level matching preserves word order and context
• You get more precise results, especially for longer texts

The technical bit? Instead of one vector, you get multiple vectors capturing different semantic aspects.

When should you use them?
✓ When exact phrase matching matters
✓ For search tasks where word order is crucial
✓ When you need nuanced understanding of longer texts

The trade-off? They need more memory and compute - a multi-vector embedding can be 4x larger than traditional ones. But for many use cases, that precision boost is absolutely worth it.

author: Paolo Perrone
subtitle: No BS AI/ML Content | ML Engineer with a Plot Twist 🥷100M+ Views 📝
content:
Agents are here—and building them is a whole new level of pain:

1️⃣ Building agents is a whole different beast

We’re asking them to solve dynamic search problems in enterprise environments—with fuzzy constraints, under time pressure. It’s like this:

Given a task P, data D, and tools T = {t1…tn}, the agent must figure out the right sequence of tool invocations over D to complete P.

That means reasoning over:
⇨ Which tools to use (retrieval, graph traversal, log search…)
⇨ How to chain them in multi⇨ hop workflows, with smart backtracking
⇨ How to coordinate across agents with different ACLs and incomplete views
⇨ When to stop—without looping or hallucinating, _and_ without a reward function

 2️⃣ Agents don’t get second chances

Humans can tolerate latency from other humans, but not from software. This means, you’ll need:

⇨ A semantic cache that maps task → toolchain. This avoids rethinking solved paths. Bonus points if you store reusable sub-paths
⇨ A fast, low-loss way to shrink massive corpora (TB+) down to something workable
⇨ Durable execution and async-await for agents (Temporal, anyone?)
⇨ Agent-to-agent broadcasting, especially when ACLs and context are fragmented

3️⃣ Pricing is a minefield
Not all tasks are created equal. Diagnosing a multi-region outage ≠ finding a broken link.

But most usage-based models price them the same. That’s misaligned.

⇨ Startups will need new pricing strategies—either value-based or usage-weighted by task complexity. 
⇨ Both are hard to get right _and_ explain.

Agentic software isn’t just “smarter software”
It’s a whole new game—and we’re still figuring out the rules

author: Aadit Sheth
subtitle: Co-founder, The Narrative Company. Storytelling and comms for world-class companies on X & LinkedIn
content:
Stanford dropped a 70-minute masterclass on how GPT works.

Here’s what you’ll learn in this lecture:

1. What Are Transformers?

•  They’re not robots, they’re attention-based neural networks.
•  Built to process sequences all at once, not step-by-step like RNNs.
•  Powering everything from ChatGPT to AlphaFold to robot control systems.

2. Why They Work So Well

•  Self-attention lets the model “look” at every part of the input, dynamically.
• Multi-head attention finds different patterns in parallel.
•  Layer norms + residuals make deep training stable and scalable.

3. Three Types of Transformer Models

•  GPT (decoder-only): Generates text one token at a time.
•  BERT (encoder-only): Understands and classifies input sequences.
•  T5 (encoder-decoder): Translates, summarizes, and more,  input to output mapping.

4. How GPT Actually Works (in Code)

•  Karpathy walks through GPT in just 300 lines of PyTorch.
•  Uses the Tiny Shakespeare dataset to teach language modeling character by character.
•  Covers batching, loss functions, and training loops, all from scratch.

5. The Limitations & What’s Next

•  Transformers are still bound by context length limits (e.g., 2K tokens).
•  Quadratic attention cost makes long documents expensive.
• Next wave is Long-context models, plugin memory, and diffusion alternatives.

AI isn’t magic. But this lecture feels like it.

Share this with anyone curious about how transformers are changing the world.

content:
🚀 Boosting 2-bit LLMs with EoRA: I tested NVIDIA’s training-free adapter method on Qwen3 & Qwen2.5 👇

- EoRA compensates quantization loss using a lightweight LoRA adapter. No fine-tuning needed. I applied it to 2-bit Qwen models quantized with AutoRound.
- Qwen3-32B (2-bit, group size 128) gained +7.5 points on IFEval after adding an EoRA adapter. Qwen3-14B showed similar gains.
- Qwen2.5-72B also improved with an EoRA rank of 256. Lower ranks didn’t help as much on this bigger model.

Adapter overhead? Minimal for Qwen3-14B:
  +257MB (rank 32)
  +514MB (rank 64)

Takeaway:
EoRA makes 2-bit LLMs actually usable: not far from FP16 performance, ~5.5x smaller, and zero training cost.

Bonus: EoRA adapters are great QLoRA starting points for low-cost fine-tuning.

You shouldn’t use structured output mode on LLMs for reasoning tasks.

We’re open sourcing Osmosis-Structure-0.6B: an extremely small model that can turn any unstructured data into any format. (Links in comments!)

We found that structured output mode drastically worsens model performance on reasoning tasks, such as when agents structure data from a conversation in order to use APIs / MCPs.

We trained the model on 500K+ tasks where the model needed to format data into a structured output.

With Osmosis-Structure-0.6B, we saw a 4X jump in accuracy on benchmarks like AIME (1983-2024) and DAPO-Math-17K for Claude Sonnet 4.

Why this matters: multi-agent/model architecture for AI agents is increasingly popular. It works well since we’re now able to train small models to perform just as well as foundation models on domain-specific tasks and workflows.

author: Niels Rogge
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer at ML6 & Hugging Face
content:
When people ask me "Which framework should I use for developing AI agents? Should I use OpenAI Agent SDK? Google's Agent Development Kit? LangGraph or Pydantic's Agent framework?"

My answer to that is: they are all mostly similar, and you shouldn't use any of them. Start by using LLM APIs directly, and build from there. Working with vanilla LLM APIs makes it much easier to see what the model gets as input, and what it produces as output at each step of the process. It also allows to have better control over the amount of tokens consumed/produced, allows for better guardrailing, and more. This is also what Anthropic recommends in their blog post "Building effective agents".

Usually, it's not a good idea to just give a single prompt and a set of tools to an LLM. It will quickly get lost, and it's incredibly hard to see what's going on under the hood with each of those agentic frameworks, as they abstract away a lot for you.

When developing robust agentic applications, I recommend building "workflows", which are predefined sequences of steps. LLMs can be invoked in one or multiple steps, with clearly defined inputs and outputs. This is typically what LLMs are good at: given the right context, they are capable of producing the desired output, like converting a PDF to a JSON containing the key fields, or producing a summary of a long piece of text. The idea is that you as a human are still determining the workflow, as opposed to a fully autonomous agent which is determining its own workflow.

Philipp Schmid wrote a really nice blog post on "agentic patterns", things you can include in those workflows. You can get really creative with them! For example, you can invoke an LLM 5 times in parallel and perform a majority vote to get more reliable results. Or you could invoke an LLM to provide feedback to the output of a previous LLM step, or route the input to a selected LLM which is equipped with the appropriate tools.

- "Building effective AI agents": https://lnkd.in/eHuMGU3S
- "Agentic patterns": https://lnkd.in/e6wfN9_G

content:
Post #6: Building LLM from Scratch
𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝗔𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗠𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗺 - 𝗕𝗲𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗰𝗲𝗻𝗲

Let's break it down - 
Imagine the sentence: "𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝘁 𝗿𝗮𝗻"

When trying to understand the word "ran", the model does three things:
𝟭. 𝗦𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱 - How related is each word to "ran"
𝟮. 𝗡𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲𝘀 - They all add up to 1 (like weights or probabilities)
𝟯. 𝗕𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝘃𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 - More relevant words like "cat" contribute more to understanding the word "ran"

This is the 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗺 - a powerful idea that lets the model weigh and mix the words based on their relationships.

Inspired by Sebastian Raschka's "Building Large Language Models from Scratch", I've created a minimal working example in PyTorch and explained each line in layman terms. Please find the implementation attached to this post. Hope it helps!

author: Tanner Norton
subtitle: Deep Learning Engineer | Scientist Engineer III | Master of Science in Computer Science
content:
How do you make a small model perform like a large one?
Let's talk about the idea of knowledge distillation. The animation below shows a small "student" model learning to mimic a larger, more accurate "teacher" model.
Left: Teacher’s decision boundary
 Middle: Student learning over time
 Right: Error between student and teacher
Instead of learning from just the correct label, the student learns from the teacher’s soft probabilities—confidence values that tell it how sure the teacher is. These soft targets provide richer signal than hard 0/1 labels.
This allows a smaller model to:
Learn faster
Generalize better
Preserve most of the teacher’s behavior
Distillation is especially valuable when deploying models to edge devices, real-time systems, or anywhere size and speed matter.
If you're building production ML systems, this is a technique worth knowing. Let me know if you'd like the Python code for this demo.

Claude 4’s system prompt leaked - 10,000 words detailing exactly how the model is told to think, respond, and behave.

It reveals how today’s leading models aren’t just trained on what to say, but on how to behave.

The prompt is filled with multi-layered logic: instructions to explain limitations before answering, stay on-topic across long chats, invoke tools like APIs and web search with precision, and shut down harmful or off-policy requests without escalating. It repeats constraints, scopes answers, and reinforces values not by chance, but by design.

This is how AI alignment looks in practice: a mix of philosophy, programming, and safety engineering, embedded into the system itself. Not just to avoid “hallucinations,” but to simulate thoughtfulness, restraint, and even emotional intelligence.

LLMs are no longer just prediction engines. They’re becoming systems with behavior stacks, memory scaffolds, and guardrails coded through language.

Every AI output is the result of careful constraint not just capability and the more we understand how models are shaped, the better we can use them wisely.

author: Aksel Joonas Reedi
subtitle: Building AI Agents @ Hugging Face 🤗
content:
1.5 months into my internship at Hugging Face, and I just shipped my first research contribution 🚀

I've been diving deep into how AI agents execute actions. The current state-of-the-art choices are:
→ JSON agents (reliable but too rigid)
→ CodeAgents (flexible, but parsing errors kill performance)

But what if I told you I found a third option that beats both? 👇


The problem I discovered: 🤕

After analyzing 15,724 agent traces across GAIA, MATH, Frames & SimpleQA, I found that parsing errors in the first action reduce success rates by 21.3%. That’s a lot!

JSON agents avoid this but lack support for loops and state, which are usually required in real-world use cases. CodeAgents are expressive but fragile when extracting Python from markdown.

My approach: Structured CodeAgents 👷🧠

Instead of generating code in markdown blocks, what if agents generated both thoughts AND code in a structured JSON format?

The results were surprising:
Parsing errors went to 0, and performance doubled compared to JSON agents. Structured generation consistently wins for capable models. 📈

Claude-4-Sonnet: 32% → 65% → 68% (JSON → Code → Structured)
GPT-4o: 34% → 53% → 54%
Qwen-235B: 45% → 48% → 56%

But there’s a bit of a catch ⚠️:

There's a "structure tax." Smaller models completely fail when forced to handle JSON formatting + Python syntax + reasoning simultaneously. The cognitive overhead is too much. The Python generated in JSON tags usually has syntax errors and breaks down the agent.

What this means for agent builders:
Choose your architecture based on your model's capability. For frontier models, structured generation is a win. For smaller models, stick with simpler approaches.

Full research details in my blog post: https://lnkd.in/dN8Mj5D4 

Big thanks to Aymeric Roucher, Amir Mahla, and Albert Villanova for the mentorship and support 🤗
#AI #MachineLearning #Research #HuggingFace #Agents

author: Andreas Horn
subtitle: Head of AIOps @ IBM || Speaker | Lecturer | Advisor
content:
𝗪𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻 “𝗟𝗟𝗠.” ⬇️

In 2025, the AI landscape has evolved far beyond just large language models. Knowing which model to use for your specific use case — and how — is becoming a strategic advantage.

Let’s break down the 8 most important model types and what they’re actually built to do: ⬇️

1. 𝗟𝗟𝗠 – 𝗟𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹
→ Your ChatGPT-style model.
Handles text, predicts the next token, and powers 90% of GenAI hype.
🛠 Use case: content, code, convos.

2. 𝗟𝗖𝗠 – 𝗟𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹
→ Lightweight, diffusion-style models.
Fast, quantized, and efficient — perfect for real-time or edge deployment.
🛠 Use case: image generation, optimized inference.

3. 𝗟𝗔𝗠 – 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹
→ Where LLM meets planning.
Adds memory, task breakdown, and intent recognition.
🛠 Use case: AI agents, tool use, step-by-step execution.

4. 𝗠𝗼𝗘 – 𝗠𝗶𝘅𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘁𝘀
→ One model, many minds.
Routes input to the right “expert” model slice — dynamic, scalable, efficient.
🛠 Use case: high-performance model serving at low compute cost.

5. 𝗩𝗟𝗠 – 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹
→ Multimodal beast.
Combines image + text understanding via shared embeddings.
🛠 Use case: Gemini, GPT-4o, search, robotics, assistive tech.

6. 𝗦𝗟𝗠 – 𝗦𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹
→ Tiny but mighty.
Designed for edge use, fast inference, low latency, efficient memory.
🛠 Use case: on-device AI, chatbots, privacy-first GenAI.

7. 𝗠𝗟𝗠 – 𝗠𝗮𝘀𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹
→ The OG foundation model.
Predicts masked tokens using bidirectional context.
🛠 Use case: search, classification, embeddings, pretraining.

8. 𝗦𝗔𝗠 – 𝗦𝗲𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗔𝗻𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹
→ Vision model for pixel-level understanding.
Highlights, segments, and understands *everything* in an image.
🛠 Use case: medical imaging, AR, robotics, visual agents.

Understanding these distinctions is essential for selecting the right model architecture for specific applications, enabling more effective, scalable, and contextually appropriate AI interactions.

While these are some of the most prominent specialized AI models, there are many more emerging across language, vision, speech, and robotics — each optimized for specific tasks and domains.

LLM, VLM, MoE, SLM, LCM → GenAI
LAM, MLM, SAM → Not classic GenAI, but critical building blocks for AI agents, reasoning, and multimodal systems

author: Abhinand Balachandran
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer | Kaggle Master
content:
🚀 𝙎𝙥𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙚𝙚𝙠𝙚𝙣𝙙 𝙤𝙥𝙩𝙞𝙢𝙞𝙯𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝘾𝙐𝘿𝘼 𝙠𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙚𝙡𝙨 𝙛𝙧𝙤𝙢 𝙨𝙘𝙧𝙖𝙩𝙘𝙝 — 𝙘𝙝𝙖𝙨𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙮 𝙢𝙞𝙘𝙧𝙤𝙨𝙚𝙘𝙤𝙣𝙙!

After years of using PyTorch abstractions, I tried matrix multiplication from scratch in C++/CUDA and optimized it one level at a time. Started on my RTX 2060, then moved to an A100 for final benchmarking.

Basic CUDA matmul kernel → 𝟯𝟱𝗺𝘀
After optimizations → 𝟳.𝟱𝗺𝘀

Breaking the matrix multiplication into shared-memory tiles gave a 𝟱𝘅 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗽 — thread blocks now work together on fast on‑chip data instead of hammering slow global memory. With some final low-level tuning like __restrict__ pointers, loop unrolling, tile width, read-only cache hints, I was able to squeezed out another tiny fraction of performance.

But here's what really got me: writing the parallel code yourself changes everything. You stop taking GPU acceleration for granted. You start thinking in warps, memory hierarchies, and thread synchronization. You feel every optimization working.

When you use PyTorch, this is all abstracted away (for the better). But implementing the kernels yourself? You understand why certain operations are fast, others aren't, and how memory bandwidth and memory hierarchy of the chip affects performance.

cuBLAS still crushed me at 𝟬.𝟯𝟮𝗺𝘀 — a humbling reminder of what best-in-class optimization looks like. But getting under 8ms consistently after just a couple of days writing CUDA felt pretty incredible for a learning exercise. We're not even utilizing TF32 and Tensor Cores yet, so it's not really a fair comparison by any means. There's definitely room to push sub-1ms with more advanced optimizations.

This is basic CUDA territory, but every optimization taught me something new and deep.🔥

#CUDA #GPU #HighPerformanceComputing #Optimization #Nvidia

author: Leonie Monigatti
subtitle: Sr. Developer Advocate @ Elastic | I help devs build search agents
content:
A quick mental model for choosing the right loss function when fine-tuning an embedding model:

𝟭. 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 (𝗲.𝗴., 𝗶𝗻 𝗤𝗔 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀)
MultipleNegativesRankingLoss

𝟮. 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗿/𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗿)
TripletLoss

author: Val Andrei Fajardo
subtitle: AI Engineering & Research Lead @ Carlyle | Manning Author | Ex LlamaIndex | PhD UWaterloo
content:
🚀 Very Excited to Introduce FedRAG!

Today, I'm pleased to share my latest open-source project that I have been working on since joining Vector Institute this past January.

FedRAG is a framework for fine-tuning RAG systems. It endeavours to simplify the fine-tuning of RAG systems across centralized (i.e typical) as well as federated architectures.

⬢ Why RAG Fine-tuning?
Most existing popular frameworks, including LlamaIndex, focus mainly on RAG inference rather than training or full-fledged fine-tuning. FedRAG aims to fill this gap. Yet, there has been recent work that demonstrated improved performance of RAG systems post fine-tuning (e.g., see RA-DIT by Lin, Xi Victoria et al. (2023)—we've implemented RA-DIT in FedRAG!).

⬢ Why Federated Learning?
Inspired by the emerging decentralized trends such as Anthropic's MCP, and Google's A2A, we decided to incorporate federated learning in anticipation of the need to train on distributed datasets.

⬢ Brief Summary
FedRAG is PyTorch native, meaning that retriever and generator models are ~torch.Modules and you can fine-tune with ~torch.Datasets and ~torch.DataLoaders

With that being said, FedRAG also works well with Hugging Face's ecosystem. Meaning you can use any ~PreTrainedModel or ~PeftModel as the generator and ~SentenceTransformer as the retriever.

Integrations to other core tooling in the RAG ecosystem also exist! You can use Qdrant as your storage solution for the RAG's knowledge store. And, after fine-tuning you can bridge the RAG system to a LlamaIndex ~ManagedIndex to leverage their powerful features and ecosystem.

Finally, for federation, we use `flwr` (Flower Labs) as our federated learning backend. With FedRAG, converting centralized training tasks to federated ones can be done with a simple `.get_federated_task()` method call.

Learn more about FedRAG in our blog post: https://lnkd.in/e9_PJVHh

⬢ A Final Note
This is very much a v0.0.x release — we're just getting started and would love your thoughts, feedback, and contributions as we build this tool together!

author: Reuven Cohen
subtitle: ♾️ Agentic Engineer / CAiO @ Cognitum One
content:
Introducing FACT: Fast Augmented Context Tools (3.2x faster, 90% cost reduction vs RAG) 

RAG had its run, but it’s not built for agentic systems. Vectors are fuzzy, slow, and blind to context. They work fine for static data, but once you enter recursive, real-time workflows, where agents need to reason, act, and reflect. RAG collapses under its own ambiguity.

That’s why I built FACT: Fast Augmented Context Tools. 

Traditional Approach:
User Query → Database → Processing → Response (2-5 seconds)

FACT Approach:
User Query → Intelligent Cache → [If Miss] → Optimized Processing → Response (50ms)

It replaces vector search in RAG pipelines with a combination of intelligent prompt caching and deterministic tool execution via MCP. Instead of guessing which chunk is relevant, FACT explicitly retrieves structured data, SQL queries, live APIs, internal tools, then intelligently caches the result if it’s useful downstream.

The prompt caching isn’t just basic storage. 

It’s intelligent using the prompt cache from Anthropic and other LLM providers, tuned for feedback-driven loops: static elements get reused, transient ones expire, and the system adapts in real time. Some things you always want cached, schemas, domain prompts. Others, like live data, need freshness. Traditional RAG is particularly bad at this. Ask anyone force to frequently update vector DBs. 

I'm also using Arcade.dev to handle secure, scalable execution across both local and cloud environments, giving FACT hybrid intelligence for complex pipelines and automatic tool selection.

If you're building serious agents, skip the embeddings. RAG is a workaround. FACT is a foundation. It’s cheaper, faster, and designed for how agents actually work: with tools, memory, and intent.

To get started point your favorite coding agent at: https://lnkd.in/gek_akem

author: Vinija Jain
subtitle: ML Leadership @ Google | Ex-Meta, Amazon, Oracle, PANW | Stanford AI | EMNLP Outstanding Paper Award Recipient
content:
🧐 Multimodal with just fine-tuning? ByteDance makes it happen with VoRA.

The new Vision as LoRA (VoRA) paper introduces a bold, streamlined approach to building multimodal LLMs—no vision encoder, no connector, no architecture bloat. Just LoRA.

Instead of bolting a vision tower onto an LLM, VoRA injects vision understanding directly into the LLM using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). That means:

🔹 No new inference overhead- LoRA layers are merged into the LLM after training.
🔹 Frozen base LLM- Only LoRA + visual embeddings (~6M params) are trained, preserving language ability and ensuring stability.
🔹 Image inputs at native resolution- No resizing, no tiling hacks—VoRA leverages the LLM’s flexible token handling.
🔹 Bidirectional attention for vision- Instead of using causal masks across all tokens, VoRA allows vision tokens to attend freely—boosting context modeling.

To teach the LLM visual features:
🔹 VoRA uses block-wise distillation from a pretrained ViT, aligning intermediate hidden states across layers. This improves visual alignment while keeping the LLM’s core untouched.
🔹 The training objective combines distillation loss (cosine similarity between ViT + LLM visual features) and standard language modeling loss over image-caption pairs.

What does this get you?
🔹 A modality-agnostic architecture ready for extension to audio, point clouds, and beyond.

This might be one of the most efficient takes yet on vision-language modeling. Excited to see how this evolves.

📄 Paper + Code: https://lnkd.in/gwZr33Vj 

Follow Aman Chadha and I for more updates!

author: Niels Rogge
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer at ML6 & Hugging Face
content:
TimesFM, the Time Series Foundation Model by Google is now available in the Hugging Face Transformers library!

TimesFM is very similar to a GPT model like ChatGPT, except it is trained to predict the next values in a time-series, as opposed to the next text token. The model is pre-trained on a large collection of time-series collected by Google. This involves both synthetic data as well as 100 billion actual time-points from various domains like Google Trends and Wikipedia Page views. 

After pre-training, we can use it to forecast new values of a given time-series, like predicting the value of temperature or sales values. This is called "zero-shot prediction" since we don't update the weights of the model, we just use it out-of-the-box for making predictions on new, unseen data, much like prompting a large language model (LLM) or vision-language model (VLM). Interestingly, the authors claim that it outperforms models like DeepAR which are explicitly trained on time-series.

The blog post linked below is a great explainer for knowing how TimesFM works. The idea is to "patchify" a time-series into smaller pieces which serve as the "tokens".

We've uploaded notebooks on both inference as well as fine-tuning on custom data.

author: Mary Newhauser
subtitle: Member of Technical Staff @ Fastino Labs
content:
Fine-tuning generative LLMs used to be a drag.

Then it got efficient.

Parameter Efficient Fine-tuning (PEFT) has played a huge role in this. PEFT techniques allow you to train models for your specific needs without updating or retraining the entire model from scratch.

So what are the main benefits of PEFT?
✅ Less computational costs: fine-tuning PEFT approaches can make training models easier for a wide variety of hardware limitations and requirements.
✅ Better memory usage because all pretrained parameters frozen, and only new adaptor weights are trained.
✅ Avoids catastrophic forgetting: Freezing pretrained parameters means that knowledge is not forgotten when updating new weights during fine-tuning.

Here are 3 examples of common PEFT techniques:
• LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation): Freezes the original model weights and injects low-rank trainable matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture.
• Prefix Tuning: Optimizes a sequence of continuous task-specific vectors (the "prefix") prepended to the input, while keeping the language model parameters frozen.
• Prompt Tuning: Similar to prefix tuning, but optimizes continuous prompts added to the input text to guide the model towards the desired task.

Hugging Face's 🤗 PEFT library is the best open source resource out there for all things PEFT! Their developer guide on the docs page also has a great overview of various techniques.

author: Lysandre Debut
subtitle: COSO - Chief Open Source Officer at Hugging Face
content:
The Transformers library is undergoing it's largest pivot to date 🙌

It now cements its role as the central model definition, irrespective of the backend and runner. One ground truth to bring more reliability across the ecosystem.

This comes into play as Transformers becomes a backend of:

- most popular inference engines like vLLM, SGLang, TGI, TensorRT, ...
- training frameworks like Axolotl, Unsloth, DeepSpeed, FSDP, PyTorch-Lightning, ...
- and adjacent modeling libraries like llama.cpp, MLX, ONNX, ...

Transformers is the pivot across frameworks: if a model is integrated, then you're certain it is handled by the rest of the ecosystem. 

In a field where ML releases are more and more frequent, keeping track of integrations in all downstream libraries can become a headache.

By having Transformers as a backend, you get immediate access to all 300+ supported architectures, and you're ensured immediate access to upcoming model releases.

This often means day-0 access, but also community-fixes, and a shared baseline for evaluation.

This means that we'll strive to continuously improve Transformers so that:

-  Integrations are simpler & faster
- Models continue being adaptable, customizable
- Model definitions remain simple, easily augmented by downstream libraries.

Read more about it in the following blog post: https://lnkd.in/eQjmcWxF

author: Mary Newhauser
subtitle: Member of Technical Staff @ Fastino Labs
content:
Are we “over” pre-trained LLMs? I don’t know.

But if you’re not fine-tuning, you’ll be left behind. This fine-tuning guide is my best arXiv find this year. 🥹

The Ultimate Guide to Fine-Tuning LLMs takes you from data preparation all the way to monitoring and maintenance. It also explains over 14 individual fine-tuning techniques, including Mixture of Agents, half fine-tuning, pruning, and PEFT methods.

And in case you don’t want to read the whole guide, I’ve summarized some of them here (insanely simplified due to character limits!):

🎯 Task-Specific Fine-Tuning: Adapts a pre-trained LLM for a specific task by training on relevant data.

📚 Domain-Specific Fine-Tuning: Tailors a LLM to understand and generate text in a specialized field by training on domain-specific data.

🤏 Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT): Adapts LLMs by only training a small subset of (additional) parameters.

🧊 Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA): Freezes original weights and applies changes via low-rank matrices.

4️⃣ QLoRA: LoRA extension that uses 4-bit quantization for better memory efficiency.

🧭 Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA): Fine-tunes models by decomposing weight updates into magnitude and direction, applying LoRA to the latter to achieve full fine-tuning performance.

🌓 Half Fine-Tuning (HFT): balances knowledge retention and new learning by freezing half of an LLM's parameters per fine-tuning round.

🧠 Mixture of Experts (MoE): Combines outputs from specialized subnetworks ("experts") for computation.

🦙 Lamini Memory Tuning: Uses a Mixture of Experts (adapters) as individual memory banks to store specific information and reduce hallucinations.

🤖 Mixture of Agents (MoA): Combines outputs of multiple LLM agents (like MoE but with agents).

🛡️ Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO): Reinforcement learning method used to train agents to make optimal decisions through reward signals.

🗣️ Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO): Directly aligns LLMs with human preferences using a classification objective on preferred and rejected responses.

✂️ Pruning: Reduces LLM size and complexity by eliminating unnecessary components.

🔗 Full article here: https://lnkd.in/gab8d3Z2

Also, I'm making a list of open source libraries that leverage these methods, so if you can recommend one, drop it in the comments!

author: Aditya Naganath
subtitle: Partner at Kleiner Perkins
content:
As agentic products hit the market, sharing some early observations:

1. They're much harder to build than traditional software. 

a) We're asking these products to solve dynamic search problems in enterprise environments, under real-world but hard to encode constraints. And they must do so fast - humans can tolerate latency from other humans, but not from software. 

b) In other words -  Given a task P, a corpus of raw data D, and a family of tools T = {t1, t2..., tn}, the agent must learn an optimal policy that yields an accurate permutation of tool invocations over D to complete task P. 

This isn’t trivial. The system must reason over:

- What tools to use (retrieval, summarization, log search, graph traversal…)
- How to compose them into multi-hop workflows with intelligent backtracking. 
- How to coordinate multiple agents that each have different permissions within T, and thus differing implicit context over D, from each other. 
- When to stop — without hallucinating or looping. Remember, this is particularly hard when you don't have an explicit reward function upfront to optimize against. 

2. To be viable in production, these agents must be fast.

- You need a semantic cache. One that persists a global map of P -> {ta, tb...., tk} for every validated piece of work performed by the system. This avoids forcing the system to reason from first principles for every incremental task, especially those inside our posterior distribution. In fact, a semantic cache could even store successful sub-paths, but this gets complicated fast. 
- You need a clever way of shrinking the search space, D, to something smaller that is not very lossy. Especially useful when D can be PB / TB scale.
- We need "async-await" and durable execution for agents. I've heard OpenAI's Codex (recent launch) leverages Temporal. 
- You need to have agents broadcasting work to each other, especially when some agents have different ACLs than others and context sharing is critical. 

3. Pricing is tricky because not all units of work are equal.

Some tasks are low-value and low-risk. Others (e.g. “diagnose the root cause of a multi-region outage” or “triage a lateral movement alert”) are high-value, high-risk (a wrong conclusion is costly) and harder to get right.

Most usage-based pricing models treat these as equivalent and don’t account for outcome value. Startups need to figure out how to price units of work - either on a case by case basis (tricky to communicate to the buyer) or on a basis that accurately mirrors the expected value delivered across various scenarios.

author: Rahul Agarwal
subtitle: Staff ML Engineer | Meta, Roku, Walmart | 1:1 @ topmate.io/MLwhiz
content:
Few Lessons from Deploying and Using LLMs in Production

Deploying LLMs can feel like hiring a hyperactive genius intern—they dazzle users while potentially draining your API budget. Here are some insights I’ve gathered:

1. “Cheap” is a Lie You Tell Yourself: Cloud costs per call may seem low, but the overall expense of an LLM-based system can skyrocket.

Fixes: 
- Cache repetitive queries: Users ask the same thing at least 100x/day
- Gatekeep: Use cheap classifiers (BERT) to filter “easy” requests. Let LLMs handle only the complex 10% and your current systems handle the remaining 90%.
- Quantize your models: Shrink LLMs to run on cheaper hardware without massive accuracy drops
- Asynchronously build your caches — Pre-generate common responses before they’re requested or gracefully fail the first time a query comes and cache for the next time.

2. Guard Against Model Hallucinations: Sometimes, models express answers with such confidence that distinguishing fact from fiction becomes challenging, even for human reviewers.

Fixes: 
- Use RAG - Just a fancy way of saying to provide your model the knowledge it requires in the prompt itself by querying some database based on semantic matches with the query. 
- Guardrails: Validate outputs using regex or cross-encoders to establish a clear decision boundary between the query and the LLM’s response.

3. The best LLM is often a discriminative model: You don’t always need a full LLM. Consider knowledge distillation: use a large LLM to label your data and then train a smaller, discriminative model that performs similarly at a much lower cost.

4. It's not about the model, it is about the data on which it is trained: A smaller LLM might struggle with specialized domain data—that’s normal. Fine-tune your model on your specific data set by starting with parameter-efficient methods (like LoRA or Adapters) and using synthetic data generation to bootstrap training.

5. Prompts are the new Features: Prompts are the new features in your system. Version them, run A/B tests, and continuously refine using online experiments. Consider bandit algorithms to automatically promote the best-performing variants.

What do you think? Have I missed anything? I’d love to hear your “I survived LLM prod” stories in the comments!

author: Sai Meghana Yerramsetty
subtitle: SDE @Amazon
content:
🚀 I Built a Transformer from Scratch Using Just CUDA & Numba
(No PyTorch. No TensorFlow)

I just finished implementing a fully GPU-accelerated Transformer encoder block from first principles. Here’s why I did it—and what I learned:

I’ve trained LLMs, fine-tuned BERT, and deployed attention models. But I realized:
- What do queries, keys, and values actually do in memory?
- Why softmax? Why LayerNorm?
- How does attention really work?

So I dug in.

1. Ground Zero:
    - Started with 3Blue1Brown’s visual explanations
    - Reverse-engineered "Attention Is All You Need" (paper)
    - Studied Karpathy’s nanoGPT and Jay Alammar’s Illustrated Transformer

2. CUDA Deep Dive: 
    - Learned CUDA from scratch: threads, blocks, shared memory
    - Wrote custom kernels for:
            Matrix multiplication (naive → tiled optimization)
            Softmax (with numerical stability tricks)
            LayerNorm (mean/variance per token)

Hardest part? Debugging GPU kernels (printf debugging doesn’t work here!)

3. Parallel Attention Heads
    - Each head gets its own Q, K, V projections
    - Processes sequences independently in GPU threads
    - Custom CUDA kernel for scaled dot-product attention

4. Positional Encoding Revelation
Unlike RNNs:
    - No recurrence → needed positional awareness
    - Implemented sinusoidal encoding in pure NumPy
    - Discovered the beauty of frequency-based positioning

5. Stabilizing the Model
Every sublayer gets:
    - Residual Connections (input + output)
    - LayerNorm (custom CUDA kernel)
    - ReLU (hand-written GPU implementation)

Next Steps - Building the decoder block

Full code for the Encoder Block is on GitHub - https://lnkd.in/gDEyyMu6

🗣️ LLaMA-style language decoder

author: Abhishek Divekar
subtitle: Sr. Applied Scientist @Amazon (9+ YoE) || Published in AAAI, EMNLP || MSCS UT Austin || AI Olympiad Coach, Team India 2025
content:
When I interview ML Scientists, I check for depth over rote memorization.

Testing obscure theory a candidate hasn't touched in 5+ years ago is, at best, a weak indicator of success. 
Instead, I start with the interviewee's most recent flagship project or paper; work that spanned several months. From there, I start digging. I ask questions about low-level details, then gradually widen the scope to more general theory that naturally connects to their project.

I often ask them to write a common equation (convexity condition, attention mechanism, etc.) and explain each term; it's an effective way to separate fresh-from-bootcamp grads from serious practitioners.

The goal is always to gauge depth of understanding. ML has evolved into a largely "automated" discipline, where developers can obtain decent results using simple APIs.

An ML Scientist, however, often operates at the frontier of what's possible; they need both the skill and the inclination to dive deep into a problem and emerge with a solution that can bring 10x impact.

subtitle: I teach AI Agents and Lead Gen | Lead Gen Man(than) | 100K+ students
content:
Agentic Architectures are the hottest thing under the sun right now. 

And you're still confused which Agentic Architecture to choose?

Simply put, Agentic Architectures are a 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 via a 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗰𝗵.

What this means for 𝘺𝘰𝘶:
You can now build a 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 using multiple agents organized in patterns that fit your specific needs.

Agentic Architectures are organizational frameworks, allowing AI systems to efficiently distribute workloads, share knowledge, and combine specialized capabilities. No more one-size-fits-all approaches!

Let's understand first Single Agent System and Multi-Agent System. Each approach has distinct advantages:

Single-Agent System:
- 𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 with one AI agent connecting directly to tools & memory
- 𝗟𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 without inter-agent communication overhead
- 𝗘𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 with fewer components to integrate
- 𝗜𝗱𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝗿 focused, domain-specific tasks with clear boundaries

Multi-Agent System:
- 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 across specialized AI agents
- 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 that can grow with complexity
- 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗹 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 for improved performance on complex tasks
- 𝗜𝗱𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝗿 cross-domain problems requiring multiple types of expertise

Multi-agent systems are more implementable as they allow for custom architectures, distributed workloads, tailored precisely to your problem's complexity.

Multi-Agent System Patterns
1️⃣ Parallel: Multiple agents process simultaneously for maximum speed and throughput.

2️⃣ Sequential: Agents work in sequence, each refining previous outputs for complex tasks.

3️⃣ Loop: Circular flow enables iterative improvement until desired quality is reached.

4️⃣ Router: One agent directs inputs to specialized paths based on content analysis.

5️⃣ Aggregator: Consolidates multiple inputs into comprehensive unified outputs.

6️⃣ Network: Interconnected agents share knowledge bidirectionally for complex reasoning.

7️⃣ Hierarchical: Manager-worker structure handles complexity through delegated subtasks.

Multi-agent systems win because you can mix-and-match patterns to solve exactly your problem.

Agentic Architecture examples:
1️⃣ Hierarchical: Parent-child agent delegation with clear authority flows

2️⃣ Human-in-the-loop: AI systems with human oversight at critical points

3️⃣ Shared tools: Multiple agents accessing common resources efficiently

4️⃣ Sequential: Agents working in chain order, each building on previous outputs

5️⃣ Database with tools: Centralized knowledge with specialized access methods

6️⃣ Memory transformation using tool: Raw data conversion into structured AI memory

Over to you: Which agentic architecture pattern you like?

content:

I stopped jump-starting an ML project on a Jupyter when I realized:

❌ It discourages code reusability.
❌ It is difficult to do version control properly.

Now, I start an ML project by first setting up a project directory like this! ↓

↳ data/ # Your CSV and JSON files reside here
↳ notebook/ # Your ipynb files reside here
↳ src/ # Place your ML functions/objects in src
↳ tests/ # Unit tests your code in src
↳ main.py # Glues all the operations of training a model

✅ 𝗗𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝘁 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗯𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀. 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝗿𝗰!

Remember the key steps to modeling - extracting and preprocessing data, performing EDA, building features, training the model, and evaluating. Each step often involves custom code or wrappers on top of existing libs like Sklearn.

Modularize it in src/, then import it in notebooks and the main file.

✅ 𝗗𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝗽𝘂𝘀𝗵 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴.

Unit testing ensures that your code is reliable. It outputs what it's supposed to do. Whenever I submit a code change to production, I run Pytest to ensure nothing breaks!

author: Ed Collins
subtitle: Founding Machine Learning Engineer @ Fifth Dimension AI
content:
A good litmus test for whether an engineer has worked with AI in production systems is a simple question: how do you ensure safe JSON output?

If you’re using AI to make code-level decisions at runtime, you’ll need its conclusions in a machine-readable form. JSON is the most common of these.

But since LLMs are generative, they’re not guaranteed to output valid JSON, even when asked. You might get triple backticks. Single quotes instead of double. Unescaped characters. A friendly preamble before the JSON. A refusal to answer. Or the model might just ignore the instruction entirely. Something in the user’s prompt might throw it off. The list goes on.

Engineers who’ve worked with this in production know the edge cases - the strange behaviours, brittle responses, and unexpected failures. An inexperienced engineer might suggest “just ask for JSON” or “just use JSON mode”, but that’s not enough. We’ve seen invalid output from models even in JSON mode, and not all models support it anyway.

There are three techniques we’ve come to rely on that now work so well, we don’t even use JSON mode anymore: prefill, repair, and tenacity.

Prefill the assistant’s response with the opening of the JSON you want — this is by far the most reliable technique we’ve found.

Repair the output with a library like json-repair, handling common cases like XML wrappers or markdown fences.

Catch all parsing errors and retry with the same prompt using a library like tenacity. Because LLMs are non-deterministic, a second attempt will often succeed where the first didn’t.

We’ve been using this setup in production for over six months now. We haven’t seen a single JSON error in that time.

subtitle: Self-host your inference, save $$$, own your AI | xYouTube
content:
This paper is wild. 🤯

Stanford researchers found a very simple way to make any open LLM a strong reasoning model.

They did two key things:
1️⃣ Used just 1,000 carefully chosen reasoning examples for training
2️⃣ Added a "Wait" command when the model tries to stop thinking too early

Their results beat OpenAI's o1 model on math tests by up to 27%.

The approach is also cheap and fast:
▪️ it took only 26 minutes of training
▪️ and cost less than $30.

This shows that making AI better at reasoning doesn't need complex methods or huge datasets. Simple tricks can work remarkably well.

author: Aurimas Griciūnas
subtitle: Founder @ SwirlAI • Ex-CPO @ neptune.ai (Acquired by OpenAI) • UpSkilling the Next Generation of AI Talent • Author of SwirlAI Newsletter • Public Speaker
content:
𝗠𝗖𝗣 𝘃𝘀. 𝗔𝟮𝗔

Two days ago Google announced an open A2A (Agent2Agent) protocol in an attempt to normalise how we implement multi-Agent system communication.

As always, social media is going crazy about it, but why?

Let’s review the differences and how both protocols complement each other (read till the end).

𝘔𝘰𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘱𝘪𝘦𝘤𝘦𝘴 𝘪𝘯 𝘔𝘊𝘗:

𝟭. MCP Host - Programs using LLMs at the core that want to access data through MCP.

❗️ When combined with A2A, an Agent becomes MCP Host.

𝟮. MCP Client - Clients that maintain 1:1 connections with servers.
𝟯. MCP Server - Lightweight programs that each expose specific capabilities through the standardized Model Context Protocol.
𝟰. Local Data Sources - Your computer’s files, databases, and services that MCP servers can securely access.
𝟱. Remote Data Sources - External systems available over the internet (e.g., through APIs) that MCP servers can connect to.

𝘌𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘈2𝘈:

Where MCP falls short, A2A tries to help. In multi-Agent applications where state is not necessarily shared

𝟲. Agents (MCP Hosts) would implement and communicate via A2A protocol, that enables:

➡️ Secure Collaboration - MCP lacks authentication.
➡️ Task and State Management.
➡️ User Experience Negotiation.
➡️ Capability discovery - similar to MCP tools.

𝗛𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀:

❗️ I believe creators of MCP were planning to implement similar capabilities to A2A and expose agents via tools in long term.
❗️ We might just see a fight around who will win and become the standard protocol long term as both protocols might be expanding.

Let me know your thoughts in the comments. 👇

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
💭 Dream-7B: Don't sleep on diffusion language models

I've wanted to talk about it for a while, but I was waiting for the model weights. Diffusion models are exciting because they refine the entire text sequence in parallel rather than generating tokens sequentially.

The authors claim that Dream 7B matches or exceeds similar-sized autoregressive models on general, math, and coding tasks. They used a smart initialization with an autoregressive model to accelerate training dramatically.

However, the model is not very impressive in practice. It fails to solve simple equations and feels quite confused (e.g., it told me it has been trained by "OpenAI 2").

I want to believe it, but diffusion language models are still way, way behind. This is also the case in terms of inference speed, where theoretical advantages are far from being realized, leading to sluggish answers.

It's still an interesting academic work with innovations in terms of dynamic noise levels, for example. Thanks to the authors for releasing the weights!

author: Andrés Marafioti
subtitle: Multimodal Research Lead @ Hugging Face | 10+ YOE in AI R&D
content:
Just read the 𝗤𝘄𝗲𝗻𝟮.𝟱-𝗢𝗺𝗻𝗶 technical report, and it's incredibly impressive. Here are some highlights:

Qwen2.5-Omni is a unified end-to-end multimodal model that can understand and generate text, images, audio, and video—providing both text and natural speech responses in real-time.

At its heart lies the innovative 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗲𝗿-𝗧𝗮𝗹𝗸𝗲𝗿 architecture:

𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗲𝗿: A large language model that processes multimodal inputs and generates textual responses.
𝗧𝗮𝗹𝗸𝗲𝗿: An autoregressive speech decoder that converts Thinker's representations into real-time speech tokens.

Key technical details:

𝗔𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗼 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴: Converts audio into 128-channel mel-spectrograms (16kHz, 25ms window, 10ms hop), encoded via a modified Whisper model. Audio is processed in 2-second blocks using streaming-compatible attention to minimize latency.
𝗩𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗼 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴: Uses a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder with dynamic frame sampling, treating each frame like an image. Synchronization with audio is achieved using TMRoPE (Time-aligned Multimodal RoPE), a novel positional embedding method aligning temporal, height, and width axes across all modalities.
𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗼 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Utilizes a sliding-window DiT model along with a modified BigVGAN decoder, maintaining context-aware audio streaming through a receptive field of 2 lookback and 1 lookahead blocks.

Training was conducted in multiple stages, initially locking the language model and training the audio and vision encoders separately. Later stages integrated everything using diverse multimodal data, including sequences up to 32k tokens.
Post-training involved reinforcement learning to enhance Talker's stability and reduce hallucinations, alongside multi-speaker fine-tuning for improved prosody and natural speech quality.
The model achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks such as OmniBench and AV-Odyssey, excelling in tasks involving text, image, audio, and video modalities. Remarkably, end-to-end speech instruction following nearly matches text-based instruction performance—a significant achievement.
Overall, Qwen2.5-Omni is a highly ambitious and elegantly integrated multimodal model. The Thinker-Talker separation and TMRoPE positional embedding provide innovative solutions to challenging problems in multimodal understanding and generation.
However, I'd love to see more detailed ablation studies and experimental validations for some architectural choices. Empirical evidence would further strengthen the impressive claims made.

Major congratulations to the Qwen team. Qwen2.5-Omni marks a substantial step forward for real-time, unified multimodal AI assistants.

author: Andrés Marafioti
subtitle: Multimodal Research Lead @ Hugging Face | 10+ YOE in AI R&D
content:
Today, we share the tech report for 𝗦𝗺𝗼𝗹𝗩𝗟𝗠: 𝗥𝗲𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀. 
🔥 Explaining how to create a 𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘆 𝟮𝟱𝟲𝗠 𝗩𝗟𝗠 that uses less than 1GB of RAM and outperforms our 80B models from 18 months ago! 

Here are the coolest insights from our experiments:
✨ Longer context = Big wins: Increasing the context length from 2K to 16K gave our tiny VLMs a 60% performance boost!
✨ Smaller is smarter with SigLIP: Surprise! Smaller LLMs didn't benefit from the usual large SigLIP (400M). Instead, we use the 80M base SigLIP that performs equally well at just 20% of the original size!
✨ Pixel shuffling magic: Aggressively pixel shuffling helped our compact VLMs "see" better, achieving the same performance with sequences 16x shorter!
✨ Learned positional tokens FTW: For compact models, learned positional tokens significantly outperform raw text tokens, enhancing efficiency and accuracy.
✨ System prompts and special tokens are key: Introducing system prompts and dedicated media intro/outro tokens significantly boosted our compact VLM’s performance—especially for video tasks.
✨ Less CoT, more efficiency: Turns out, too much Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data actually hurts performance in small models. They dumb
✨ Longer videos, better results: Increasing video length during training enhanced performance on both video and image tasks.

author: Abhishek Divekar
subtitle: Sr. Applied Scientist @Amazon (9+ YoE) || Published in AAAI, EMNLP || MSCS UT Austin || AI Olympiad Coach, Team India 2025
content:
When I give advice about ML Science interviews, I often stress just one thing: focus on demonstrating mathematical depth.
Too many people who work in AI (or study AI) have a 100-foot view of concepts but not a zero-foot view of them.
A good example is LLM decoding. In an interview, if I notice a candidate has worked on LLMs (so, 50% of people nowadays), I will ask which decoding strategy they have used (usually greedy, top-p or top-k). Then, I will give them a vocabulary of next-token logits predicted by an LLM, and ask them to walk me through the mathematical computation which goes on for top-p vs top-k decoding, and write the equation for each.
Many candidates fail this, or take super long (>10 mins is long for this question). The interview inevitably goes south from there...as an interviewer, I don't have much confidence in a candidate who can't explain a concept they have supposedly worked on for multiple months.
On the flipside, great candidates can reproduce equations (and know the purpose of each piece) and intelligently discuss alternative approaches. I will often vouch for these candidates. Ultimately, I want to work with people who demonstrate expertise, since I will never be an expert in everything. There are colleagues I can learn from and who will complement any team they join.
Work on developing a "zero-foot" view.

content:
Steal my recipe on how I hyperparameter tune my models👇

I often see that tuning model params provide a 1-10% lift in the model performance.

Here are 3 strategies I employ:

𝗧𝗶𝗽 𝟭 - 𝗦𝗽𝗹𝗶𝘁 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻-𝘃𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗱-𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘀

Don't train an ML model on the train set then tune model parameters on the test set. The test set is only for final evaluation. Instead, tune the params on a validation set, then evaluate on the test set.

𝗧𝗶𝗽 𝟮 - 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗵 

When tuning tree-based models like the Random Forest or XGBoost, I find that tree-size and depth usually bring the biggest gains in performance. All other parameters tend to be marginal.

𝗧𝗶𝗽 𝟯 - 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗥𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗺 𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗼𝗿 𝗕𝗮𝘆𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Unless the parameter search space is small, don't bother with grid search. It takes too long. Use Random Search or Bayesian Optimization. Personally, I use HyperOpt for Bayesian tuning.

🚀 MCPs are exploding. Here’s a small proof point: a few weeks ago, I quietly published a crate we use internally at LangDB — async-mcp(https://lnkd.in/dZCTnfzm), a Rust implementation of the Model Context Protocol (MCP). No launch post, no tweets. And yet... 3,700+ downloads in just a few weeks.
This crate is an unofficial implementation of MCP, built async-first using Tokio (a vibed-out fork of an earlier repo we credited in the README). We implemented several transports, including an in-memory transport using channels that powers some of our internal workflows. 

Up next: support for the authorization spec (https://lnkd.in/du8gRX5r), which we believe is a game-changer for trusted agent infra.

🦀 Why Rust?
- Official implementations are mostly in JS/TS.
- We love Rust.
- MCP is to LLM agents what HTTP was to the web. We wanted efficiency, safety, and control at the systems level — Rust gives us that.

🧠 How LangDB Uses MCP
LangDB connects to MCP servers at the AI Gateway level. That means you can offload fallback logic, tool execution orchestration, and more to the gateway, powered by virtual models and workflows just by using open AI compatible APIs or ofcourse just like another MCP. content:
Uber used RAG and AI agents to build its in-house Text-to-SQL, saving 140,000 hours annually in query writing time. 📈
Here’s how they built the system end-to-end:

The system is called QueryGPT and is built on top of multiple agents each handling a part of the pipeline.

1. First, the Intent Agent interprets user intent and figures out the domain workspace which is relevant to answer the question (e.g., Mobility, Billing, etc).

2. The Table Agent then selects suitable tables using an LLM, which users can also review and adjust.

3. Next, the Column Prune Agent filters out any unnecessary columns from large tables using RAG. This helps the schema fit within token limits.

4. Finally, QueryGPT uses Few-Shot Prompting with selected SQL samples and schemas to generate the query.

QueryGPT reduced query authoring time from 10 minutes to 3, saving over 140,000 hours annually!

Multi-agent system (MAS) are agents that interact, communicate, and collaborate to achieve a shared goal, which would to be difficult or unreliable for a single agent to accomplish.

Benchmark:
- Selected five popular, open-source MAS (MetaGPT, ChatDev, HyperAgent, AppWorld, AG2)
- Chose tasks representative of the MAS intended capabilities (Software D Development, SWE-Bench Lite, Utility Service Tasks, GSM-Plus) total of 150 tasks
- Recorded the complete conversation logs, human annotators reviews, Cohen's Kappa score to ensure consistency and reliability, LLM-as-a-Judge Validation


Multi Agent Failure modes: 
1. Disobey Task Spec: Ignores task rules and requirements, leading to wrong output.
2. Disobey Role Spec: Agent acts outside its defined role and responsibilities.
3. Step Repetition: Unnecessarily repeats steps already completed, causing delays.
4. Loss of History: Forgets previous conversation context, causing incoherence.
5. Unaware Stop: Fails to recognize task completion, continues unnecessarily.
6. Conversation Reset: Dialogue unexpectedly restarts, losing context and progress.
7. Fail Clarify: Does not ask for needed information when unclear.
8. Task Derailment: Gradually drifts away from the intended task objective.
9. Withholding Info: Agent does not share important, relevant information.
10. Ignore Input: Disregards or insufficiently considers input from others.
11. Reasoning Mismatch: Actions do not logically follow from stated reasoning.
12. Premature Stop: Ends task too early before completion or information exchange.
13. No Verification: Lacks mechanisms to check or confirm task outcomes.
14. Incorrect Verification: Verification process is flawed, misses critical errors.



How to improve Multi-Agent LLM System:
📝 Define tasks and agent roles clearly and explicitly in prompts.
🎯 Use examples in prompts to clarify expected task and role behavior.
🗣️ Design structured conversation flows to guide agent interactions.
✅ Implement self-verification steps in prompts for agents to check their reasoning.
🧩 Design modular agents with specific, well-defined roles for simpler debugging.
🔄 Redesign topology to incorporate verification roles and iterative refinement processes.
🤝 Implement cross-verification mechanisms for agents to validate each other.
❓ Design agents to proactively ask for clarification when needed.
📜 Define structured conversation patterns and termination conditions.

author: Aritra Roy Gosthipaty
subtitle: MLE @ 🤗 Hugging Face
content:
Bringing Efficiency to LLMs with Fine-Tuning

LayerSkip, introduced in the 2024 paper by Mostafa Elhoushi et al. (arXiv:2404.16710), is a brilliant technique to accelerate large language model (LLM) inference without compromising accuracy.

By training models with layer dropout and early exit loss, LayerSkip enables early exits during inference and leverages self-speculative decoding—using the same model to draft and verify tokens.

This cuts latency, reduces memory usage, and delivers massive throughput gains. So why hasn’t LayerSkip taken off immediately in the community? The catch lies in its original design: it requires pre-training a model from scratch with LayerSkip’s methodology.

Pre-training is computationally expensive and impractical for many, which likely slowed its adoption despite its cleverness.

That’s where our work comes in. I teamed up with Mostafa Elhoushi, to integrate it with Hugging Face's TRL library—specifically the SFTTrainer.

Instead of pre-training, we’ve made it possible to fine-tune existing models with LayerSkip. This shift eliminates the heavy upfront cost while preserving the technique’s inference-time efficiency gains. Fine-tuning is faster, cheaper, and more accessible, opening the door for broader experimentation and adoption.

We’ve released this research project under TRL at https://lnkd.in/gbBQwWfv

Our goal? To empower the community to train their own LayerSkip-enhanced models and share feedback. Want adapters or other features? Let us know—we’re all ears.

The Magic Behind PyTorch’s Backprop: Automatic Differentiation

Ever wondered how PyTorch computes gradients so efficiently? 🤔 The secret lies in automatic differentiation! 🚀

⚙️ What is Automatic Differentiation? 

When computing derivatives, there are three main approaches:

📏 Numerical Differentiation: Uses finite differences to approximate derivatives
🧮 Symbolic Differentiation: The process you learn in calculus, where mathematical expressions are manipulated algebraically (similar to how it’s done in SymPy).
⚡ Automatic Differentiation: Tracks operations, builds a computational graph, and applies the chain rule 

💡 Types of Automatic Differentiation: 

🔹 Forward Mode: Computes derivatives from inside to outside
🔹 Reverse Mode: Computes function outputs first, then backpropagates gradients from outside to inside
