author: Weaviate
subtitle: 58K followers
content:
The secret to more accurate AI retrieval isn't bigger models.

It's smarter vector representations that preserve context.

But what makes multi-vector models unique? How do they differ from traditional models, and why are they gaining traction?

𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀

• Project entire queries, documents or images into single vectors.
• Each entire item is compressed into 𝘢 𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘨𝘭𝘦 𝘱𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘵 in a vector space.
• While efficient for fast retrieval, they can oversimplify complex data structures, especially in contextually rich documents.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗩𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗰𝗵

• Break down queries, documents or images into 𝘮𝘶𝘭𝘵𝘪𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘴𝘮𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘳 𝘷𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘴, for each token or image patch.
• This allows for more granular and nuanced matching between queries and documents/images.
• Token or patch embeddings are compared later, via 𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯.

𝗟𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

• Each query vector is compared against all document/image patch vector via a similarity score.
• The highest similarity is recorded (MaxSim), so the most relevant comparisons are saved.
• All of these highest similarity scores are added together to form the final score.

Late interaction ensures that the model captures more detailed relationships between the query and the data.

🟢 The model can zero in on specific parts of a document that are most relevant to the query.

🟢 Contextual dependencies can be captured by token/patch level embeddings, enabling more nuanced query/document relationships.

🔴 Requires storing a vector for each token or patch in the database.

ColBERT is a multi-vector model for text, whereas models like ColPali and ColQwen extended this approach for images and more complex documents like PDFs - and can understand text and images within documents via an OCR-style approach, using vision language models instead of regular language models.

Learn more about multi-vector models in Weaviate: https://lnkd.in/dSHqVjys

author: Andrés Marafioti
subtitle: Multimodal Research Lead @ Hugging Face | 10+ YOE in AI R&D
content:
VLMs connect a vision encoder to a language model using a linear layer—meaning each visual feature becomes one token.

To reduce the number of tokens, SmolVLM and SmolDocling use pixel shuffle—but how does it work?

🔄 Pixel shuffle rearranges the encoded image, trading spatial resolution for channels. Instead of assigning one token per "pixel" feature, we merge features before tokenization, reducing sequence length while keeping information density high.

Instead of keeping a high-res grid like (64×64×1), we rearrange the information:
📏 (64×64×1) → (32×32×4) → (16×16×16) → (8×8×64)
Then, a linear layer merges this compacted representation into tokens before feeding them to the transformer.

Why does this matter?
✅ Fewer tokens → Faster inference & lower compute cost
✅ Local features get merged → More meaningful representations
✅ Memory-efficient → Great for on-device VLMs & multimodal AI

🚀 SmolVLM uses tricks like this to stay lightweight & efficient!

subtitle: Staff ML Engineer | Meta, Roku, Walmart | 1:1 @ topmate.io/MLwhiz
content:
Few Lessons from Deploying and Using LLMs in Production

Deploying LLMs can feel like hiring a hyperactive genius intern—they dazzle users while potentially draining your API budget. Here are some insights I’ve gathered:

1. “Cheap” is a Lie You Tell Yourself: Cloud costs per call may seem low, but the overall expense of an LLM-based system can skyrocket.

Fixes: 
- Cache repetitive queries: Users ask the same thing at least 100x/day
- Gatekeep: Use cheap classifiers (BERT) to filter “easy” requests. Let LLMs handle only the complex 10% and your current systems handle the remaining 90%.
- Quantize your models: Shrink LLMs to run on cheaper hardware without massive accuracy drops
- Asynchronously build your caches — Pre-generate common responses before they’re requested or gracefully fail the first time a query comes and cache for the next time.

2. Guard Against Model Hallucinations: Sometimes, models express answers with such confidence that distinguishing fact from fiction becomes challenging, even for human reviewers.

Fixes: 
- Use RAG - Just a fancy way of saying to provide your model the knowledge it requires in the prompt itself by querying some database based on semantic matches with the query. 
- Guardrails: Validate outputs using regex or cross-encoders to establish a clear decision boundary between the query and the LLM’s response.

3. The best LLM is often a discriminative model: You don’t always need a full LLM. Consider knowledge distillation: use a large LLM to label your data and then train a smaller, discriminative model that performs similarly at a much lower cost.

4. It's not about the model, it is about the data on which it is trained: A smaller LLM might struggle with specialized domain data—that’s normal. Fine-tune your model on your specific data set by starting with parameter-efficient methods (like LoRA or Adapters) and using synthetic data generation to bootstrap training.

5. Prompts are the new Features: Prompts are the new features in your system. Version them, run A/B tests, and continuously refine using online experiments. Consider bandit algorithms to automatically promote the best-performing variants.

What do you think? Have I missed anything? I’d love to hear your “I survived LLM prod” stories in the comments!

author: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D.
subtitle: Research @ Netflix
content:
Many recent frontier LLMs like Grok-3 and DeepSeek-R1 use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. To learn how it works, let’s pretrain an MoE-based LLM from scratch in PyTorch…

nanoMoE is a simple (~500 lines of code) but functional implementation of a mid-sized MoE model that can be pretrained on commodity hardware in less than a week. This repository is based upon Andrej Karpathy’s nanoGPT, but has been modified to support MoE models. 

Expert layer: Most of the details for nanoMoE are implemented at the model architecture level. nanoMoE uses a decoder-only transformer architecture, but we have modified the feed-forward component of the architecture to use several (8) experts instead of a single feed-forward layer.

Each expert shares the same architecture as the original feed-forward neural net. We can implement these experts efficiently by computing their output in parallel via a batch matrix multiplication operation in PyTorch.

Routing: To determine which tokens go to which experts, we implement a linear routing mechanism, which is standard for MoEs. This mechanism takes the token vector as input and predicts the top K experts for this token along with their probabilities. Then, we can use the output of the router to construct fixed-size batches (based on expert capacity) for each expert. 

Auxiliary losses: To ensure that nanoMoE pretraining is stable and all experts are utilized, we use both the load balancing auxiliary loss (proposed by Switch transformer, encourages balanced utilization of experts instead of repeatedly using the same experts for every token) and the router z-loss (proposed by ST-MoE paper, avoids router logits become large and causing round-off errors). These standard auxiliary losses are widely used in the MoE literature. 

Best practices: Aside from using the auxiliary losses outlined above, we adopt a few other tricks to make sure that nanoMoE pretraining is stable:
- Properly tuning scaling factors for auxiliary losses vs. core language modeling loss.
- A special weight initialization scheme for MoEs proposed by the Switch Transformer.
- Always using full precision (float32) in the router.

For a full explanation of nanoMoE along with a reproducible implementation and all related experiments, check out the blog post or github repository (in image).

content:
Why are companies shifting towards the Agentic RAG approach?

They are prioritizing Agentic RAG over traditional retrieval approaches to build more autonomous and intelligent systems. 

Well, traditional RAG systems are constrained by static workflows and lack the adaptability required for multi-step reasoning and complex task management.

Agentic RAG represents an advanced approach that enhances traditional RAG systems by integrating intelligent agents capable of autonomous decision-making and multi-step reasoning. 

Unlike conventional RAG models that primarily utilize LLMs for straightforward question answering, Agentic RAG employs specialized agents to navigate complex queries requiring detailed analysis and planning. 

These agents function similarly to expert researchers, adeptly retrieving relevant information from multiple sources, comparing data, and synthesizing comprehensive responses. 

This dynamic approach allows for improved contextual understanding and adaptability, enabling the system to respond more effectively to diverse user needs. 

The architecture of Agentic RAG includes components such as an input layer for user queries, retrieval mechanisms that leverage various tools (like web searches and APIs), and a generation phase where coherent responses are crafted based on the retrieved information. 

By allowing agents to evaluate which tools to use and when to re-retrieve data, Agentic RAG significantly enhances the flexibility and efficiency of information retrieval processes. 

Moreover, it supports real-time adjustments based on user intent, making it particularly valuable in environments where understanding nuanced queries is essential. 

Applications of Agentic RAG span various fields, including research assistance, customer support, and knowledge management, where its ability to deliver precise and contextually relevant answers can greatly enhance productivity and decision-making. 

Overall, Agentic RAG marks a substantial evolution in AI technologies, transforming passive information retrieval into an active investigative process that leverages external knowledge for superior outcomes.

author: Leo (Leonid) Boytsov
subtitle: Machine learning scientist and engineer speaking πtorch & C++. Past AWS AI, Carnegie Mellon University. Opinions are sampled from my own 100 trillion parameter LM.
content:
It seems to me that several people have made this observation already. It is much easier to train R1 from new Qwen models compared to, e.g., old Llama ones. So, it's not just RL that makes a difference.

Moreover, it is a very interesting observation that without "natural" intermediate rewards, R1's RL is not much different from supervised fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories.

The way it works: Using a current model/policy we roll out the existing trajectory into the future and record whether it was successful or not. If none or few of these roll outs are successful, there is simply no signal to update the policy! So the quality of base model seems to be crucial for success.

At the same time, after obtaining N successful and M unsuccessful rollouts, updating the policy is just a classification problem (see a link in the comments).

"The real source of strength in R1 may thus be that (1) the base model has been pre-trained with enough intermediate token data on the relevant domains to provide k reasonable trajectories for each synthetic data problem such that at least some of them actually end up in solutions and (2) availability of the verifiers that provide strong reward signal--that can be used to push either an SFT or an iterative SFT/RL phase."

author: Maxime Labonne
subtitle: Head of Post-Training @ Liquid AI
content:
⚛️ Atom of Thoughts for Markov LLM Test-Time Scaling

AoT tackles an efficiency problem in LLM reasoning: models waste resources tracking extensive reasoning history, when only the current reasoning state matters for solving complex problems.

→ AoT introduces a Markov process approach to LLM reasoning where each state depends only on its immediate predecessor, eliminating the need to track complex historical dependencies throughout the reasoning process.

→ The framework decomposes questions into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure, then contracts subquestions into an independent atomic state, focusing computational resources on current reasoning rather than historical information.

→ AoT can function both as a standalone reasoning framework and as a plug-in enhancement for existing test-time scaling methods like Chain-of-Thought and Forest of Thoughts.

→ Experiments across six benchmarks showed significant performance improvements, especially in multi-hop reasoning tasks where AoT enabled gpt-4o-mini to outperform dedicated reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 by 10.6% on HotpotQA.

The Markov property implementation tackles a genuine bottleneck instead of just tweaking existing approaches. The theoretical foundation is solid, but it looks like a poor initial decomposition would lead to cascading errors.

Lost in all the GPU jargon? Let's simplify it!

Ordered from lowest-level (most control) to highest-level (most convenience):

🔍 𝙇𝙤𝙬-𝙇𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙡 (𝙈𝙖𝙭𝙞𝙢𝙪𝙢 𝘾𝙤𝙣𝙩𝙧𝙤𝙡)

🔹 PTX: NVIDIA's Parallel Thread Execution instruction set - the assembly language for CUDA GPUs.
🔹 CUDA: NVIDIA's base programming model. Write C++ kernels that execute directly on GPU hardware using thread blocks and shared memory.
🔹 HIP: AMD's portable C++ API that allows code to run on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs with minimal changes.

🔧 𝙈𝙞𝙙-𝙇𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙡 (𝘽𝙖𝙡𝙖𝙣𝙘𝙚 𝙤𝙛 𝘾𝙤𝙣𝙩𝙧𝙤𝙡/𝘾𝙤𝙣𝙫𝙚𝙣𝙞𝙚𝙣𝙘𝙚)

🔹 CUTLASS: NVIDIA's C++ template library for matrix operations with efficiently tiled implementations.
🔹 OpenCL: Cross-platform framework for heterogeneous computing across different hardware (cpu, gpu, ...).
🔹 Triton: OpenAI's Python DSL that compiles to efficient kernels with automatic tiling and optimizations.

⚡ 𝙃𝙞𝙜𝙝-𝙇𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙡 (𝙈𝙖𝙭𝙞𝙢𝙪𝙢 𝘾𝙤𝙣𝙫𝙚𝙣𝙞𝙚𝙣𝙘𝙚)

🔹 cuBLAS/cuDNN: Pre-optimized libraries for linear algebra and deep learning operations.
🔹 ROCm Libraries: AMD's optimized libraries (rocBLAS, MIOpen) equivalent to NVIDIA's offerings.
🔹 NCCL: NVIDIA's library for multi-GPU communication patterns in distributed training.
🔹 XLA: Google's accelerated linear algebra compiler for hardware-optimized operations.
🔹 TensorRT: NVIDIA's inference optimizer that fuses operations and quantizes for deployment.

The lower you go, the more control but higher complexity. The higher you go, the easier to use but less flexibility for custom optimizations.

author: Rahul Agarwal
subtitle: Staff ML Engineer | Meta, Roku, Walmart | 1:1 @ topmate.io/MLwhiz
content:
Few Lessons from Deploying and Using LLMs in Production

Deploying LLMs can feel like hiring a hyperactive genius intern—they dazzle users while potentially draining your API budget. Here are some insights I’ve gathered:

1. “Cheap” is a Lie You Tell Yourself: Cloud costs per call may seem low, but the overall expense of an LLM-based system can skyrocket.

Fixes: 
- Cache repetitive queries: Users ask the same thing at least 100x/day
- Gatekeep: Use cheap classifiers (BERT) to filter “easy” requests. Let LLMs handle only the complex 10% and your current systems handle the remaining 90%.
- Quantize your models: Shrink LLMs to run on cheaper hardware without massive accuracy drops
- Asynchronously build your caches — Pre-generate common responses before they’re requested or gracefully fail the first time a query comes and cache for the next time.

2. Guard Against Model Hallucinations: Sometimes, models express answers with such confidence that distinguishing fact from fiction becomes challenging, even for human reviewers.

Fixes: 
- Use RAG - Just a fancy way of saying to provide your model the knowledge it requires in the prompt itself by querying some database based on semantic matches with the query. 
- Guardrails: Validate outputs using regex or cross-encoders to establish a clear decision boundary between the query and the LLM’s response.

3. The best LLM is often a discriminative model: You don’t always need a full LLM. Consider knowledge distillation: use a large LLM to label your data and then train a smaller, discriminative model that performs similarly at a much lower cost.

4. It's not about the model, it is about the data on which it is trained: A smaller LLM might struggle with specialized domain data—that’s normal. Fine-tune your model on your specific data set by starting with parameter-efficient methods (like LoRA or Adapters) and using synthetic data generation to bootstrap training.

5. Prompts are the new Features: Prompts are the new features in your system. Version them, run A/B tests, and continuously refine using online experiments. Consider bandit algorithms to automatically promote the best-performing variants.

What do you think? Have I missed anything? I’d love to hear your “I survived LLM prod” stories in the comments!

Been playing with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) lately - it's this new standard for building AI tools that work with LLMs. Cool concept, but after a few days of tinkering, I decided to take a different route.

So what's MCP anyway?

MCP lets AI apps access your custom tools and data in a standardized way. You build a server that exposes:
- Data sources the AI can read
- Functions the AI can execute
- Template prompts for common tasks

It's pretty slick for AI apps that need to hook into your tools.

Why I built something different?

Don't get me wrong - MCP is interesting! But I kept hitting walls when building stuff I actually wanted to deploy:
- Premature ecosystem
- Not super friendly with cloud deployments
- Required learning a whole new protocol
- Felt over-engineered for many use cases

My alternative: A FastAPI Tools Server

Instead, I put together a FastAPI template for AI tools that's been working amazingly well for me:

- REST API foundation that works literally everywhere
- Simple decorator for exposing tools to AI systems
- Docker-ready for easy deployment
- Uses uv for crazy fast dependency management

The best part? I can focus on building cool AI tools instead of wrestling with protocol specs.

I'm sharing this template for anyone else building AI tools who wants something that "just works" today. Check it out at the link below.

author: Philipp Schmid
subtitle: AI Developer Experience at Google DeepMind 🔵 prev: Tech Lead at Hugging Face, AWS ML Hero 🤗 Sharing my own views and AI News
content:
After Matryoshka Embeddings comes Matryoshka Quantization. 👀 A quantization method from Google DeepMind that enables to train a single model that can be served at different integer precision levels (int8, int4, int2) achieving performance, achieving up to 10% improvement for 2-bit.

How Matryoshka Quantization (MatQuant) works, simplified: 
1️⃣ Start with a pre-trained model (e.g., Gemma 2) and choose quantization method (QAT or OmniQuant) 
2️⃣ Configure nested integer representations (int8 → int4 → int2) where lower bits are subsets of higher bits
3️⃣ Nested Quantization: Apply the base method (OmniQuant or QAT) to get the highest bit-width (e.g., int8) representation. 
4️⃣ Use a slicing operator to extract lower-precision weights (int4, int2) from the higher-precision representation by taking the most significant bits. 
5️⃣ Calculate a weighted loss that combines the losses for each target bit-width (int8, int4, int2). 
6️⃣ Optimize the model parameters (or auxiliary parameters for OmniQuant) using the combined multi-scale loss. 
7️⃣ Use the outputs of the higher-precision model (e.g., int8) to guide the training of the lower-precision models (e.g., int2). (Optional) 
8️⃣ During inference, dynamically mix'n'match layers with different precisions (e.g., some layers at int8, others at int4 or int2) for an optimal accuracy/cost trade-off.

Insights
💡 Single model can use multiple precision levels (8-bit to 2-bit) without retraining 
📈 Up to 10% accuracy improvement for int2 models compared to other methods 
🔄 Co-distillation from int8 to int2 provides additional 1.65% accuracy boost 
🎯 Mix'n'Match enables optimal accuracy-compute trade-offs 
🚀 Enables dynamic precision switching based on hardware constraints 
🔧 Works with both QAT and OmniQuant quantization approaches 
⚡ Int2 FFN-quantized Gemma-2 9B outperforms int8 FFN-quantized Gemma-2 2B

author: Pavel Iakubovskii
subtitle: ML Engineer, ex-Hugging Face | Kaggle Competitions Master | 20k+ stars on GitHub
content:
🔥 Small tweaks, massive speedup! I optimized a pose estimation pipeline and took it from 9 FPS → 47 FPS!

I used 🤗 Transformers with RT-DETR as the detector and ViTPose for keypoint detection. Initially, it ran at 117ms per frame (~9 FPS) on my GPU, too slow for real-time applications.

🔍 What is ViTPose, and why do we need a detector?
ViTPose is a top-down pose estimation model that works on cropped images of people rather than the full scene. It requires a detector like RT-DETR to first locate individuals before estimating their keypoints.
This top-down approach allows for multi-person pose estimation and typically yields higher accuracy. However, it can be computationally expensive when dealing with multiple people, as ViTPose needs to process each crop separately.

⚡ Optimizing the Pipeline
By applying 4 key optimizations, I achieved 22ms per frame (~47 FPS)! Here’s what made the difference:

✅ Lower precision (FP32 → BF16/FP16) for better hardware utilization.
✅ Optimizing the model with torch.compile, 🤗 Transformers models are already designed to avoid graph breaks, making them well-suited for compilation.
✅ Using the ‘fast’ image processor from 🤗 Transformers (torch-based instead of numpy-based).
✅ Rewriting preprocessing with `roi_align` for more efficient crop extraction and resizing.

Originally, I just wanted to squeeze out a little more speed, but I didn’t expect to 5x the FPS with just a few tweaks!

💡 Want to see the full pipeline? Check out the notebook (link in the first comment)!

author: Himanshu Bamoria
subtitle: Co-founder Gooseworks (Y Combinator W23)
content:
🚀 Implementing Self-Reflective RAG with OpenAI, LangGraph LangChain, and FAISS 

We published a ready-to-use Colab notebook and a step-by-step guide for Self-reflective RAG. 

Self-reflective RAG is an advanced RAG technique that uses an arbitrary LLM to adaptively retrieve documents on demand. ⚡️

Standard RAG has its limitations:
❌ Inefficient retrieval – It fetches documents for every query, even when unnecessary, leading to information overload and lower output quality.

❌ Irrelevant results – Not all retrieved documents are useful, and feeding irrelevant data to the LLM reduces response accuracy.

⚡️ Self-reflective RAG lets LLM decide whether retrieval is necessary for a query. If yes, it also guides the model on how to critically evaluate the retrieved information. 🎯

Self-reflection uses Reflection tokens that help take logical reasoning throughout the entire workflow. There are 4 types of reflection tokens: 

1️⃣ Retrieve
2️⃣ ISREL (is relevant)
3️⃣ ISSUP (is supported)
4️⃣ ISUSE (is useful)

Check out our detailed blog that explains the entire concept and Colab notebook in comments 👇

The only AI books that matter for production:

Core Infrastructure (Required):
1. "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" - Martin Kleppmann
Real talk: Your AI system is a data system. This is your bible.
Focus: Chapters 1-4 (fundamentals), 6 (partitioning), 10-11 (batch/stream)

2. "Fundamentals of Database Engineering" - Hussein Nasser
Why: Your vector DB will break. Fix it with this.
Key: Storage engines, indexing, transaction models

3. "Building Machine Learning Systems with Python" - Luis Pedro Coelho
Skip theory. Focus: Chapters on deployment, testing, monitoring

Production Engineering (Pick Based on Stack):

4. "Production Kubernetes" - Josh Rosso
If running containerized AI: This is mandatory.
Skip intro. Jump to: Scaling, monitoring, troubleshooting

5. "Building ML Pipelines" - Hannes Hapke
Actually useful. Focus on:
- Data validation
- Model monitoring
- Pipeline testing

Optional But Valuable:

6. "System Design Interview" - Alex Xu

• Academic papers without code
• Books without production focus

Read in this order:
1. Kleppmann (data systems)
2. Nasser (databases)
3. Stack-specific production book
4. Everything else when needed

➡️With the advent of OpenAI o1 and Deepseek, COT- a slow-thinking reasoning technique have been adapted widely.

1. Associative memory mechanism:

author: Richard Meng
subtitle: CEO @ Roe | Catching fin-crimes with vectors
content:
If this isn’t Deep Research, I don’t know what is. Here's how we systematically analyzed Uber’s historical product and service developments using over 600-pages+ SEC 8-K filings:

1. Start with SEC 8K filings PDFs with zero metadata.
2. Identify key metadata—such as the quarter and ticker symbol ($UBER)—strictly from the first two pages of each filing.
3. Find the pages relevant to the new product and services. We did not use a vector search here because it will not be for such an obscure query!
4. Summarize the pages from Step 3. into abstracts with O1 model. We generate 20 abstracts for $UBER, one abstract per filing.
5. Final step: Aggregate the abstracts from Step 4. Based on the ticker $UBER, we aggregated 20 abstracts from Uber into a 2000-word research report.

The entire process—from metadata extraction to insights generation—is strictly governed by SQL, ensuring full control over: Metadata management, File selection, Page selection.

This methodology guarantees complete transparency and verifiability, making every insight traceable to its source.

author: Tsun-Yi Yang
subtitle: Founder and CEO of MIMI AI :) | Ex-Meta, Ex-Amazon
content:
In my early career in Meta, I was told that nobody care much about quantization, people care about good performance even with much more computational cost. 

I know it's false by heart, the truth of neural network (or LLM) is that scaling law exists, but you should not blindly inflate your computational resources. Yes... it will still work with much more power/money... but it shouldn't be.

I am glad to see in Microsoft they already crack the key problem of quantization, and I believe this paper is the foundation of next generation LLM. What is that? It's quite simple. FP4 training.

If you can achieve "almost" the same results as FP16 by FP4, there is a high chance that you can scale your model by 4 times in training. Meaning your next generation "small model" would be 4x larger than right now, which is basically the current "medium model".

And if you are greedy enough (which you should), your "large model" would also be 4x larger than the current large model. This is in algorithm/code training level, meaning that you don't need to have more money to buy more gpus. Just BANG! Directly 4x larger. So yeah, the scaling of LLM is not stoping any time soon IMO.

I read their paper and I found it fascinating. There are two key equations only. Not super trivial, but the direction is easy to understand which I would like to share.

The key equation is equation (7) and (8). A Differentiable Gradient Estimator (DGE). It replace the old Straight Through Estimator (STE).

Why is it good? In quantization LLM, people usually keep the forward inference the normal quantization way, which keeps the efficiency of the low precision network. While focusing on improving the backward propagation, so the gradient would learn things that particularly improve the low-precision LLM or neural network.

So Straight Through Estimator (STE) made a very very simple assumption. Basically that you treat the derivate f'(x) approximation as 1. Which is a easy but false assumption which introduce so much error in updating the model. So the proposed Differentiable Gradient Estimator (DGE) basically design a similar function as FP4 quantization, so it is actually smooth and differentiable.

To understand it very simply, think of a step function, and how sigmoid function mimic the step and yet smooth so it can be differentiable. DGE is basically a specialized function which serves FP4 only.

Apart from that, they also find Outlier Clamping and Compensation method (OCC) is working very efficiently. It is basically clip/clamp out the overly large/small value out of the activation value. Very very simple but it works. This also works in GAN, and Deepseek in different context so ;).

Understanding the paper is not that hard, but the real impact will come once this is integrated in either pytorch, huggingface, or any kernel that they might be developing. Imagine you have 4x gpus now :).

Really looking forward to this.

author: Aurimas Griciūnas
subtitle: Founder @ SwirlAI • Ex-CPO @ neptune.ai (Acquired by OpenAI) • UpSkilling the Next Generation of AI Talent • Author of SwirlAI Newsletter • Public Speaker
content:
Here is why you need to understand 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗥𝗔𝗚 as an AI Engineer.

Simple naive RAG systems are rarely used in real world applications. To provide correct actions to solve the user intent, we are always adding some agency to the RAG system - it is usually just a bit of it.

It is important to 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗹𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝘇𝘇 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 and understand that there is 𝗻𝗼 𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗯𝗹𝘂𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗻𝘁 to add this agency to your RAG system and you should adapt to your use case. My advice is to think in systems and engineering flows.

Let’s explore some of the moving pieces in Agentic RAG:

𝟭. Analysis of the user query: we pass the original user query to a LLM based Agent for analysis. This is where:

➡️ The original query can be rewritten, sometimes multiple times to create either a single or multiple queries to be passed down the pipeline.
➡️ The agent decides if additional data sources are required to answer the query.

𝟮. If additional data is required, the Retrieval step is triggered. In Agentic RAG case, we could have a single or multiple agents responsible for figuring out what data sources should be tapped into, few examples:

➡️ Real time user data. This is a pretty cool concept as we might have some real time information like current location available for the user.
➡️ Internal documents that a user might be interested in.
➡️ Data available on the web.
➡️ …

𝟯. If there is no need for additional data, we try to compose the answer (or multiple answers or a set of actions) straight via an LLM.
𝟰. The answer gets analyzed, summarized and evaluated for correctness and relevance:

➡️ If the Agent decides that the answer is good enough, it gets returned to the user.
➡️ If the Agent decides that the answer needs improvement, we try to rewrite the user query and repeat the generation loop.

✅ Remember the Reflection pattern from my last Newsletter article? This is exactly that. 👆

The real power of Agentic RAG lies in its ability to perform additional routing pre and post generation, handle multiple distinct data sources for retrieval if it is needed and recover from failures while generating correct answers.

What are your thoughts on Agentic RAG? Let me know in the comments! 👇

author: Richard Meng
subtitle: CEO @ Roe | Catching fin-crimes with vectors
content:
> 90% PDF chatbots rely on vector-search-based RAG, but they shouldn’t:

Here is how you build a chatbot without RAG: 

1) Work closely with your business team to pinpoint what questions they actually want to know.
2) Extract rich document and page-level metadata based on those questions.
Example: If you're analyzing SEC filings for risks, use an LLM to identify the stock symbol and filing date from the first page. Then, locate pages containing "Risks."
3) When a question comes in, fetch the relevant documents and pages using metadata, then feed raw pages into the LLM for the final answer.

Why We Use ZERO Vectors (And You Should Too)
1) The LLM captures deeper semantic context than the embedding model
2) Pages are processed as a whole, preserving context across tables, graphs, and multi-page sections.
3) When a better, cheaper LLM drops, swap it in and rerun on pages—no dealing with vector storage, chunking, or endless RAG tweaks.

Just Remember: You're Not (re)Building Google Search. 
You should build a stable chatbot that works 99% of the time for your business team.

author: Richard Meng
subtitle: CEO @ Roe | Catching fin-crimes with vectors
content:
We've spoken with 30 companies who developed RAG-based chatbots on PDF documents. Every single one has failed:

Core issues:
1) In vector space, "non-dairy products" is often closer to "milk" than "meat," this is a fundamental flaw of vector embedding search because they're very lossy.
2) Splitting documents into smaller chunks disrupts coherence, breaking cross-references and context.
3) Adopting new RAG architectures, re-embedding chunks with new models, and rerankers requires continuous, costly data (re)engineering efforts.
4) No Support for Aggregations – Vector search struggles with queries requiring aggregation (e.g., max, min, total), making it unreliable for analytical use cases.

As a result, companies band-aid their chatbots by writing complex heuristics to patch these failures. Ironically, many end up going back to rule-based chatbots.

Our advice is simple - Do You Even Need RAG?

LLM models are dirt cheap now and quite comparable to embedding models.

If your documents are small: just load them directly into the LLM context.
If your documents are large: Enrich with rich metadata and query the right documents and pages based on the metadata.

Chatting on documents must be redesigned.

author: Pierre-Carl Langlais
subtitle: Co-founder Pleias
content:
I release today the first Google Colab notebook to train a reasoning LLM with the new Reinforcement Learning algorithm from DeepSeek, GRPO. In less than 2 hours you can transform a very small model, Qwen 0.5 (500 million parameters) into a tiny math reasoning machine. To this date, this is probably the closest reproduction of R1 and o1 post-training cycle you can easily run (on a A100).
https://lnkd.in/dcyiypVf

The notebook is based on a script by William Brown that significantly improves on Llama 1B capacities for math. This is a typical reinforcement learning approach based on thousands of examples from the gsm8k dataset. The model has to find the solution, reason over it for some time (this is the absolute basic form of inference time compute) and rewarding the good reasoning traces.

To make it work effectively on Colab, I implemented the following changes:
* Use vllm over the default inference from trl. Since you have to generate the reasoning "drafts" at each step (16 in all), inference time is one of your made bottleneck. vllm improves it by a factor 10. This is still some experimental as I had to run simultaneously training and a separate inference on one GPU — not much past example, you will get a warning, but it "just works".
*Switch llama 1b to Qwen 0.5b, a smallest yest still capable model. I have also a working example for Qwen 1.5b but with had to scale down the hyperparameters. Using LORA peft should make it possible to train on Colab even with larger models, but not working at the moment (compatibility issue with vllm).
*Dropping flash attention and a few other things.

Reinforcement learning is probably one of the main factor behind DeepSeek success (and before that). Yet, there are compatively little accessible ressources for individual researchers and hobbyists. Both the rise of small models, ready to use methods from trl/Hugging Face, and fast inference with vllm is changing that. For now my notebook requires a A100 but even the free inference in t4 should be feasible for very small model (with some code change).

Having accessible scripts that run easily is obviously great to better understand how the new reasoning models are made. But it goes beyond that. There's a lot to do at the intersection of RL, reasoning and *something*. Right now, most of the research is focused on math and programming, but there is so much more that could be could be done in other domains. 

We have multiple projects under way at pleias that leverage reasoning diversity by combining synthetic data generation, custom evaluation/verification, RL and some form of mechanistic interpretability. We have been impressed by the  capacities of very tiny models in a wide number of applications from RAG to data processing at scale. Stay tuned for much much more.

author: Avi Chawla
subtitle: Co-founder DailyDoseofDS | IIT Varanasi | ex-AI Engineer MastercardAI | Newsletter (150k+)
content:
4 strategies for multi-GPU training explained visually.

By default, deep learning models only utilize a single GPU for training, even if multiple GPUs are available.

An ideal way to proceed (especially in big-data settings) is to distribute the training workload across multiple GPUs.

The graphic below depicts four common strategies for multi-GPU training:

1) Model parallelism
- Different parts (or layers) of the model are placed on different GPUs.
- Useful for huge models that do not fit on a single GPU.
- However, model parallelism also introduces severe bottlenecks as it requires data flow between GPUs when activations from one GPU are transferred to another GPU.

2) Tensor parallelism
- Distributes and processes individual tensor operations across multiple devices or processors.
- It is based on the idea that a large tensor operation, such as matrix multiplication, can be divided into smaller tensor operations, and each smaller operation can be executed on a separate device or processor.
- Such parallelization strategies are inherently built into standard implementations of PyTorch and other deep learning frameworks, but they become much more pronounced in a distributed setting.

3) Data parallelism
- Replicate the model across all GPUs.
- Divide the available data into smaller batches, and each batch is processed by a separate GPU.
- The updates (or gradients) from each GPU are then aggregated and used to update the model parameters on every GPU.

4) Pipeline parallelism
- This is often considered a combination of data parallelism and model parallelism.
- So the issue with standard model parallelism is that 1st GPU remains idle when data is being propagated through layers available in 2nd GPU:
- Pipeline parallelism addresses this by loading the next micro-batch of data once the 1st GPU has finished the computations on the 1st micro-batch and transferred activations to layers available in the 2nd GPU.
- The process looks like this:
↳ 1st micro-batch passes through the layers on 1st GPU.
↳ 2nd GPU receives activations on 1st micro-batch from 1st GPU.
↳ While the 2nd GPU passes the data through the layers, another micro-batch is loaded on the 1st GPU.
↳ And the process continues.
- GPU utilization drastically improves this way. This is evident from the animation below where multi-GPUs are being utilized at the same timestamp (look at t=1, t=2, t=5, and t=6).

author: Jim Fan
subtitle: NVIDIA Director of AI & Distinguished Scientist. Co-Lead of Project GR00T (Humanoid Robotics) & GEAR Lab. Stanford Ph.D. OpenAI's first intern. Solving Physical AGI, one motor at a time.
content:
Thoughts about o3: I'll skip the obvious part (extraordinary reasoning, FrontierMath is insanely hard, etc). I think the essence of o3 is about *relaxing a single-point RL super intelligence* to cover more points in the space of useful problems. The world of AI is no stranger to RL achieving god-level stunts.

AlphaGo was a super intelligence. It beats the world champion in Go - well above 99.999% of regular players. 
AlphaStar was a super intelligence. It bests some of the greatest e-sport champion teams on StarCraft. 
Boston Dynamics e-Atlas was a super intelligence. It performs perfect backflips. Most human brains don't know how to send such surgically precise control signals to their limbs.

Similar statement can be made for AIME, SWE-Bench, and FrontierMath - they are like Go, which requires exceptional domain expertise above 99.99....% of average people. o3 is a super intelligence when operating in these domains.

The key difference is that AlphaGo uses RL to optimize for a simple, almost trivially defined reward function: winning the game gives 1, losing gives 0. Learning reward functions for sophisticated math and software engineering are much harder. o3 made a breakthrough in solving the reward problem, for the domains that OpenAI prioritizes. It is no longer an RL specialist for single-point task, but an RL specialist for a bigger set of useful tasks.

Yet o3's reward engineering could not cover ALL distribution of human cognition. This is why we are still cursed by Moravec's paradox. o3 can wow the Fields Medalists, but still fail to solve some 5-yr-old puzzles like the one below. I am not at all surprised by this cognitive dissonance, just like we wouldn't expect AlphaGo to win Poker games.

Huge milestone. Clear roadmap. More to do.

content:
NVIDIA Data Science ("DL Engineer") Interview Question:
How are Word2Vec embeddings created?

Word2Vec embedding is created through a two-layer neural network that processes text to produce word vectors12.  Here's how it works-

𝗜𝗻𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:
A large corpus of text is read and preprocessed
Words are tokenized and mapped to their contexts.

𝗡𝗲𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲:
The network has an input layer, a hidden layer, and an output layer
Two main architectures are used: Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW) and Skip-gram.

𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀:
CBOW predicts a target word from context words.
Skip-gram predicts context words given a target word.
The network learns by adjusting weights to minimize prediction errors.

𝗩𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:
The hidden layer's weights form the word embeddings.
Each word is represented as a vector in a high-dimensional space (typically 100-300 dimensions).

𝗦𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲:
Words with similar contexts end up close to each other in the vector space.
The resulting embeddings capture semantic relationships between words.

The training process involves iterating over the text corpus multiple times, refining the word vectors to better predict words based on their contexts. The final embeddings can then be used for various natural language processing tasks.

author: Nirmal Budhathoki
subtitle: Security Data Scientist @ Microsoft | Data Science, Cloud Security, Machine Learning | Mentor
content:
How can you use autoencoders for anomaly detection?

In my previous post, I covered similar question of using PCA for anomaly detection. This is another popular question in ML focused data science interview (asked in #Google MLE role). 

Link to my post covering PCA: https://lnkd.in/gUwBMdcX

Let me start with reconstruction error (re). If we transform our data using some function, we should be able to reconstruct it with minimal loss. The re is the error as difference between original data point and its reconstruction. Because anomalies are rare, their contribution into the transformation process (function) will always be low, which in-turn will produce high re. In fact, we don't even need anomaly data to train model, we only train on normal data points. This is similar to one-class SVM in our traditional ML world. I posted this on past: https://lnkd.in/gHUeCy5T?

Now, let's understand how autoencoder works. An autoencoder is a neural network designed to compress input data through a bottleneck layer and decode it to reconstruct it as accurately as possible. Below are important points to highlight: 

📌 Compression: Autoencoders learn to compress input data thru bottleneck layer into a lower-dimensional representation.

📌 Training on Normal Data: The model is trained exclusively on non-anomalous (normal) data to learn its patterns and features.

📌 Reconstruction Error: During inference, the reconstruction error (difference between input and output) is calculated.

📌 Anomaly Identification: High reconstruction errors indicate that the input data deviates from the patterns learned during training, signaling potential anomalies.

📌 Threshold Setting: A reconstruction error threshold is set to classify data as normal or anomalous.

A brilliant book that teaches you to think mathematically, helping you avoid common logical pitfalls in data analysis and machine learning. 

4. "A First Course in Probability" by Sheldon Ross
Understanding probability is fundamental to machine learning. This book is a great introduction to probabilistic thinking and statistical inference. 

5. "The Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book" by Andriy Burkov
A concise yet comprehensive overview of machine learning concepts, perfect for quick reference and as a primer for understanding the field. It’s a great starting point for anyone new to the field.

6. "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" by Martin Kleppmann
A well-known book among software engineers, however also necessary for ml engineers to grasp the fundamentals of scalable system design.

author: Charles Packer
subtitle: Co-Founder & CEO at Letta
content:
Introducing the AI agents stack: breaking down today’s tech stack for building AI agents into three key layers: (1) agent hosting/serving, (2) agent frameworks, (3) LLM models & storage.

Sarah Wooders and I got so tired of seeing bad “market maps” for LLM / AI agents shoved in our feeds that either had layouts that made no sense or were littered with random companies on them (ie that don’t have serious community adoption), or both. As researchers / engineers actually working in the agents space, we decided to make a serious attempt at making one of these market map diagrams that actually reflects real world usage by today’s developers building AI agents.

Basically - if you’re starting a vertical agents company today (November 2024), what software are you most likely to use to build out your “agents stack”?

In our opinion, the AI/LLM agents stack is a significant departure from the standard LLM stack. The key difference between the two lies in managing state: LLM serving platforms are generally stateless, whereas agent serving platforms need to be stateful (retain the state of the agent server-side).

Building stateful services is a lot harder of an engineering challenge compared to building developer SDKs, so unsurprisingly very few agent serving platforms actually exist today (Letta being one of them).

For a full breakdown of the stack, check out our full post (link in comments).

content:
When working with ASR, we often find that clients face cost, quality, and speed challenges. 

Most of the time, you compromise on one to achieve the other. And that's fine. If you don't mind a slight downgrade in quality, implementing Whisper to transcribe multiple languages should be obvious.

Not really. While Whisper saves on costs, latency is an issue, and there's that pesky task of inferring speaker labels if you want to get serious about your downstream tasks.

Recently, we've seen excellent examples of both Whisper-based transcription and diarization. Particularly Guillaume Klein's (https://lnkd.in/eJsWRUbX) faster-whisper library (https://lnkd.in/emQ7Xq5c) and Minh Chien Vu's (https://lnkd.in/eycqQbpz) simple but effective diarization method (https://lnkd.in/eswcgdBt).

It's exciting to go from YouTube URL to a fully diarized transcript in a few minutes, but as we tinkerers know, things start to fall apart when you want to deploy something into production.

That "last mile" is the most annoying, so we've open-sourced our Dockerized implementation of Guillaume's and Chien's work - Whisper-based transcription and diarization based on agglomerative clustering. 

We call it Wordcab-Transcribe. Check all the features here: https://lnkd.in/eU4EqhD7

We tested the container locally and deployed it as an endpoint on Cortex (https://lnkd.in/eksBPN9Y), so our team can use it for a fraction of the cost of production ASR solutions.

It pairs well with Wordcab's self-hosted summary models - it costs pennies per hour to transcribe, diarize, and summarize our team's conversations.

The repo is a WIP - there's a lot we want to add and improve, but it works out of the box and performs surprisingly well. You will see the performance chart soon. Find links to the repo and our blog about the project here:

author: Hassan Taherian
subtitle: PhD in Computer Science
content:
My Latest Work on Speaker Diarization and Separation

Challenges in Overlapped Speech Recognition: Traditional automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often struggle with overlapped speech, as they are designed for single-talker speech.

Introducing SSND: We propose a novel framework, "Speaker Separation via Neural Diarization" (SSND) for multi-channel conversational speaker separation. This approach significantly enhances ASR performance in environments with multiple speakers.

How SSND Works: SSND uses an end-to-end neural diarization to detect individual speech activities. It then creates a sequence of embeddings to allocate speakers to the outputs of a separation model. This method addresses  the permutation ambiguity problem during the diarization phase through location-based training, rather than during the separation process.

Advantages Over CSS: Unlike Continuous Speaker Separation (CSS), SSND can efficiently process longer segments with multiple speakers. This makes it more effective and suitable for speaker-attributed ASR systems.

Benchmark Results: We evaluated SSND on the LibriCSS dataset and achieved state-of-the-art results in both diarization and ASR, outperforming all  existing methods by a large margin.

author: VAIBHAV SHANKAR SHARMA
subtitle: Serial Entrepreneur | Fintech Innovator | Product Strategist | Transforming Global Security through Cutting-Edge Technology
content:
Source-Disentangled Neural Audio Codec (SD-Codec): A Novel AI Approach that Combines Audio Coding and Source Separation

Neural audio codecs have completely changed how audio is compressed and handled, by converting continuous audio signals into discrete tokens. This technique uses generative models trained on discrete tokens to produce complicated audio while maintaining the excellent quality of the audio. These neural codecs have significantly improved audio compression, making it possible to store and transfer audio data more effectively without compromising sound quality.

However, a lot of the neural audio codec models that are currently in use were not designed to distinguish between distinct sound domains. Instead, they were trained on sizable and varied audio datasets. For example, the harmonics and structure of spoken language are very different from those of music or ambient noise. The inability to distinguish between different audio domains makes it difficult to model data effectively and manage sound production. These models find it challenging to handle the distinctive qualities of various audio formats, which might result in less-than-ideal performance, particularly in applications that need exact control over sound production.

In order to overcome these issues, a team of researchers has introduced the Source-Disentangled Neural Audio Codec (SD-Codec), a unique technique that combines source separation and audio coding. The goal of SD-Codec is to enhance current neural codecs by specifically identifying and classifying audio signals into distinct domains. Unlike other latent space compression techniques, SD-Codec allocates discrete representations, or distinct codebooks, to various audio sources, including music, sound effects, and voice. Because of this division, the model is better able to recognize and maintain the distinctive qualities of each form of audio.

SD-Codec improves the interpretability of the latent space in neural audio codecs by simultaneously learning how to separate and resynthesize audio. In addition to helping to preserve high-quality audio resynthesis, it gives additional control over the audio creation process by making it easier to distinguish between various sources. Because SD-Codec can separate sources inside the latent space, it can manipulate the audio output more precisely, which is very useful for applications that need to generate or edit detailed audio.

Based on experimental results, SD-Codec successfully disentangles various audio sources and performs at a competitive level in terms of audio resynthesis quality. This separation capacity results in better interpretability, which makes it simpler to comprehend and manipulate the generated audio.

author: Abhishek Dileep
subtitle: Ex-Sony | IIT MANDI Research Scholar
content:
TasNet Model :  Time domain Audio source separation for real time single channel Audio source separation

This model was proposed as an alternative to the classical method of using spectrogram features for the extraction of features of the model and using the waveform in time domain. The whole audio is broken down in L segments of audio clips and then given to the model piece by piece

The encoder is given the segment which is a 1D-conv with a relu and sigmoid both activation function added to it and passed a layer called the segmentation layer. The output of the encoder layer is a non negative matrix that can essentially considered as a weighted matrix of the mix of sounds (source audio clip in our case). Now this segmentation layer has been referred from previous spectrogram models where the objective is to find a mask over the given audio segment for each and every source present in the audio mixture. This task is taken care by a Deep LSTM layer which is very useful at capturing long range temporal data. We then pass it to the decoder whose job is to reconstruct the encoded audio clip from the masked output values into multiple sources of audio clip. This Decoder will provide us with different speaker output as our output waveform

subtitle: AI Developer Experience at Google DeepMind 🔵 prev: Tech Lead at Hugging Face, AWS ML Hero 🤗 Sharing my own views and AI News
content:
How are Anthropic 's model so good at coding? Is it the dataset or the a special RLHF technique? 🤔 Reinforcement learning with execution feedback (RLEF) from Meta could provide some insights. RLEF uses iterative code synthesis with test execution and feedback to determine reward signals.

Implementation
1️⃣ LLM generates code solutions for instruction
2️⃣ Code is executed and evaluated on public test cases
3️⃣ Feedback based on the result is provided from tests back to model
4️⃣ LLM tries to fix the code based on the feedback
5️⃣ Process repeats until either, public tests pass or the turn limit is reached
6️⃣ The final reward signal for PPO is based on private test cases per sample

Insights
😒 Requires a dataset of code instructions with public and private unit tests
✅ LLM trained to optimize for both first-attempt success and error correction
🦙 RLEF improved Llama 3.1 70B on CodeContests from 27.5% to 40.1% with 1@3 (up to 3 corrections)
🚀 RLEF Llama 3.1 70B outperformed AlphaCodium using GPT-4

author: Niels Rogge
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer at ML6 & Hugging Face
content:
Both Microsoft and Apple released interesting new multimodal models on Hugging Face recently which do a very similar thing: turning screenshots of user interfaces (UIs) into structured data.

💥 Microsoft released OmniParser. OmniParser consists of 2 models, applied in sequence:
- an object detection model (YOLOv8), fine-tuned for Interactable Region Detection (identifying interactable regions from the UI screen). This way, one can apply the Set of Marks approach: feed a multimodal LLM like GPT-4V a screenshot overlayed with bounding boxes of interactable regions, rather than the screenshot alone.
- an image captioning model (BLIP-2/Florence-2), fine-tuned for describing each of the detected interactable regions. This way, one can feed GPT-4V not only the screenshot with overlayed bounding boxes, but also the corresponding captions, which explain what each of the regions can be used for.

Funny enough, I shared about OmniParser on X and it is currently number 3 in top trending models :)

💥 In similar fashion, Apple released Ferret-UI (shown below): a new multimodal large language model (MMLM) tailored for enhanced understanding of mobile UI screens, equipped with referring, grounding, and reasoning capabilities. The authors leverage 2 pre-trained large language models (Gemma-2B and LLaMa-8B) to make the model understand and reason about screenshots of user interfaces, classify widgets, etc.

The goal of these models, you ask? Simple: to improve LLM based UI agents: when operating an LLM to perform tasks on a computer, it needs to understand not only the current place it's looking at (whether it's the screen of a desktop, laptop, or mobile phone), but also make sure it can take the appropriate action to achieve a certain goal. Hence these models "augment" the screenshot with additional contextual information. For example, if you want the model to place an order, you want it to look at the "confirm order" button, making sure it reliably can click on it, irregardless of the UI. 

This is very similar to the "Computer Use" feature that Anthropic released last week.

UI-based LLM agents will be a thing, and this is only the beginning!

author: Niels Rogge
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer at ML6 & Hugging Face
content:
Let's go!! Meta released a new video LLM on Hugging Face, and it sets a new SOTA (state-of-the-art) for open-source video understanding. 🔥

The model is called LongVU, a new multimodal large language model capable of processing long videos (for things like answering questions about it, summarizing it, identifying important passages, etc). 

LongVU is capable of processing very long videos thanks to various clever compression techniques, which increasingly reduce the amount of tokens used to represent a video (and which a Transformer needs to process in parallel).

First, the authors employ DINOv2, a self-supervised image model open-sourced by Meta as well, to remove redundant frames that exhibit high feature similarity across time. Next, features for the remaining frames are combined with features from SigLIP, an important vision encoder open-sourced by Google. The large language model (text decoder part of LongVU) is conditioned on these features.

Next, after temporal reduction, the authors employ spatial reduction (reducing the width and height dimensions of certain video features). Based on the embeddings of the text query (e.g. "What did this man put on the pizza?"), less important frames get their features' resolution reduced, whereas the most important frames's features keep their original resolution.

Finally, spatial token compression (STC) is performed to further reduce the amount of tokens. This is based on a technique where a non-overlapping window is slided over the tokens, where tokens which exhibit high cosine similarity with the first frame of each window are removed.

In terms of performance, the model gets SOTA results on EgoSchema, MVBench and VideoMME and MLVU. Only on VideoMME, the gap with closed-source (GPT-4o and Gemini) is still large, but it's quite impressive to see the results.

author: Jim Fan
subtitle: NVIDIA Director of AI & Distinguished Scientist. Co-Lead of Project GR00T (Humanoid Robotics) & GEAR Lab. Stanford Ph.D. OpenAI's first intern. Solving Physical AGI, one motor at a time.
content:
Not every foundation model needs to be gigantic. We trained a 1.5M-parameter neural network to control the body of a humanoid robot. It takes a lot of subconscious processing for us humans to walk, maintain balance, and maneuver our arms and legs into desired positions. We capture this “subconsciousness” in HOVER, a single model that learns how to coordinate the motors of a humanoid robot to support locomotion and manipulation.

We trained HOVER in NVIDIA Isaac, a GPU-powered simulation suite that accelerates physics by 10,000x faster than real time. To put the number in perspective, the robots undergo 1 year of intense training in a virtual “dojo”, but take only ~50 minutes of wall clock time on one GPU card. The neural net then transfers zero-shot to the real world without finetuning.

HOVER can be *prompted* for various types of high-level motion instructions that we call “control modes”. To name a few:
- Head and hand poses - can be captured by XR devices like Apple Vision Pro.
- Whole-body poses - via MoCap or RGB camera.
- Whole-body joint angles - Exoskeleton.
- Root velocity command - Joysticks. 

What HOVER enables:
- A unified interface for us to control the robot using whichever input devices are convenient at hand.
- An easier way to collect whole-body teleoperation data for training. 
- An upstream Vision-Language-Action model to provide motion instructions, which HOVER translates to low-level motor signals at high frequency.

HOVER supports any humanoid that can be simulated in Isaac. Bring your own robot, and watch it come to life!

It's a big teamwork from NVIDIA GEAR Lab and collaborators: Tairan He, Wenli Xiao, Toru Lin, Zhengyi Luo, Zhenjia Xu, Zhenyu Jiang, Jan Kautz, Changliu Liu, Guanya Shi, Xiaolong Wang

Team leads: Jim Fan, Yuke Zhu

content:
This came unexpected! OpenAI released Swarm, a lightweight library for building multi-agent systems. Swarm provides a stateless abstraction to manage interactions and handoffs between multiple agents and does not use the Assistants API. 👀

How it works:
1️⃣ Define Agents, each with its own instructions, role (e.g., "Sales Agent"), and available functions (will be converted to JSON structures).
2️⃣ Define logic for transferring control to another agent based on conversation flow or specific criteria within agent functions. This handoff is achieved by simply returning the next agent to call within the function.
3️⃣ Context Variables provide initial context and update them throughout the conversation to maintain state and share information between agents.
4️⃣ Client.run() initiate and manage the multi-agent conversation. Needs initial agent, user messages, and context and returns a response containing updated messages, context variables, and the last active agent.

Insights
🔄 Swarm manages a loop of agent interactions, function calls, and potential handoffs.
🧩 Agents encapsulate instructions, available functions (tools), and handoff logic.
🔌 The framework is stateless between calls, offering transparency and fine-grained control.
🛠️ Swarm supports direct Python function calling within agents.
📊 Context variables enable state management across agent interactions.
🔄 Agent handoffs allow for dynamic switching between specialized agents.
📡 Streaming responses are supported for real-time interaction.
🧪 The framework is experimental. Maybe to collect feedback?
🔧 Flexible and works with any OpenAI client, e.g. Hugging Face TGI or vLLM hosted models.

author: Victoria Slocum
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer @ Weaviate
content:
ColBERT, ColPali, and ColQwen all use this “Col” - contextualized late interaction - function. But how does it actually work?

A model first generates token-level embeddings for each query and document token - and then we can use the fancy equation to get a similarity score between the query and document.
Let’s go through the process step by step, emojis correlate to the function in the image:
🟢 For each query token, compare it to every token in a document using dot product, similar to cosine similarity
🔵 Find the highest similarity score (MaxSim) for each query token-document pair.
🔴 Sum up all the MaxSim scores from each query token to get the total similarity score between the full query and document.
🟠 Obtain the overall similarity score for a query and document pair

In the case of ColPali, instead of document tokens, the document image is split into patches, but it functions exactly the same besides that!

Big day for local LLM fans!

- Hugging Face announced a collaboration with Ollama, the popular software tool to run LLMs 100% privately offline on your laptop. It is now possible to run any GGUF model from the 🤗 hub using Ollama. Let me explain: GGUF is a format to store the weights of a large language model in an efficient format (using the .gguf extension). This is heavily used by the llama cpp framework, which implements models like LLaMa in C++, a fast programming language, enabling these models to be run at home on your laptop. The GGUF format supports various forms of so-called "quants", short for "quantizations", which significantly shrink the size of the models while keeping performance degradation to a minimum. The 🤗 hub hosts a huge amount of these GGUF models in various quantized formats (currently more than 43k!). Now, all you need to do to run a GGUF model from the hub is run "ollama run hf://hf. co/{username}/{reponame}:latest" and it will pull the weights from the hub onto your machine. See the video by the on-device LLM 🐐 Vaibhav Srivastav below.

- Mistral AI released 2 new models optimized for edge use cases, 3B and 8B parameter variants. The models are called Ministral, come with a 128k token context window and are optimized for agentic use cases (function calling). author: Victoria Slocum
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer @ Weaviate
content:
Naive chunking vs late chunking vs late interaction (ColBERT) - what’s the difference?

1️⃣ Naive chunking divides a document into fixed-size segments, or chunks, based on metrics like sentences, or token count. The chunks are embedded independently, which may split meaningful units of information, potentially reducing retrieval accuracy or resulting in lost context.
2️⃣ Late chunking delays the chunking process until after the document is embedded. This means that the resulting chunks maintain full document context, but it still only requires the same storage resources and pipeline configurations as naive chunking.
🔍 Query time: Both naive and late chunking result in embedded chunks that can be directly compared with the query vector in similarity search.

3️⃣ ColBERT uses a late interaction architecture, where it tokenizes both the query and document and embeds each token separately, without any sort of pooling step. This approach allows for fine-grained matching between query and document terms and doesn’t result in lost context like naive chunking, but has a higher resource cost because it requires storing every token embedding.
🔍 Query time: ColBERT compares all document tokens with query tokens using a MaxSim operator.

subtitle: Coder at day, creator at night | AI Agents, Automation, Software and Computer Vision | I Help Companies and 100k+ People Build Systems
content:
Monocular 3D Object Detection with MonoPSR 🔥🏎  The physical world is 3D so if we want to take our computer vision models into the real world, we often need to do a mapping from 2D to 3D. 

Some of the earlier approaches have been using LIDAR to map the 2D detection from standard object detection models into 3D space. In the most recent research we have AI depth estimations models instead of expensive 3D sensors. Based on 3D data, camera information like the intrinsic parameters and 2D detection from the images, you can take all of that and map it into 3D space. 


Key ideas for MonoPSR👇 

Shared feature map is created by concatenating features from feature map, and features learned from image patches. 

Proposal depth initialized from the bbox height and real height of objects. This leads to more accurate depth estimation. It is even possible to regress the residual distance directly from the patch.

Proposal stage to first estimate the physical dimension and orientation and then depth estimation.

The proposal stage is highly practical for 3D object detection. Together with the refinement module the performance can be boosted even further. First depth z is calculated from the intrinsics and estimated bbox and the regressed physical height of the object. Then the x and y can be estimated by reprojecting the center of the 2d bbox to the plane at depth z.

author: Aymeric Roucher
subtitle: Building Agents, formerly at Hugging Face | Polytechnique - Cambridge
content:
📜 Old-school RNNs can actually rival fancy transformers!

Remember good old RNNs (Recurrent Neural Networks)? Well, researchers from Mila - Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute and Borealis AI just have shown that simplified versions of decade-old RNNs can match the performance of today's transformers.

They took a fresh look at LSTMs (from 1997!) and GRUs (from 2014). They stripped these models down to their bare essentials, creating "minLSTM" and "minGRU". The key changes:
❶ Removed dependencies on previous hidden states in the gates
❷ Dropped the tanh that had been added to restrict output range in order to avoid vanishing gradients
❸ Ensured outputs are time-independent in scale (not sure I understood that well either, don't worry)

⚡️ As a result, you can use a “parallel scan” algorithm to train these new, minimal RNNs, in parallel, taking 88% more memory but also making them 200x faster than their traditional counterparts for long sequences

🔥 The results are mind-blowing! Performance-wise, they go toe-to-toe with Transformers or Mamba.

And for Language Modeling, they need 2.5x fewer training steps than Transformers to reach the same performance! 🚀 

🤔 Why does this matter?

By showing there are simpler models with similar performance to transformers, this challenges the narrative that we need advanced architectures for better performance!

💬 François Chollet wrote in a tweet about this paper:
“The fact that there are many recent architectures coming from different directions that roughly match Transformers is proof that architectures aren't fundamentally important in the curve-fitting paradigm (aka deep learning)”
“Curve-fitting is about embedding a dataset on a curve. The critical factor is the dataset, not the specific hard-coded bells and whistles that constrain the curve's shape.”

It’s the Bitter lesson by Richard Sutton striking again: don’t try fancy thinking architectures, just scale up your model and data!

Read the paper 👉 https://lnkd.in/eQiV_8nZ

author: Mohamed Mekkouri
subtitle: ML Research @WhiteCircle | prev Hugging Face 🤗 | Making LLMs Safer & Faster
content:
🚀 Exciting breakthrough in Extreme Quantization!

At Hugging Face, we've finally cracked the code for BitNet — no pretraining needed! By fine-tuning a Llama3 8B model, we’ve achieved results close to Llama 1 & 2 7B on key downstream tasks.

What makes this special?
BitNet, introduced by Microsoft Research, replaces traditional linear layers in attention and feed-forward networks with BitLinear layers using ternary or binary precision, making it an exciting approach for quantization.

However, while the original papers propose pre-training models from scratch with Quantization Aware Training (QAT), that’s resource-intensive. Our vision is to make these models more accessible and open, allowing the community to get involved and experiment more.

Our approach?
We started with Llama3 8B, applied quantization, but early attempts showed that quantization caused the model to lose its learned information. After experimenting with various methods, we discovered Warmup Quantization, a technique that gradually introduces quantization into the model. By using a lambda parameter that shifts from 0 to 1, we controlled the level of quantization and evaluated different scheduling techniques. Linear scheduling performed best in general.

Results?
After fine-tuning on 10B tokens and 100B tokens, we achieved performance comparable to Llama 1 & 2 7B on several downstream tasks (except Hellaswag and Winogrande). 
This is just the beginning of The Era of Extreme Quantization!

🔍 Want to dive deeper? Check out the full blogpost to learn more about BitNet and how we’ve made this work without pretraining!

AI didn’t get here by chance. Historically, each key research paper fixed what the last one couldn’t. 

These were the 6 papers that shaped the history of LLMs and Transformers. Read the summary to understand key problems they solved : 


2003 – Bengio et al., 𝘈 𝘕𝘦𝘶𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘗𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘢𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘤 𝘓𝘢𝘯𝘨𝘶𝘢𝘨𝘦 𝘔𝘰𝘥𝘦𝘭 (12,600 citations)
Summary: "Laid the foundation for neural networks in language modeling, but could only predict a single word from a fixed input."
Link: https://lnkd.in/gi5bszmb

2014 – Sutskever et al., 𝘚𝘦𝘲𝘶𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘚𝘦𝘲𝘶𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘯𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘕𝘦𝘶𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘕𝘦𝘵𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘴 (35,350 citations)
Summary: "Enabled machine translation with encoder-decoder LSTMs. But still faced the 'encoder bottleneck,' fitting entire sentences into one vector."
Link: https://lnkd.in/gQ23JM2H

2014 – Bahdanau et al., 𝘕𝘦𝘶𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘔𝘢𝘤𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘦 𝘛𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘴𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 (20,390 citations)
Summary: "Solved the encoder bottleneck by introducing the attention mechanism, allowing the model to focus on relevant parts of the input."
Link: https://lnkd.in/gMEZP6m6

2017 – Vaswani et al., 𝘈𝘵𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘴 𝘈𝘭𝘭 𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘕𝘦𝘦𝘥 (77,250 citations)
Summary: "Took it further by removing RNNs entirely, showing that self-attention alone could outperform all previous models."

2020 – Brown et al., 𝘓𝘢𝘯𝘨𝘶𝘢𝘨𝘦 𝘔𝘰𝘥𝘦𝘭𝘴 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘍𝘦𝘸-𝘚𝘩𝘰𝘵 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘯𝘦𝘳𝘴 (𝘎𝘗𝘛-3) (8,800 citations)
Summary: "Scaled transformers to billions of parameters, enabling few-shot learning, but faced challenges with generating human-like responses consistently."
Link: https://lnkd.in/g4cABNVD

2021 – Ramesh et al., 𝘋𝘈𝘓𝘓·𝘌: 𝘊𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘐𝘮𝘢𝘨𝘦𝘴 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘛𝘦𝘹𝘵 𝘋𝘦𝘴𝘤𝘳𝘪𝘱𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 (1,590 citations)

author: Joinal Ahmed
subtitle: AI / ML Engineering Leader | Google Developer Expert - Cloud AI & GenAI | GenAI, RAG, MLOps, Cloud AI | Ex-Microsoft, Google & AWS
content:
🔥 The buzz in town is all about graph-based RAG approaches, and this paper from Microsoft  paves the way forward! 
Here's why everyone's talking about it:

TL;DR: Microsoft researchers introduce "Graph RAG," a novel approach combining retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with graph-based indexing to enable large language models (LLMs) to answer global questions about entire text corpora. This method outperforms traditional RAG in comprehensiveness and diversity of answers, especially for datasets around 1 million tokens.

Key design elements:
🧠 LLM-driven graph index creation (entities, relationships, claims)
🌳 Hierarchical community detection in the graph
📝 Pre-generation of community summaries at multiple levels
🗺️ Map-reduce query answering using community summaries

Improvements achieved:
📈 72-83% win rate in comprehensiveness over naïve RAG
🎨 62-82% win rate in diversity over naïve RAG
💪 Competitive performance with 26-33% fewer tokens for low-level summaries
🚀 Up to 97% token reduction for root-level summaries with modest performance trade-off

Scenarios where Graph RAG is apt:
📚 Analyzing large document collections (e.g., scientific literature, intelligence reports)
🧩 Supporting data sensemaking activities requiring multiple global queries
🕸️ Domains with complex entity relationships (e.g., corporate structures, historical events)
🔍 Situations requiring both high-level overviews and detailed drill-downs

This Microsoft paper paves the way by addressing limitations of traditional RAG for global, corpus-wide questions and introducing a scalable method for creating and leveraging graph-based knowledge indexes. 
🌟 It opens up exciting possibilities for more effective AI-assisted analysis of large document sets across various domains, from scientific discovery to intelligence analysis.

author: Prerit Munjal
subtitle: Platform Engineering Leader • Senior TPM at Groupon • ex-CTO • Building AI Solutions with ROI
content:
Optimise your docker image by 95% not just in size but also in security.

1. 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝘀.

Stage 1 will build an artifact consisting of all the required libraries & dependencies. Stage 2  will use a slim/scratch base image and copy only the artifact from Stage 1 resulting in up to 95% less image size.

2. 𝗣𝗶𝗰𝗸 𝘀𝗹𝗶𝗺 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀.

Slim images don’t have any unnecessary components like shell utilities, libraries, or metadata. It will reduce the size and the attack surface area.

3. 𝗕𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗳𝗶𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗟𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴.

Always order the instructions from least changing to most changing i.e. use COPY instruction much later in the Dockerfile.

4. 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿𝘀. 

Commands like RUN COPY ADD create layers. Fewer layers = Small Size = Faster Build Times.

5. 𝗡𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗿𝘂𝗻 𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗼𝗼𝘁 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿.

By default, every image runs with root privileges, so make sure you run the image as a non-pseudo user[may break your application, some processes need root privileges]

6. 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘃𝘂𝗹𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 using tools like Trivy & Scout.

Avoid CRITICAL and HIGH vulnerabilities.

Tip: To see individual layers of an image use tools like Dive.

subtitle: AI Developer Experience at Google DeepMind 🔵 prev: Tech Lead at Hugging Face, AWS ML Hero 🤗 Sharing my own views and AI News
content:
OCR-2.0 is coming, and Generative AI and multimodal LLMs will power it! 🔍 GOT (General OCR Theory) is a 580M end-to-end OCR-2.0 model that outperforms all existing methods.

GOT consists of a Vision-Encoder to convert images into transformers images into tokens and a decoder for generating OCR outputs in various formats (e.g., plain text, markdown, Mathpix). GOT is designed to handle complex tasks like sheets, formulas, and geometric shapes

Implementation
1️⃣Vision Encoder Pre-training: The encoder (VitDet) trained using scene text and document OCR data to recognize both slice and whole-page inputs.
2️⃣ Joint-Training: The encoder is connected to the decoder (Qwen-0.5B) and both are trained on more general OCR tasks (e.g., formulas, sheet music, geometry).
3️⃣ Post-Training: Fine-tuned the model with specific tasks, such as fine-grained OCR, multi-page PDFs, and dynamic resolution, using new synthetic datasets.

Insights
🧠 Encoder-Decoder with 80M (VitDet) Encoder and 500M (Qwen2) Decoder with 8k context
🥇 Achieves a 0.035 edit distance and 0.972 BLEU score on plain OCR
📊 Outperforms LLaVA-NeXT and Qwen-VL-Max in document and scene text OCR
🧮 Can extract LaTeX formulas from Arxiv and convert them to Mathpix format
📃 Supports dynamic resolution and multi-page OCR
🖼️ Input resolutions up to 1024x1024

author: Victoria Slocum
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer @ Weaviate
content:
There’s tons of techniques out there for compressing existing vectors, but what about training an embedding model to create smaller, denser vectors out of the box? 🤔

In regular vector embeddings, all dimensions are equally important, but in Matryoshka embeddings, earlier dimensions store more information than later dimensions. This means, for example, you can only use a slice, like the first 8, 16, 32, etc. dimensions of a vector that originally had 1536 dimensions, and still retain much of the information.

The video below has a vector space with 10k random samples, reduced down to a 3D space using PCA. Each frame is a different number of dimensions being used, from 4-dims to all 3072-dims. You can see that by the time it’s using 512 dims, the structure of the vector space is already well defined. It’s a great visualization for how the underlying data representation/vector-space changes as more and more dimensions of a Matryoshka embedding are used!

If you want to dive deeper, check out this blog by Leonie Monigatti and Zain Hasan: https://lnkd.in/ekB7iwEq
