Remember scaling laws? These are empirical laws that say "the bigger your model, the better it gets". More precisely, "as your compute increases exponentially, loss decreases in a linear fashion". They have wild implications, suggesting that spending 100x more training compute would make you super-LLMs. That's why companies are racing to build the biggest AI superclusters ever, and Meta bought 350k H100 GPUs, which probably cost in the order of $1B.

But think of this : we're building huge reasoning machines, but only ask them to do one pass through the model to get one token of the final answer : i.e., we expend a minimal effort on inference. That's like building a Caterpillar truck and making it run on a lawnmower's motor. 🚚🛵 Couldn't we optimize this? 🤔

💡 So instead of scaling up on training by training even bigger models on many more trillions of tokens, Google researchers explored this under-explored avenue : scaling up inference compute.

They combine two methods to use more compute : either a reviser that iterated to adapt the model distribution, or generate N different completions (for instance through Beam Search) and select only the best one using an additional verifier model.

They use a Palm-2 model (released in May 23) on the MATH dataset : Palm-2 has the advantage of getting a low performance on MATH, but not zero, so that improvements will be noticeable.

And the results show that for the same fixed amount of inference compute:
💥 a smaller model with more effort on decoding beats a x14 bigger model using naive greedy sampling.

That means that you can divide your training costs by 14 and still get the same perf for the same inference cost!

Take that, scaling laws. Mark Zuckerberg, you're welcome, hope I can get some of these H100s.

author: Damien Benveniste, PhD
subtitle: Building AI Agents
content:
Should you learn more about Vector databases? Probably!

Vector databases are often used for recommender engines, where we learn vector representations of users and items we want to recommend. This allows to quickly find similar items by using an approximate nearest neighbor search. As long as we can learn a vector representation of a piece of data, we can index it in a vector database. With the recent advent of LLMs, it became easier to compute vector representations of text documents, capturing the semantic meaning of that text, and vector databases make it easier to find semantically similar text documents.

When looking for the nearest neighbors, it is often not important to be perfectly accurate. Product Quantization (PQ) is a way to quantize the vector space to represent vectors with less precision. The idea is to cluster vectors and index the cluster centroids instead of the vectors themselves. When looking for the nearest neighbors to a query vector, we just need to pull the vectors from the closest clusters. It is a faster search, and indexing the vectors takes much less memory space.

We first need to partition each vector into smaller vectors and run a K-means algorithm on each partition. Instead of indexing the vectors, we index the centroid of the clusters they belong to. If we use 2 clusters per partition and have 6 vectors, that's 3X data compression. Obviously, compression would be much higher with more vectors. Each vector now maps to a set of clusters and their related centroids.

If we want to find the nearest neighbors from a query vector, we measure the squared Euclidean distance for each cluster in each partition and return the vectors with the lowest summed squared Euclidean distances.

Instead of having to iterate through each vector, we just need to iterate through the clusters' centroids. There is a balance between search latency and accuracy. The more clusters we use, the better the hash will be and the more accurate the returned nearest neighbors, but it will increase the search latency as we will need to iterate through more clusters.

This is still a brute force approach as the algorithm scales with the number of clusters, but it can be used in combination with other algorithms to have blasting fast retrieval.

author: Basel Hossam
subtitle: SWE @ Siemens EDA
content:
To deepen my understanding of Deep Q-Learning, I decided to implement it in code using PyTorch and test it on the Flappy Bird environment. The work was highly inspired by the paper “Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning”.

One major difference from the paper is that instead of using convolutional layers to process snapshots of the game, I opted to work with features provided directly by the flappy-bird-gym enviroment, such as player’s rotation, velocity and last pipe’s horizontal position. This approach allowed me to achieve efficient training without overextending my computational resources.

One particularly effective strategy was forcing the bird to go down during the early stages of exploration (high epsilon), which significantly increased training speed. The results have been very promising, even though there were further improvements, such as integrating dueling Deep Q-Networks.

This project has been a valuable exercise in applying theory to practice, and I’m excited to explore more deep reinforcement learning algorithms.

content:
𝗔 𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗰𝗸 𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗼𝗻 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁/𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴! 
 
In traditional ML systems, it is easier to backtrack to a problem compared to Generative AI ones based on LLMs. 
 
When working with LLMs, their generative nature can lead to complex and sometimes unpredictable behavior. 
 
𝗔 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁? 
 
"Log prompts or entire chains with representative metadata when testing/evaluating your LLM." 
 
𝘖𝘯𝘦 𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘮 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘐 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘐'𝘷𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘶𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘢𝘴𝘬 𝘪𝘴 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗠𝗟 - 𝗟𝗟𝗠. 
 
🔹 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗮 𝗳𝗲𝘄 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹: 
 
→ 𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗧𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀 
Here you might have a query that represents the larger text, the LLMs response which is the summary, and you could calculate the ROUGE score inline between query & response and add it to the metadata field. 
 
Then you can compose a JSON with query, response, and rouge_score and log it to comet. 
 
→ 𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗤&𝗔 𝗧𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀 
Here, you could log the Q&A pairs separately, or even add an evaluation step using a larger model to evaluate the response. Each pair would be composed of Q, A, GT, and True/False to mark the evaluation. 
 
↳ 𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗧𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀 
You could log the query and response, and append in the metadata a few qualitative metrics (e.g. relevance, cohesiveness). 
 
↳𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗥𝗔𝗚 
If you have complex chains within your RAG application, you could log prompt structures (sys_prompt, query), and LLM responses and track the chain execution step by step. 
 
↳ 𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗡𝗘𝗥 
You could define the entity fields and log the query, response, entities_list, and extracted_entities in the same prompt payload. 
 
↳𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀 
CometML LLM also allows you to log images associated with a prompt or a chain. If you’re working with GPT4-Vision for example, you could log the query and the generated image in the same payload. 
 
Also, besides the actual prompt payload, you could inspect the processing time per each step of a chain. 
 
For example, a 3-step chain in an RAG application will have: 
1. query the Vector DB 
2. compose the prompt, and pass it to the LLM 
3. compose the response and return  
 
When logging the chain to CometML, you can see the processing time/chain step.

subtitle: I Can Help You with AI, Data Projects 👉atliq.com | Helping People Become Data/AI Professionals 👉 codebasics.io | Youtuber - 1M+ Subscribers | Ex. Bloomberg, NVIDIA
content:
What is Federated Learning?

Let's understand this by looking at how Google Keyboard (Gboard) uses this machine-learning technique to predict the next word.

[A] Local Training: When you type on Gboard, it trains a local neural network model on your device to improve next-word predictions.

[B] Secure Sharing: Only the model updates (gradients) are sent to a centralized server. This means what you type stays on your phone, preserving your data privacy. The server aggregates updates from many devices to build a new, improved model.

[C] Model Improvement: The improved model is sent back to mobile devices, and the process repeats.

This way, the centralized model improves based on data from thousands of devices without compromising individual privacy.

It's like a bunch of chefs contributing to a grand recipe by sharing tips without revealing their secret ingredients.

For more in-depth information, check out Google's research paper on Federated Learning in the comments.

author: Damien Benveniste, PhD
subtitle: Building AI Agents
content:
Not too long ago, the largest Machine Learning models most people would deal with merely reached a few GB in memory size. Now, every new generative model coming out is between 1B and 1T parameters! 

To get a sense of the scale, one float parameter, that's 32 bits or 4 bytes, so those new models can scale between 4 GB to 4 TB in memory, each running on expensive hardware. And during the backpropagation algorithm, those models can need as much as 10 times this amount of memory. Because of the massive scale increase, there has been quite a bit of research to reduce the model size while keeping performance up. There are 5 main techniques to compress the model size.

- Model pruning is about removing unimportant weights from the network. The game is to understand what "important" means in that context. A typical approach is to measure the impact on the loss function of each weight. This can be done easily by looking at the gradient and second-order derivative of the loss. Another way to do it is to use L1 or L2 regularization and get rid of the low-magnitude weights. Removing whole neurons, layers, or filters is called "structured pruning" and is more efficient when it comes to inference speed.

- Model quantization is about decreasing parameter precision, typically by moving from float (32 bits) to integer (8 bits). That's 4X model compression. Quantizing parameters tends to cause the model to deviate from its convergence point, so it is typical to fine-tune it with additional training data to keep model performance high. We call this "Quantization-aware training". When we avoid this last step, it is called "Post training quantization", and additional heuristic modifications to the weights can be performed to help performance.

- Low-rank decomposition comes from the fact that neural network weight matrices can be approximated by products of low-dimension matrices. A N x N matrix can be approximately decomposed into a product of 2 N x 1 matrices. That's an O(N^2) -> O(N) space complexity gain! 

- Knowledge distillation is about transferring knowledge from one model to another, typically from a large model to a smaller one. When the student model learns to produce similar output responses, that is response-based distillation. When the student model learns to reproduce similar intermediate layers, it is called feature-based distillation. When the student model learns to reproduce the interaction between layers, it is called relation-based distillation. 

- Lightweight model design is about using knowledge from empirical results to design more efficient architectures. That is probably one of the most used methods in LLM research.

--
👉 LLM Masterclass starts Aug 15th: https://lnkd.in/e3YdK6DT

author: Abhinav Kimothi
subtitle: Director Data Science @ Sigmoid | LLMs, RAG, Agents
content:
The technique of enhancing the parametric memory of an LLM by creating access to an explicit non-parametric memory, from which a retriever can fetch relevant information, augment that information to the prompt, pass the prompt to an LLM to enable the LLM to generate a response that is contextual, reliable, and factually accurate is called Retrieval Augmented Generation.

To construct a RAG-enabled system there are several components that need to be assembled. This includes creation and maintenance of the non-parametric memory, or a knowledge base, for the system. The other pipeline facilitates real-time interaction by sending the prompts to and accepting the response from the LLM, with retrieval and augmentation steps in the middle. Evaluation is yet another critical component, ensuring the effectiveness of the system. All these components of the system are supported by a robust service infrastructure.

Indexing Pipeline creates the knowledge base or the non-parametric memory of RAG-based applications. Indexing Pipeline needs to be set-up before the real-time user interaction with the LLM can begin

To leverage this knowledge base for accurate and contextual responses a Generation Pipeline including the steps of retrieval, augmentation and generation is created.

Together, these pipelines form the backbone of a RAG-enabled system, enabling seamless interaction with users and delivering contextually relevant responses

author: Edward Schmuhl
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer @ Growth Team Weaviate ✨
content:
What are Cross Encoders?

Cross-encoders are a type of machine learning model used to determine the similarity between two items, such as a query and a document. Here's a closer look at what they are and how they function:

- Joint Encoding: Cross-encoders take a pair of items (e.g., a query and a document) and encode them together as a single input. By considering the entire pair simultaneously, they capture complex relationships and interactions between the two items.

Similarity Scoring: After encoding the pair, the model outputs a similarity score, indicating how closely related the items are. In a search engine, a higher score signifies greater relevance of the document to the query.

- High Accuracy: Since cross-encoders analyze the entire pair together, they provide highly accurate assessments of similarity. They are great for capturing nuances and detailed relationships between items.

Computational Intensity: One drawback is that cross-encoders are computationally intensive. They require significant processing power to jointly encode and score each pair of items, which can be slow, especially for large datasets. Additionally, Cross-Encoders don’t generate embeddings that could be used for indexing or further processing.

For more exploration of this topic, check out Zain Hasan review of the paper "Adaptive Retrieval and Scalable Indexing for k-NN Search with Cross-Encoders", which discusses how to combine the benefits of both bi-encoders and cross-encoders.

author: Ahsen Khaliq
subtitle: ML @ Hugging Face
content:
Microsoft presents SpreadsheetLLM

Encoding Spreadsheets for Large Language Models

paper page: https://lnkd.in/eqvykDdT

Spreadsheets, with their extensive two-dimensional grids, various layouts, and diverse formatting options, present notable challenges for large language models (LLMs). In response, we introduce SpreadsheetLLM, pioneering an efficient encoding method designed to unleash and optimize LLMs' powerful understanding and reasoning capability on spreadsheets. Initially, we propose a vanilla serialization approach that incorporates cell addresses, values, and formats. However, this approach was limited by LLMs' token constraints, making it impractical for most applications. To tackle this challenge, we develop SheetCompressor, an innovative encoding framework that compresses spreadsheets effectively for LLMs. It comprises three modules: structural-anchor-based compression, inverse index translation, and data-format-aware aggregation. It significantly improves performance in spreadsheet table detection task, outperforming the vanilla approach by 25.6% in GPT4's in-context learning setting. Moreover, fine-tuned LLM with SheetCompressor has an average compression ratio of 25 times, but achieves a state-of-the-art 78.9% F1 score, surpassing the best existing models by 12.3%. Finally, we propose Chain of Spreadsheet for downstream tasks of spreadsheet understanding and validate in a new and demanding spreadsheet QA task. We methodically leverage the inherent layout and structure of spreadsheets, demonstrating that SpreadsheetLLM is highly effective across a variety of spreadsheet tasks.

author: Aymeric Roucher
subtitle: Building Agents, formerly at Hugging Face | Polytechnique - Cambridge
content:
𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐝𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐧𝐢𝐪𝐮𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐡𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐮𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 👏

DoLa decoding, which made a conference paper at ICLR '24, has just been merged in Transformers by João Gante and Yung-Sung Chuang.
This new decoding method is simple yet extremely impressive!

Reminder: Decoder LLMs (the GPT kind of LLM, the most common one) generate their outputs one token at a time: at each step, given a current text, they compute, for each token in their vocabulary, a "logit" that should represent the probability that this token is coming next.
Then the decoder either picks the highest logit token (greedy decoding) or samples one with a probability defined by the logits (sampling). The token gets appended to the current text, and the decoder compute logits again, and the cycle continues.

The authors of DoLa wanted to improve that simple method. 

They knew this established fact that transformer LMs encode low-level info (like base syntax) in early layers and more high-level info like knowledge in the later layers.

💡 This gave them their key idea: During decoding, rather than picking the token with the highest logit, 𝘄𝗵𝘆 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗽𝗶𝗰𝗸 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿𝘀?

Implementation is actually quite simple: at each step, you get the layer for which the logits diverge most from your final layer, and this chosen layer becomes the premature layer. Then you subtract the logits from the premature layer to your final layer, in order to reward tokens for which the logits progressed most. And this lets you pick your next token.

Their test settings:
➤ Test 4 sizes of Llama-1 models (7b to 65B)
➤ Benchmarks on multiple choice QA (TruthfulQA, FACTOR) and open-ended QA (TruthfulQA-open-ended, GSM8K)

✨ 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲!
🚀 𝟱% - 𝟮𝟬% 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝘀
🚀 For instance on TruthfulQA / Open-ended, across all model sizes the increase in truthfulness is 14 base points, which is 𝗮𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝟰𝟬% 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴!

🤔 Wouldn't decoding take longer because of this added contrasting step? 👉 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝗴𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲, 𝟭 𝘁𝗼 𝟴% 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆.

The paper has additional insights such as how token confidence evolves across layers for different types of tokens: I recommend to read it!

subtitle: Building Agents, formerly at Hugging Face | Polytechnique - Cambridge
content:
𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗱𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 "𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴" 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗴𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 ⛔

It's trendy to share models "fine-tuned for function calling"; but from my observations, this fine-tuning is not necessary or sufficient to build good agent systems.

To name only a few of these models:
🐦‍⬛ Nexusflow/𝗡𝗲𝘅𝘂𝘀𝗥𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗻-𝗩𝟮-𝟭𝟯𝗕
⌘ CohereForAI/𝗰𝟰𝗮𝗶-𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱-𝗿-𝗽𝗹𝘂𝘀
⛵️ mistralai/𝗠𝗶𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹-𝟴𝘅𝟮𝟮𝗕-𝗜𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁-𝘃𝟬.𝟭

Here "Fine-tuned for function-calling" generally means "fine-tuned to generate function calls in correct JSON for extremely simple tasks". In other terms, it means "improve the formatting of the tool calls".

Yet I discovered two things while improving Transformers Agents:
🧐 Even when used as JSON agents, these fine-tuned models don't perform very well
🏅 𝙂𝙤𝙤𝙙 𝙗𝙖𝙨𝙚 𝙢𝙤𝙙𝙚𝙡𝙨 𝙥𝙚𝙧𝙛𝙤𝙧𝙢 𝙗𝙚𝙩𝙩𝙚𝙧 𝙬𝙞𝙩𝙝𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙖𝙣𝙮 𝙛𝙞𝙣𝙚-𝙩𝙪𝙣𝙞𝙣𝙜, 𝙟𝙪𝙨𝙩 𝙥𝙡𝙖𝙞𝙣 𝙥𝙧𝙤𝙢𝙥𝙩𝙞𝙣𝙜. (Llama-3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet) 

👇 The graph below shows the count of errors for my GPT-4o validation run on the GAIA benchmark: 𝙰𝚐𝚎𝚗𝚝𝙿𝚊𝚛𝚜𝚒𝚗𝚐𝙴𝚛𝚛𝚘𝚛 and 𝙰𝚐𝚎𝚗𝚝𝙴𝚡𝚎𝚌𝚞𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗𝙴𝚛𝚛𝚘𝚛 are the ones caused by either not giving the action in a correct format or giving incorrect arguments, so they're the ones that should be reduced by this type of fine-tuning.
➤ As you can see, their count is already close to 0!
And given that GPT-4o is certainly not fine-tuned for our Code tool calling format, this shows that "function calling fine-tuning" is not necessary!

That said, fine-tuning would help bring this error count down to a real 0, thus improving perf a bit (see how more AgentErrors is correlated with the answer being false).
🔶 But even after this fine-tuning, the hardest part for the agent is still to 𝙥𝙡𝙖𝙣 𝙜𝙤𝙤𝙙 𝙩𝙖𝙨𝙠-𝙨𝙤𝙡𝙫𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙩𝙧𝙖𝙟𝙚𝙘𝙩𝙤𝙧𝙞𝙚𝙨 𝙤𝙫𝙚𝙧 𝙨𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙖𝙡 𝙨𝙩𝙚𝙥𝙨.

So I think the real improvements for an agent system will come from:
➤ 𝗨𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 (waiting for Llama-3-405B)
➤ 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘅 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 rather than naive one-step actions (possibly using RL!)

𝙍𝙚𝙖𝙙 𝙢𝙮 𝙘𝙤𝙡𝙡𝙚𝙘𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙤𝙛 𝙥𝙖𝙥𝙚𝙧𝙨 𝙤𝙣 𝙖𝙜𝙚𝙣𝙩𝙨 👉 https://lnkd.in/eas9KBxD

author: Nikhil Rana
subtitle: Sr. Consultant, AI @ Google Cloud | Ex AB-InBev | Ex-JP Morgan
content:
Last saturday at the AI Converge event, I had a chance to discuss some aspects of fine-tuning a code SLM(Small Language Model). One of the questions regarding how some of these models were pre-trained was around the concept of FIM or Fill in the Middle.

What's FIM or Fill in the Middle? ◀ 🔽 ▶
Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) is a simple yet powerful data augmentation technique that enables an LLM to learn infilling text without changing their model architecture or without compromising their standard left-to-right generative capability.

But how does it benefit an LLM? 🧠
Better code completion: Imagine a coding assistant that can seamlessly fill in missing lines of code, complete functions, or even write docstrings!
More coherent natural language generation: LLMs with FIM can also generate more coherent and engaging text, especially when it comes to tasks like writing creative stories or completing long-form articles.
More efficient training: The best part is that FIM can be learned "for free" during pretraining, meaning that it does not require any extra compute cost. This makes it an incredibly efficient way to improve LLM performance.

There are 2 approaches to FIM training depending on how a document is split and concatenated to create an training example:
PSM (Prefix-Suffix-Middle)
SPM (Suffix-Prefix-Middle)

The choice of SPM or PSM affects the efficiency of inference and how the model processes the information. For e.g. if you check out the model card/paper of CodeGemma, it mentions that the models are trained to work with both PSM and SPM modes and its FIM settings are 80% to 90% FIM rate with 50-50 PSM/SPM. This makes it a balanced and flexible model for building a code completion AI assistant.

As a best practice, it's important to understand how an LLM or SLM has been pre-trained to make sure it is the right model for your LLM workflow or fine-tuning task.

CodeGemma FIM configuration: https://lnkd.in/gjZckrhe

author: Iryna Kondrashchenko
subtitle: Co-Founder @ DataForce Solutions | Building LUML: The unified platform to track, deploy, and monitor AI models
content:
📝 Named entity recognition in just two lines of code

🎉 Scikit-LLM's latest update introduces two new NER methods: dense and sparse. Being provided with the text and entities to be extracted, the library performs tagging, parsing the output and presenting it in a human readable way, where each entity is highlighted and the explanation is displayed on hovering over the entity.

🤔 What is a sparse tagging approach?
In sparse mode, only a list of entities is produced which is then mapped to the text via regex. In most of the scenarios, the usage of sparse mode should be preferable for the following reasons:
🔸 lower number of output tokens (cheaper to use);
🔸 strict validation -> it is guaranteed that the output is invertible and only contains the specified entities;
🔸 higher accuracy, especially with smaller models.

🤔 What is a dense tagging approach?
In dense mode, the model produces a tagged output right away. Dense mode should only be used when the following conditions are met:
🔸 a larger model is used (e.g. gpt-4);
🔸 the text is expected to contain multiple (distinct) instances of lexically ambiguous words.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗣𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗻 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲?

With a repository template, you can create a new repository with the same directory structure, branches, CI/CD, and files from the original template.

It integrates the necessary tools and configuration to build quality code and automate tasks.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻𝗲?

𝟏. 𝚂𝚊𝚟𝚎𝚜 𝚝𝚒𝚖𝚎: You don't need to set up the project structure and tools from scratch.

𝟐. 𝙲𝚘𝚗𝚜𝚒𝚜𝚝𝚎𝚗𝚌𝚢: Ensures a uniform project setup, which is helpful if you work in a team.

𝟑. 𝙱𝚎𝚜𝚝 𝚙𝚛𝚊𝚌𝚝𝚒𝚌𝚎𝚜: Uses tools to enforce standards to improve your code's quality, readability, and maintainability.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄

𝟏. Create a new repository from the template with Cookiecutter.
𝟐. Create a branch and develop a feature using pre-commits.
𝟑. Create Pull Requests (PR) when the feature is finished and tested.
𝟒. The CI system will trigger and use all the code quality tools.
𝟓. After the code review and adjustments, if the CI passes, we merge the code.
𝟔. If not, we fix the issues until all the checks pass.

author: Raphaël MANSUY
subtitle: Data Engineering | DataScience | AI & Innovation | Author | Follow me for deep dives on AI & data-engineering
content:
Introducing Multi-Head RAG: A Novel Approach to Solving Multi-Aspect Problems with Large Language Models ...

In the rapidly evolving field of natural language processing, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful technique for enhancing the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). 

By integrating a retrieval system that fetches relevant documents from a large corpus, RAG enables LLMs to provide more accurate and relevant responses. However, existing RAG solutions often struggle with queries that require information from multiple, distinct aspects.

👉 Harnessing the Power of Multi-Head Attention

To address this challenge, the research team has developed Multi-Head RAG (MRAG), a novel approach that leverages the multi-head attention layers in transformers to improve the retrieval of multi-aspect documents. Unlike traditional RAG systems that use a single embedding from the last decoder layer, MRAG utilizes multiple embeddings from different attention heads, capturing various facets of data.

Here's a step-by-step example of how MRAG works:

1. During data preparation, MRAG constructs multi-aspect embeddings for each text chunk using the activations from the multi-head attention layer.
2. These embeddings are stored in a data store, with each single-aspect embedding pointing to the original text chunk.
3. When a query is received, MRAG generates a multi-aspect embedding of the query using the same embedding model.
4. The retrieval engine then finds the nearest multi-aspect embeddings in the data store using a special multi-aspect retrieval strategy.
5. The retrieved documents are then used to provide a more accurate and relevant response to the query.

By using embeddings from multiple attention heads, MRAG can effectively retrieve documents that cover different aspects of a query, even when the embeddings of these documents are far apart in the embedding space.

👉 Impressive Performance and Real-World Applications

The results show up to a 20% improvement in relevance over standard RAG baselines, highlighting the significant potential of this approach.

👉 Seamless Integration and Efficiency

One of the key advantages of MRAG is its seamless integration with existing RAG frameworks and data stores. 

It does not require additional storage or multiple inference passes, making it cost-effective and energy-efficient. 

This ease of integration and efficiency makes MRAG a practical choice for organizations looking to improve their information retrieval systems without incurring high costs.

author: Srimouli Borusu
subtitle: Staff Applied Scientist - AI @Walmart | Ex-BITS | Ex-ISB
content:
Understanding the Subtleties of Batch Normalization in Neural Networks 👨‍🎓 
------------------------------------------------------------------------
As machine learning practitioners, we often rely on batch normalization to stabilize and accelerate the training of deep neural networks. However, there's a subtle detail about batch normalization that is frequently overlooked but crucial to understand.

The Impact of Batch Normalization on the Learning Rate
Batch normalization adjusts the mean and variance of each mini-batch during training, which helps in mitigating issues like internal covariate shift. But here's the often-missed point: batch normalization effectively changes the dynamics of the learning rate.

Why? 😕 
When batch normalization scales the inputs of a layer, it indirectly scales the gradients during backpropagation. This scaling can lead to an effective increase or decrease in the learning rate, depending on the variance of the batch. Specifically, batch normalization includes a learnable parameter gamma (γ) for each feature, which scales the normalized output. If γ is large, it amplifies the gradients, and if γ is small, it diminishes them.

An Example ✍ 
Consider a simple neural network layer with an input x and a batch normalization layer applied to it. The normalized output is:
x̂ = (x - μ) / σ
Where μ and σ are the mean and standard deviation of the batch. The output of the batch normalization layer is then:
y = γx̂ + β
During backpropagation, the gradient with respect to the input x is influenced by γ:
∂L/∂x = γ * ∂L/∂y
If γ is initialized or learned to be large, the gradients flowing back will be scaled up, effectively increasing the learning rate for the parameters of the previous layers. Conversely, a small γ reduces the effective learning rate.

Why This Matters 🤔 
This interaction means that careful tuning of the learning rate and batch normalization parameters is essential. Ignoring this can lead to either too rapid updates (risking overshooting minima) or too slow convergence. Understanding this nuance can help in setting better hyperparameters and achieving more stable and faster training.

Takeaway 😇 
Next time you're fine-tuning your neural network, consider the hidden interplay between batch normalization and your learning rate. A deeper understanding of these subtleties can make a significant difference in your model's performance and training efficiency.

There are plenty of videos on YouTube that walks through the basics. It will give you a passive, but high-level overview of what are the building blocks of the topics. I don't linger watching the entire video end-to-end. I skip around to get the gist. Videos by Andrej Karpathy is a great place to start

𝟯. 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗵
I jot down the math to see what the model is doing each step along the way. In essence, a model is just data transformation, using X to convert to y.

And, every model is composed of a two-stage process from how it generates the predictions to how it trains the model weights to improve the predictions.

Understanding this part, you can now understand how different models use different sets of mathematical and statistical theories to achieve these.

In GPT case, the main ingredient is the decoder block consisting of multi-headed attention for generating prediction and back propagation with adam optimizer for optimizing the weights.

𝟰. 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗶𝘁
Code it from scratch. Hugging Face or loading pre-trained models are great in applications, but they won't help you understand what actually happens under the hood.

Load tensorflow or pytorch, then work through the code line by line. Look up "X" model from scratch on Github, and you will find plenty of repos that shows authors rebuilding a model from scratch for your guidance.

𝟱. 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆 𝗶𝘁
Don't just end it from here. Think about how you would deploy this model if this was an actual project. 

Build an API with your solution, then deploy your solution to AWS using lambda or load balancer.

content:
Wanna learn how to deploy ML models to production?

Let's go step-by-step, with a real-world example 🧵↓
 
 
𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲

Imagine today is your first day as an ML engineer at Uber, and your task is to improve the ML service that predicts the Estimated Time of Arrival (ETA), which gives users an estimate of when their driver will arrive.

𝗔𝘀 𝗮 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿

You
> define the problem
> talk to other data engineers and ML engineers in the team
> expand the set of model features, and
> train a promising ML model.

You are happy with the results, so it is time to deploy

So far you have 4 things:

> the model pickle

> a predict function, that maps input features to output predictions, using the model artifact.

> A FastAPI wrapper around your Python code, to build the REST API, and

> A Dockerfile to package everything in an isolated box.

How do you deploy this code as a production ready API?


𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 -> 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗟𝗢𝗽𝘀 𝘄𝗮𝘆

Let’s go step by step

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟭 → Push code to new branch and open Pull Request (PR)

Use git and Github to track code changes.

I recommend you develop your code in a non-master branch, where you work, and push changes to remote.

Once you are happy with the results, you open a Pull Request


𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟮 → Continuous Integration (CI)

The CI pipeline is a github action that is triggered automatically every time you open a Pull Request.

The end goal is to make sure that your new code version, and model artifact are actually good and deserve to be promoted to production.

The CI steps in this case are:

> Unit tests, e.g. make sure you feature engineering functions work as expected

> Trains the model and generates the model artifact.

> Validates the ML model performance and possible biases, using a library like PyTest or Giskard

At the end, the pipeline checks can either

→ fail, so you need to work further on your code, or move to another project with higher priori

→ pass, so your model is ready to be deployed. In this case,

the CI pipeline pushes the model to your model registry, from where it can later be deployed, and

your branch “my_new_model” gets merged to master.


𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟯 → Continuous Deployment (CD)

The Continuos Deployment (CD) pipeline is another github action that is triggered automatically after successful completion of the CI pipeline.

The role of the CD pipeline is to deploy the Dockerfile you wrote as a production ready API.

In this case, our github action

> Pushes the Docker image to Uber’s docker registry,
> Triggers the deployment to your compute platform, for example
    - Kubernetes, with kubectl
    - AWS Lambda, or
    - Serverless platforms, like Beam or Cerebrium that do not require Docker images.

content:
The next LLM Agents will be Python and not JSON-based! 🐍 CodeAct proposes a new framework to generate executable Python code instead of JSON for more challenging controll flows. It is not only more accurate but also reduces the number of actions for complex tasks. 🤯

LLM agents are typically prompted to produce actions by generating JSON, which limits and restricts flexibility (e.g., using multiple tools or loops). CodeAct uses executable Python code to consolidate LLM agents' actions into a unified “action space”. 💡

Implementation
1️⃣ Provide a system prompt that explains the CodeAct framework, including a few shot examples and the tools (Python function signature or docstring).
2️⃣ User prompts LLM with request or task
3️⃣ LLM generates a Python code as the action, based on the provided “tools”
4️⃣ Execute the code with a Python interpreter. (be cautious here)
5️⃣ Captures the output or error messages and provides this information to the LLM
6️⃣ LLM then decides to modify its previous code or generate the response for the user

Steps 3-6 are repeated until the LLM decides to submit a final response or reaches a predefined number of interactions.

Insights
🚀 Outperforms existing method with up to 20% higher success rates
⚡ Requires up to 30% fewer actions to solve tasks
🤖 GPT-3.5 CodeAct matches GPT-4 JSON performance
🛠️ Use of error messages allows self-debugging and improves performance
📚 Created CodeActInstruct dataset, consisting of 7,000+ multi-turn interactions
💬 Including datasets like OpenOrca and ShareGPT to keep general language understanding
🧩 Use of Python code allows complex control flows with loops or conditions

author: Damien Benveniste, PhD
subtitle: Building AI Agents
content:
Can we mix the concepts of Multihead-Attentions and Mixture-of-Experts together into one Attention layer? You bet we can!

Many multihead attention layer implementations are now sparse, meaning that we don't use all the Keys and Values in the computation of the resulting hidden states. This leads to sub-quadratic time complexity if you are careful in the way you select the Keys and Values. Typically, we use a heuristic approach to select those, but what about we let the model decide what are the best to select?

If you think about the Mixture-of-Expert architecture, the model uses a gate to learn what the best experts to use for each token. So we could do the same for the multihead-attention, but in that situation, the "experts" are the Keys and Values.

In that code, the gate maps from `hidden_size` to `num_heads`, so the `gate_score` has a dimension of (batch_size, seq_length, num_heads). If we decide that we want only the top 10% best keys and values, we can just look at that tensor to find the top 10% highest numbers. The `torch.topk` gives exactly that, and we can now `gather` the top Keys and Values. Note that this is done per head, which means that each head will choose different Keys and Values, and the learning remains quite heterogeneous.

The typical time complexity of an Attention layer is O(seq_length^2 * hidden_size), but here it is O(seq_length * K * hidden_size) where K is the number of Keys and Values selected for the computation.

Should I call that the Gated-Multihead-Attention layer or the MoE-Multihead-Attention layer?

author: Armand Ruiz
subtitle: building AI systems @meta
content:
Forget RAG, welcome Agentic RAG 
 
𝗡𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗥𝗔𝗚 
In Native RAG, the most common implementation nowadays, the user query is processed through a pipeline that includes retrieval, reranking, synthesis, and generation of a response.  
 
This process leverages retrieval and generation-based methods to provide accurate and contextually relevant answers. 
 
𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗥𝗔𝗚 
Agentic RAG is an advanced, agent-based approach to question answering over multiple documents in a coordinated manner. It involves comparing different documents, summarizing specific documents, or comparing various summaries.  
 
Agentic RAG is a flexible framework that supports complex tasks requiring planning, multi-step reasoning, tool use, and learning over time. 
 
𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 
- Document Agents: Each document is assigned a dedicated agent capable of answering questions and summarizing within its own document. 
 
- Meta-Agent: A top-level agent manages all the document agents, orchestrating their interactions and integrating their outputs to generate a coherent and comprehensive response. 
 
𝗙𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗕𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗳𝗶𝘁𝘀 
- Autonomy: Agents act independently to retrieve, process, and generate information. 
 
- Adaptability: The system can adjust strategies based on new data and changing contexts. 
 
- Proactivity: Agents can anticipate needs and take preemptive actions to achieve goals. 
Applications 
 
Agentic RAG is particularly useful in scenarios requiring thorough and nuanced information processing and decision-making. 
 
A few days ago, I discussed how the future of AI lies in AI Agents. RAG is currently the most popular use case, and with an agentic architecture, you will supercharge RAG!

author: Victoria Slocum
subtitle: Machine Learning Engineer @ Weaviate
content:
Product Quantization (PQ) is still one of my favorite types of vector compression algorithms because of its versatility, performance, and dynamic rates of compression. There’s a reason it was the first (but certainly not the last) type of quantization algorithm to be introduced in Weaviate!

The underlying concept is clustering - a vector is split up into a segment of a certain size, and that segment is assigned to the closest centroid that best represents it. This means that a lot of the general information is still retained, just a little fuzzier.

Because the algorithm still retains the general sense of the original vector, you can use PQ to get way higher levels of compression than other algorithms and still get decent recall out of the box. With a rescoring or reranking algorithm added on, it ends up being very good 👀

Interested in learning more about vector quantization techniques? I definitely recommend talk from Etienne Dilocker: https://lnkd.in/e_tuNv9d

author: Sebastian Raschka, PhD
subtitle: ML/AI research engineer. Author of Build a Large Language Model From Scratch (amzn.to/4fqvn0D) and Ahead of AI (magazine.sebastianraschka.com), on how LLMs work and the latest developments in the field.
content:
Building an LLM from Scratch is in the final stages. I'm currently working on Chapter 6, finetuning a GPT-like LLM to classify SPAM messages. 

And while I'm polishing up the main content, I wanted to share some bonus experiments along with some interesting takeaways:

1. Training the Last vs. First Output Token (row 1 vs 2): Training the last output token results in significantly better performance compared to the first. This improvement is expected due to the causal self-attention mask.

2. Training the Last Transformer Block vs. Last Layer (row 1 vs 3): Training the entire last transformer block is much more effective than training only the last layer.

3. Training All Layers vs. Last Transformer Block (row 1 vs 4): Training all layers shows a modest improvement of 2% over just training the last transformer block, but it requires almost three times longer in terms of training duration.

4. Using Larger Pretrained Models (row 1 vs 5, and row 1 vs 6): Employing a 3x larger pretrained model leads to worse results. However, using a 5x larger model improves performance compared to the initial model, as was anticipated.

5. Using a Model with Random Weights vs. Pretrained Weights (row 1 vs 7): Utilizing a model with random weights yields results that are only slightly worse by 1.3% compared to using pretrained

6. Padding Input to Full Context Length vs. Longest Training Example (row 1 vs 8): Padding the input to the full supported context length results in significantly worse

I've kept the LLM and dataset small on purpose, so you can run the training on a regular laptop like a MacBook Air M3 in about 15 minutes in case you don't have access to a GPU.

author: Chip Huyen
subtitle: AI x stuff
content:
LinkedIn has published one of the best reports I’ve read on deploying LLM applications: what worked and what didn’t.

1. Structured outputs
They chose YAML over JSON as the output format because YAML uses less output tokens. Initially, only 90% of the outputs are correctly formatted YAML. They used re-prompting (asking the model to fix its YAML responses), which increased the number of API calls significantly.

They then analyzed the common formatting errors, added those hints to the original prompt, and wrote an error fixing script. This reduced their errors to 0.01%.

2.  Sacrificing throughput for latency
Originally, they focused on TTFT (Time To First Token), but realized that TBT (Time Between Token) hurt them a lot more, especially with Chain-of-Thought queries where users don’t see the intermediate outputs.

They found that TTFT and TBT inversely correlate with TPS (Tokens per Second). To achieve good TTFT and TBT, they had to sacrifice TPS.

3. Automatic evaluation is hard
One core challenge of evaluation is coming up with a guideline on what a good response is. For example, for skill fit assessment, the response: “You’re not a good fit for this job” can be correct, but not helpful.

Originally, evaluation was ad-hoc. Everyone could chime in. That didn’t work. They then have linguists build tooling and processes to standardize annotation, evaluating up to 500 daily conversations and these manual annotations guide their iteration.

Their next goal is to get automatic evaluation, but it’s not easy.

4. Initial success with LLMs can be misleading
It took them 1 month to achieve 80% of the experience they wanted, and additional 4 months to surpass 95%. The initial success made them underestimate how challenging it is to improve the product, especially dealing with hallucinations. They found it discouraging how slow it was to achieve each subsequent 1% gain.

Autonomous Driving on Wet Road Surface using LIDAR Image Matching-based Localization System. 

The road surface in the observation image is distorted because of the weak reflectivity of laser beams in these challenging weather conditions. This causes lateral and longitudinal errors by image matching techniques between map and observation sensory data (as demonstrated by the correlation matrix). 
As the image-matching results are integrated into the localization module in a probabilistic format, the lateral and longitudinal mismatching are recovered in the system output without influencing the localization accuracy.

content:
New release from MIT for Deep Learning based Structure from Motion achieving COLMAP-level accuracy. 🔥🔥 FlowMap: High-Quality Camera Poses, Intrinsics, and Depth via Gradient Descent

FlowMap is the first self-supervised, end-to-end differentiable SfM method that provides COLMAP-level accuracy for 360° scenes. The model solves for precise camera poses, camera intrinsics, and per-frame dense depth of a video sequence. This process normally requires unique image features across multiple view points, matching and triangulation to obtain camera poses and project the points to 3D space for reconstruction.

It outperforms prior gradient-descent based bundle adjustment methods and surprisingly performs on par with COLMAP which has been the state-of-the-art SfM method for at least a decade.

author: Jim Fan
subtitle: NVIDIA Director of AI & Distinguished Scientist. Co-Lead of Project GR00T (Humanoid Robotics) & GEAR Lab. Stanford Ph.D. OpenAI's first intern. Solving Physical AGI, one motor at a time.
content:
The moat of software AI agents is not the thin wrapper layer (Devin, SWE-Agent), but the underlying LLM. Instead of benchmarking the wrapper, I think SWE-Bench is excellent for evaluating coding LLMs instead:

Hold the agent layer fixed and vary only the LLM backend. Provide all tools: LLM-friendly command line, editor, web browser. Specify a maximum token budget and internet query budget. 

How do GPTs, Gemini's, Claude's, Command R, Mistral, Llama compare with each other on solving real-world software engineering problems, with human-level tool access? This is a MUCH more realistic benchmark than HumanEval. It tests an LLM's ability to search StackOverflow, read documentations, self-reflect, self-correct, and carry out long-term consistent plans.

In the Voyager (LLM playing Minecraft) paper, we did such an experiment where we held the Voyager algorithm fixed and swapped out the GPT-4 backend (orange curve) with 3.5 (green curve). It makes a world of difference.

With a bad LLM, neither Devin nor Voyager matters - you won't get good performance any way. Conversely, with a much stronger LLM (eyeing GPT-5), we can probably get to L4-L5 software automation with just a bit of extra effort.

author: Julian Schmidt
subtitle: Research Engineer – Autonomous Driving
content:
Check out the newly released source code of our IEEE Intelligent Vehicles Symposium 2023 research paper on lane distance-based evaluation of trajectory prediction models: https://lnkd.in/ejCW5dKc

Currently established metrics are based on Euclidean distance, which means that errors are weighted equally in all directions. Euclidean metrics are insufficient for structured environments like roads, since they do not properly capture the agent’s intent relative to the underlying lane. In order to provide a reasonable assessment of trajectory prediction approaches with regard to the downstream planning task, we propose a new metric that is lane distance-based: Lane Miss Rate (LMR). LMR implicitly weights Euclidean error relative to the lane and goes into the direction of capturing intents of traffic agents.

📝 Paper: https://lnkd.in/gCKqvyTr

🎨 Figure: Scenario where all predictions (red) are a miss in terms of LMR. The predictions do not cover the lane of the ground-truth (green), hence LMR results in a miss. Euclidean Miss Rate (orange circle), however, weights error equally in all directions. This results in one prediction not being detected as a miss, despite being located on the wrong lane.

Many thanks to all the people involved, especially Thomas, who supported me throughout.

subtitle: Head of Developer Relations | GTM Advisor | 250K+ Community Builder | Published O’Reilly Author | Open Source Contributor | andrewmadson.com
content:
Hey, Data Analysts!

Are you upskilling in Machine Learning and AI. Hooray!

You need to understand MLOps to be successful (short for Machine Learning Operations). MLOps is a set of practices that combines ML development with software engineering and operations to streamline the entire ML lifecycle.

The MLOps architecture can be divided into three main phases:

1. ML Design: This phase focuses on understanding the business use case, exploring and preparing the data, and designing the ML solution.

2. ML Development: In this phase, data scientists conduct experiments, develop and select models, and prepare them for deployment.

3. MLOps: MLOps involves data engineering, ML engineering, and a continuous loop of model verification, packaging, deployment, and monitoring.

Within the MLOps phase, several key components work together to ensure the smooth operation of ML models in production:

➡️ Data and ML Metadata Store: Centralized repositories for storing and managing data and model metadata.
➡️ ML Engineering: Developing and maintaining the infrastructure and pipelines for ML model deployment and monitoring.
➡️ Feature Store: Enabling reuse and consistency of features across models and projects.
➡️ Model Registry: Versioning, tracking, and managing ML models throughout their lifecycle.
➡️ Model Serving: Deploying models as scalable and accessible services for inference.
➡️ Performance Monitoring: Monitor model performance and data drift to ensure optimal results.
➡️ ML Prediction: Generating predictions using the deployed models to drive business value.

If you're involved in ML projects, understanding MLOps is crucial for success. Start by assessing your current knowledge, identify areas for improvement, and gradually implement MLOps principles within your process.

content:
Can LLMs learn to reason better by practicing? 🤖💭 A recent paper from Meta evaluates the effectiveness of RL methods, Expert Iteration (IE), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), and Return-Conditioned RL. Meta studies this by fine-tuning the Llama 2 model, using various reinforcement learning techniques for reasoning (Math).

𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀
🔍 Evaluate Sparse Reward, +1 if the final answer is correct, and Dense Reward (matching intermediate steps in a reference solution). Sparse perform equally well then Dense
🏆 Expert Iteration* (EI) performed the best among the tested RL algorithms in most cases.
⚖️ There is limited benefit of continued supervised fine-tuning beyond a certain point.
🚧 RL only slightly improves SFT (~7%), indicating a limit to the exploration and solution discovery capabilities of these models. (Prompted: 5%, SFT: 41%, RL: 48%)
📈 The RL improves maj@1* and pass@n* scores, suggesting more generalization
🥇 Expert Iteration (IE)* slightly outperforms PPO in improving LLM reasoning (math)
🤖 Explored synthetic data generation to grow diverse sets of examples with filtering, but with worse results due to false positives
❓ Not many details on the train dataset (size, prompts, template)

author: Connor Shorten
subtitle: Research Scientist at Weaviate
content:
Unfortunately, Large Language Models will not consistently follow the instructions that you give them. This is a massive problem when you are building AI systems that require a particular type of output from the previous step to feed into the next one!

For example, imagine you are building a blog post writing system that first takes a question and retrieved context to output a list of topics. These topics have to be formatted in a particular way, such as a comma-separated list or a JSON of Topic objects, such that the system can continue writing the blog post!

I am SUPER excited to share the 4th video in my DSPy series, diving into 3 solutions to structuring outputs in DSPy programs: (1) TypedPredictors, (2) DSPy Assertions, and (3) Custom Guardrails with the DSPy programming model!

TypedPredictors follow the line of thinking around JSON mode and using Pydantic BaseModels to interface types and custom objects into a JSON template for LLMs. The output can then be validated to provide a more structured retry prompt to correct the output structure!

DSPy Assertions are one of the core building blocks of DSPy, offering an interface to input a boolean-valued function and a retry prompt which is templated alongside the past output to retry the call to the LLM!

Custom Guardrails with the DSPy Programming Model are one of the things I love the most about DSPy — we have unlimited flexibility to control these systems however we want. The video will also show you how to write custom guardrails and retry Signatures and discussion around using TypedPredictors for your Custom Guardrails and potentially feeding your Custom Guardrails into a DSPy Assertion.

I had so much fun exploring this topic! Further seeing how well OpenAI’s GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-Turbo, Cohere’s Command R, and Mistral 7B hosted with Ollama perform with each Structured Output strategy! I also found monitoring structured output retries to be another fantastic application of Arize Phoenix! I hope you find the video useful!

Video: https://lnkd.in/efCPjZqh

If interested, all the code examples for this DSPy series can be found here! - https://lnkd.in/gUermCGn 💻

author: Andrew Jardine
subtitle: Adaptive ML - (X-Hugging Face 🤗)
content:
Need to run 🦙 #Llama faster?.......turns out you can just delete half the layers 🤯......... almost no impact on accuracy, but reduces cost significantly 👇👇

New research by Meta, Cisco and Massachusetts Institute of Technology combines pruning, quantization and PEFT across various #opensource models to improve efficiency. Surprisingly, results show you can delete 20% to 50% of the model layers without impacting performance, while memory and compute declines linearly with layers pruned. 

Interestingly, results also suggest that shallow layers are disproportionately important for models results, allowing deletion of deeper layers with minimal impact.

Method:
1️⃣ Test Llama, Qwen, Mistral and Phi families of models from 70B to 2B
2️⃣ Use similarity score to identify model layers for removal
3️⃣ Progressively delete layers with lowest angular distance
4️⃣ Apply post-pruning QLoRA tune on C4 dataset
5️⃣ Test against MMLU and BoolQ benchmarks 

Insights:
🔹 Llama 70B: limited drop in accuracy after 40% layers removed
🔹 Llama 13B: limited drop in accuracy after 50% layers removed
🔹 Other models: limited drop in accuracy after 20-30% layers removed
🔹 Memory / inference cost reduces linearly with layers pruned
🔹 Shallow layers disproportionately impact model results
🔹 Suggests current training might not leverage deeper layers effectively

Paper 👉 https://lnkd.in/g4kix3HH

Retrieval Augmented Generation + Chain of Thought (COT) ⇒ Retrieval Augmented Thoughts (RAT) 🤔 RAT uses an iterative chain of thoughts prompting with retrieved information to mitigate hallucination and improve factual correctness. 🔄 

𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:
1️⃣ Prompt LLM with a question using zero-shot CoT.
2️⃣ Retrieve information using the question and each CoT reasoning step
3️⃣ Revise CoT steps* based on the retrieved context relevant to the prompt
4️⃣ Generate a response using revised CoT steps and context.
*𝘗𝘳𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘵𝘴 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘤𝘭𝘶𝘥𝘦𝘥 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘗𝘢𝘱𝘦𝘳.

🚀 RAT is better than simple RAG, CoT on Code Generation, Creative Writing or task planning

content:
Can we combine multiple fine-tuned LLMs into a single MoE? 🤔 Earlier today Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B a combined MoE of smaller models and probably further trained was released. Meta also explores in their paper “Branch-Train-MiX” if we can combine individual “experts” (LLMs) into a single Mixture-of-Experts (MoE).

𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
1️⃣ Select pre-trained LLM as the seed model, e.g. Llama 2 7B
2️⃣ Fine-tune individual LLMs on dedicated task, domain or language
3️⃣ Combine feedforward parameters of LLMs (2️⃣) in MoE layers and average the remaining parameters
4️⃣ Fine-Tune combined MoE to learn token-level routing (assuming experts are frozen), allowing the model to activate the appropriate experts for different inputs selectively.

𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀
📚 Experts can be trained independently
🦙 BTX is a 3x7B Llama (est. 17B) that outperforms Llama 2 13B
⚡ During inference, ~11B parameters are active
🌱 More efficient, uses ~1/3 of the training compute of llama 13B (since llama 7b is reused)
🌐 Can be used to create domain experts' MoEs
🥇 Top-2 routing yields the best results

Paper: https://lnkd.in/eQkCBuwd
Community implementation: https://lnkd.in/eyUSAFnW

3. **Q&A with Fine-tuned Microsoft Phi-2:** Opting for a space-optimized solution, we leveraged a fine-tuned Microsoft/phi-2 for user queries. Our dataset, compiled using GPT, ensured accurate responses for complex medical report queries.
 
4. **Specialized LLM Chains:** Implementing diverse LLM chains via LangChain for distinct tasks. Memory-equipped chains for chat functionalities and memory-free chains for patient guidance, all running on distributed servers for lightning-fast retrieval.

author: Mahesh Deshwal
subtitle: Senior AI Research Engineer || NLP (Gen AI, LLM Agents as you might know) | Deep Learning | Currently working on AI Evals, Alignment, Safety, Trust & Responsibilities: Basically guardrails & all the hard part remaining
content:
There were some amazing insights last night from Predibase on fine tuning adapters (LoRA/qLoRA) for LLMs. They discussed about fine tuning adapters for 30 tasks (700 Adapters in total) and beating GPT-4 in almost every one of those tasks with a LoRA rank of 8. So for a PHi-2 model, Rank of 196 gives you somewhere around 10% trainable params. I know these numbers by heart as I’ve been struggling to fine tune my own Phi-2 adapters for a long time
Still waiting on that technical writeup that they promised me 😆 Anyways, few things that caught my eye were:

1. Usually, Instruction Fine tuned and “aligned” models (DPO/PPO/RLHF) usually are better performer. For example, Mistral-7-b-instruct and Zephyr usually beat Mistral-7b. That is a empirically known thing BUT here it was opposite. Best fine tuned Adapters were those which used vanilla as a base model.

2. This one is even more interesting. In the end, the LoRA adapters, usually, compensated for the amount of knowledge gained. So the knowledge gained is higher for small models and lower for bigger models.

3. If you look at fine margins, Mistral-7B outperforms Phi-2 in most tasks which, IMO, says that Phi-2 might have a direct or indirect data leakage in benchmarks.

4. Simpler the data and task, more it is closer to GPT-4.


They didn’t mention it anywhere but few thing that I have found myself over the past 3 weeks are that:

For reasoning and logic related tasks, your full fine-tuning makes the model worse. Means LoRA performs better than full fine tuning. Can be because of catastrophic forgetting.

A bigger model is slower to train BUT it gets fine tuned in less number of training steps reaching same or better metric. Maybe because of the already gained knowledge.

Training data size compensates for the number of training steps (which is very basic thing for me to mention. Everyone knows it).

Anyways it was good to invest an hour on it. Haven't tried their platform though.

PS: I took some screenshots from it Justin 😁

author: Andrii Maurin
subtitle: Founder at Grindset Software
content:
👀 How do we train 70B models? The models of such sizes would take around 140 GB of VRAM unquantized. And that is without taking into account optimizer parameters that would push memory requirements far higher.

Traditionally high-level training was accomplished with something called the Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) model from Pytorch in which every parameter is copied onto every GPU in the system. This speeds up the training but doesn’t solve the main problem — memory requirements.

Fortunately, a few years ago folks from AI at Meta (Facebook Research back then) came up with the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) model. It shards the model’s parameters across workers and can optionally offload part of the training computation to the CPUs. But why does it matter now all of a sudden?

Meet QLoRA — a simple but brilliant combination of two critically important advances in modern neural networks: quantization and LoRA. In a nutshell, it’s a technique that trains LoRA adapters on top of the quantized base model. This greatly reduces the memory footprint for the training, as LoRAs are typically only a few percent of the model’s parameter count.

And now engineers from Answer.AI (founded by Jeremy Howard and Eric Ries) combined FSDP and QLoRA to allow us to fine-tune 70B models on two 3090s GPUs. Essentially we’re squeezing at least 200 GB of memory needed before optimizations into under 48 GBs of VRAM — something that was not even thought of only a few months ago!

What's the impact of this is gonna be? 👇

#LLM #AI #research

author: Hamza Tahir
subtitle: CTO at ZenML, building Kitaru — open-source infrastructure for autonomous agents.
content:
Most people think that productionalizing LLMs is just about deploying the Langchain/LLamaindex app but they're missing this crucial detail.

Focusing on the app reminds of the famous MLOps diagram where the tiny code block was at the center and there were a bazillion components around it. There's a lot more to it!

Having 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗥𝗔𝗚 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 in production is very difficult, and requires automated workflows that are observable and repeatable.

I've been doing some system architecture thinking lately, and come up with the following components, that form a bigger picture of a LLMOps system in production.

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟭: 𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗰 𝗥𝗔𝗚
We need an indexing pipeline that loads the data from proprietary sources and index it in a vector database. This is important to automate as your data may change rapidly, and you need your application to be fetching the latest data.

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟮: 𝗥𝗔𝗚 + 𝗧𝘄𝗼-𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹
Reranking is a technique that allows you to retrieve the most relevant documents to send to your LLM. The reranker can be a simple ML model that is trained on proprietary data. We need a pipeline to train this raranking model.

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟯: 𝗘𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗱𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗲
Finetuning embeddings is a good tradeoff between basic RAG vs finetuning the LLM itself. This can result in tremendous improvements in retreival. This requires a finetuning pipeline that can also generate synthetic data.

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟰: 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗲 (𝗼𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻)
Finetuning or pretraining the LLM from scratch is probably the most technically complex but can result in results that are specific to your domain or data. This requires the typical training pipeline that most ML Engineers are used to.

I have not even gotten into the evaluation and guardrails components that will make this diagram even more complex! However, its a good start. Once you have these pipelines working, you can be extra sure that your RAG system is more robust and specialized to your use-case.

Did I miss a structural component? Comment below to let me know! 

P.S. If you're looking to build these sorts of pipelines, hit me up. I'm looking to work with people who are dealing with LLMOps challenges in production!

author: Erich Silva
subtitle: Data Engineer | Analytics and ML | Data Platform Engineering
content:
A '𝚙𝚒𝚙 𝚒𝚗𝚜𝚝𝚊𝚕𝚕 𝚕𝚕𝚊𝚖𝚊–𝚒𝚗𝚍𝚎𝚡' today installs 131 dependencies. 😳

I was analyzing the footprint of a few LLM frameworks, and regardless of the reasons, it’s a shame how bloated some of the popular libraries have become.

The plot draws attention to LlamaIndex, but if you look at LangChain numbers (more in the comments), you will see that its implementation (langchain, langchain_core, and langchain_community) currently spans 2385 unique files and 160k lines of code. These numbers alone are not proxies for anything, but they definitely steer me away from considering LangChain for a production workflow.

But it shouldn’t be an all-or-nothing situation. 🤔

Frameworks are great for exploration due to their abstractions, and thanks to open source, widely adopted libraries are often up to speed with latest research.

Ultimately, the decision to bring dependencies from a sandbox to higher environments should be a matter of assessing the trade-offs between flexibility (e.g., easily switching from a remote LLM provider to another, with LiteLLM, or from a dated RAG architecture to a novel one with LlamaIndex) and sustainment (Wrapping your application around frameworks that are showing signs of conflicting development directions might not be a good idea).

If you want to hear another take on this subject, I recommend the ‘frameworkless’ RAG implementation demo by Francesco Saverio Zuppichini on the Qdrant YouTube channel. I share a lot of his opinions about whether or not to adopt a framework in your application.

#llm #llamaindex #langchain #generatieveai 
—
Some notes about the analysis.

LlamaIndex has modular install options for the core library and select integrations, but the results below are from a pip install llama-index as documented in their Getting Started.

This is not intended to be an apples-to-apples comparison, as each framework solves different problems and aims at different levels of abstraction.

The current release of PyTorch and HuggingFace’s Transformers were included for perspective.

author: shubh sehgal
subtitle: AI/ML Engineer | Building Production ML & LLM Systems | MS AI @ RIT (80% Merit Scholarship) | Research Assistant @ CLaSP, RIT | Former Data Scientist at actyv.ai®
content:
Over the past 2-3 weeks, I've been diving into the world of deploying machine learning models into production environments and I'm thrilled to share the progress on my latest project - The Seismic Magnitude Prediction project, an automated ML pipeline for earthquake analysis using the ANSS Data API.

The Airflow Deployment on EC2 hosts our data ingestion pipeline, facilitating intuitive workflow definition and monitoring for smooth execution. Leveraging Airflow's architecture, data retrieval from API occurs at set intervals, ensuring continuous ingestion. Data formatting and transformation align raw data with desired schema for downstream processing. Processed data is archived onto Amazon S3, ensuring reliable storage for subsequent stages. Through event-driven architecture, a Lambda function triggers pre-processing operations, facilitating timely data preparation for analysis, culminating in actionable insights stored in the final S3 bucket.

GitHub Actions is configured to run a cron job in the CI workflow every day. The feature pipeline involves fetching data from a cleaned/transformed S3 bucket and conducting automated feature testing using the "Great Expectations" library. Successful feature tests result in features being pushed into the Hopsworks feature store and forming a feature group. These features are automatically retrieved for the training pipeline, where model training commences. The best model for the regression problem is pushed into the Hopsworks model registry, including all associated metrics, alongside the capability to upload various performance evaluation graphs such as learning curves and metric comparisons for monitoring purposes.

Finally, an API endpoint for inference is established using Flask.

Special thanks to Pau Labarta Bajo for his "3 real-world ML apps you can build TODAY" youtube video, from where I got the idea to implement this project.

If you have any suggestions or views regarding this project, I'd love to hear from you!

author: Eden Marco
subtitle: LLMs @ Google Cloud | AI Engineering | Opinions stated here are my own, not those of my company
content:
🚨 Demo Alert: risks when deploying insecure LLM agents 🤖 
      (Spoiler: total environment compromise!)🚨

In a recent demo, I showcased what happens when deploying an LLM Agent to the cloud without taking basic security measures. 

(btw Used LangSmith by LangChain🦜🔗 for tracing)

The outcome was alarming☠️
an exploitable application with access to my entire cloud environment.

Why did this happen? 🤔

Lack of Least Privilege Principle:
The deployment didn't limit the ReAct agent to a specific service account or role with tight IAM permissions. Instead, it operated under the Compute Engine Service Account, which has extensive capabilities across the cloud environment.

Insecure Tool Usage:
The application used ShellTool + PythonREPL with unsanitized user input, leading to a vulnerability where a simple adversarial prompt could create a virtual machine within the project.

A few Improvements? (not a closed list)
1️⃣ Implement a custom role with scoped permissions for the agent.
2️⃣ Inspect and sanitize user input rigorously.
3️⃣ Override the class and specially the   ```_run``` method in tools like ShellTool/PythonREPL (which are inherently insecure and categorized under langchain_experimental due to their security risks) to include custom RBAC enforcement.


🛑 TLDR: 
Agents 🤖 can do amazing things, and with frameworks like LangChain 🦜🔗 , LangGraph, they are super easy to implement, but can expose our application to a lot of security risks. Before we go live to production we have to make sure our system is E2E designed against security issues.

author: Alex Razvant
subtitle: Senior AI Engineer | Writing The AI Merge Newsletter
content:
If you're looking for a 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲, 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹-𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀-𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲 on how to productionalize LLMs - stop here!

Many  LLM articles/repositories focus on a single component, either fine-tuning, inference, or deployment of pre-existing models.

The available end-to-end resources, target the theoretical aspects and recommend tools to use when building a GenAI LLM solution.

There are too few workshops on how to engineer an end-to-end LLM product.

To mitigate this gap, Alex Vesa, Paul Iusztin, and I, have started working on a course that covers a production-ready LLM solution that encapsulates all the required modules, starting from data pipelines down to deployment and monitoring.

author: Leonie Monigatti
subtitle: Sr. Developer Advocate @ Elastic | I help devs build search agents
content:
If you haven’t been living under a rock, you have already noticed that the developer community is currently super excited about DSPy.

DSPy is a framework developed by Stanford NLP researchers (Omar K.) to help you build LLM-based applications.

In contrast to similar frameworks, DSPy aims to tackle the fragility problem of developing LLM-based applications by prioritizing programming over prompting.

DSPy does this by introducing the following concepts:
- Hand-written prompts and fine-tuning are abstracted and replaced by signatures
- Prompting techniques, such as Chain of Thought or ReAct, are abstracted and replaced by modules
- Manual prompt engineering is automated with optimizers (teleprompters) and a DSPy Compiler

Below, you can see what the code and information flow of a DSPy program for a naive RAG pipeline would look like.

author: Davide Scaramuzza
subtitle: Professor of Robotics and Perception at the University of Zurich
content:
Check out our #PAMI paper with code "Dense Continuous-Time  Optical Flow from Event Cameras," where we show how to regress *continuous-time* trajectories of every pixel from #eventcameras alone or event plus frames! The key idea is to iteratively estimate per-pixel polynomials using a recurrent lookup and update scheme. 
Paper: https://lnkd.in/dDJtYiBX 
Code: https://lnkd.in/dwnJGJm4
DOI: https://lnkd.in/d-3mJA2x

We present a method for estimating dense continuous-time optical flow from event data. Traditional dense optical flow methods compute the pixel displacement between two images. Due to missing information, these approaches cannot recover the pixel trajectories in the blind time between two images. We show that it is possible to compute per-pixel, continuous-time optical flow using events from an event camera. Events provide temporally fine-grained information about movement in pixel space due to their asynchronous nature and microsecond response time. We leverage these benefits to predict pixel trajectories densely in continuous time via parameterized Bézier curves. To achieve this, we build a neural network with strong inductive biases for this task: First, we build multiple sequential correlation volumes in time using event data. Second, we use Bézier curves to index these correlation volumes at multiple timestamps along the trajectory. Third, we use the retrieved correlation to update the Bézier curve representations iteratively. Our method can optionally include image pairs to boost performance further. To train and evaluate our model, we introduce a synthetic dataset (MultiFlow) that features moving objects and ground truth trajectories for every pixel. Our quantitative experiments suggest that our method successfully predicts pixel trajectories in continuous time and is competitive in the traditional two-view pixel displacement metric on MultiFlow and DSEC-Flow. Open source code and datasets are released to the public.

Kudos to Mathias Gehrig and Manasi Muglikar
#computervision #eventcamera

author: Alex Razvant
subtitle: Senior AI Engineer | Writing The AI Merge Newsletter
content:
𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲'𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝗻𝗱-𝘁𝗼-𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗬𝗼𝗹𝗼 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲! 
 
After challenges with optimizing and compiling 𝙔𝙊𝙇𝙊 𝙢𝙤𝙙𝙚𝙡𝙨 𝙩𝙤 𝙏𝙚𝙣𝙨𝙤𝙧𝙍𝙏 on multiple GPUs mainly due to version mismatches between ONNX, ORT, TensorRT, and so on - I had to automate this process. 
 
This pipeline 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗺𝗲 𝟯-𝟰 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀 to implement but 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝘀𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗲𝘁𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 whenever I had to optimize YOLO models. 
 
𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲’𝘀 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀: 
 
→ 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗰 𝗣𝘆𝗧𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗵-𝘁𝗼-𝗢𝗡𝗡𝗫 
Either have a single .py script that converts the .pt 2 .onnx or add each YOLO branch (v5, v7, v8) as submodules to use the exporter for each architecture directly. 
 
→ 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗙𝗶𝗹𝗲 
I have a config.json file where I specify the TensorRT version I need, the ONNX Operator Set, and metadata fields to save the model as (e.g. 𝙈𝙊𝘿𝙀𝙇_𝘽𝘼𝙏𝘾𝙃_𝙂𝙋𝙐_𝘿𝘼𝙏𝘼𝙏𝙔𝙋𝙀...). 
 
→ 𝗢𝗡𝗡𝗫 𝗦𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗖𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸 
Once triggering the .pt to .onnx conversion, I run several tests on the integrity of the model and its configuration.  
 
→ 𝗦𝗽𝗶𝗻-𝘂𝗽 𝗧𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗼𝗿𝗥𝗧  
Once the .onnx model is validated, I start the TensorRT container, copy the .onnx model, convert the model to .engine, copy it back to the host path then remove the container. 
 
→ 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗮𝘃𝗲 
I save the .engine based on the specified model metadata in my .json config. 
 
→ 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗡𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗮 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳 𝗔𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘇𝗲𝗿 
PerfAnalyzer is a tool that profiles your .engines and finds the best configuration for your target GPU. I test various use cases, like optimal batch size, min/optimal/max load of concurrent requests, GPU stats under workload, and many more. 
 
→ 𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘀 𝗗𝗮𝘀𝗵𝗯𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱 
The last step includes the performance-metrics parsing and generating charts around the key metrics like Queries-per-Second (QPS), Concurrency Analysis, and Precision Accuracy. 
 
𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘆: 
→𝘔𝘢𝘯𝘶𝘢𝘭 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘴 𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘸𝘢𝘳𝘥 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘥𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘱𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘥𝘭𝘺 𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘣𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘦𝘳𝘳𝘰𝘳. 
→ 𝘕𝘰 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦𝘹 𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘣𝘦𝘵𝘸𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘖𝘕𝘕𝘟, 𝘊𝘜𝘋𝘕𝘕, 𝘊𝘜𝘋𝘈 - 𝘢𝘶𝘵𝘰𝘮𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘪𝘵.

author: Jim Fan
subtitle: NVIDIA Director of AI & Distinguished Scientist. Co-Lead of Project GR00T (Humanoid Robotics) & GEAR Lab. Stanford Ph.D. OpenAI's first intern. Solving Physical AGI, one motor at a time.
content:
I've been asked what's the biggest thing in 2024 other than LLMs. It's Robotics. Period. We are ~3 years away from the ChatGPT moment for physical AI agents. We've been cursed by the Moravec's paradox for too long, which is the counter-intuitive phenomenon where "tasks that humans find easy are extremely hard for AI, and vice versa".

2024 will be remembered as the first year that the AI community fights back big time against the curse. We will not win immediately, but we will be on the path of winning.

In 2023, we've caught a glimpse of the future foundation models and platforms for robots:
- Multimodal LLMs with robot arms as a physical I/O device: VIMA, PerAct, RvT (NVIDIA), RT-1, RT-2, PaLM-E (Google), RoboCat (DeepMind), Octo (Berkeley, Stanford, CMU), etc.
- Algorithms that bridge the gap between System 2 high-level reasoning (LLMs) and System 1 low-level control: Eureka (NVIDIA), Code as Policies (Google), etc.
- Insane amounts of progress on robust hardware: Tesla Optimus, Figure, 1X, Apptronik, Sanctuary, Agility+Amazon, Unitree, etc. 
- Data has always been the Achilles' heel of robotics. The research community is coming together to curate the next ImageNet, such as the Open X-Embodiment (RT-X) dataset. It's still not diverse enough, but a baby step is a major step.
- Simulation and synthetic data will play a critical role in solving robot dexterity and even computer vision in general.
(1) NVIDIA Isaac can simulate reality at 1000x faster than real-time. The incoming data stream scales as compute scales.
(2) Photorealism can be enabled by hardware-accelerated raytracing. The realistic renderings also come with groundtruth annotations for free, such as segmentation, depth, 3D pose, etc.
(3) Simulators can even multiply real-world data to create much larger datasets, greatly reducing the expensive human demonstration efforts. MimicGen (NVIDIA) is a representative example.

I'm all in, personally. The best is yet to come.

author: Andrew Ng
subtitle: DeepLearning.AI, AI Fund and AI Aspire
content:
The LVM (large vision model) revolution is coming a little after the LLM (large language model) one, and will transform how we process images. But there’s an important difference between LLMs and LVMs:
- Internet text is similar enough to proprietary text documents that an LLM trained on internet text can understand your documents. 
- But internet images – such as Instagram pictures – contain a lot of pictures of people, pets, landmarks, and everyday objects. Many practical vision applications (manufacturing, aerial imagery, life sciences, etc.) use images that look nothing like most  internet images. So a generic LVM trained on internet images fares poorly at picking out the most salient features of images in many specialized domains. 

That’s why domain specific LVMs – ones adapted to images of a particular domain (such as semiconductor manufacturing, or pathology) – do much better. At Landing AI, by using ~100K unlabeled images to adapt an LVM to a specific domain, we see significantly improved results, for example where only 10-30% as much labeled data is now needed to achieve a certain level of performance. 

For companies with large sets of images that look nothing like internet images, I think domain specific LVMs can be a way to unlock considerable value from their data. Dan Maloney and I share more details in the video.

How do companies actually use LLMs in production?
